It uses an instrument called the "bandoneon," a relative of the accordion.

world-dance:6.fact: Dancers hardly move their upper bodies and do quick steps with just their feet.
world-dance:6.about:
There are "hard shoes," which strike the floor, and soft "soft shoes."
The show "Riverdance" made it famous around the world.

world-dance:7.fact: A classical dance from India. It tells stories with hand shapes and eye movements.
world-dance:7.about:
A classical dance from South India with more than 2,000 years of history.
There are dozens of hand shapes called "mudras," and dancers combine them to tell stories.

world-dance:8.fact: At summer festivals, everyone dances together in a circle.
world-dance:8.about:
At Obon, local people gather and dance in a circle around a tower called a yagura.
"Gujō Odori" in Gifu is famous for more than 30 nights of dancing in summer, with some nights going on until morning.

world-dance:9.fact: A dance from Tokushima. Its chant, "The dancers are fools and the watchers are fools…," is famous.
world-dance:9.about:
A dance from Tokushima with more than 400 years of history. Every August, more than a million people come to watch.
Dancers chant "Erai yatcha, erai yatcha, yoi yoi yoi yoi!"

world-dance:10.fact: A dance born in Kōchi. Dancers shake clappers called "naruko."
world-dance:10.about:
"Yosakoi" means "come in the evening" in the old Tosa dialect.
In Hokkaido, the "YOSAKOI Sōran Festival," mixed with the Sōran-bushi song, is hugely popular too.

world-dance:11.fact: An Okinawan dance. Dancers dance while beating drums.
world-dance:11.about:
A traditional Okinawan performance for welcoming and sending off the spirits of ancestors at Obon.
Dancers beat big and small drums and parade through town to sanshin and singing.

world-dance:12.fact: It comes from a song of Hokkaido's fishermen. It is a popular dance at sports days too.
world-dance:12.about:
It comes from a song herring fishermen sang while pulling in their nets.
To the chant "Yāren sōran sōran," dancers copy the movements of pulling nets and rowing boats.

#paintings-france: Paris is the "city of art." Painters who cared about light and colour gathered there.

paintings-france:0.fact: A painting by Monet. The word "Impressionism" came from its title.
paintings-france:0.about:
Monet painted the morning at the port of Le Havre in France with quick brushstrokes.
At an exhibition, someone made fun of it, saying "This is just an impression (a sketch)," and that's how the name "Impressionism" was born.

paintings-france:1.fact: Monet built a Japanese-style bridge and pond in his garden and painted them again and again.
paintings-france:1.about:
Monet loved Japanese ukiyo-e prints and collected more than 200.
In the garden of his house at Giverny, he dug a pond, built a Japanese-style arched bridge and painted the view many times.

paintings-france:2.fact: Degas painted lots of people practising ballet.
paintings-france:2.about:
Degas liked painting dancers in natural moments, practising or resting, more than on stage.
Like a photo, his paintings have bold layouts where people are cut off at the edges.

paintings-france:3.fact: Cézanne said, "I want to astonish Paris with an apple."
paintings-france:3.about:
Cézanne set out apples and studied them for days. Apples don't rot quickly, so he could take his time.
His idea of "seeing nature as cylinders, spheres and cones" influenced later artists like Picasso.

paintings-france:4.fact: A big painting Seurat made over 2 years by putting down tiny dots.
paintings-france:4.about:
A big painting (3 m wide) of people relaxing on a Sunday on an island in a river in Paris.
Up close you see little dots of colour, but from far away they look like people and trees.

paintings-france:5.fact: A painting by Rousseau. He never went to a jungle. He imagined it while visiting botanical gardens.
paintings-france:5.about:
Rousseau taught himself to paint while working at a government office, so he was a "Sunday painter."
He painted imaginary jungles by looking at botanical gardens, animal books and zoos.

paintings-france:6.fact: Millet painted people picking up wheat that had fallen in a field.
paintings-france:6.about:
A painting of three women picking up ears of wheat left in a field after the harvest.
Millet kept painting the people who worked in the countryside with great care.

paintings-france:7.fact: A work Matisse made by cutting out coloured paper. It forms a spiral shape.
paintings-france:7.about:
When illness made it hard to hold a brush, Matisse made his art by cutting coloured paper with scissors.
He said he was "drawing with scissors" and created a new kind of art.

#paintings-netherlands: The Netherlands has close ties to Nagasaki. Many masters of light and colour came from there and its neighbours.

paintings-netherlands:0.fact: A painting by Vermeer, with beautiful soft light from the window.
paintings-netherlands:0.about:
A woman pouring milk in a kitchen. In the light from the window, the bread and jug seem to sparkle.
Vermeer put down tiny dots of light to show the feel of each thing.

paintings-netherlands:1.about:
A view of Delft, the town where Vermeer was born and grew up. The contrast between cloud shadows and sunlight is beautiful.
There are only about 35 works by Vermeer in the world.

paintings-netherlands:2.fact: A huge group portrait by Rembrandt, more than 3 m tall and 4 m wide.
paintings-netherlands:2.about:
A group portrait of members of the town guard. The people lit up by light stand out from the darkness.
It is actually a daytime scene, but the varnish on the surface turned dark, so it came to be called "The Night Watch."

paintings-netherlands:3.fact: Rembrandt painted dozens of pictures of his own face during his life.
paintings-netherlands:3.about:
From when he was young until he was old, he painted his own face again and again.
If you line the paintings up, you can see how one person's life changed.

paintings-netherlands:4.fact: One of Van Gogh's most famous works. He painted sunflowers in a vase many times.
paintings-netherlands:4.about:
Van Gogh painted 7 "Sunflowers" pictures. One is at the SOMPO Museum of Art in Tokyo.
In about 10 years as a painter, Van Gogh left more than 2,000 works.

paintings-netherlands:5.fact: Van Gogh painted it to celebrate the birth of his nephew. You can see the influence of Japanese ukiyo-e.
paintings-netherlands:5.about:
He painted almond blossoms, a sign of spring, against a blue sky.
It was a painting for his newborn nephew's room, full of the joy of new life.

paintings-netherlands:6.fact: A painting of Van Gogh's room. He used bright colours to show the feeling of "rest."
paintings-netherlands:6.about:
The bedroom in the yellow house where he lived in Arles in southern France. Van Gogh liked this painting so much that he painted it 3 times.
The walls and furniture look a little crooked, which is very Van Gogh.

paintings-netherlands:7.fact: A painting by Mondrian, made with only black lines and red, yellow and blue.
paintings-netherlands:7.about:
While painting trees, Mondrian made the shapes simpler and simpler until he arrived at just vertical and horizontal lines and 3 colours.
This design is used on all sorts of things, like clothes and furniture.

paintings-netherlands:8.fact: Escher drew strange pictures, like stairs that keep going up but end where they started.
paintings-netherlands:8.about:
Escher was a master at drawing shapes that can't really exist as if they were real.
Hands drawing each other, birds that slowly turn into fish… the more you look, the stranger they get.

paintings-netherlands:9.fact: A painting of a winter village by Bruegel from Belgium. There are people skating too.
paintings-netherlands:9.about:
Hunters and dogs coming home over a snowy hill, and villagers skating and playing on a frozen pond.
It shows winter life in Europe more than 400 years ago very clearly.

#japanese-painters: Japanese painters created beautiful pictures in many ways, with ink, gold leaf, woodblock prints and more.

japanese-painters:0.fact: A master of ink painting who painted mountains and rivers with only ink.
japanese-painters:0.about:
A painter-monk of the Muromachi period. He went to China (Ming) to study painting and perfected a Japanese style of ink painting.
A famous story says that as a boy he drew a mouse on the floor with his tears.

japanese-painters:1.fact: "Pine Trees." A National Treasure gently painted in ink, showing a pine forest in the mist.
japanese-painters:1.about:
From Nanao, Ishikawa. He went to Kyoto and did great work while competing with the Kanō school.
"Pine Trees" uses only shades of ink to show pine trees dimly appearing in the mist.

japanese-painters:2.fact: "Irises." Purple irises line up on a gold background.
japanese-painters:2.about:
Born into a kimono shop family in Kyoto, he painted bold designs like kimono patterns.
The name of the "Rinpa" school comes from the "rin" in Kōrin.

japanese-painters:3.fact: He was good at painting things that looked real. His cute puppy paintings are famous too.
japanese-painters:3.about:
A painter in Kyoto in the Edo period. He valued drawing from life (drawing what you see).
His paintings of round little puppies are still hugely popular for being so cute.

japanese-painters:4.fact: He painted roosters, fish and flowers in fine detail and bright colours.
japanese-painters:4.about:
At 40, he handed the family business to his younger brother and threw himself into painting.
His 30 "Colourful Realm of Living Beings" paintings show roosters, fish, flowers and insects in bright colours.

japanese-painters:5.fact: He kept painting until he was nearly 90 and is said to have left more than 30,000 works.
japanese-painters:5.about:
He is said to have moved house more than 90 times and changed his name more than 30 times in his life.
"Hokusai Manga" is full of drawings of people moving, animals, tools and more, and it was used like a drawing textbook.

japanese-painters:6.fact: He was good at rainy and snowy scenes. Van Gogh copied Hiroshige's prints too.
japanese-painters:6.about:
He was born into a family of firefighters in Edo. He drew travel scenes and famous places in gentle colours.
Hiroshige's blue is called "Hiroshige blue" and was popular in Europe.

japanese-painters:7.fact: A great master of Japanese-style painting who painted Mt. Fuji hundreds of times.
japanese-painters:7.about: A Japanese-style painter who worked from the Meiji to the Shōwa period. He created a new style called "mōrōtai," which shows things with blurred colour instead of lines.

japanese-painters:8.fact: Known for calm landscapes in blue and green.
japanese-painters:8.about:
A Japanese-style painter known for calm landscapes in blue and green.
He also painted the sliding-door paintings at Tōshōdai-ji temple in Nara. His paintings with a white horse are famous too.

japanese-painters:9.fact: He made the "Tower of the Sun" for the 1970 Osaka Expo. His famous words are "Art is an explosion!"
japanese-painters:9.about:
He is known for saying "Art is an explosion!" The Tower of the Sun was the symbol of the 1970 Osaka Expo.
At Shibuya Station in Tokyo, there is also his huge mural, "The Myth of Tomorrow."

japanese-painters:10.fact: Born in Nagano. She is known around the world for her polka-dot works.
japanese-painters:10.about:
Since she was a child, she has turned into art her experiences of seeing the world around her covered in dots.
She also worked in America, and today she is one of the most popular Japanese artists in the world.

#sculpture-world: Big statues, small statues, strange statues. Let's tour the world's famous sculptures.

sculpture-world:0.fact: Stone statues on Easter Island in Chile. Some are more than 10 m tall.
sculpture-world:0.about:
There are about 900 moai on Easter Island. The biggest is nearly 20 m tall and was left unfinished.
Researchers are still studying how they were moved.

sculpture-world:1.fact: A lion's body with a human face. It sits in front of the pyramids in Egypt.
sculpture-world:1.about:
It is 73 m long and 20 m tall, carved from one huge rock.
It was buried in sand for thousands of years, and there were times when nothing below its neck could be seen.

sculpture-world:2.fact: Statues of soldiers made of clay, each with a different face.
sculpture-world:2.about:
Besides soldiers, there are statues of horses and chariots. When they were made, they were painted in bright colours.
Digging still continues, and new statues are still being found.

sculpture-world:3.fact: A bronze statue about 11 m tall. It was made more than 750 years ago and is a National Treasure.
sculpture-world:3.about:
It used to be inside a big building, but earthquakes and a tsunami destroyed the building, and it has sat outside for more than 500 years.
You can even go inside the statue and look around.

sculpture-world:4.fact: Copenhagen, Denmark. It was made from a story by Hans Christian Andersen.
sculpture-world:4.about:
At about 1.25 m tall, it is smaller than you might think. It sits on a rock by the sea.
Andersen was a Danish writer who also wrote "The Ugly Duckling."

sculpture-world:5.fact: The symbol of Singapore. It has a lion's head and a fish's body, and water sprays from its mouth.
sculpture-world:5.about:
The name Singapore means "lion city." The fish body stands for the old fishing village.
It is about 8.6 m tall, and posing with it spraying water is a popular photo spot.

sculpture-world:6.fact: Expo '70 Commemorative Park, Osaka. A 70 m tower made by Okamoto Tarō.
sculpture-world:6.about:
It has 3 faces: the golden face on top is the future, the face on the front is the present, and the black face on the back is the past.
Inside, you can see the "Tree of Life," which shows the evolution of living things.

sculpture-world:7.fact: A huge mirror-like work in Chicago, USA. It is called "The Bean."
sculpture-world:7.about:
It was made of 168 stainless steel plates joined so that you can't see the seams.
The sky, the buildings and you yourself are reflected in its surface, all stretched and bent. It's lots of fun.

sculpture-world:8.fact: In front of Shibuya Station in Tokyo. A statue of the Akita dog who kept waiting for his owner. It is famous as a meeting place.
sculpture-world:8.about:
Even after his owner, Professor Ueno Hidesaburō, died, Hachi kept going to Shibuya Station for about 10 years.
In 2015, a statue of Professor Ueno and Hachi meeting again was made at the University of Tokyo.

#nagasaki-city: Nagasaki: a city of hills, a harbour and culture from abroad. Which places have you been to?

nagasaki-city:0.fact: A garden with the oldest Western-style wooden house in Japan (1863).
nagasaki-city:0.about:
A garden with the house of Glover, a Scottish merchant who worked in Nagasaki at the end of the Edo period, and other old houses.
From the hilltop you can see the whole of Nagasaki Harbour and the city. Glover was one of the people who helped Japan modernise.

nagasaki-city:1.fact: A stone bridge that looks like a pair of glasses when it's reflected in the river. Try to find the heart-shaped stone!
nagasaki-city:1.about:
One of the oldest stone arch bridges in Japan, built by a Chinese monk in 1634.
Heart-shaped stones are set into the stone walls of the river, and people say finding one brings happiness.

nagasaki-city:2.fact: One of Japan's three great Chinatowns, along with Yokohama and Kobe.
nagasaki-city:2.about:
A Chinatown that grew up near the "Tōjin Yashiki," where Chinese people lived in the Edo period.
It is lined with shops selling champon, sara udon and kakuni manjū, and it is a venue for the Lantern Festival.

nagasaki-city:3.fact: A cobblestone slope in an area where many foreigners used to live.
nagasaki-city:3.about: A cobblestone slope in Higashi-Yamate, where foreigners lived in the Meiji period. People in Nagasaki back then called all Westerners "Oranda-san" (Dutch people), so it got this name.

nagasaki-city:4.fact: A way of getting around for people in Nagasaki since 1915. It is also called the "ching-ching train."
nagasaki-city:4.about:
On Nagasaki's streetcars, one ride costs the same however far you go.
For more than 100 years, they have carried the people of this hilly city in their daily lives.

nagasaki-city:5.fact: An aquarium where you can meet many kinds of penguins.
nagasaki-city:5.about:
One of the top aquariums in the world for the number of penguin species.
It also has a "Penguin Beach" where penguins swim in the natural sea nearby.

nagasaki-city:6.fact: A park praying for world peace. Many people visit from around the world.
nagasaki-city:6.about:
A park made to wish for world peace. It has the big "Peace Statue," with its right hand pointing to the sky and its left hand stretched out level.
There are also statues sent by countries from around the world.

nagasaki-city:7.fact: A harbour that has been connected to the world for a long time. Huge cruise ships come here too.
nagasaki-city:7.about:
A harbour opened in 1571 for Portuguese ships. After that, Nagasaki grew as Japan's window to other countries.
Today, lots of big cruise ships from around the world come here.

#nagasaki-food: Nagasaki has lots of dishes influenced by China, Portugal and the Netherlands.

nagasaki-food:0.fact: Full of vegetables and seafood. It is said to have been made up by a Chinese cook for students from China.
nagasaki-food:0.about:
Thick noodles in soup made from pork and chicken bones, with more than 10 ingredients like cabbage, bean sprouts, kamaboko, squid and shrimp.
The noodles are cooked right in the soup.

nagasaki-food:1.fact: Crispy thin noodles with a thick sauce poured on top.
nagasaki-food:1.about:
The ingredients of champon are made into a thick sauce and poured over noodles. There are two kinds: crispy thin noodles and soft thick noodles.
Many people in Nagasaki eat it with Worcestershire sauce.

nagasaki-food:2.fact: A Nagasaki Western-style dish with pilaf, spaghetti and tonkatsu all on one plate.
nagasaki-food:2.about:
There are many ideas about where its name came from, but no one really knows.
It's called a "kids' meal for grown-ups" and is a popular menu item at Nagasaki's Western-style restaurants.

nagasaki-food:3.fact: Sweet and salty stewed pork in a fluffy bun.
nagasaki-food:3.about: It comes from a Chinese dish, "dongpo pork." It is one of the dishes of shippoku cuisine.

nagasaki-food:4.fact: A cake that came from Portugal and was born in Nagasaki.
nagasaki-food:4.about: A simple cake made from eggs, sugar, flour and starch syrup. Some castella shops in Nagasaki have been open since the Edo period.

nagasaki-food:5.fact: A sherbet-like ice cream sold by ringing a little "chirin chirin" bell.
nagasaki-food:5.about:
It is sold at stalls with parasols, and sometimes the lady will scoop it into the shape of a rose.
It's crunchy and refreshing, a taste of summer memories in Nagasaki.

nagasaki-food:6.fact: Nagasaki's milkshake isn't a drink. It's a dessert like shaved ice that you eat with a spoon.
nagasaki-food:6.about:
It is made by mixing eggs, sugar, milk and ice, and you eat it with a spoon like sherbet.
People say it became an icy dessert because Nagasaki summers are hot and the city is full of hills.

nagasaki-food:7.fact: Hamburgers came from Americans and became Sasebo's famous food.
nagasaki-food:7.about: Each shop makes its own by hand, with lots of bacon, egg and vegetables in a big bun. They take pride in making each one after you order.

nagasaki-food:8.fact: Thin, chewy udon made by brushing on camellia oil and stretching the noodles.
nagasaki-food:8.about:
Thin, chewy udon that is said to be one of Japan's three great udon.
It is usually eaten with "ago" (flying fish) broth. "Jigoku-daki," where you scoop the noodles straight out of the pot, is famous too.

nagasaki-food:9.fact: Nagasaki grows the most loquats in Japan.
nagasaki-food:9.about:
The loquat is a fruit that came from China. Nagasaki loquats are said to have started in the Edo period, when a woman in Nagasaki planted seeds she got from a Chinese ship.
"Mogi loquats" are Nagasaki's best-known kind, and they are in season in early summer.

#wasei-eigo: Some words sound like English but don't work in English. They are "wasei-eigo" (Japanese-made English). What's the real English?

wasei-eigo:0.fact: In Japanese it's "konsento," but in English "consent" means "agreement." The holes for electricity are an outlet (US) or a socket (UK).
wasei-eigo:0.about:
The thing you plug in is a plug, and the place you plug it into is an outlet (US) or a socket (UK).
The shape of sockets is different in each country, so you need an adapter when you travel abroad.

wasei-eigo:1.fact: In Japanese it's "manshon," but in English a mansion is a "huge house." A normal home in a block of flats is an apartment.
wasei-eigo:1.about:
In English, "mansion" makes people think of a big house with a pool and a large garden.
"I live in a manshon" is "I live in an apartment."

wasei-eigo:2.fact: In Japanese it's "bebī kā," but in English it's a stroller (US) or a pram (UK).
wasei-eigo:2.about: "Bebī kā" is a word made in Japan. In English, a "baby car" might sound like a toy car for babies.

wasei-eigo:3.fact: In Japanese it's "nōto pasokon," but in English it's a laptop. "Notebook" can just mean a paper notebook.
wasei-eigo:3.about:
"Laptop" means a computer you can use on top of your lap.
A computer on a desk is a desktop computer.

wasei-eigo:4.fact: In Japanese it's "shāpu penshiru," but in English it's a mechanical pencil. It's the invention that gave the company "Sharp" its name.
wasei-eigo:4.about: Around 1915, Hayakawa Tokuji, the founder of Sharp, started selling the "Ever-Ready Sharp Pencil," an improved version of his propelling pencil.

wasei-eigo:5.fact: In Japanese, cheating on a test is "kanningu," but in English "cunning" means "sly." Cheating on a test is cheating.
wasei-eigo:5.about:
"Cunning" means sly or crafty. Doing something unfair on a test is "cheating."
In English, "cheat" is a verb that means to do something unfair.

wasei-eigo:6.fact: In Japanese it's "gasorin sutando," but in English it's a gas station (US) or a petrol station (UK).
wasei-eigo:6.about:
In America, petrol is called gas, and in the UK it's called petrol.
The "stand" part is "station" in English.

wasei-eigo:7.fact: In Japanese they're "furaido poteto." In America they're French fries, and in the UK they're chips.
wasei-eigo:7.about:
British "chips" are American "French fries." American "chips" are "crisps" in the UK (potato chips).
Even in English, the words can change from country to country.

wasei-eigo:8.fact: In Japanese it's "petto botoru." PET is the name of a kind of plastic. In English it's a plastic bottle.
wasei-eigo:8.about:
PET is short for polyethylene terephthalate. In English it's a plastic bottle or a water bottle.
If you say "pet bottle," people might think it's a bottle for a pet!

wasei-eigo:9.fact: The Japanese word "waishatsu" came from "white shirt," because that's what it sounded like.
wasei-eigo:9.about:
In English, a shirt with a collar and buttons is a dress shirt or a button-down shirt.
A T-shirt is just "T-shirt" in English too.

wasei-eigo:10.fact: In Japanese, people say "mai pēsu," but in English you'd say "I do things at my own pace."
wasei-eigo:10.about:
To describe a "mai pēsu" person in English, you'd say something like "He does things at his own pace."
"My pace" by itself doesn't make sense in English.

wasei-eigo:11.fact: In Japanese, "naību" means delicate, but in English "naive" means "inexperienced." A delicate person is sensitive.
wasei-eigo:11.about:
In English, "naive" often has a slightly bad meaning: "not knowing much about the world because you lack experience."
The Japanese "naību" (delicate) is "sensitive" in English.

#words-from-japanese: Lots of English words came from Japanese. People around the world use them too!

words-from-japanese:0.fact: All over the world, people say "tsunami."
words-from-japanese:0.about:
Around the time of the huge Indian Ocean earthquake in 2004, "tsunami" started being used in news all over the world.
In English it is also called a tidal wave, but now "tsunami" is the usual word.

words-from-japanese:1.about:
In English it's pronounced something like "carry-oh-key."
People enjoy karaoke boxes all over the world, just like in Japan.

words-from-japanese:2.fact: "E" (picture) + "moji" (character). It has nothing to do with the English word emotion!
words-from-japanese:2.about: In 2015, the Oxford Dictionaries chose the 😂 emoji as their "Word of the Year."

words-from-japanese:3.fact: The fifth taste, discovered in 1908 by Ikeda Kikunae in kombu broth.
words-from-japanese:3.about:
Glutamic acid in kombu, inosinic acid in katsuobushi and guanylic acid in shiitake mushrooms make umami.
Today, chefs around the world value "umami."

words-from-japanese:4.fact: Japan's "kawaii" (cute) culture is used just as it is in English too.
words-from-japanese:4.about:
From the 2000s, it spread around the world along with Japanese fashion and characters.
It is in the Oxford English Dictionary too.

words-from-japanese:5.fact: In English, "futon" can also mean something like a sofa bed.
words-from-japanese:5.about: In English-speaking countries, a futon is often a thick mattress on a wooden frame, a piece of furniture that works as both a sofa and a bed.

words-from-japanese:6.fact: "Tycoon," meaning a powerful businessperson, comes from the Japanese word "taikun" (great lord).
words-from-japanese:6.about:
At the end of the Edo period, foreigners called the shogun "taikun."
The word entered English and came to mean "a very important person in business."

words-from-japanese:7.fact: "Honcho," meaning "leader," comes from the Japanese word "hanchō" (squad leader).
words-from-japanese:7.about:
It is said that American soldiers in Japan after World War II took the Japanese word "hanchō" home with them.
In English, people say "the head honcho" (the top boss).

words-from-japanese:8.fact: The Japanese art of growing trees in small pots. It has fans all over the world.
words-from-japanese:8.about:
It started from Chinese "penjing" and grew into a unique art in Japan.
Some bonsai are hundreds of years old and are passed down in families from generation to generation.

words-from-japanese:9.fact: It is eaten all over the world as a healthy food.
words-from-japanese:9.about:
Tofu, made from soybeans, was born in China and came to Japan.
It has lots of protein and is popular with vegetarians too.

words-from-japanese:10.fact: Japanese manga and anime became words used around the world just as they are.
words-from-japanese:10.about:
Japanese manga is read from right to left. Many versions abroad are still read from right to left too.
In English, "anime" means Japanese animation.

words-from-japanese:11.fact: Even at the Olympics, Japanese words like "hajime" (begin) are used.
words-from-japanese:11.about: In judo matches everywhere in the world, the referees use Japanese words like "hajime" (begin), "matte" (wait) and "ippon" (full point).

#sdgs: 17 goals for everyone in the world to reach by 2030. What can we do?

sdgs:0.fact: A world where everyone can get the things they need to live.
sdgs:0.about:
Hundreds of millions of people in the world live on less than about 300 yen a day.
The goal is a world where homes, food, schools and medical care reach everyone.

sdgs:1.fact: Finishing your school lunch is also a step towards valuing food.
sdgs:1.about:
About a third of all the food made in the world is said to be thrown away.
Not leaving food and not buying too much are things we can do.

sdgs:2.fact: Wash your hands, gargle, and go to bed early and get up early. Take care of your body.
sdgs:2.about:
Washing your hands is the simplest way to prevent colds and infections.
In many areas of the world, there are no hospitals nearby.

sdgs:3.fact: Some children in the world can't go to school.
sdgs:3.about:
More than 200 million children in the world can't go to school.
Being able to read books and study is an important right.

sdgs:4.fact: A world where boys and girls can try whatever they like.
sdgs:4.about:
The goal is a society where what you can do and your dreams aren't decided by "because you're a boy" or "because you're a girl."
Let's share the housework at home too.

sdgs:5.fact: Turn off the water while you brush your teeth.
sdgs:5.about:
More than 2 billion people in the world can't drink safe water. Some children spend hours every day fetching water.
Japan is one of the few countries in the world where you can drink tap water straight from the tap.

sdgs:6.fact: Switch off electricity you aren't using.
sdgs:6.about: Burning oil and coal gives off carbon dioxide. It's important to make more electricity from the power of the sun, wind and water.

sdgs:7.fact: The goal is a world where everyone can work safely.
sdgs:7.about:
Ending "child labour," where children are made to work instead of going to school, is part of this goal.
The goal is a society where everyone can work safely and find meaning in their work.

sdgs:8.fact: Making life better with new technology.
sdgs:8.about:
It's also important that everyone in the world can use the internet and new technology.
Ideas and technology can solve problems in society.

sdgs:9.fact: Respecting differences and leaving no one behind.
sdgs:9.about:
The goal is a society where everyone is valued, whatever their country, age, or whether they have a disability.
"Leave no one behind" is the motto of the SDGs.

sdgs:10.fact: Towns where everyone can keep living safely.
sdgs:10.about:
Building towns where everyone can keep living: barrier-free towns, towns that can stand up to disasters, towns with lots of green.
In hilly cities like Nagasaki, finding ways to make life easier for older people is important too.

sdgs:11.fact: Take good care of things and recycle.
sdgs:11.about:
Makers think about ways of making things without waste, and users think about using things carefully for a long time.
Look at the recycling marks and sort your rubbish correctly.

sdgs:12.fact: Going out by bike or on foot is kind to the Earth too.
sdgs:12.about:
The Earth's average temperature is slowly rising, and there are more heavy rains and heatwaves.
What each person does, like saving electricity and walking instead of driving, matters.

sdgs:13.fact: Don't throw rubbish in the sea. Use less plastic.
sdgs:13.about:
It's important not to catch too many sea creatures and not to pollute the sea.
Picking up rubbish on the beach is one way to protect the sea.

sdgs:14.fact: Protect forests and the places where animals live.
sdgs:14.about:
When forests shrink, animals lose their homes and soil gets washed away.
Let's plant trees and protect the homes of living things.

sdgs:15.fact: A world where problems are solved by talking.
sdgs:15.about:
The goal is a peaceful, fair society where everyone can live without fear.
Settling arguments with words is also a step towards peace.

sdgs:16.fact: Countries, companies and schools all work together.
sdgs:16.about:
The 17 goals can't be reached unless countries, companies, schools and each of us work together.
Connecting with friends around the world is one step.

#bosai: Japan has lots of earthquakes and typhoons. Let's be prepared, just in case.

bosai:0.fact: Remember "o-ka-shi-mo": don't push, don't run, don't talk, don't go back.
bosai:0.about:
School evacuation drills are practice so that you don't panic when it's real.
Listen carefully to your teacher and move quickly and quietly.

bosai:1.fact: First get low, protect your head and stay still. Get under a desk.
bosai:1.about:
Most earthquake shaking stops within 1 minute. If you rush outside, you might get hurt by things falling down.
When you're outside, move away from concrete block walls and vending machines.

bosai:2.fact: Get ready water, food, a torch, a radio, a first-aid kit and more.
bosai:2.about:
Pack everything in a backpack and keep it somewhere you can grab it quickly.
It's good to add family photos, a note of contact numbers and a whistle too.

bosai:3.fact: 3 litres per person per day is a good guide. It's safest to store enough for at least 3 days.
bosai:3.about:
When the water stops, you don't just need drinking water. You also need water for the toilet and for washing your hands.
Keeping water in the bathtub is one way to be prepared.

bosai:4.fact: Check the dangerous places and evacuation sites in your town on a map.
bosai:4.about:
Maps made by your city or town show places that are dangerous in floods, landslides and tsunamis.
Nagasaki has lots of slopes and cliffs, so watch out for landslides in heavy rain.

bosai:5.fact: The green sign marks an evacuation site. Decide on a place where your family will meet too.
bosai:5.about:
Evacuation site signs use pictograms understood all over the world, so people from other countries can understand them too.
There is also a "tsunami evacuation building" sign, for escaping to high places in a tsunami.

bosai:6.fact: Bring things in from outside, close the windows and evacuate early.
bosai:6.about:
Weather forecasts show where a typhoon will go days in advance.
Close the storm shutters, bring things in from the balcony and get torches ready in case of a power cut.

bosai:7.fact: If you call 171, you can leave a message for your family.
bosai:7.about:
In a big disaster, phone calls are hard to get through. Call 171 and enter your home phone number to leave a voice message.
You can try it out on days like the 1st of every month.

bosai:8.fact: September 1st is Disaster Prevention Day. Check your preparations with your family.
bosai:8.about:
This day became Disaster Prevention Day because of the Great Kantō Earthquake on September 1st, 1923.
On this day, talk with your family about evacuation sites and how to contact each other.

#animal-families: Animals have all kinds of families too. Some have fathers who raise the babies, and some have grandmothers as leaders!

animal-families:0.fact: The leader of the herd is the oldest grandmother elephant.
animal-families:0.about:
An African elephant herd is a family of grandmothers, mothers, aunts and children. The grandmother leader knows well where to find water and food.
A baby elephant stays in its mother's tummy for about 22 months. When the males grow up, they leave the herd.

animal-families:1.fact: The father keeps the egg warm on his feet for about 2 months.
animal-families:1.about:
In the Antarctic winter, while the mother goes to the sea to find food, the father keeps the egg on his feet, wrapped in the skin of his belly.
For about 2 months, the father eats nothing and survives the cold. Many fathers huddle together to block the wind.

animal-families:2.fact: The babies are born from a pouch on the father's tummy.
animal-families:2.about:
In seahorses, the mother puts her eggs into the pouch on the father's tummy.
The father protects the eggs in his pouch and gives birth to hundreds of babies. It's an unusual animal where the father gives birth.

animal-families:3.fact: A pack is a family of a father, a mother and their children.
animal-families:3.about:
A group of wolves is called a "pack." Usually it's a family of a father, a mother and their children from a few years.
Older brother and sister wolves help look after their younger brothers and sisters. They talk to their family by howling.

animal-families:4.fact: They take turns being the lookout and the babysitter.
animal-families:4.about:
Meerkats live in big family groups. They all take turns standing on their back legs as the lookout and staying with the babies as the babysitter.
When the lookout spots something like a hawk, it calls out to warn everyone.

animal-families:5.fact: A grandmother orca leads her family to places where there are fish.
animal-families:5.about:
Orcas live in families centred on their mothers, and they sometimes stay together all their lives.
Grandmother orcas know where the fish are from long experience, and in years with little food, they lead the family from the front.

animal-families:6.fact: It's the father who carries the twin babies on his back.
animal-families:6.about:
Marmosets, small monkeys from South America, often have twins.
The father and older brothers and sisters carry the babies on their backs and only pass them to the mother when she feeds them milk.

animal-families:7.fact: They live as a family, with a sea anemone as their home.
animal-families:7.about:
Clownfish live as a family inside a sea anemone. The anemone's stingers sting other fish, but clownfish are protected by their slimy bodies.
They have an amazing system: the biggest fish in the group becomes the mother.

animal-families:8.fact: Females stay in the troop they were born in all their lives.
animal-families:8.about:
In a troop of Japanese macaques, females stay in the troop they were born in, and males move to another troop when they grow up.
"Culture," like bathing in hot springs or washing sweet potatoes, is known to be passed from mothers to children.

#family-names-world: "My family name is ___." What family names mean, and the order of names, are different in each country.

family-names-world:0.fact: People say the most common are 1st Satō, 2nd Suzuki and 3rd Takahashi.
family-names-world:0.about:
Common family names in Japan include Satō, Suzuki, Takahashi, Tanaka, Itō and Watanabe. There are said to be about 1.8 million people called Satō.
In Nagasaki, Yamaguchi and Tanaka are said to be common. The most common names are different from area to area.

family-names-world:1.fact: Tanaka means "in the rice fields." Japan is said to have more than 100,000 family names.
family-names-world:1.about:
Many Japanese family names come from what the place where people lived was like. Tanaka is "in the rice fields," Yamamoto is "at the foot of the mountain" and Matsushita is "under the pine tree."
In the Meiji period, everyone came to have a family name. Japan has one of the largest numbers of family names in the world.

family-names-world:2.fact: Kim, Lee and Park together make up about half the population!
family-names-world:2.about:
In South Korea, just three family names, Kim, Lee and Park, make up about half the population.
Because there are so few family names, the place a family comes from has also been treated as important. Most family names are one character long.

family-names-world:3.fact: Wang, Li and Zhang are each used by about 100 million people.
family-names-world:3.about:
In China too, Wang, Li and Zhang are common, and each is said to be used by about 100 million people.
Like in Japan, the family name comes first. Almost all family names are one character, and there is even a book of family names called the "Hundred Family Surnames."

family-names-world:4.fact: Smith (blacksmith) is the most common family name in the UK and the USA.
family-names-world:4.about:
Many English family names come from old jobs. Smith is a "blacksmith" who hammers iron, Baker is a "bread maker," Taylor is a "tailor" and Cooper is a "barrel maker."
Smith is the most common family name in the UK, the USA and Australia.

family-names-world:5.fact: Instead of a family name, people call themselves "son of ___" or "daughter of ___."
family-names-world:5.about:
Many people in Iceland don't share a family name. Boys add "-son" (son) and girls add "-dóttir" (daughter) to their father's first name.
That's why the phone book was in order of first names, not family names.

family-names-world:6.fact: Many people have two family names: their father's and their mother's.
family-names-world:6.about:
In Spain and Latin America, many people use two family names side by side: their father's and their mother's.
For example, "Picasso" in the painter Pablo Picasso's name is his mother's family name. Names can get very long!

family-names-world:7.fact: In Japan, China and South Korea, the family name comes first. In English, the first name usually comes first.
family-names-world:7.about:
In Japan, China, South Korea, Hungary and some other countries, the family name comes first. In English-speaking countries, the first name usually comes first.
Since 2020, the Japanese government writes names in English with the family name first, like "Sato Ken." Either way is fine as long as you say your name clearly.

#family-celebrations: From birth to growing up, and beyond. Families around the world celebrate all kinds of milestones.

family-celebrations:0.fact: On the seventh night after a baby is born, the family writes the baby's name and puts it on display.
family-celebrations:0.about:
A celebration held on the seventh night after a baby is born. The chosen name is written on a "naming paper" and displayed at home.
Long ago, it was hard for babies to grow up healthy, so families celebrated that the baby had made it this far.

family-celebrations:1.fact: About 100 days after birth. The family wishes that "the baby will never go hungry."
family-celebrations:1.about:
A celebration about 100 days after birth, where the baby pretends to eat a meal.
The family wishes that "the baby will never go without food all their life" and prepares a feast with red bean rice and sea bream. In some areas, they touch a small stone with chopsticks and wish for "strong teeth."

family-celebrations:2.fact: On the first birthday, the baby carries about 2 kg of mochi on their back.
family-celebrations:2.about:
On the first birthday, the baby carries mochi made from one "shō" of rice (about 1.8 kg) on their back.
"Isshō" (one shō) sounds like "isshō" (a whole life), so it carries the wish "may you never go hungry all your life." The family watches the baby walk and tumble.

family-celebrations:3.fact: A Korean first-birthday celebration. People guess the baby's future from what the baby picks up.
family-celebrations:3.about:
In South Korea, on the first birthday (dol), things like thread, a brush, money and a microphone are put in front of the baby.
If the baby picks up thread, it means a long life; a brush means they will love studying. It's a fun fortune-telling game, very much like Japan's "erabitori."

family-celebrations:4.fact: Children's growth at ages 3, 5 and 7 is celebrated around November 15th.
family-celebrations:4.about:
Families celebrate their children's growth at ages 3, 5 and 7 around November 15th. Many families wear kimono and take photos.
Long, thin "chitose ame" candy carries the wish "may you stay healthy for a long time."

family-celebrations:5.fact: In Mexico and other countries, a girl's 15th birthday is celebrated in a big way.
family-celebrations:5.about:
In Mexico and Latin America, a girl's 15th birthday is celebrated in a big way as "a step towards adulthood."
She wears a dress and dances a waltz with her family, and lots of relatives and friends come to the party.

family-celebrations:6.fact: In Japan, the whole town celebrates young people becoming adults.
family-celebrations:6.about:
Since 2022, people in Japan legally become adults at 18. Many towns hold a "Gathering for 20-Year-Olds" for young people who are 20.
The second Monday of January is "Coming of Age Day," a national holiday. Some people wear furisode kimono or hakama.

family-celebrations:7.fact: A celebration at age 60. People wear a red sleeveless jacket.
family-celebrations:7.about:
The combination of the 12 zodiac animals and the 10 "heavenly stems" goes around once every 60 years, back to the year you were born. So turning 60 is called "kanreki" (the calendar returns).
It means "going back to being a baby," so people are given a red jacket and hat.

family-celebrations:8.fact: A celebration at age 88. The character "米" looks like 八十八 (88)!
family-celebrations:8.about:
The 88th birthday celebration is called "beiju." If you split the character "米" (rice), it looks like "八・十・八" (8, 10, 8).
There are other names from the shapes of characters too, like "kiju" for 77 and "hakuju" for 99 (take 一 away from 百 (100) and you get 白).

family-celebrations:9.fact: A celebration of 50 years of marriage.
family-celebrations:9.about:
The 50th wedding anniversary is called the "golden wedding," and the 25th is the "silver wedding." In English they are called golden wedding and silver wedding too, and they are celebrated all over the world.
The whole family gathers to say "thank you" for the couple's long journey together.

#generations: Great-grandpa, grandpa, dad, and you. Life has changed a lot from generation to generation.

generations:0.about:
A picture of family connections in the shape of a tree is called a "family tree."
Your grandparents are your grandfather and grandmother, and their parents are your great-grandfather and great-grandmother. Your parents' brothers and sisters are your uncles and aunts, and their children are your cousins.

generations:1.fact: Ten generations ago, you had a whopping 1,024 ancestors!
generations:1.about:
You have 2 parents, 4 grandparents, 8 great-grandparents… the number doubles every time you go back.
Ten generations ago (about 250 to 300 years ago, in the Edo period), you'd have 1,024 ancestors. If even one of them hadn't been there, you might not be here.

generations:2.fact: When your great-grandparents were children, rice was cooked on a kamado stove.
generations:2.about:
Old kitchens had a "kamado," a stove made of earth or bricks. People burned firewood to cook rice, and watching the fire was one of the jobs children helped with.
There is still an old song about how to cook tasty rice on a kamado: "First a small flame, then a big flame in the middle."

generations:3.fact: In the 1950s, everyone dreamed of a TV, a washing machine and a fridge.
generations:3.about:
In 1950s Japan, the black-and-white TV, the electric washing machine and the electric fridge were called the "three sacred treasures," and everyone wanted them.
In the 1960s, the colour TV, the air conditioner and the car became the "new three treasures." The 1964 Tokyo Olympics helped colour TVs spread.

generations:4.fact: People made calls by putting a finger in a numbered hole and turning the dial.
generations:4.about:
Old phones had a "dial": you put your finger in the hole for each number and turned it. Homes had one phone, often in the entrance or the hallway.
Towns had lots of public phones, and you put in 10-yen coins to make a call. Even now, we say we "dial" a phone number.

generations:5.fact: An old calculating tool that children still learn at elementary school.
generations:5.about:
The soroban came from China and was made easier to use in Japan. In the Edo period, children learned it at terakoya schools.
It is still taught in elementary school maths. People who are good at the soroban can calculate very fast in their heads by imagining one.

generations:6.fact: In 1979, a small player that let you listen to music outside was born in Japan.
generations:6.about:
In 1979, Sony in Japan released the "Walkman," which let you listen to cassette tapes outdoors, and it became hugely popular around the world.
When your parents were children, CD and MD (MiniDisc) players were used too.

generations:7.fact: Today's elementary school students each use their own tablet or computer at school.
generations:7.about:
From around 2020, elementary and junior high school students in Japan were each given a tablet or computer (the GIGA School program).
When your grandparents were children, there were only blackboards and notebooks. What will elementary school students be using 100 years from now?

#pets-as-family: Pets are important members of the family. Around the world, there are famous animals that people loved.

pets-as-family:0.fact: Hachi the Akita waited at Shibuya Station every day for his owner to come home.
pets-as-family:0.about:
Hachi the Akita went to Shibuya Station every day to meet his owner, Professor Ueno. Even after the professor stopped coming home, Hachi kept waiting at the station for about 10 years.
The story is known all over Japan, and there is a statue of Hachikō in front of Shibuya Station. It was even made into a movie in America.

pets-as-family:1.fact: A cat that became stationmaster at Kishi Station in Wakayama. Lots of people came to see her.
pets-as-family:1.about:
Tama, a cat who lived at Kishi Station in Wakayama, was made "stationmaster" in 2007. People came from all over Japan and the world to see her in her hat.
The railway line, which had been in trouble because so few people used it, came back to life thanks to Tama. Now "Nitama" has taken over.

pets-as-family:2.fact: A dog that travelled on mail trains in America.
pets-as-family:2.about:
Around 1888, a dog called Owney who had settled in at an American post office rode mail trains along with the mail bags.
Everywhere he went, he was given medals and tags as souvenirs, and he travelled all over America. He was loved as a lucky charm of the postal service.

pets-as-family:3.fact: In 1925, sled dogs carried medicine through the snow to a town.
pets-as-family:3.about:
In the winter of 1925, an illness spread in a town in Alaska called Nome. Teams of sled dogs ran a relay of about 1,000 km through blizzards to deliver medicine.
There is a statue of Balto, who ran the last stretch, in Central Park in New York, and Togo, who ran the longest stretch, is honoured too.

pets-as-family:4.fact: Dogs usually live about 10 to 15 years.
pets-as-family:4.about:
Dogs usually live about 10 to 15 years. Small dogs often live longer than big dogs.
One year for a dog is like several years for a person, so at 2 a dog is already an adult. Daily walks, good food and check-ups at the vet help them live long, healthy lives.

pets-as-family:5.fact: Cats that live indoors sometimes live more than 15 years.
pets-as-family:5.about:
Cats that are cared for indoors often live more than 15 years. Some cats live past 20.
Cats are said to sleep more than 12 hours a day. They are lively at dawn and dusk because those were their hunting times in the wild.

pets-as-family:6.fact: A giant tortoise on the island of St Helena. He is more than 190 years old.
pets-as-family:6.about:
Jonathan, a giant tortoise living on St Helena in the Atlantic Ocean, is said to have hatched around 1832, and he is thought to be the oldest living land animal in the world.
He can hardly see now, but he recognises the people who look after him by smell and sound. Some tortoises live more than 100 years.

pets-as-family:7.fact: If you take good care of them, they live more than 10 years.
pets-as-family:7.about:
Goldfish are a kind of carp. They were born in China and came to Japan about 500 years ago. Yamatokōriyama in Nara is famous for goldfish.
If you raise them carefully in a big tank, they can live more than 10 years and grow over 30 cm. Goldfish scooping at summer festivals is part of summer in Japan.

pets-as-family:8.fact: Japan has more pet dogs and cats than children under 15.
pets-as-family:8.about:
There are about 16 million pet dogs and cats in Japan, more than the number of children under 15 (about 14 million).
Now more people keep cats than dogs. When you get a pet, it's important to look after it as part of your family until the very end.

#animal-superpowers: "A cheetah can run fast." Animals' bodies hide amazing powers that people don't have.

animal-superpowers:0.fact: It goes from 0 to 100 km per hour in only about 3 seconds! The fastest animal on land.
animal-superpowers:0.about:
A cheetah can run at about 100 km per hour, but only for a few hundred metres at full speed. Its thin body, long legs and long tail for balance are the secrets of its speed.
Unlike other cats, its claws always stick out, gripping the ground like spikes.

animal-superpowers:1.fact: When it dives at prey, it goes more than 300 km per hour.
animal-superpowers:1.about:
A peregrine falcon folds its wings and dives from high in the sky, sometimes going faster than 300 km per hour. It's faster than the Shinkansen, the fastest animal in the world.
Little bumps inside its nostrils protect its breathing from the super-fast wind.

animal-superpowers:2.fact: It can jump about 9 m in one hop.
animal-superpowers:2.about:
With its thick back legs and long tail, a red kangaroo can jump about 9 m long and about 3 m high.
The long tendons in its legs store energy like springs, so hopping is less tiring than walking. It can't walk backwards.

animal-superpowers:3.fact: It can jump more than 100 times its body length.
animal-superpowers:3.about:
A flea's body is about 2 to 3 mm long, but it can jump more than 30 cm. For a person, that would be like jumping over a school building.
Its legs have a rubbery substance called "resilin" that stores energy and releases it all at once.

animal-superpowers:4.fact: The only bird that can fly backwards.
animal-superpowers:4.about:
A hummingbird beats its wings about 50 to 80 times a second, so it can stay still in the air and fly backwards.
It has a long, thin beak and a long tongue for drinking nectar from flowers. The smallest hummingbird weighs about 2 g, the same as two 1-yen coins.

animal-superpowers:5.fact: It shoots water from its mouth to knock insects off leaves.
animal-superpowers:5.about:
Archerfish live in rivers and mangroves in places like Southeast Asia. A groove in its mouth lets it shoot a thin jet of water at insects 1 to 2 m away.
Light bends when you look out of water, but it's an expert that takes that into account when it aims.

animal-superpowers:6.fact: Its tongue shoots out faster than a sports car accelerates!
animal-superpowers:6.about:
A chameleon's tongue stretches about as long as its body and catches insects in an instant. The smaller the chameleon, the faster it is, and the tongue speeds up much faster than a sports car.
It can also move its left and right eyes separately to look in two directions at once.

animal-superpowers:7.fact: Its punch is so fast that light and bubbles appear in the water.
animal-superpowers:7.about:
A mantis shrimp's punch is about 80 km per hour. It's so fast that bubbles form in the water, and when they collapse, they give off light and heat.
It's strong enough to break shells. Its eyes are amazing too: they can tell apart far more colours than ours.

animal-superpowers:8.fact: It can walk on glass walls and even ceilings.
animal-superpowers:8.about:
The soles of a gecko's feet have millions of hairs too tiny to see. These hairs stick tightly to walls, so it can walk on glass and ceilings.
Scientists are copying this to research things like tape that doesn't use glue.

animal-superpowers:9.fact: It changes colour in an instant and can even open jar lids.
animal-superpowers:9.about:
An octopus's skin has lots of little bags of colour, so it can change its colour and pattern in an instant to hide.
It has 3 hearts, and its arms have lots of nerves, so each arm moves almost as if it can think for itself. One octopus at an aquarium even opened a jar lid.

animal-superpowers:10.fact: It sleeps with half of its brain at a time, so it can rest while swimming.
animal-superpowers:10.about:
Dolphins have to come up to the surface to breathe. So they sleep with one half of the brain at a time, taking turns, and keep swimming with one eye open.
Newborn babies and their mothers are known to swim for a while with almost no sleep.

animal-superpowers:11.fact: It makes more than 600 volts of electricity with its body.
animal-superpowers:11.about:
Most of the body of the electric eel, which lives in rivers in South America, is made of organs that make electricity. It gives off several times the electricity of a home socket (100 volts in Japan).
It uses electricity to stun fish and to sense what's around it in muddy water. It's not really an eel but a different kind of fish.

animal-superpowers:12.fact: It uses echoes of sound to find insects even in total darkness.
animal-superpowers:12.about:
Bats make high sounds that people can't hear and use the echoes to learn where things are and what shape they are. This is called "echolocation."
Some bats eat hundreds of insects an hour. Dolphins also "see" what's around them with sound in the same way.

animal-superpowers:13.fact: It can go in a straight line by looking at the light of the Milky Way.
animal-superpowers:13.about:
Dung beetles roll dung into balls and push them in a straight line so others can't steal them.
A study in 2013 found that dung beetles in South Africa use the light of the Milky Way in the night sky to find their way. It was the first time this was discovered in an animal.

animal-superpowers:14.fact: If it loses a leg, the leg grows back.
animal-superpowers:14.about:
The axolotl (Mexican salamander) can regrow its legs, tail and even parts of its heart when they are lost.
In the wild it lives only in a lake in Mexico City, and people worry it will die out. How it rebuilds its body is helping medical research too.

animal-superpowers:15.fact: A tiny creature that survived even after being sent into space.
animal-superpowers:15.about:
Tardigrades are creatures smaller than 1 mm. When they dry out, they curl up into a "barrel" shape and can stay like that, as if asleep, for years.
In 2007, some were sent into space in an experiment and came back alive. They live in places near us too, like in moss.

#how-animals-move: "It can swim. It can't fly." Swimming, flying, running, crawling: animals' bodies are made for the way they move.

how-animals-move:0.fact: It wiggles its body from side to side and pushes water with its tail fin.
how-animals-move:0.about:
Fish bend their bodies into an S shape and push water backwards with their tail fins to move forward. Their other fins are for turning and stopping.
Many fish have an air bag inside called a "swim bladder" to control how deep they float.

how-animals-move:1.fact: Even without legs, it can move in 4 ways.
how-animals-move:1.about:
Snakes move by catching their scales on the ground. They have 4 ways of moving: wiggling, stretching and squeezing like an accordion, crawling in a straight line, and going sideways across sand (sidewinding).
A snake has 200 to more than 400 bones in its backbone, far more than a person (about 33).

how-animals-move:2.fact: Its bones are hollow, so it is very light.
how-animals-move:2.about:
Birds' bones are hollow, so they are very light. The shape of the wings changes how air flows and creates a force that lifts the body (lift).
Aeroplane wings work the same way. Some birds, like ostriches and penguins, don't fly.

how-animals-move:3.fact: It holds its body up with 3 of its 6 legs at a time, in a triangle.
how-animals-move:3.about:
Insects move 3 of their 6 legs at the same time: the front and back legs on one side and the middle leg on the other side. They always make a triangle with 3 legs, so they don't fall over easily.
This way of walking is used in six-legged robots too.

how-animals-move:4.fact: Its long back legs work like springs.
how-animals-move:4.about:
A frog's back legs can be longer than its body. It stores energy in its tendons and jumps all at once. Some frogs can jump more than 10 times their body length.
In the water, it swims with its webbed back feet. Breaststroke is a lot like the way frogs swim.

how-animals-move:5.fact: It opens and closes its bell to push water out.
how-animals-move:5.about:
A jellyfish opens its bell to fill it with water, then squeezes it shut to push the water out, and the push moves it along. It has no brain, no heart and no bones.
Jellyfish are very old creatures that have been in the sea for more than 500 million years.

how-animals-move:6.fact: It uses its wings like flippers to "fly" through the water.
how-animals-move:6.about:
A penguin's wings are like stiff flippers, and it flaps them to swim underwater, just like a bird flying in the sky.
Gentoo penguins are said to swim at about 36 km per hour. Their bodies are shaped like a teardrop, so the water doesn't hold them back much.

how-animals-move:7.fact: At full speed, all four of its legs leave the ground.
how-animals-move:7.about:
Long ago, people didn't know whether all four of a horse's legs leave the ground at the same moment when it runs at full speed.
In 1878, the photographer Muybridge lined up lots of cameras to take a series of photos and proved that "all four leave the ground." This also became one of the beginnings of movies.

how-animals-move:8.fact: It twists its body as it falls and lands on its feet.
how-animals-move:8.about:
When a cat falls, it first turns its head to look down, then twists the front half and then the back half of its body, and lands on its feet.
Its flexible backbone and the way it moves its body are so amazing that physicists have studied them. But high places are dangerous for cats too.

#human-skills-world: "I can play kendama." Around the world, there are lots of amazing skills that people learn by practising.

human-skills-world:0.fact: Japan is an unusual country where many elementary schools have unicycles.
human-skills-world:0.about:
In Japan, many elementary schools have unicycles, and lots of children ride them at break time. This is an unusual sight in the world.
At world unicycle championships, Japanese riders do well in events like freestyle. Riding builds balance and core strength.

human-skills-world:1.fact: Skipping with two ropes. Japanese teams do well at world championships!
human-skills-world:1.about:
Two ropes are turned in opposite directions, and you jump inside them. It grew from a children's game in New York, USA, into a sport.
Double dutch is popular in Japan, and some Japanese teams have won world championships. Rhythm and teamwork are important.

human-skills-world:2.fact: The kendama we know today was born in Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima.
human-skills-world:2.about:
Games where you catch a ball on a cup or a spike are found all over the world, but the kendama of today was born around 1919 in Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima.
Now it's very popular in America and Europe too, and world championships are held in Hatsukaichi. There are said to be thousands of tricks.

human-skills-world:3.fact: Experts can keep more than 10 balls in the air.
human-skills-world:3.about:
Juggling is a skill seen all over the world since long ago. Wall paintings in ancient Egypt even show people throwing balls.
Experts can keep more than 10 balls going. Jugglers use all kinds of things, like balls, clubs and rings.

human-skills-world:4.fact: Japanese players have won the world championship many times.
human-skills-world:4.about:
The yo-yo is a very old toy that is said to have existed even in ancient Greece.
At the World Yo-Yo Contest held every year in America, Japanese players have won many times. "String tricks," where the yo-yo keeps spinning, look like a dance.

human-skills-world:5.fact: The world record is less than 4 seconds!
human-skills-world:5.about:
The Rubik's Cube was invented in 1974 by Mr Rubik in Hungary. There are more than 43 quintillion ways to mix up the colours on its 6 sides!
The speedcubing world record is less than 4 seconds, and there's even a blindfolded event.

human-skills-world:6.fact: People imagine a soroban in their heads and calculate super fast.
human-skills-world:6.about:
People who are good at the soroban calculate by imagining its beads in their heads. This is called "anzan" (mental arithmetic).
In "flash anzan," where numbers flash on a screen one at a time, some experts can add up dozens of numbers in a few seconds.

human-skills-world:7.fact: On La Gomera in Spain, people can talk by whistling.
human-skills-world:7.about:
On La Gomera, one of Spain's Canary Islands, people have used "Silbo," which shows words with high and low whistles.
It's a clever way to send your voice far across mountains and valleys. Now it's taught at school too, and it's on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

human-skills-world:8.fact: You can play a tune with a single leaf.
human-skills-world:8.about:
A leaf whistle is played by holding a leaf to your lips and blowing so it vibrates and makes a sound. Hard, smooth leaves, like camellia or oak leaves, work well.
Skilled people can play songs on one leaf. Children in Japan and around the world have enjoyed it for a long time.

human-skills-world:9.fact: From one sheet of paper, you can make animals and even insects. Today there are experts all over the world.
human-skills-world:9.about:
Origami developed in Japan, and today it's called "origami" in English too. Yoshizawa Akira created many new designs and spread a way of showing folds with diagrams.
Today, ideas from origami are even used for satellite solar panels and for folding maps (the Miura fold).

#body-can: Your body is amazing too! Let's compare it with animals and find out its secrets.

body-can:0.fact: A tiny organ deep in your ear senses when your body tilts.
body-can:0.about:
Deep inside your ear are small rings filled with liquid, called the "semicircular canals." When your head tilts, the liquid moves and your brain senses which way your body is facing.
You get dizzy after spinning because the liquid keeps moving even after you stop.

body-can:1.fact: From seeing something to moving takes about 0.2 seconds.
body-can:1.about:
It takes about 0.2 seconds from seeing something to your body moving. You can measure how fast you react by trying to catch a ruler a friend drops.
Athletes react faster through practice, and they also learn to predict their opponent's moves.

body-can:2.fact: The human world record is 8.95 m, almost the same as a kangaroo!
body-can:2.about:
The long jump world record is 8.95 m, jumped by Mike Powell of the USA in 1991. That's about the length of a classroom!
A red kangaroo's jump is about 9 m too. With practice and a run-up, people can jump as far as animals.

body-can:3.fact: The fastest person runs about 44 km per hour, about half as fast as a cheetah.
body-can:3.about:
The fastest person in the 100 m runs at about 44 km per hour. That's about as fast as pedalling a bike as hard as you can.
A cheetah goes about 100 km per hour. But people have other special skills that animals can't copy.

body-can:4.fact: People can cool down by sweating, so we are good at running a long way.
body-can:4.about:
People can sweat all over their bodies to cool down, so we are animals that are very good at running long distances.
In a marathon on a hot day, people can sometimes even beat horses. Every year in the UK there is a race where people and horses compete.

body-can:5.fact: If you tickle yourself, it doesn't really tickle.
body-can:5.about:
If you tickle your own armpit, it doesn't really tickle. Your brain already knows how your hand will move, so it isn't surprised.
When a friend tickles you, you don't know where they'll touch, so it tickles.

body-can:6.about:
About 1 in 10 people in the world is left-handed. This number doesn't change much between countries or over time.
Lots of everyday tools, like scissors, ticket gates and pencil sharpeners, are made for right-handed people, so left-handed tools are made too.

body-can:7.fact: Your jaw muscle is very strong for its size.
body-can:7.about:
The jaw muscle called the "masseter" can make a very strong force for its size. The force of biting with your back teeth can even be about the same as your body weight.
Chewing well makes saliva, which helps digestion. Some people say to "chew each mouthful 30 times."

body-can:8.fact: When you practise again and again, the connections in your brain get stronger.
body-can:8.about:
When you practise something again and again, the connections between the nerve cells in your brain get thicker and stronger. That's why things you couldn't do before slowly become things you can do.
This keeps happening even when you're a grown-up. "I can't do it" really means "I can't do it yet!"

#robots-can: "Robots can … Robots can't …" Let's look at what robots are good at and what they still find hard.

robots-can:0.fact: Japan is a country that makes lots of factory robots.
robots-can:0.about:
In car and electronics factories, lots of robot arms do welding, putting things together and painting.
Japan is one of the countries that makes the most factory robots in the world, and companies like FANUC and Yaskawa Electric are famous.

robots-can:1.fact: It remembers the shape of the room and cleans by itself.
robots-can:1.about:
Cleaning robots spread after the "Roomba" went on sale in America in 2002. It uses sensors to find walls and steps, makes a map of the room and cleans.
When it's finished, it goes back to its charger by itself. Now there are also robots that mop floors and clean windows.

robots-can:2.fact: A doctor controls it, so operations can be done through small cuts.
robots-can:2.about:
Robots that help with operations are controlled by a doctor sitting a little way away. The robot's thin arms stop shaky hands, so operations can be done through small cuts.
The important thing is that the robot doesn't decide things by itself: a doctor is always moving it.

robots-can:3.fact: It has been driving on Mars for years, studying rocks and soil.
robots-can:3.about:
NASA's Mars rovers "Curiosity" and "Perseverance" landed on Mars in 2012 and 2021. They drill rocks and take photos, looking for signs that there was water on Mars long ago.
Perseverance also carried a small helicopter, "Ingenuity," which was the first to fly in the sky of another planet.

robots-can:4.fact: It explores the deep sea floor, where people can't go.
robots-can:4.about:
The deep sea is pitch dark and the weight of the water (water pressure) is huge, so it's very hard for people to go there. So robots controlled from far away explore the sea floor.
JAMSTEC, a Japanese research organisation, is a world leader in studying deep-sea creatures and the sea floor.

robots-can:5.fact: A Japanese robot that could walk and run on two legs.
robots-can:5.about:
ASIMO, announced by Honda in 2000, walked smoothly on two legs, and later it could run, climb stairs and carry a tray.
It was shown all over the world and helped push forward research on human-shaped robots. It retired in 2022.

robots-can:6.fact: A dog-shaped robot born in Japan is known all over the world.
robots-can:6.about:
"aibo," a robot dog released by Sony in 1999, got people talking all over the world. A new aibo came out in 2018.
It remembers people's faces and gets happy when you pat it. Lots of people feel it's part of the "family," even though it's a robot.

robots-can:7.fact: Folding laundry is very hard for robots!
robots-can:7.about:
Robots are good at carrying heavy things and doing the same job tens of thousands of times. But they are still very bad at folding crumpled laundry and holding soft things.
Sometimes the things people think are "easy" are the hardest for robots.

#jhs-life-japan: You'll be in junior high school soon! "I want to join the ___ club." What will change in junior high?

jhs-life-japan:0.fact: The stand-up-collar school uniform has kept the same style since the Meiji period.
jhs-life-japan:0.about:
A "gakuran" is a school uniform with a stand-up collar that goes around the neck. It started when it was used as a university uniform in the Meiji period.
One idea is that "ran" comes from "ranpuku" (Dutch clothes), the Edo-period word for Western clothes. It might be a word linked to Dejima in Nagasaki.

jhs-life-japan:1.fact: It was first worn by sailors. It became a school uniform in the 1920s.
jhs-life-japan:1.about:
The sailor uniform was first worn by sailors in navies like Britain's. Some say the big collar was for hearing sounds in the wind at sea.
In Japan, it spread as a uniform for girls' schools in the 1920s. Around the world, it's known as a picture of "Japanese school."

jhs-life-japan:2.fact: In junior high school, a different teacher teaches each subject.
jhs-life-japan:2.about:
In elementary school, your homeroom teacher teaches many subjects, but in junior high school each subject, like Japanese, maths, English and science, is taught by a specialist teacher.
Subject names change too: "sansū" (arithmetic) becomes "sūgaku" (mathematics). You'll have more English lessons, and the sentences in the textbook get longer.

jhs-life-japan:3.fact: After school, you do sports or cultural activities with your teammates.
jhs-life-japan:3.about:
Club activities are things you do after school or on days off with friends who like the same things. There are sports clubs and culture clubs.
It's unusual for schools to have so many sports and music teams like in Japan, and people from other countries are sometimes surprised.

jhs-life-japan:4.fact: Older students are "senpai," and younger students are "kōhai."
jhs-life-japan:4.about:
In junior high school, students in older years are called "senpai," and students in younger years are called "kōhai." In clubs, senpai teach you, and one day you'll teach your kōhai.
"Senpai" is so well known around the world that it is sometimes understood in English too.

jhs-life-japan:5.fact: A few times a year, there are tests in all your subjects.
jhs-life-japan:5.about:
In junior high school, there are "regular tests" once or twice a term, testing all your subjects together.
Before tests, clubs stop and you make a plan and study. Making a "study plan" is a junior high school skill too.

jhs-life-japan:6.fact: A trip with friends for several days, a big memory of junior high school.
jhs-life-japan:6.about:
School trips are said to have started with a Tokyo school's trip in 1886. Travelling with friends for several days is a very Japanese school event.
For junior high school, Kyoto, Nara and Tokyo are popular. At some schools, groups make their own plans and explore the city by themselves.

jhs-life-japan:7.fact: The whole class practises a song and performs it.
jhs-life-japan:7.about:
Many junior high schools have a "chorus contest," where each class practises a song and they compete. Students are the conductor and the piano player too.
Classes practise every morning before the big day, and the feeling when all the voices come together becomes a memory for life.

jhs-life-japan:8.fact: Students think of ways to make their school better themselves.
jhs-life-japan:8.about:
The student council is a group of student representatives who think of ideas to make the school better and carry them out. The president and secretary are chosen in a student election.
With greeting campaigns, running school events and volunteering, students make their school themselves.

#club-origins-sports: "I want to join the volleyball team." When and where were the sports of junior high school clubs born?

club-origins-sports:0.fact: The first event at the ancient Olympics was a sprint.
club-origins-sports:0.about:
The first ancient Olympics on record were held in 776 BC in Olympia, Greece. The only event was a sprint of about 192 m called the "stadion."
The word "stadium" comes from this "stadion." Running, jumping and throwing are the most basic parts of sport.

club-origins-sports:1.fact: Practising with bamboo swords and armour spread in the Edo period.
club-origins-sports:1.about:
Kendo comes from samurai sword training. In the Edo period, a way of practising with bamboo swords (shinai) and armour, so people could strike each other without getting hurt, spread.
Now people do kendo all over the world, and there are world championships. It's a martial art that begins and ends with a bow.

club-origins-sports:2.fact: The first rules were made in England.
club-origins-sports:2.about:
People played ball-kicking games all over the world, but in 1863 the "Football Association" was set up in England, and the rule of not using your hands was decided.
That's why it's called "football" in the UK, and "soccer" in America and Japan. It's the most popular sport in the world.

club-origins-sports:3.fact: An American teacher taught it to Japanese students.
club-origins-sports:3.about:
Around 1872, an American teacher, Horace Wilson, taught baseball to students at a school in Tokyo. The Japanese word "yakyū" is said to have been spread by Masaoka Shiki and Chūman Kanoe.
The Kōshien high school baseball tournament has more than 100 years of history and is a summer tradition in Japan.

club-origins-sports:4.fact: Named after a big house in England called "Badminton."
club-origins-sports:4.about:
Games where people hit a shuttlecock back and forth have been around for a long time. Around 1873, the game was played at a big country house in England called "Badminton House," and its name became the name of the sport.
A shuttlecock is made of 16 bird feathers. A smash can go faster than 400 km per hour!

club-origins-sports:5.fact: Kanō Jigorō started it in Tokyo.
club-origins-sports:5.about:
In 1882, Kanō Jigorō opened the Kōdōkan in Tokyo and created "judo," based on jūjutsu. Its idea is "beating a bigger opponent with gentle strength."
Kanō became the first IOC (International Olympic Committee) member from Asia. Judo has been an Olympic sport since the 1964 Tokyo Games.

club-origins-sports:6.fact: It was born in England as tennis on a table.
club-origins-sports:6.about:
Around the 1880s, a kind of tennis played on a table was born in England. Some say books were first used as the net and a cork as the ball.
It was called "ping-pong" because of the sound it makes. It came to Japan in 1902.

club-origins-sports:7.fact: Tennis with a rubber ball. It was born in Japan!
club-origins-sports:7.about:
In the Meiji period, tennis balls had to be bought from abroad and were expensive, so in Japan cheap rubber balls were used instead. This was the start of soft tennis.
It's a sport born in Japan, and now it's popular in Asian countries like South Korea and Taiwan too.

club-origins-sports:8.fact: It started in America with peach baskets as the goals.
club-origins-sports:8.about:
In 1891, an American teacher, James Naismith, thought it up as a sport people could play in a gym in winter. The first goals were peach baskets, and each time someone scored, the ball was taken out with a ladder.
The first game was 9 players against 9, and the score was 1–0.

club-origins-sports:9.fact: It was made in America as a gentler sport than basketball.
club-origins-sports:9.about:
In 1895, an American, William Morgan, thought it up as a sport that was less rough than basketball. Its first name was "Mintonette."
Japan's women's team won the gold medal at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and were called the "Witches of the Orient."

club-origins-sports:10.fact: A relay where runners pass on a sash. It was born in Japan.
club-origins-sports:10.about:
Ekiden began in 1917 with a relay of about 500 km from Kyoto to Tokyo over 3 days. It got its name from "tenma," the Edo-period system of relaying horses between post towns.
This race where runners pass on a sash is called "ekiden" abroad too. The Hakone Ekiden at New Year is famous.

#club-origins-culture: "I like music. I want to join the brass band." Not just sports clubs! Let's see what's fun about culture clubs.

club-origins-culture:0.fact: Japanese school brass bands are famous around the world for their high level.
club-origins-culture:0.about:
Japan has lots of school brass bands, and many bands from all over the country take part in the All Japan Band Competition, which has been held since 1940.
Trumpets, clarinets, saxophones, percussion and many other instruments play together to make one piece of music. Sometimes they march and play at the same time.

club-origins-culture:1.fact: A contest where schools across Japan compete in singing, with more than 90 years of history.
club-origins-culture:1.about:
The NHK National School Music Competition started in 1932, and every year elementary, junior high and high school choirs compete with their singing.
Voices are split into parts by how high or low they are to make harmony. It's music you can make with no instruments, just your body.
