Uranus's axis is tilted about 98 degrees, so it goes around the Sun lying on its side. One trip around takes about 84 years.
So its north pole gets sunlight for about 42 years, and then it's night for the next 42 years. Each season lasts about 21 years!

#seasons-72: Long ago in Japan, the year was split into 72 small seasons. Each one has a name like "The swallows arrive."

seasons-72:0.fact: The start of spring. Spring winds from the east melt the ice.
seasons-72:0.about:
On the calendar, spring begins at Risshun. The first of the 72 micro-seasons is "The east wind melts the ice," the time when soft winds from the east start to melt the ice on ponds.
The day before Risshun is "Setsubun," when people throw beans.

seasons-72:1.fact: Insects that spent the winter underground come outside.
seasons-72:1.about:
"Keichitsu" means "insects that were shut away underground open their doors and come out."
In fact, frogs and insects start moving around March, when the ground warms up. The English word "spring" also means "to jump out."

seasons-72:2.fact: Day and night are the same length. Sparrows start building nests.
seasons-72:2.about:
The micro-season around the spring equinox is "Sparrows start to nest," when sparrows begin building their nests.
Around this time, cherry blossoms start to open across Japan. When 5 or 6 flowers open on a special "sample tree," weather office staff announce that the blossoms have started.

seasons-72:3.fact: Swallows fly in from the countries to the south.
seasons-72:3.about:
Seimei is the time when "everything is pure and bright." Its micro-season is "The swallows arrive," when swallows come back from the countries to the south.
In China and Okinawa, families gather at their family graves around this time and share a feast, called the "Qingming Festival" (Shīmī in Okinawa).

seasons-72:4.fact: The start of summer. Frogs start croaking in the rice fields.
seasons-72:4.about:
Rikka is the start of summer, around Children's Day. Its micro-season is "Frogs start singing," when water fills the rice fields and frogs begin to croak.
It's also the season for new tea, and tea picked on "the 88th night" is thought to bring a long life.

seasons-72:5.fact: Rice-planting time. Fireflies start to fly.
seasons-72:5.about:
Bōshu is the time to sow the seeds of plants with "awns" (bristles), like rice and wheat. It's rice-planting season.
One of its micro-seasons is "Rotten grass becomes fireflies." People long ago believed rotting grass turned into fireflies.

seasons-72:6.fact: The longest days. There's an unusual plant that dies back in summer.
seasons-72:6.about:
The micro-season around the summer solstice is "The self-heal withers." Self-heal (utsubo-gusa) is a plant that dies back in summer, when other plants are growing thick.
At the winter solstice it's the opposite: "The self-heal sprouts." It's a clever pair of names at the two ends of the year.

seasons-72:7.fact: The hottest time of the year.
seasons-72:7.about:
Taisho is the hottest time of the year. Its micro-season is "The paulownia begins to bear fruit," when paulownia trees start producing seeds.
On the "Day of the Ox" in this period, there's a custom of eating eel to stop summer tiredness.

seasons-72:8.fact: It may still be hot, but on the calendar it's the start of autumn.
seasons-72:8.about:
Risshū is the start of autumn on the calendar. Hot days continue, but its micro-season is "A cool breeze arrives," and you might feel a cool wind in the morning or evening.
From this day, summer greeting cards change from "shochū mimai" (midsummer greetings) to "zansho mimai" (late-summer greetings).

seasons-72:9.fact: Summer thunder ends, and the sky turns autumnal.
seasons-72:9.about:
The micro-season around the autumn equinox is "Thunder lowers its voice." Summer evening showers and thunder become rarer.
The sky feels higher, and you start to see wispy clouds and "fish-scale" clouds. Moon-viewing happens around this time too.

seasons-72:10.fact: The start of winter. Sasanqua camellias begin to flower.
seasons-72:10.about:
Rittō is the start of winter. Its micro-season is written "The camellias begin to open," but the flowers here are actually sasanqua camellias.
They're the winter flowers that appear in the children's song "Takibi" (Bonfire). In the north, the first snow starts to fall.

seasons-72:11.fact: The shortest day. The plant that died in summer sprouts.
seasons-72:11.about:
The micro-season around the winter solstice is "The self-heal sprouts." The self-heal that died back in summer starts to sprout. Before the coldest time of year, the next life has already begun.
Knowing the 72 seasons helps you notice the little changes every day.

#haiku-seasons: Haiku capture the seasons in 17 sounds: 5-7-5. It's one of the shortest kinds of poem in the world.

haiku-seasons:0.fact: A short Japanese poem made of 17 sounds: 5, 7 and 5.
haiku-seasons:0.about:
A haiku is one of the shortest kinds of poem in the world, made of 17 sounds: 5, 7 and 5. It was born in the Edo period, and in the Meiji period Masaoka Shiki named it "haiku."
It captures something you saw or felt in just a few words. Now haiku are written all over the world, and in English they're called "haiku" too.

haiku-seasons:1.fact: A haiku usually includes one "kigo," a word that shows the season.
haiku-seasons:1.about:
A kigo is a word that shows the season. "Cherry blossom" is spring, "cicada" is summer, "moon" is autumn and "snow" is winter. A book that collects season words is called a "saijiki."
It's fun that some don't match how we feel today because of the old calendar: "watermelon," for example, is an autumn word.

haiku-seasons:2.fact: "Furuike ya / kawazu tobikomu / mizu no oto" (An old pond / a frog jumps in / the sound of water)
haiku-seasons:2.about:
Matsuo Bashō was a haiku poet of the Edo period, called the "god of haiku." "An old pond / a frog jumps in / the sound of water" is the most famous haiku in the world.
The "plop" of a frog jumping into a quiet old pond makes you feel the stillness. "The Narrow Road to the Deep North," about his journey through Tōhoku, is famous too.

haiku-seasons:3.fact: "Katatsumuri / sorosoro nobore / Fuji no yama" (Little snail / climb slowly, slowly / up Mount Fuji)
haiku-seasons:3.about:
Kobayashi Issa wrote lots of haiku that looked kindly at small creatures. "Skinny frog / don't give up! / Issa is here" is famous too.
"Little snail / climb slowly, slowly / up Mount Fuji" gives the feeling of "it's fine to go slowly, just keep heading for your big goal."

haiku-seasons:4.fact: "Na no hana ya / tsuki wa higashi ni / hi wa nishi ni" (Rapeseed flowers / the moon in the east / the sun in the west)
haiku-seasons:4.about:
Yosa Buson was an Edo-period haiku poet who was also a great painter. That's why his haiku bring colours to mind, like paintings.
"Rapeseed flowers / the moon in the east / the sun in the west" describes a huge scene: a field of yellow rapeseed flowers, with the moon rising in the east and the sun setting in the west.

haiku-seasons:5.fact: "Kaki kueba / kane ga naru nari / Hōryū-ji" (I bite a persimmon / and a bell rings out / at Hōryū-ji)
haiku-seasons:5.about:
Masaoka Shiki made haiku new in the Meiji period. He valued "shasei," describing things just as you see them. He loved baseball and is known for turning baseball words into Japanese.
"I bite a persimmon / and a bell rings out / at Hōryū-ji" is an autumn haiku about hearing the temple bell of Hōryū-ji while eating a persimmon in Nara.

haiku-seasons:6.fact: In English they're "haiku" too. They're written in schools all over the world.
haiku-seasons:6.about:
There are haiku in English too. English counts sounds differently, so they're often written as short, three-line poems.
Schools all over the world have haiku lessons, and astronauts have even written haiku in space. The Japanese word "haiku" is in English dictionaries too.

haiku-seasons:7.fact: There are lots of contests where elementary students across Japan send in haiku.
haiku-seasons:7.about:
Japan has lots of contests where children send in haiku, and hundreds of thousands of poems come in every year. In one contest, the winning haiku are printed on green tea bottles.
Try turning "something you saw, a sound you heard, or something you felt" into 5-7-5 with a season word!

#shun-food: "Watermelon is a summer fruit." The time when a food is tastiest and most plentiful is called "shun."

shun-food:0.fact: The time when a food is tastiest and has the most nutrients.
shun-food:0.about:
"Shun" is the time when a food is most plentiful, tastiest and full of nutrients. Foods in season are cheaper too.
Now we can buy all kinds of things all year because of greenhouses and imports, but knowing what's in season lets you taste the changing seasons.

shun-food:1.fact: Spring. Young bamboo that sometimes grows more than 1 m in a day.
shun-food:1.about:
Bamboo shoots are the young sprouts of bamboo. They poke out of the ground in spring, and one was recorded growing more than 1 m in a day. One idea is that the kanji 筍 is used because a shoot becomes bamboo in 10 days (one "jun," 旬).
The trick to tasty bamboo shoots is boiling them right after you dig them up.

shun-food:2.fact: Their real season is spring to early summer. Japan has a huge number of varieties.
shun-food:2.about:
The real season for strawberries is spring to early summer, but in Japan, greenhouse strawberries are everywhere from around Christmas.
Japan is said to have more than 300 varieties, like "Amaou" and "Tochiotome," and they're popular abroad too. The little seeds on the outside of a strawberry are actually each a fruit.

shun-food:3.fact: Early summer. Nagasaki grows the most loquats in Japan!
shun-food:3.about:
Loquats are a fruit in season in early summer. Nagasaki grows the most loquats in Japan, and "Mogi loquats" are especially famous.
They're said to have started when a woman in Mogi planted seeds that came to Nagasaki from China in the Edo period. It's a taste that spread from Nagasaki all over Japan.

shun-food:4.fact: Summer. About 90% water, so it helps prevent heatstroke too.
shun-food:4.about:
Watermelons are a fruit from Africa, and they're about 90% water. They're perfect for getting water into your body in hot summers.
Kumamoto grows the most in Japan. There are even square watermelons and black watermelons. It's a mystery of "contrast" in taste that a little salt makes watermelon taste sweeter.

shun-food:5.fact: Summer. They're actually soybeans picked while they're young.
shun-food:5.about:
Edamame are soybeans picked while they're still young and green. When they become soybeans, they're used to make tofu, miso, soy sauce and natto.
In English they're called "edamame" too, and they're sold in American supermarkets.

shun-food:6.fact: Autumn. In kanji, it's written "autumn sword fish."
shun-food:6.about:
Pacific saury is a fish in season in autumn, and its kanji 秋刀魚 mean "autumn sword fish." That's because its long, thin, shiny silver body looks like a sword.
The rakugo comedy story "The Saury of Meguro" is famous too. Recently, changes in the sea have meant fewer are caught.

shun-food:7.fact: Autumn. In English, they're sometimes called "kaki."
shun-food:7.about:
Persimmons are a fruit from East Asia, and in Japan they've long been loved as a taste of autumn. In some countries, they're called "kaki" in English too.
They're so full of nutrients that there's a saying: "When persimmons turn red, doctors turn pale." Bitter persimmons become sweet when they're dried.

shun-food:8.fact: Winter. A winter classic to eat under the kotatsu.
shun-food:8.about:
Mikan oranges are a fruit in season in winter. Wakayama, Ehime and Shizuoka are the main growing areas, and Nagasaki is one too.
In America and Canada, they're called "satsumas," after Satsuma (old Kagoshima). The white strings (the albedo) are full of nutrients too.

shun-food:9.fact: Winter. A "promotion fish" that changes its name as it grows.
shun-food:9.about:
Yellowtail is a "promotion fish" that changes its name as it gets bigger. It depends on the area, but the names go something like wakashi → inada → warasa → buri.
"Kan-buri," winter yellowtail, is rich and very tasty. It's caught in the seas around Gotō in Nagasaki too, and fish farming is common.

#animals-through-seasons: Living things sense the changing seasons, so they migrate, sleep or change colour.

animals-through-seasons:0.fact: They fly thousands of kilometres from Southeast Asia to reach Japan in spring.
animals-through-seasons:0.about:
Swallows spend the winter in warm countries like those in Southeast Asia, and in spring they fly thousands of kilometres back to Japan. Sometimes they return to the same nest as last year.
There's a saying, "When swallows fly low, it will rain," because insects fly lower in damp air.

animals-through-seasons:1.fact: In the rainy season, the rice fields are full of frogs singing together.
animals-through-seasons:1.about:
In the rainy season, when the rice fields are filled with water, frogs croak to call a partner. The ones croaking are the males.
Japanese tree frogs puff up their throats like balloons to make loud calls. They often croak before rain, so they're called "rain frogs" in Japanese.

animals-through-seasons:2.fact: Around June, they glow around clean rivers.
animals-through-seasons:2.about:
Genji fireflies glow around clean rivers in June. The light on their tails is "cold light" that gives off almost no heat, and it's a signal to other fireflies.
The timing of their flashes is different in eastern and western Japan, so people say fireflies have "dialects." Fireflies are a sign that a river is clean.

animals-through-seasons:3.fact: They live underground for years, and above ground for only a few weeks.
animals-through-seasons:3.about:
Cicada larvae spend years underground, growing by drinking sap from tree roots. When they come up and become adults, they live only a few weeks.
In America, there are cicadas that come out in their billions all at once, every 13 or 17 years. Only the males sing.

animals-through-seasons:4.fact: They spend summer in the mountains and come down to the villages in autumn.
animals-through-seasons:4.about:
Autumn darter dragonflies are born in rice fields, and then they spend the hot summer high in the cool mountains. In autumn, they turn red and come back down to the villages.
They're a Japanese autumn insect, well known from the children's song "Akatombo" (Red Dragonfly), with music by Yamada Kōsaku.

animals-through-seasons:5.fact: More than 10,000 cranes come to Izumi in Kagoshima in winter.
animals-through-seasons:5.about:
Every winter, more than 10,000 hooded cranes and white-naped cranes fly from places like Siberia to the Izumi Plain in Kagoshima. It's the biggest place in Japan for cranes to spend the winter.
Most of the world's hooded cranes gather here. The local people have protected them carefully for a long time.

animals-through-seasons:6.fact: They fly from Siberia to lakes in Hokkaido and Niigata.
animals-through-seasons:6.about:
In winter, swans fly thousands of kilometres from Siberia to places like Hokkaido, Tōhoku and Hyōko Lake in Niigata.
In spring, they go back north and raise their chicks in Siberia. Some swans wear numbered rings around their necks so researchers can learn their migration routes.

animals-through-seasons:7.fact: During winter, they stay in their dens without eating anything.
animals-through-seasons:7.about:
Bears eat lots of nuts in autumn to get fat, and in winter they spend months in their dens without eating or even going to the toilet.
Mother bears give birth to tiny babies while hibernating, and in spring they come out of the den together.

animals-through-seasons:8.fact: At Jigokudani in Nagano, Japanese macaques warm up in hot springs.
animals-through-seasons:8.about:
At Jigokudani Monkey Park in Nagano, Japanese macaques get into the hot spring to warm up in winter. They're famous around the world as "snow monkeys."
Japanese macaques are the most northern-living monkeys in the world (apart from humans).

animals-through-seasons:9.fact: In winter its fur is pure white, and in summer it's brown.
animals-through-seasons:9.about:
The stoat is a member of the weasel family that lives in places like Japan's high mountains. In winter its fur turns pure white, with only the tip of its tail staying black. In summer its back is brown.
It's a change of clothes to make it harder to spot in the snow. Rock ptarmigans and mountain hares turn white in winter too.

#home-objects-history: "This is my kitchen. We have a rice cooker." When were the handy machines in our homes invented?

home-objects-history:0.fact: A light from the Edo period: an oil flame surrounded by paper.
home-objects-history:0.about:
In the Edo period, homes were lit by "andon," lamps made of paper stretched over a wooden frame. Oil like rapeseed oil burned inside, but they were only a tiny fraction as bright as a light bulb today.
That's why people long ago went to bed soon after sunset and got up at sunrise.

home-objects-history:1.fact: Bamboo from Kyoto was used in Edison's light bulbs.
home-objects-history:1.about:
To make a light bulb that would shine for a long time, Edison tried thousands of materials for the filament. The best was bamboo from Yawata, near Kyoto.
Light bulbs with bamboo filaments are said to have shone for more than 1,000 hours. Today, LEDs that last even longer are the most common.

home-objects-history:2.fact: The first vacuum cleaner was a big machine pulled by a horse.
home-objects-history:2.about:
In 1901, Booth in the UK made a cleaner that "sucked up" dust. It was so big that it was pulled by a horse to the front of a house, and the hose was put in through the window.
Later, small vacuum cleaners for use at home were invented, and now we have robots that clean by themselves.

home-objects-history:3.fact: It was invented to take the dampness out of a printing factory.
home-objects-history:3.about:
In 1902, Carrier in the USA invented a machine that cooled and dried the air so that paper in a printing factory wouldn't stretch and shrink in the damp. This was the start of air conditioning.
Japanese summers are hot and humid, so now almost every home has an air conditioner.

home-objects-history:4.fact: From scrubbing on a washboard by hand to machines spun by motors.
home-objects-history:4.about:
Long ago, people washed clothes by scrubbing them by hand in a tub on a washboard. Around 1908, an electric washing machine with a motor went on sale in America.
They spread in Japan in the 1950s. Time spent on housework dropped a lot, and life changed.

home-objects-history:5.fact: Takayanagi Kenjirō showed the character "イ" on a screen.
home-objects-history:5.about:
In 1926, Takayanagi Kenjirō in Shizuoka succeeded in showing the katakana character "イ" on a cathode-ray tube. It was a pioneer of electronic television.
Takayanagi is called "the father of Japanese television." TV broadcasting in Japan began in 1953.

home-objects-history:6.fact: Japan's first electric fridge was made.
home-objects-history:6.about:
Long ago, people bought ice from the ice seller and kept food cold in wooden "ice boxes." In 1930, the first electric fridge was made in Japan.
But it was expensive, and it only spread to most homes in the 1960s. Now big fridges with freezers and vegetable drawers are normal.

home-objects-history:7.fact: It was discovered when a chocolate bar melted in someone's pocket.
home-objects-history:7.about:
In 1945, an American engineer, Spencer, noticed during radar research that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. He had discovered that radio waves (microwaves) heat food.
A microwave oven makes heat by shaking the water inside food. In Japan, people call it "chin suru," after the "ding" sound.

home-objects-history:8.fact: Rice cooks at the press of a switch. A great Japanese invention!
home-objects-history:8.about:
In 1955, Toshiba in Japan released an automatic electric rice cooker. You press the switch, and it turns itself off when the rice is cooked.
People no longer had to watch the fire of a kamado, and housework got much easier. Now rice cookers are used across Asia and around the world.

home-objects-history:9.fact: It spread in Japan and surprises travellers from around the world.
home-objects-history:9.about:
A Japanese company improved an American medical product and in 1980 began selling a toilet seat that washes your bottom with warm water.
Warm seats, lids that open by themselves, flushing sounds… Japanese toilets have become a "speciality" that surprises visitors from abroad.

home-objects-history:10.fact: Japanese researchers made it, and white LED lights were born.
home-objects-history:10.about:
Red and green LEDs had been around for a long time, but blue LEDs were so hard to make that people said "it's impossible this century."
In the 1990s, research by Akasaki Isamu, Amano Hiroshi and Nakamura Shūji made bright blue LEDs possible, and white LED lights were born. The three won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014.

#japanese-home: "My room is upstairs." Tatami, shōji, kotatsu: Japanese homes are full of wisdom that suits the climate and the way people live.

japanese-home:0.fact: The size depends on the area. Kyoma mats are bigger than Edoma mats!
japanese-home:0.about:
Tatami are Japanese floor mats made of igusa rush. The size of a room is described by the number of mats, like "6 tatami."
But the size of one mat is different in each area: "Kyōma" in the Kansai region is about 191 cm × 95 cm, and "Edoma" in the Kantō region is about 176 cm × 88 cm. So a 6-tatami room is bigger in Kyoto!

japanese-home:1.fact: Paper doors soften the light and divide rooms however you like.
japanese-home:1.about:
Shōji are doors with thin washi paper on a wooden frame, and they let soft light through. Fusuma are doors covered in thick paper that divide one room from another.
If you take the fusuma out, two rooms become one big room. It's a handy idea for when the family gets together.

japanese-home:2.fact: The place where you take off your shoes, the "border" between inside and outside.
japanese-home:2.about:
The genkan is where you take off your shoes before stepping up into the house. It's an important "border" between inside and outside, and the floor is one step higher.
Taking off shoes is a smart way to keep tatami and floors clean in a rainy, damp climate. Line up your shoes with the toes pointing outwards.

japanese-home:3.fact: A special spot in a Japanese-style room for displaying a hanging scroll or flowers.
japanese-home:3.about:
The tokonoma is a raised alcove in one corner of a Japanese-style room, where a hanging scroll, a flower arrangement or seasonal decorations are displayed.
It's polite to seat a guest in the "kamiza," the place of honour near the tokonoma. Many homes don't have a tokonoma now.

japanese-home:4.fact: A veranda that connects the house and the garden. Cool in summer, sunny in winter.
japanese-home:4.about:
The engawa is a wooden veranda running along the outside of the house, gently connecting the house and garden.
In summer the breeze makes it cool, and in winter the sun makes it warm. It was also a place to chat with the neighbours.

japanese-home:5.fact: A Japanese winter heater that dates back to the Muromachi period.
japanese-home:5.about:
The kotatsu was born around the Muromachi period. Long ago, a frame was put over a sunken hearth and covered with a quilt. Now it has an electric heater.
The family gathering around one kotatsu and eating mikan oranges is a classic winter scene in Japan.

japanese-home:6.fact: Wash your body first, then get into the bath. The family shares the water.
japanese-home:6.about:
In a Japanese bath, you wash your body outside the tub first, then soak in the clean water. That's why the family can take turns using the same water.
Soaking up to your shoulders to warm up and relax is part of Japanese culture. In many countries, people just take a shower.

japanese-home:7.fact: Fold it away in the morning, and your bedroom becomes a different room in the day.
japanese-home:7.about:
A futon is bedding you lay on the floor to sleep on. If you fold it and put it in the cupboard in the morning, the room you slept in can be a living room or study room in the day.
Hanging futons outside on sunny days is very Japanese. In English it's "futon" too, but abroad it can mean a sofa bed.

japanese-home:8.fact: "3LDK" means 3 rooms + a living room, dining area and kitchen.
japanese-home:8.about:
"3LDK," which you see in Japanese home adverts, means a home with 3 rooms plus an L (living room), a D (dining area) and a K (kitchen).
In English-speaking countries, homes are usually described by the number of bedrooms, like "3-bedroom."

japanese-home:9.fact: Japanese homes are built to strict rules so they can stand up to earthquakes.
japanese-home:9.about:
Japan has lots of earthquakes, so there are strict rules about how strong buildings must be (earthquake-resistance standards). The rules were made stronger in 1981 and have been updated since.
Tall buildings also use systems that absorb or reduce shaking, called "seismic isolation" and "seismic damping."

#rooms-world: Kitchens, bathrooms, bedrooms… The same rooms can look and work completely differently in another country!

rooms-world:0.fact: Many homes in South Korea have a fridge just for kimchi.
rooms-world:0.about:
In South Korea, people make lots of kimchi and keep it for a long time, so many homes have a fridge just for kimchi. It copies the temperature of the old way of storing it in jars buried in the ground.
"Kimjang," when families and neighbours make huge amounts of kimchi at the start of winter, is on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

rooms-world:1.fact: A classic in Italian kitchens: a pot that makes coffee on the stove.
rooms-world:1.about:
The moka pot was born in Italy in 1933. When the water at the bottom boils, steam pushes the hot water up and coffee is made.
It's a classic tool found in almost every Italian kitchen.

rooms-world:2.fact: About 3 million saunas in a country of about 5.5 million people!
rooms-world:2.about:
Finland is said to have about 3 million saunas for its population of about 5.5 million. Even flats have saunas.
After warming up in the sauna, some people jump into a lake or the snow. Finnish sauna culture is on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

rooms-world:3.fact: A steam bath where you warm your body on a warm stone.
rooms-world:3.about:
A Turkish hammam is a bath where you lie on warm marble under a domed ceiling and warm your body in the steam.
It carries on the tradition of ancient Roman baths, and it was also a place where townspeople met and chatted. Scrubbing and bubble massages are famous too.

rooms-world:4.fact: In Brazil and Mexico, some people sleep in hammocks instead of beds.
rooms-world:4.about:
In northern Brazil and on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, some people still sleep in hammocks instead of beds. In hot places, the breeze keeps you cool, and you're off the ground, away from insects and animals.
Hammocks were invented by the Indigenous peoples of the Americas, and European sailors used them on ships too.

rooms-world:5.fact: Korean underfloor heating. People live sitting on the floor.
rooms-world:5.about:
Ondol is Korea's traditional underfloor heating. Long ago, hot smoke from the kitchen stove was sent under the floor to warm the rooms.
That's why sitting and sleeping on the floor has been a part of Korean life. Today, most homes heat the floor with hot water pipes.

rooms-world:6.fact: The door of a Mongolian ger always faces south.
rooms-world:6.about:
A Mongolian ger is a round home, and the door is always built facing south. That's to avoid the cold north wind and let sunlight in.
There's a stove in the middle, and its chimney goes out through the skylight. Everyone in the family has their own place to sit, and the north side at the back is the most important seat.

rooms-world:7.fact: A Middle Eastern guest room. Guests sit on floor cushions and are made welcome.
rooms-world:7.about:
Homes in Arab countries in the Middle East have a room for guests called a "majlis." Cushions are laid out on the floor and along the walls, and people sit and talk.
Guests are first offered coffee and dates (the fruit of the date palm). It's a culture that treasures welcoming guests.

rooms-world:8.fact: Homes in America and Canada often have basements.
rooms-world:8.about:
Homes in America and Canada often have basements. In cold areas, foundations are dug deep enough not to freeze, so people began using that space as a room.
Basements are used as playrooms, storerooms and laundry rooms. In areas with lots of tornadoes, they're also a safe place to shelter.

#how-home-works: Turn the tap and water comes out; press a switch and the lights come on. Behind it all is lots of science and work.

how-home-works:0.fact: Dam → water treatment plant → water pipes. Japan is one of the few countries where you can drink tap water.
how-home-works:0.about:
Tap water is taken from dams and rivers, cleaned with sand and chemicals at a water treatment plant, and sent to homes through water pipes. Nagasaki City's water is also water stored in dams and then cleaned.
In Japan, you can drink tap water straight from the tap. Not many countries in the world can do this.

how-home-works:1.fact: At sewage plants, tiny living things clean the water.
how-home-works:1.about:
Water from toilets and baths goes through sewer pipes to a sewage treatment plant. There, tiny living things you can't see (microbes) eat the dirt and clean the water.
The cleaned water goes back into rivers and the sea. Not pouring oil down the drain is an important way to help protect water.

how-home-works:2.fact: It uses the way a liquid takes in heat when it turns into a gas.
how-home-works:2.about:
When sweat dries, your body feels cool, doesn't it? When a liquid turns into a gas, it takes heat from its surroundings. Fridges use this.
In pipes inside the fridge, a coolant turns into a gas and takes in heat, and outside it turns back into a liquid and gives the heat away. That's why the back of a fridge is warm.

how-home-works:3.fact: Eastern Japan is 50 hertz and western Japan is 60 hertz. Japan has two kinds of electricity!
how-home-works:3.about:
Electricity is made at power stations, sent along power lines at very high voltage, and stepped down little by little at substations before it reaches homes.
In the Meiji period, eastern Japan bought generators from Germany and western Japan bought them from America. That's why the east still uses 50 hertz and the west uses 60 hertz.

how-home-works:4.fact: Gas has no smell of its own. A smell is added on purpose for safety.
how-home-works:4.about:
The gas we use at home has almost no smell to begin with. A bad smell is added on purpose so that people notice straight away if it leaks.
If you smell gas, don't light a flame or touch light switches. Open the windows and tell a grown-up.

how-home-works:5.fact: The air between the panes of glass stops heat getting through.
how-home-works:5.about:
Double-glazed windows have a layer of air between two panes of glass. Air doesn't let heat through easily, so in winter the room stays warm, and in summer the heat outside is kept out.
Almost all homes in Hokkaido have double- or triple-glazed windows. They also get less condensation.

how-home-works:6.fact: The bumps on a key line up the pins inside at exactly the right height.
how-home-works:6.about:
Inside many locks are rows of small pins of different lengths. When you put in the right key, its bumps push the pins to exactly the right height, and the lock can turn.
This idea is said to go back to wooden locks in ancient Egypt, about 4,000 years ago.

how-home-works:7.fact: A "siphon" makes the water rush away all at once.
how-home-works:7.about:
In a flush toilet, water from the tank rushes in all at once, and the water in the curved pipe gets pulled along by a "siphon," so everything flushes away.
Japanese toilets are designed to flush with little water, and some use less than half the water of older toilets.

how-home-works:8.fact: A vacuum wall stops heat getting through, so hot things stay hot.
how-home-works:8.about:
A vacuum flask has a double wall, and the space in between has no air: it's a "vacuum." Heat hardly travels through a vacuum, so hot things stay hot and cold things stay cold.
It was invented in 1892 by Dewar in the UK for experiments. Japanese companies also spread light, tough water bottles around the world.

#chores-world: "I wash the dishes. I can cook curry." Every country has its own ways of doing jobs at home and at school.

chores-world:0.fact: In Japan, children clean their own classrooms.
chores-world:0.about:
In Japanese schools, children clean their classrooms, hallways and toilets themselves every day. It helps them learn to take care of the places they use.
In many countries, cleaning staff do the cleaning, so Japan's "cleaning time" is praised and copied abroad.

chores-world:1.fact: At the football World Cup, Japanese fans picking up rubbish made the news.
chores-world:1.about:
At the football World Cup, Japanese supporters picking up rubbish in the stands with blue rubbish bags after matches got attention around the world. The players also leave their changing room clean and tidy.
The spirit of "leave it more beautiful than when you came" is spreading a good image of Japan around the world.

chores-world:2.fact: In Japan many homes hang washing outside, but in America dryers are normal.
chores-world:2.about:
In Japan, many homes hang their washing on balconies or in the garden. In America, clothes dryers are normal, and some towns even ban hanging washing outside.
In Europe, many homes dry washing indoors. Drying with the sun and wind is an eco-friendly way that uses no electricity.

chores-world:3.fact: Wrap, carry and store things with one cloth. You can use it again and again.
chores-world:3.about:
A furoshiki is one square cloth that can wrap boxes, bottles and even watermelons. It's said to get its name from the Edo period, when people wrapped their clothes in it to take to the public bath ("furo").
You can use it again and again, so it's getting attention around the world as an eco-friendly way to use fewer plastic bags.

chores-world:4.fact: In Kamikatsu, Tokushima, rubbish is sorted into 45 kinds.
chores-world:4.about:
Kamikatsu in Tokushima declared itself "zero waste" in 2003. The townspeople sort their rubbish into 45 kinds and take it to the rubbish station.
It recycles more than 80% of its rubbish, and visitors come from all over the world to see how.

chores-world:5.fact: In Japan, each kind of rubbish has its own collection day.
chores-world:5.about:
In Japan, each kind of rubbish has its own collection day, like "burnable rubbish on Mondays and Thursdays." Cans, bottles and plastic bottles are put out separately too.
The rules are different in each town, so people who move first check the rubbish calendar.

chores-world:6.fact: From 5th grade, children learn cooking and sewing.
chores-world:6.about:
In Japanese elementary schools, "home economics" starts in 5th grade. Children cook rice and miso soup, sew on buttons and make aprons.
It's a subject where you learn how to look after your own life. If you try what you've learned at home, your family will be happy too.

chores-world:7.fact: An American woman invented a machine that washes plates without breaking them.
chores-world:7.about:
In 1886, Josephine Cochrane in America was fed up with her servants breaking her precious plates, so she invented a dishwasher herself.
The idea of standing plates in a rack and spraying them with water is still the same today. Almost every home in Europe and America has one.

chores-world:8.fact: Some families give pocket money for helping out, and some don't.
chores-world:8.about:
In some families, you get pocket money for helping out, and in others, "we're a family, so of course we help." Both ideas are found all over the world.
Thinking about how to use your pocket money is the first step in learning about money.

#inside-japanese-school: "Where is the music room? — It's on the second floor." Even the school you go to every day is full of things the world finds unusual!

inside-japanese-school:0.fact: Few countries in the world change shoes inside school.
inside-japanese-school:0.about:
In Japanese schools, you change from outdoor shoes into indoor shoes at the shoe lockers. It's the same idea as taking off your shoes when you go into a house.
In many countries, people wear their shoes into the classroom. Indoor shoes keep the school building clean and make cleaning easier.

inside-japanese-school:1.fact: A room where you can get help with injuries or feeling unwell. A special teacher works there.
inside-japanese-school:1.about:
The nurse's office has a special teacher called a "yōgo kyōyu" (school nurse teacher) who treats injuries and helps when you feel unwell. Health check-ups are done here too.
Having this kind of teacher at every school is a big feature of Japanese schools.

inside-japanese-school:2.fact: Big desks, taps and gas burners. A room for experiments.
inside-japanese-school:2.about:
The science room has big lab benches, taps, gas burners, microscopes and models of the human body. For safety, you stand up when you do experiments.
Practising how to use alcohol lamps and test tubes properly is an important part of learning in the science room.

inside-japanese-school:3.fact: Portraits of composers on the wall. Why are they there?
inside-japanese-school:3.about:
Many music rooms have portraits of composers like Bach, Mozart and Beethoven on the walls. It's an old custom to help children feel closer to the musicians they meet in their textbooks and lessons.
There are lots of instruments too, like a piano, xylophones and percussion.

inside-japanese-school:4.about:
Books in Japanese school libraries have numbers from 0 to 9 from the "Nippon Decimal Classification (NDC)." For example, 4 is natural science, 7 is the arts and 9 is literature.
Once you know the numbers, it's easier to find books in any library. In Japan, the law says every elementary and junior high school must have a library.

inside-japanese-school:5.fact: In a disaster, it becomes a shelter for people in the area.
inside-japanese-school:5.about:
The gym isn't only for PE lessons and assemblies. In earthquakes and heavy rain, it becomes a shelter where people from the area gather.
That's why some gyms keep emergency supplies like water and blankets.

inside-japanese-school:6.fact: Many Japanese elementary schools have a pool. That's rare in the world!
inside-japanese-school:6.about:
Many elementary schools in Japan have an outdoor pool, with swimming lessons in summer. They spread in this country surrounded by sea to help prevent water accidents.
Not many countries in the world have pools at schools, and people from abroad are sometimes surprised.

inside-japanese-school:7.fact: Children raise rabbits and chickens and grow vegetables.
inside-japanese-school:7.about:
At Japanese elementary schools, children raise rabbits and chickens and grow morning glories and cherry tomatoes in the school garden.
By taking turns caring for living things, they learn about the value of life and about responsibility.

inside-japanese-school:8.fact: The school chime and lunchtime broadcasts come from here.
inside-japanese-school:8.about:
The broadcasting room has microphones and equipment, and the school chime, lunchtime broadcasts and event announcements come from here.
The Japanese school chime, "kin-kon-kan-kon," is based on the melody of the bells of Big Ben in London.

inside-japanese-school:9.fact: All the teachers' desks are together in one room.
inside-japanese-school:9.about:
In Japanese schools, all the teachers' desks are together in one room called the "shokuin-shitsu" (staff room). That way, teachers can talk things over quickly.
In countries like America, each teacher often has their own classroom and works there.

inside-japanese-school:10.fact: The word comes from the Dutch "ransel" (backpack).
inside-japanese-school:10.about:
The name "randoseru" is said to come from the Dutch word "ransel," meaning backpack. It's a word that came from the Netherlands in the Edo period.
School randoseru are said to have started around 1885, in the Meiji period, at Gakushūin in Tokyo. Now people from abroad love them too, calling them "kawaii."

#libraries-world: Libraries are treasure chests of the world's knowledge. Some even deliver books by camel or boat!

libraries-world:0.fact: A library in ancient Egypt that tried to collect all the books in the world.
libraries-world:0.about:
Around 300 BC, a library was built in Alexandria, Egypt, that tried to collect books from all over the world. It's even said that books on ships arriving at the port were copied.
It was later lost, but in 2002 a new "Library of Alexandria" opened in the same city.

libraries-world:1.fact: The "Long Room" in Ireland is lined with about 200,000 old books.
libraries-world:1.about:
The "Long Room" of Trinity College Library in Dublin, Ireland, has about 200,000 old books on wooden shelves about 65 m long.
The "Book of Kells," a beautiful handwritten book from about 1,200 years ago, is kept here too.

libraries-world:2.fact: The biggest library in the world, with more than 170 million items.
libraries-world:2.about:
The Library of Congress in Washington, USA, is the biggest library in the world, with more than 170 million items, including books, maps, photos and recordings.
It's said that if you put all its shelves in a line, they would stretch more than 1,000 km. It has books in more than 450 languages.

libraries-world:3.fact: A copy of every book published in Japan is sent here.
libraries-world:3.about:
The National Diet Library is the biggest library in Japan. By law, books and magazines published in Japan are sent here and kept forever.
It has a main library in Tokyo, the Kansai-kan in Kyoto, and the International Library of Children's Literature in Ueno, Tokyo.

libraries-world:4.fact: About 6,000 round windows in its walls. It's called "the cake box."
libraries-world:4.about:
Kanazawa Umimirai Library in Ishikawa has about 6,000 small round windows in its white walls, and it's called "the cake box."
Soft light comes in through the windows, so it feels like reading in a bright forest. It's been featured as one of the world's beautiful libraries.

libraries-world:5.fact: Inside a pure white cube, floors of books are stacked up.
libraries-world:5.about:
From outside, Stuttgart City Library in Germany is a pure white box. Inside is an amazing space with white stairs and bookshelves stacked floor upon floor.
It opened in 2011, and people come from all over the world to see the building.

libraries-world:6.fact: In Kenya, camels carry books to faraway villages.
libraries-world:6.about:
In northeastern Kenya, a mobile library where camels carry books began in 1996. Camels can take books to desert villages where there are no roads.
Children in the villages look forward to the day the camels come.

libraries-world:7.fact: A Colombian teacher went around villages with books on donkeys.
libraries-world:7.about:
Luis Soriano, an elementary school teacher in Colombia, started the "Biblioburro," going around mountain villages with books loaded on two donkeys.
He keeps bringing stories to children who have no other chance to read books.

libraries-world:8.fact: In Norway, a boat full of books visits villages in the fjords.
libraries-world:8.about:
In western Norway, since 1959, a book boat called "Epos" has visited small villages in the fjords.
When the boat arrives at the harbour, children choose books and enjoy storytelling and puppet shows.

libraries-world:9.fact: In Japan too, vans full of books come to parks and schools.
libraries-world:9.about:
In Japan too, "mobile libraries," vans with bookshelves, visit parks, schools and community halls in areas far from a library.
In places with lots of islands and mountains, like Nagasaki, mobile libraries do an important job.

libraries-world:10.fact: People put books in a little box in front of their house and swap them freely.
libraries-world:10.about:
It started in America in 2009, when someone put a small wooden box in front of their house with a sign saying "Take a book, leave a book."
Now there are tens of thousands of "Little Free Libraries" in more than 100 countries.

#school-buildings-world: On boats, in forests, and even in space! Around the world, children learn in all kinds of places.

school-buildings-world:0.fact: In Bangladesh, children can learn on boat schools even when floods cover the roads.
school-buildings-world:0.about:
Bangladesh has lots of rivers, and in the rainy season roads and villages are flooded. So "floating schools," with classrooms inside boats, were created.
The boats go around villages to pick up children, and solar panels give them electricity. They started around 2002.

school-buildings-world:1.fact: In the mountains of Nepal, some children walk for hours to get to school.
school-buildings-world:1.about:
In mountain villages in Nepal's Himalayas, some children walk for hours along mountain paths to get to school.
Around the world, some children cross rivers or walk over rope bridges to get to school. It makes us think about how important it is to be able to go to school.

school-buildings-world:2.fact: Denmark and Germany have kindergartens where children spend all day in the forest.
school-buildings-world:2.about:
Denmark and Germany have "forest kindergartens," where children spend the whole day in the forest, even on rainy and snowy days.
Climbing trees, looking for bugs and making campfires help them build thinking skills and strong bodies in nature. They've spread to Japan too.

school-buildings-world:3.fact: A Western-style school building from the Meiji period. It was the first school building to become a National Treasure.
school-buildings-world:3.about:
The old Kaichi School in Matsumoto, Nagano, is a Western-style school building built in 1876. Local carpenters copied Western buildings and added their own ideas.
In 2019, it became the first school building to be made a National Treasure. Now it's a museum about the history of education.

school-buildings-world:4.fact: A place of learning said to be "the oldest school in Japan."
school-buildings-world:4.about:
Ashikaga Gakkō in Ashikaga, Tochigi is said to be "the oldest school in Japan." From the Muromachi period to the Sengoku period, people from all over Japan came to study there.
It's said that the missionary Francis Xavier described it to Europe as "the biggest school in Japan."

school-buildings-world:5.fact: In places with lots of islands, like Nagasaki, some schools have only a few students.
school-buildings-world:5.about:
Nagasaki has more islands than any other prefecture in Japan. Some small island schools have only a few students in the whole school.
Teachers and children are close, and there are lessons about the island's nature and fishing. Some children from cities even move to island schools for "island study."

school-buildings-world:6.fact: Denmark has a school with almost no classroom walls.
school-buildings-world:6.about:
Near Copenhagen in Denmark, there's a school with almost no classroom walls. Children study sitting on big staircases, or learn in groups wherever they like.
Around the world, the idea of "designing school buildings to fit how children learn" is spreading.

school-buildings-world:7.fact: In crowded cities, some schools have playgrounds and pools on the roof.
school-buildings-world:7.about:
In big cities with little space, like Tokyo and Hong Kong, some schools have playgrounds and pools on their roofs.
High fences keep everyone safe while they exercise close to the sky.

school-buildings-world:8.fact: A lesson came from the space station to children in Japan.
school-buildings-world:8.about:
Japanese astronauts have taught lessons from the International Space Station (ISS) to children on the ground. They showed experiments like balls of water floating in the air.
The space station is about 400 km above the Earth. A "classroom in space" is the highest classroom in the world.

#big-small-animals: "big / bigger / the biggest" Let's compare the biggest and smallest living things on Earth!

big-small-animals:0.fact: About 30 m long. The biggest animal in the history of the Earth.
big-small-animals:0.about:
The blue whale grows to about 30 m long and more than 100 tonnes. It's the biggest animal in the history of the Earth, even including dinosaurs. Its heart is about the size of a small car.
But its food is tiny krill. It eats several tonnes a day.

big-small-animals:1.fact: About 2 g. One of the smallest mammals.
big-small-animals:1.about:
Kitti's hog-nosed bat lives in caves in Thailand and Myanmar. It weighs about 2 g and is about 3 cm long, the weight of two 1-yen coins.
It's about the size of a bumblebee, so in English it's called the "bumblebee bat."

big-small-animals:2.fact: About 1.5 kg. The biggest bird's egg.
big-small-animals:2.about:
An ostrich egg is about 15 cm long and weighs about 1.5 kg, the same as about 25 chicken eggs. The shell is so hard that sometimes it won't break even if a person stands on it.
But compared with the size of the bird, an ostrich egg is actually on the small side.

big-small-animals:3.fact: About the size of a pea. The smallest bird's egg.
big-small-animals:3.about:
The bee hummingbird of Cuba is the smallest bird in the world, and its egg is about 6 mm long, about the size of a pea.
Its nest is much smaller than a coffee cup and is made with spider silk.

big-small-animals:4.fact: A huge deep-sea squid more than 10 m long.
big-small-animals:4.about:
The giant squid is a deep-sea squid that can be more than 10 m long, including its long arms. Its eyes are about 25 cm across, among the biggest of any animal.
In 2004, Japanese researchers took the world's first photos of a live giant squid in the deep sea.

big-small-animals:5.fact: About 8 mm even as an adult. One of the smallest fish in the world.
big-small-animals:5.about:
Paedocypris is a fish that lives in swamps on islands like Sumatra in Indonesia. Even adults are only about 8 mm long, so it's one of the smallest fish in the world.
It lives in swamps of brown, acidic water, and when the water nearly dries up, it's thought to survive in the mud.

big-small-animals:6.fact: About 30 cm long and 3 kg. The biggest frog.
big-small-animals:6.about:
The Goliath frog lives in countries like Cameroon in Africa. It's about 30 cm long and can weigh more than 3 kg, making it the biggest frog in the world.
Males have been found to move stones in rivers to make ponds for laying eggs.

big-small-animals:7.fact: About 7 mm long. A frog that fits on a 1-yen coin!
big-small-animals:7.about:
This frog, found in Papua New Guinea in 2009, is about 7.7 mm long. It's one of the smallest vertebrates (animals with a backbone) in the world.
It lives among fallen leaves in the forest and calls with a high voice like an insect.

big-small-animals:8.fact: The biggest animal on land. It weighs more than 6 tonnes.
big-small-animals:8.about:
The African elephant is the biggest animal on land. Males weigh more than 6 tonnes and are more than 3 m tall at the shoulder.
Its trunk has tens of thousands of muscles, so it can suck up water, grab things and smell.

big-small-animals:9.fact: About 2 g. One of the lightest mammals on land.
big-small-animals:9.about:
The Etruscan shrew is a tiny mammal that lives in Europe and Asia and weighs about 2 g.
Its heart beats more than 1,000 times a minute, and it can't survive unless it keeps eating. It eats almost twice its body weight every day.

#fast-slow: "fast / slow, faster / the fastest" The fastest and the slowest things on Earth.

fast-slow:0.fact: About 390 km per hour in a dive. The fastest animal.
fast-slow:0.about:
A peregrine falcon diving at its prey has been recorded at about 390 km per hour. It's much faster than the Shinkansen, the fastest animal on Earth.
In Japan, you can see them on seaside cliffs and city buildings too.

fast-slow:1.fact: It moves only a few metres a minute, the slowest mammal.
fast-slow:1.about:
The three-toed sloth is a very slow animal that sometimes moves only a few dozen metres in a day. Leaves have few nutrients, so it lives in a way that uses little energy.
Algae grow in its fur and turn it green, which helps it hide in the forest. But it's surprisingly good at swimming.

fast-slow:2.fact: Said to be the fastest fish in the sea.
fast-slow:2.about:
The sailfish is a fish with a big back fin, and it's said to be one of the fastest fish in the sea. It chases schools of sardines with its pointed bill.
When it swims fast, it folds its back fin down, and when it's herding prey, it spreads it like a sail.

fast-slow:3.fact: About 1.5 m an hour. The slowest-swimming fish.
fast-slow:3.about:
The dwarf seahorse, a small kind of seahorse, moves only about 1.5 m in an hour, so it's thought to be the slowest-swimming fish in the world.
It swims by fluttering its back fin 30 to 70 times a second, but its body shape just isn't made for swimming. It rests by holding on to seagrass with its tail.

fast-slow:4.fact: A few dozen metres an hour. It moves along on a slimy path it makes.
fast-slow:4.about:
A snail makes slime from its foot and glides along on top of it. Its speed is a few dozen metres an hour.
It's said that thanks to this slime, it can even crawl along a knife blade without getting hurt.

fast-slow:5.fact: The Tōhoku Shinkansen runs at 320 km per hour.
fast-slow:5.about:
When the Tōkaidō Shinkansen started running in 1964, its top speed was 210 km per hour. Now the Hayabusa on the Tōhoku Shinkansen runs at 320 km per hour.
Trains on the ground that are this fast and always on time are rare in the world.

fast-slow:6.fact: A river of ice. It moves only a few centimetres to a few metres a day.
fast-slow:6.about:
A glacier is a "river of ice": snow piled up in the mountains turns to ice over hundreds of years and slowly flows under its own weight. It usually moves only a few centimetres to a few metres a day.
In 2012, it was confirmed that Japan also has small glaciers, in places like Tateyama in the Northern Alps.

fast-slow:7.fact: Light goes around the Earth 7 and a half times in 1 second. Sound travels about 340 m.
fast-slow:7.about:
Light travels about 300,000 km in one second, enough to go around the Earth 7 and a half times. Sound travels about 340 m through the air in one second.
If you count the seconds between a flash of lightning and the rumble of thunder and multiply by 340, you get how far away the lightning is in metres. 3 seconds means about 1 km.

#hot-cold: "hot / cold, hotter / the hottest" The hottest and coldest places, from space to Japan.

hot-cold:0.about:
The surface of the Sun is about 6,000°C, but its centre reaches about 15 million °C. There, hydrogen turns into helium in "nuclear fusion," making huge amounts of energy.
Its light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach the Earth.

hot-cold:1.fact: Minus 273.15°C. Nothing can be colder than this.
hot-cold:1.about:
When things get colder, the tiny particles they're made of (atoms) move more slowly. The temperature where that movement is the smallest it can be, minus 273.15°C, is called "absolute zero," and nothing can be colder.
In laboratories, scientists do experiments that cool things to very, very close to absolute zero.

hot-cold:2.fact: The highest temperature on Earth, 56.7°C, was recorded here.
hot-cold:2.about:
56.7°C, recorded in Death Valley in the USA in 1913, is the official record for the highest temperature on Earth. In summer, the ground can get hotter than 90°C.
Its name sounds scary, but in spring flowers bloom, and it's a national park visited by lots of tourists.

hot-cold:3.fact: Minus 89.2°C. The lowest temperature ever measured on the ground.
hot-cold:3.about:
At Russia's Vostok Station in Antarctica, minus 89.2°C was recorded in 1983. It's the lowest temperature ever measured on the ground.
It's said that in cold like this, your breath freezes straight away and makes a sound.

hot-cold:4.about:
In August 2025, 41.8°C was recorded in Isesaki, Gunma, setting a new record for Japan's highest temperature. Japanese summers are getting hotter every year.
A day above 35°C is called a "mōshobi" (extremely hot day). It's important to drink water, have some salt and rest somewhere cool.

hot-cold:5.about:
In January 1902, minus 41.0°C was recorded in Asahikawa, Hokkaido. It's still Japan's record for the lowest temperature.
On very cold mornings, you can sometimes see "diamond dust," water in the air that freezes and sparkles.

hot-cold:6.fact: About 460°C. The hottest planet in the solar system.
hot-cold:6.about:
Venus is the second planet from the Sun, but it's hotter than Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun, at about 460°C. That's because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps the heat.
It's an important example when we think about the Earth's "greenhouse effect."

hot-cold:7.fact: Below minus 220°C. The coldest planet in the solar system.
hot-cold:7.about:
The temperature of Uranus's atmosphere goes below minus 220°C, the lowest temperature measured on any planet in the solar system. Why it's colder than Neptune, which is further from the Sun, is still a mystery.
It looks blue-green because of methane in its atmosphere.

hot-cold:8.fact: Minus 79°C. When it melts, it doesn't become liquid; it turns straight into gas.
hot-cold:8.about:
Dry ice is carbon dioxide cooled into a solid, at minus 79°C. When it melts, it doesn't become a liquid but turns straight into a gas, so it's called "dry ice."
If you put it in water, white smoke comes out, but touching it with bare hands can hurt your skin like a burn, so be careful.

hot-cold:9.fact: People are about 36 to 37°C, and birds are about 40 to 42°C.
hot-cold:9.about:
A person's body temperature is about 36 to 37°C, and it hardly changes. On cold days and hot days, your body controls its temperature.
Birds are even warmer, about 40 to 42°C, because they use lots of energy to fly. The body temperature of snakes and lizards changes with the temperature around them.

#heavy-light: "heavy / light" From a 1-yen coin to the Earth, let's compare the mysteries of weight.

heavy-light:0.fact: Exactly 1 g. You can use it to measure weight.
heavy-light:0.about:
A 1-yen coin is made of aluminium. It weighs exactly 1 g and is exactly 2 cm across.
So a 1-yen coin can be used as a "ruler" for weight and length. If you gently place one on water, it can even float thanks to surface tension.

heavy-light:1.fact: More than 99% air. A light solid called "frozen smoke."
heavy-light:1.about:
Aerogel is a solid that is more than 99% air, and it's called "frozen smoke." It's very light, but it hardly lets heat through at all.
NASA used aerogel to make a tool on the "Stardust" space probe for catching dust from a comet.

heavy-light:2.fact: The densest metal. About 3 times heavier than iron of the same size.
heavy-light:2.about:
Osmium is the densest metal. One 1 cm cube weighs about 22.6 g, about 3 times as heavy as iron and about 8 times as heavy as aluminium of the same size.
Long ago, it was used for the tips of fountain pens.

heavy-light:3.fact: One fluffy cloud weighs as much as about 100 elephants!
heavy-light:3.about:
One fluffy cumulus cloud holds lots of tiny drops of water, and it's been calculated that together they can weigh about 500 tonnes. That's about 100 elephants!
It can still float because the drops are so tiny that rising air holds them up.

heavy-light:4.fact: More than 100 tonnes. The heaviest animal.
heavy-light:4.about:
The blue whale weighs more than 100 tonnes, and big ones are said to be over 150 tonnes, making it the heaviest animal on Earth.
It can support such a heavy body because it lives in water. On land, it would be crushed by its own weight.

heavy-light:5.about:
The bee hummingbird of Cuba weighs about 2 g, making it the lightest bird in the world. That's only as heavy as two 1-yen coins.
It flaps its wings about 80 times a second and flies from flower to flower like a bee, drinking nectar.

heavy-light:6.about:
The weight (mass) of the Earth is about 6 × 10²⁴ kg: that's 6 followed by 24 zeros.
Scientists long ago worked out the Earth's weight by measuring the tiny pull between mountains or lead balls.

heavy-light:7.fact: Iron sinks, but big iron ships float.
heavy-light:7.about:
An iron nail sinks in water, but a big iron ship floats. A ship is hollow inside and pushes away lots of water, so it gets that much "floating force" (buoyancy).
This was discovered by Archimedes in ancient Greece. It's said he had the idea in the bath and shouted "Eureka!"

#old-new: "old / new, older / the oldest" From rocks billions of years old to brand-new islands.

old-new:0.fact: Rocks in Canada are about 4 billion years old.
old-new:0.about:
The "Acasta Gneiss" in northern Canada formed about 4 billion years ago, and it's one of the oldest rocks on Earth. The Earth itself is about 4.6 billion years old.
In Australia, tiny mineral grains (zircons) 4.4 billion years old have been found too.

old-new:1.fact: One of the oldest trees in the world, more than 4,800 years old.
old-new:1.about:
Some bristlecone pines, which grow high in the mountains of the USA, are more than 4,800 years old, making them among the oldest trees in the world.
One of them has been alive since the time the pyramids were being built in Egypt. Its location is kept secret to protect it.

old-new:2.fact: A huge cedar on Yakushima. It's said to be thousands of years old.
old-new:2.about:
Yakushima's Jōmon Sugi is a huge cedar whose trunk is about 16 m around. Ideas about its age range from 2,000 to more than 7,000 years.
In 1993, Yakushima became one of Japan's first World Natural Heritage Sites. Walking to the Jōmon Sugi and back takes about 10 hours.

old-new:3.fact: One of the oldest companies in the world, started in 578.
old-new:3.about:
Kongō Gumi in Osaka is one of the oldest companies in the world. It's said to have been started in 578 by a carpenter from Baekje (in today's Korea) who was invited by Prince Shōtoku.
It built Shitennō-ji temple in Osaka and still builds temples and shrines today. Japan has a lot of companies that have lasted more than 100 years.

old-new:4.fact: A temple with the oldest wooden buildings in the world.
old-new:4.about:
Hōryū-ji in Nara has the oldest wooden buildings still standing in the world. They were built more than 1,300 years ago.
In 1993, it became one of Japan's first World Cultural Heritage Sites. Wooden buildings have lasted this long thanks to the great skill of the carpenters.

old-new:5.fact: The oldest history book in Japan.
old-new:5.about:
The "Kojiki," finished in 712, is the oldest history book in Japan that still survives. It contains myths and stories of ancient emperors.
The stories of "The White Hare of Inaba" and "Yamata no Orochi" (the eight-headed serpent) are in the Kojiki too.

old-new:6.fact: A new island that kept growing because of eruptions.
old-new:6.about:
Nishinoshima in the Ogasawara Islands, part of Tokyo, grew bigger and bigger after an eruption in the nearby sea in 2013 made new land that joined the original island.
Researchers are watching to see how plants and birds arrive on the brand-new island.

old-new:7.fact: A new element discovered in Japan. It's number 113.
old-new:7.about:
Nihonium (element 113) is a new element found by a team at RIKEN in Japan, and its name was decided in 2016. It's the first element discovered in Asia.
Its name comes from "Nihon" (Japan). Japan's name is now on the periodic table of elements.

#long-short-tall: "long / short / tall" The longest river, the tallest building, the shortest plane trip!

long-short-tall:0.fact: About 6,650 km long. It's said to be the longest river in the world.
long-short-tall:0.about:
The Nile in Africa is about 6,650 km long and is said to be the longest river in the world (people still argue about whether it or the Amazon in South America is longer).
The people of ancient Egypt grew their crops in the rich soil carried by the river's yearly floods.

long-short-tall:1.fact: 367 km long. The longest river in Japan.
long-short-tall:1.about:
The Shinano River flows from Nagano (old Shinano) to Niigata. At 367 km, it's the longest river in Japan. In Nagano it's called the "Chikuma River."
In Japan, mountains are close to the sea, so Japanese rivers are short and fast-flowing compared with the world's rivers.

long-short-tall:2.fact: About 2 m long. But it has the same number of neck bones as you: 7!
long-short-tall:2.about:
A giraffe's neck is about 2 m long, but it has the same number of neck bones as a person: 7. Each bone is just very long.
Giraffes use their necks to eat leaves high up, and males swing their necks at each other to test their strength.

long-short-tall:3.fact: 828 m tall. The tallest building in the world.
long-short-tall:3.about:
The Burj Khalifa in Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates, is 828 m tall. Finished in 2010, it's the tallest building in the world.
It's about 200 m taller than Tokyo Skytree (634 m), and on a clear day you're said to be able to see about 100 km away.

long-short-tall:4.fact: About 54 km long. It goes under the sea to connect Hokkaido and Honshu.
long-short-tall:4.about:
The Seikan Tunnel is a railway tunnel about 54 km long that opened in 1988. About 23 km of it runs under the seabed of the Tsugaru Strait.
Now the Hokkaido Shinkansen runs through it, linking Honshu and Hokkaido by train.

long-short-tall:5.fact: From island to island in Scotland, in about a minute and a half!
long-short-tall:5.about:
The plane between Westray and Papa Westray in Scotland's Orkney Islands flies about 2.7 km. With a good wind, it gets there in about a minute and a half.
The record is just 53 seconds! It's the shortest scheduled flight in the world.

long-short-tall:6.fact: The name of a hill in New Zealand has 85 letters!
long-short-tall:6.about:
The Māori name of a hill in New Zealand has 85 letters in the English alphabet, and it's known as the longest place name in the world.
It means something like "The summit of the hill where Tamatea, the traveller, played his flute for his brother…" and goes on like a story.

long-short-tall:7.fact: The Norwegian village "Å" has a one-letter name!
long-short-tall:7.about:
Norway has a village with a one-letter name: "Å." In Norwegian it means "small river."
Sweden and Denmark have places called "Å" too. The shortest place name in Japan is "Tsu" (津) in Mie.

#loud-quiet: "loud / quiet" The loudest animal on Earth and the quietest room in the world.

loud-quiet:0.fact: The unit for loudness. A whisper is about 30 decibels and shouting is about 80.
loud-quiet:0.about:
Loudness is measured in "decibels (dB)." Rustling leaves are about 20, normal talking is about 60, and under a railway bridge is about 100 decibels.
When it goes up by 10 decibels, it sounds about twice as loud to us. Listening to very loud sounds for a long time can damage your ears.

loud-quiet:1.fact: A very low, loud call that reaches hundreds of kilometres away.
loud-quiet:1.about:
The blue whale calls in a voice so low that people can hardly hear it, but it's louder than 180 decibels and is said to reach other whales hundreds of kilometres away.
In water, sound travels about 4 times faster than in air, and it carries a long way.

loud-quiet:2.fact: When it snaps its claw shut, it makes a shock wave of light and sound.
loud-quiet:2.about:
The pistol shrimp snaps its bigger claw shut incredibly fast, making a bubble in the water. When the bubble collapses, it makes a loud bang and a flash of light that can knock out small fish.
In seas with lots of pistol shrimp, the noise can even get in the way of submarines' sonar.

loud-quiet:3.fact: One of the loudest animals on land.
loud-quiet:3.about:
Howler monkeys have a special bone in their throats that makes their voices boom, and their howls reach several kilometres away. They're one of the loudest land animals.
Because they loudly announce "this is our forest," they don't need to fight.

loud-quiet:4.fact: Their calls are very loud, but too high for people to hear.
loud-quiet:4.about:
Some bats make very loud calls (ultrasound), but they're too high for human ears to hear.
They need loud calls because they find insects by the echoes. If we could hear them, we might not be able to sleep at night!

loud-quiet:5.fact: So quiet you can hear your own heartbeat.
loud-quiet:5.about:
An "anechoic chamber," covered with walls that soak up sound and keep outside noise out, is said to be the quietest room in the world. One measured minus 20 decibels, quieter than human ears can hear.
People say that inside, you can start to hear your own heartbeat and the sound of your blood flowing.

loud-quiet:6.fact: Copying owl feathers made the Shinkansen quieter.
loud-quiet:6.about:
The "pantograph," which takes electricity from the overhead wires, used to make a loud whooshing noise as the Shinkansen sped along. Engineer Nakatsu Eiji got an idea from the jagged edges of owl feathers, which let owls fly silently, and made it quieter.
The nose of the 500 Series Shinkansen copies a kingfisher's beak. It's technology that learns from nature.

loud-quiet:7.about:
When snow piles up, the town really does feel hushed. That's because the gaps between the fluffy snowflakes soak up sound like a sponge.
When the snow freezes hard, it's the opposite: sound bounces off it more easily.

#southeast-asia: Just a few hours from Japan by plane, these warm countries have rice, spices and lots of islands.

southeast-asia:0.fact: Angkor Wat is shown on its flag.
southeast-asia:0.about:
Angkor Wat in Cambodia, built about 900 years ago, is one of the biggest stone temples in the world. People come from all over the world to see it at sunrise.
It's very unusual for a country to have a building on its flag. "Amok" is a dish of fish steamed in coconut milk.

southeast-asia:1.fact: A country with no coast. The Mekong River flows through it.
southeast-asia:1.about:
Laos is the only country in Southeast Asia with no coastline. Long ago, it was called "the land of a million elephants."
Every morning, monks in orange robes walk through town collecting food offerings, which is famous. People eat sticky rice by rolling it into balls with their hands.

southeast-asia:2.fact: In Bagan, more than 2,000 old pagodas stand on the plain.
southeast-asia:2.about:
In Bagan in Myanmar, more than 2,000 pagodas and temples built hundreds of years ago stand across the plain, and it's a World Heritage Site.
People put a paste made from wood called "thanaka" on their cheeks as sunscreen. A classic breakfast is a fish noodle soup called "mohinga."

southeast-asia:3.fact: The twin "Petronas Towers" are 452 m tall.
southeast-asia:3.about:
Malaysia is a country where Malay, Chinese and Indian people live together, so you can enjoy all kinds of food and festivals.
The Petronas Twin Towers in the capital are 452 m tall. On the island of Borneo, there are rainforests where orangutans live.

southeast-asia:4.fact: A small country about the size of Tokyo's 23 wards. It has 4 official languages.
southeast-asia:4.about:
Singapore is a small city-state only a little bigger than Tokyo's 23 wards. It has 4 official languages: English, Malay, Chinese and Tamil.
Its symbol is the "Merlion," a lion on top and a fish below. The city is famous for being very clean and green.

southeast-asia:5.fact: It has a "water village" of houses standing on a river.
southeast-asia:5.about:
Brunei is a small country on the island of Borneo. Its capital has "Kampong Ayer," a water village where wooden houses stand above the river and thousands of people live.
There are even schools and shops on the water, and people get around by boat.

southeast-asia:6.fact: A new Asian country, founded in 2002.
southeast-asia:6.about:
Timor-Leste became independent in 2002, making it one of Asia's newest countries. Portuguese is one of its official languages, and it has ties with Japan too.
Its coffee, grown in the mountains, is famous and is sold in Japan too. It also has beautiful coral seas.

#south-asia: From the highest mountains in the world to coral islands in the Indian Ocean, South Asia is rich in people and nature.

south-asia:0.fact: It has Everest, the highest mountain in the world.
south-asia:0.about:
Nepal has 8 mountains over 8,000 m, including Everest (8,849 m). The Sherpa people, famous as Himalayan guides, live here too.
Its flag is the only national flag in the world that isn't a rectangle. "Momo," dumplings like Japanese gyōza, are popular.

south-asia:1.fact: Famous as a country that values its people's "happiness."
south-asia:1.about:
Bhutan is a small country in the Himalayas, known for valuing its people's "happiness" more than how rich they are.
Its name for itself means "land of the thunder dragon." "Ema datshi" is a very spicy dish of chillies cooked with cheese.

south-asia:2.fact: A tea country, famous for "Ceylon tea."
south-asia:2.about:
Sri Lanka is an island country in the Indian Ocean that used to be called "Ceylon." "Ceylon tea" is still drunk all over the world.
On top of a huge rock called Sigiriya are the ruins of an ancient king's palace.

south-asia:3.fact: Tigers live in the biggest mangrove forest in the world.
south-asia:3.about:
Bangladesh is a country rich in water, where big rivers like the Ganges meet. Lots of colourfully decorated bicycle taxis called "rickshaws" fill the streets.
The Sundarbans, on the border with India, is the biggest mangrove forest in the world, and Bengal tigers live there.

south-asia:4.fact: A very low country with more than 1,000 coral islands.
south-asia:4.about:
The Maldives is a country made of more than 1,000 coral islands, and on average it's only about 1.5 m above sea level.
People travel between islands by boat or seaplane. "Mas huni" is a breakfast of tuna mixed with coconut.

south-asia:5.fact: It has K2, the second-highest mountain in the world.
south-asia:5.about:
Pakistan has towering mountains, including K2 (8,611 m), the second-highest in the world.
Cricket is a hugely popular sport. "Biryani," rice cooked with spices and meat, is a feast for celebrations.

#west-asia: Deserts, oases and the Silk Road. Roads linking East and West have passed through this region since ancient times.

west-asia:0.fact: In Cappadocia, lots of hot-air balloons float in the sky in the morning.
west-asia:0.about:
Türkiye is a country that spreads across both Asia and Europe. In Cappadocia, more than 100 hot-air balloons floating over the strangely shaped rocks in the morning is a famous sight.
Türkiye and Japan have long been friends. In the Meiji period, people in Wakayama rescued the crew of the Turkish ship "Ertuğrul," and the story is still told.

west-asia:1.fact: Dubai has the tallest building in the world.
west-asia:1.about:
The United Arab Emirates is a country made of 7 emirates. Dubai has the tallest building in the world, the "Burj Khalifa" (828 m), and artificial islands shaped like palm trees.
Long ago, it was a small port town of pearl divers and fishing.

west-asia:2.fact: A big desert country with no rivers that flow all year.
west-asia:2.about:
Most of Saudi Arabia is desert, and it has no rivers that flow all year round. Water comes from underground and from plants that turn sea water into fresh water.
Camels have always been important animals, and there are camel races and even camel beauty contests.

west-asia:3.fact: A country where frankincense trees, with their sweet smell, grow.
west-asia:3.about:
Oman is in the southeast of the Arabian Peninsula, and it has long been known for "frankincense," a sweet-smelling tree sap.
Guests are welcomed with coffee in small cups and dates (the fruit of the date palm). Near the sea there are beaches where sea turtles lay their eggs.

west-asia:4.fact: It has Petra, an ancient city carved out of rock.
west-asia:4.about:
Petra in Jordan is a city carved out of red rock more than 2,000 years ago, and it's a World Heritage Site.
The Dead Sea is so salty that you float easily; you can even float while reading a book.

west-asia:5.fact: The country that hosted the 2022 football World Cup.
west-asia:5.about:
Qatar is a small country on a peninsula sticking out from the Arabian Peninsula. In 2022, it hosted the first football World Cup in the Middle East.
Along the seafront in the capital, Doha, there are a museum shaped like an old pearl-diving boat and other beautiful buildings.

west-asia:6.fact: Samarkand, a Silk Road city, is called "the blue city."
west-asia:6.about:
Uzbekistan is in Central Asia, where Silk Road oasis cities flourished. Samarkand's buildings are decorated with blue tiles, so it's called "the blue city."
"Plov," meat, vegetables and rice cooked in a huge pot, is a feast for celebrations.

west-asia:7.fact: The biggest country in the world with no coast.
west-asia:7.about:
Kazakhstan is the biggest country in the world with no coastline. It's about 7 times the size of Japan.
The world's first rocket carrying a person was launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome here. It's also said to be one of the places where apples first came from.

#nordic: Auroras, fjords and the midnight sun. The cold northern countries also lead the world in design and inventions.

nordic:0.fact: Famous for "fjords," deep inlets carved by glaciers.
nordic:0.about:
Norway's coast is lined with "fjords," made by glaciers carving through mountains over tens of thousands of years. In the north, you can see the aurora too.
It's said that salmon at Japanese sushi restaurants became popular after Norway started promoting it to Japan in the 1980s.

nordic:1.fact: The Nobel Prize was started by Nobel, from Sweden.
nordic:1.about:
The Nobel Prize began in 1901 because of the will of Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel. Every December, the award ceremony is held in Stockholm.
Sweden has lots of forests and lakes, and there's an idea called "the right of public access," meaning anyone may walk freely in nature.

nordic:2.fact: A country with lots of bikes. It's the home of LEGO bricks.
nordic:2.about:
In Copenhagen, the capital of Denmark, there are said to be more bikes than people, and lots of people cycle to work.
LEGO bricks were born in Denmark. "LEGO" comes from the Danish for "play well." It's also the home of Andersen's fairy tales.

nordic:3.fact: "Geysir" is where the English word "geyser" comes from.
nordic:3.about:
Iceland is an island of volcanoes and glaciers, and it uses heat from the ground for electricity and heating. "Geysir," where hot water shoots out of the ground, gave English the word "geyser."
About 400,000 people live there. "Skyr," like a thick yoghurt, is a traditional food.

nordic:4.fact: A country where almost all government services can be done online.
nordic:4.about:
Estonia is an "e-country," where almost all government services, like voting and taxes, can be done on the internet. The internet phone service Skype was also made by Estonian engineers.
The old town of Tallinn, the capital, still has its medieval streets and is a World Heritage Site.

nordic:5.fact: Said to be one of the places where the custom of decorating Christmas trees began.
nordic:5.about:
In Riga, the capital of Latvia, there's a record of a Christmas tree being decorated in 1510, so it's said to be one of "the birthplaces of the Christmas tree."
