Riga's old town is a World Heritage Site. On Midsummer night there's a festival where people sing and dance all night.

nordic:6.fact: The country where Japanese diplomat Sugihara Chiune helped many people.
nordic:6.about:
In 1940, in Kaunas, Lithuania, Japanese diplomat Sugihara Chiune kept writing visas to travel through Japan for many people who had to leave their country. He's said to have saved about 6,000 lives.
They're still remembered as "visas for life," a story that connects Japan and Lithuania.

#western-europe-2: A chocolate country, an Alpine country, a music country. They may be small, but they're full of character.

western-europe-2:0.fact: A country famous around the world for chocolate and waffles.
western-europe-2:0.about:
Belgium is famous for chocolate and waffles, and the Grand-Place, the main square in Brussels, is said to be one of the most beautiful squares in the world.
Dutch is spoken in the north, French in the south and German in part of the east. The headquarters of the EU (European Union) is in Brussels too.

western-europe-2:1.fact: An Alpine country with 4 official languages.
western-europe-2:1.about:
Switzerland is surrounded by the Alps, and it has 4 official languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
The Matterhorn, watchmaking and cheese fondue are famous. There are lots of mountain railways, so you can go up to the mountaintops by train.

western-europe-2:2.fact: A music country, where Mozart was born.
western-europe-2:2.about:
Salzburg in Austria is where Mozart was born, and the capital, Vienna, is called "the city of music," where many composers worked.
The Vienna Boys' Choir has more than 500 years of history. "Wiener Schnitzel," a thin piece of meat fried in breadcrumbs, is a famous dish.

western-europe-2:3.fact: One of the homes of Halloween.
western-europe-2:3.about:
Ireland is so green and beautiful that it's called the "Emerald Isle." Halloween grew from old autumn festivals in places like Ireland. The first jack-o'-lanterns were made from turnips.
On St Patrick's Day, March 17th, whole towns turn green. The country's symbol is the harp.

western-europe-2:4.fact: "Pan" (bread) is Portuguese. Castella came from Portugal to Nagasaki too!
western-europe-2:4.about:
About 480 years ago, Portugal was one of the first European countries to come to Japan. Many Japanese words come from Portuguese, like "pan" (bread), "botan" (button) and "kappa" (raincoat).
Castella, konpeitō sweets and tempura are also said to have come from contact with Portugal. It's a country with very deep ties to Nagasaki.

western-europe-2:5.fact: All the buses and trains in the country are free!
western-europe-2:5.about:
Luxembourg is a small country about the size of Kanagawa. In 2020, it became the first country in the world to make all its buses, trains and trams free.
People switch between three languages: Luxembourgish, French and German.

western-europe-2:6.fact: The second-smallest country in the world.
western-europe-2:6.about:
Monaco is the second-smallest country in the world after Vatican City. It's only about 4 times the size of Tokyo Disneyland.
The "Monaco Grand Prix," a car race on the town's own streets, is famous. On cliffs by the sea stand a palace and an aquarium.

#eastern-europe: Castle towns, hot spring towns, a valley of roses. In the middle of Europe are countries like something out of a fairy tale.

eastern-europe:0.fact: The country where Chopin and Marie Curie were born.
eastern-europe:0.about:
Poland is where Chopin, "the poet of the piano," and Marie Curie, who won the Nobel Prize twice, were born. An international piano competition named after Chopin is held in Warsaw.
In the Wieliczka Salt Mine, you can see an underground chapel and statues made of salt.

eastern-europe:1.fact: The word "robot" was born in Czechia.
eastern-europe:1.about:
The word "robot" was first used in 1920 in a play by Czech writer Karel Čapek. It was made from a Czech word meaning "work."
Prague, the capital, has an astronomical clock that has been running since 1410, and every hour little figures start to move.

eastern-europe:2.fact: The home of the Rubik's Cube. People say their family name first, like in Japan!
eastern-europe:2.about:
In Hungary, people say their family name first, just like in Japan. Rubik Ernő, who made the Rubik's Cube, is Hungarian too.
The capital, Budapest, was made by joining the towns of "Buda" and "Pest" on either side of the Danube, and it has lots of hot springs.

eastern-europe:3.fact: Neckties began as the scarves of Croatian soldiers.
eastern-europe:3.about:
In the 17th century, the scarves Croatian soldiers wore around their necks became fashionable in France, and they became the first neckties. The French word for necktie, "cravate," comes from "Croatia."
The town of Dubrovnik, on the Adriatic Sea, is called "the pearl of the Adriatic."

eastern-europe:4.fact: It has monasteries with outside walls covered in paintings.
eastern-europe:4.about:
In the Bukovina region of northern Romania, there are monasteries whose outside walls are covered in painted stories, and they're World Heritage Sites.
The Danube Delta, where the Danube flows into the sea, is one of Europe's great wetlands, home to more than 300 kinds of birds, including pelicans.

eastern-europe:5.fact: Rose oil from the Valley of Roses is world famous.
eastern-europe:5.about:
In Bulgaria's "Valley of Roses," roses are picked in May and June to make rose oil, which is used in perfume. Bulgaria is one of the world's top producers of rose oil.
It's famous for yoghurt too. And in Bulgaria, nodding your head up and down can mean "no," and shaking it from side to side can mean "yes."

eastern-europe:6.fact: About 60% of the country is forest. Lake Bled, with a church on an island, is famous.
eastern-europe:6.about:
Slovenia is a green country, with about 60% of its land covered in forest. A church stands on a little island in Lake Bled, like a picture postcard.
Underground there are lots of big limestone caves, where the olm, a blind salamander, lives.

#central-america-caribbean: Maya ruins, a canal that joins two oceans, Caribbean music. These are cheerful countries full of nature.

central-america-caribbean:0.fact: The national bird, the quetzal, is also the name of the money.
central-america-caribbean:0.about:
Guatemala has Tikal, a Maya ruin where pyramids rise out of the jungle. Maya people still live there today, wearing brightly coloured traditional clothes.
The quetzal, a bird with long green feathers, is the national symbol, and the money is called the "quetzal" too.

central-america-caribbean:1.fact: About 5% of the world's living things live in this small country.
central-america-caribbean:1.about:
Costa Rica is a small country, about the size of Kyushu and Shikoku put together, but about 5% of the world's living things are said to live there. Sloths, hummingbirds and red-eyed tree frogs live there too.
About a quarter of the country is protected land. Its motto is "pura vida" (pure life).

central-america-caribbean:2.fact: It has the Panama Canal, which joins the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans.
central-america-caribbean:2.about:
The Panama Canal opened in 1914, joining the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans. Ships use "locks" to change the water level, so they can go up and over the land.
Without the canal, ships would have to go all the way around South America, thousands of kilometres out of their way.

central-america-caribbean:3.fact: Cars more than 70 years old still drive around town.
central-america-caribbean:3.about:
In Havana, the capital of Cuba, American cars from the 1950s are still on the road, carefully repaired again and again.
It's the biggest island in the Caribbean, and music and dance like salsa are popular. The bee hummingbird, the smallest bird in the world, lives in Cuba too.

central-america-caribbean:4.fact: The home of reggae music. It also has lots of fast runners.
central-america-caribbean:4.about:
Jamaica is the home of reggae music. Athletics is very popular, and Usain Bolt, who holds the 100 m world record, is from Jamaica.
Blue Mountain coffee is popular in Japan too. Japan is an important buyer of this coffee.

central-america-caribbean:5.fact: There's an island with pigs that swim in the sea!
central-america-caribbean:5.about:
The Bahamas is a country of more than 700 islands, with a beautiful blue sea. On the beach of one uninhabited island, you can see pigs swimming in the sea, and they became famous around the world.
Some islands even have pink sand beaches.

central-america-caribbean:6.fact: A country with lots of players in America's Major League Baseball.
central-america-caribbean:6.about:
In the Dominican Republic, baseball is the national sport, and after the USA, it sends the most players to America's Major League Baseball.
Santo Domingo, the capital, has the oldest European-style streets in the Caribbean, and they're a World Heritage Site.

#south-america-2: The longest, thinnest country in the world, a salt flat that mirrors the sky, the highest waterfall in the world. South America is one surprise after another!

south-america-2:0.fact: About 4,300 km from north to south. The longest, thinnest country in the world.
south-america-2:0.about:
Chile is about 4,300 km from north to south but only about 180 km wide on average, making it the longest, thinnest country in the world. In the north is the Atacama, the driest desert in the world, and in the south are glaciers.
Big observatories from around the world gather under the clear skies of the Atacama, and Japan takes part too. Easter Island, with its moai statues, is part of Chile too.

south-america-2:1.fact: A country of coffee and flowers. It has more kinds of birds than any other country!
south-america-2:1.about:
Colombia is famous for growing coffee, and it also grows lots of the flowers (like carnations) that come to Japan.
With more than 1,900 kinds of birds, it has the most bird species of any country. It has coasts on both the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean.

south-america-2:2.fact: The country's name is Spanish for "equator." The Galápagos Islands belong to it too.
south-america-2:2.about:
Ecuador means "equator" in Spanish. Near Quito, the capital, there's a monument that marks the equator.
The Galápagos Islands in the Pacific Ocean are part of Ecuador too. Amazing creatures like giant tortoises and marine iguanas live there.

south-america-2:3.fact: After rain, the Uyuni Salt Flat becomes a huge mirror reflecting the sky.
south-america-2:3.about:
Bolivia's Uyuni Salt Flat is the biggest salt flat in the world. When rain leaves a thin layer of water, the sky is reflected on the ground, making a "mirror of the sky."
La Paz, where the government is, is about 3,600 m above sea level, making it the highest capital city in the world. People use cable cars to get to work.

south-america-2:4.fact: It has the highest waterfall in the world, "Angel Falls."
south-america-2:4.about:
Angel Falls in Venezuela is 979 m high, the highest waterfall in the world. It's so high that the water turns into mist on the way down.
It falls from the top of a "tepui," a flat-topped mountain like a table. Arepas (corn bread) are an everyday staple food.

south-america-2:5.fact: The country that hosted and won the first football World Cup.
south-america-2:5.about:
In 1930, Uruguay hosted the first football World Cup and won. Football is still hugely popular.
"Asado," beef slowly grilled over charcoal, is a feast. Lots of people always carry their mate tea cup with them.

south-america-2:6.fact: Many people speak Guaraní, an Indigenous language.
south-america-2:6.about:
Paraguay has two official languages, Spanish and Guaraní, an Indigenous language, and many people speak both.
The Itaipu Dam, on the border with Brazil, is one of the biggest hydroelectric power plants in the world. Many people who moved from Japan live there too.

#africa-2: Africa has more than 50 countries. The home of coffee, a pink lake, and a waterfall with the sound of thunder!

africa-2:0.fact: Said to be the home of coffee. A year has 13 months!
africa-2:0.about:
Ethiopia is said to be the home of coffee. There's a legend that a goat herder noticed his goats got lively after eating red berries. People roast and make coffee at home in a "coffee ceremony."
It has its own calendar, with 13 months in a year. "Injera," like a sour pancake, is the staple food.

africa-2:1.fact: The country with the most people in Africa. It makes lots of films too.
africa-2:1.about:
Nigeria has more than 200 million people, the most of any country in Africa. It has more than 250 ethnic groups and languages.
Its film industry is huge and is called "Nollywood"; it makes more films than almost any other country in the world.

africa-2:2.fact: It has the "Lac Rose," whose water looks pink.
africa-2:2.about:
Senegal's Lac Rose (Pink Lake) is very salty, and tiny living things in it make the water look pink.
In Wolof, people say "Nanga def?" (How are you?). "Thieboudienne," fish and rice cooked together, is the national dish.

africa-2:3.fact: A country with very clean towns. Mountain gorillas live there.
africa-2:3.about:
Rwanda is a mountainous country called "the land of a thousand hills." Plastic bags have been banned since 2008, and there's a day every month when everyone cleans the town together, so Kigali, the capital, is very clean.
Endangered mountain gorillas live in its volcanic forests.

africa-2:4.fact: The country with the most African elephants in the world.
africa-2:4.about:
About 130,000 African elephants live in Botswana, said to be the most of any country.
The Okavango Delta is a huge wetland made where river water spreads out into the desert instead of reaching the sea, and it's a World Heritage Site. Botswana is also famous for diamonds.

africa-2:5.fact: It has the Namib, said to be the oldest desert in the world.
africa-2:5.about:
Namibia's Namib Desert has existed for about 55 million years and is said to be the oldest desert in the world. Some of the red sand dunes at Sossusvlei are more than 300 m tall.
Some creatures survive on fog rolling in from the sea (like the fog-basking beetle).

africa-2:6.fact: Victoria Falls is called "the smoke that thunders."
africa-2:6.about:
Victoria Falls, on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe, is about 1.7 km wide. In the local language it's called "Mosi-oa-Tunya" (the smoke that thunders), and its spray can be seen from several kilometres away.
"Nshima," made from cornmeal, is the everyday staple food.

africa-2:7.fact: It has an ancient city of stacked stones, "Great Zimbabwe."
africa-2:7.about:
The country's name, Zimbabwe, means "houses of stone," after "Great Zimbabwe," a stone city from around the 11th to 15th centuries. It was built by stacking stones without using cement.
Zimbabwe shares Victoria Falls with Zambia.

africa-2:8.fact: It has Lake Victoria, one of the sources of the Nile.
africa-2:8.about:
Uganda is a country on the equator, on the shores of Lake Victoria, the biggest lake in Africa. One of the sources of the Nile is here.
About half of the world's mountain gorillas live in Uganda's Bwindi Forest. "Matoke," green cooking bananas, are the staple food.

#pacific-islands: Small island countries are scattered across the wide Pacific Ocean. Many have deep ties with Japan.

pacific-islands:0.fact: It has "Jellyfish Lake," where jellyfish that don't sting swim.
pacific-islands:0.about:
In Palau's Jellyfish Lake, jellyfish that were cut off from the open sea for a long time have very weak stings, and they swim around in huge numbers.
The Palauan language still has words that came from Japanese, like "daijōbu" (it's OK) and "bentō."

pacific-islands:1.fact: In 2011, it skipped a whole day to change which side of the Date Line it's on!
pacific-islands:1.about:
In December 2011, Samoa skipped the whole of December 30th to move to the west side of the International Date Line. It did this so its days of the week would match Australia and New Zealand, making business easier.
Rugby is popular, and it has a culture of traditional tattoos and dances.

pacific-islands:2.fact: Lots of players from here do well in Japanese rugby.
pacific-islands:2.about:
Tonga is a kingdom of more than 170 islands. Rugby is popular, and lots of players from Tonga play for Japanese universities and teams.
Some of the pumpkins sold in Japan in winter are grown in Tonga.

pacific-islands:3.fact: Even its highest point is only about 4.6 m above the sea.
pacific-islands:3.about:
Tuvalu is a country of coral islands, and even its highest point is only about 4.6 m above sea level. People worry about the sea level rising.
About 10,000 people live there. Its internet domain is ".tv," so it's used by TV stations and others, and that earns money for the country.

pacific-islands:4.fact: The first country in the world to welcome the New Year.
pacific-islands:4.about:
Kiribati's islands are scattered across about 4,000 km from east to west, across the equator. The Line Islands, just west of the International Date Line, are the first place in the world to start each new day.
It's an unusual country with islands in all four hemispheres: north, south, east and west.

pacific-islands:5.fact: There's a postbox under the sea!
pacific-islands:5.about:
Vanuatu has Mount Yasur, an active volcano where you can see the glow of magma from the edge of the crater.
There's a real postbox under the sea, where divers can post special waterproof postcards.

pacific-islands:6.fact: "Shell money," made of strung-together shells, is still treasured.
pacific-islands:6.about:
In the Solomon Islands, "shell money," made by polishing and stringing together tiny shells, is still used on important occasions like wedding celebrations.
Marovo Lagoon is one of the biggest saltwater lagoons in the world, surrounded by beautiful coral reefs.

#continents-oceans: "Japan is in Asia." How are the Earth's land and sea divided up?

continents-oceans:0.fact: The biggest continent. About 60% of the world's people live there.
continents-oceans:0.about:
Asia is the biggest continent, making up about 30% of the Earth's land, and about 60% of the world's people live there.
Everest, the highest mountain in the world, and the shores of the Dead Sea, the lowest land on Earth, are both in Asia.

continents-oceans:1.fact: It has 54 countries, more than any other continent.
continents-oceans:1.about:
Africa has 54 countries, more than any other continent. It has the Nile, the longest river in the world, and the Sahara, the biggest hot desert in the world.
It's thought to be where humans first came from, and the oldest human fossils have been found there.

continents-oceans:2.fact: From Canada, the USA and Mexico to the islands of the Caribbean.
continents-oceans:2.about:
North America includes Canada, the USA, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean countries. The north is an icy world near the Arctic, and the south is tropical.
Geographically, Greenland is part of North America too.

continents-oceans:3.fact: The continent of the Amazon River and the Andes Mountains.
continents-oceans:3.about:
South America has 12 countries. It has the Amazon, the river with the most water in the world, and the Andes, the longest mountain range in the world.
Portuguese is spoken in Brazil, and Spanish in most of the other countries.

continents-oceans:4.fact: A small continent with more than 40 countries.
continents-oceans:4.about:
Europe is a small continent, but it has more than 40 countries. The countries are close together, so you can cross borders by train.
It's joined to Asia by land, and the border is usually said to be around the Ural Mountains.

continents-oceans:5.fact: The continent of Australia and the Pacific islands.
continents-oceans:5.about:
Oceania is the region that includes the continent of Australia, New Zealand and the many islands of the Pacific. Australia is said to be the smallest continent.
It has lots of animals found on no other continent, like kangaroos and koalas.

continents-oceans:6.fact: A continent with no countries. About 70% of the world's fresh water is here as ice.
continents-oceans:6.about:
Antarctica is a continent covered in ice about 2,000 m thick on average, and it doesn't belong to any country. About 70% of the world's fresh water is here, as ice.
Japan does research at Shōwa Station too. There are researchers, but nobody lives there permanently.

continents-oceans:7.fact: An ocean bigger than all the world's land put together.
continents-oceans:7.about:
The Pacific is the biggest ocean in the world, covering about a third of the Earth's surface. Even if you put all the land on Earth together, the Pacific is bigger.
The deepest place, the Mariana Trench (about 10,920 m), is in the Pacific too. Its name means "peaceful ocean."

continents-oceans:8.fact: The ocean between Europe and Africa and the Americas.
continents-oceans:8.about:
The Atlantic is the second-biggest ocean in the world, between Europe and Africa on one side and the Americas on the other. Down the middle runs an undersea mountain range from north to south, and the continents are still moving apart by a few centimetres every year.
Sailors long ago crossed this ocean and reached new continents.

continents-oceans:9.fact: The ocean surrounded by Africa, Asia and Australia.
continents-oceans:9.about:
The Indian Ocean is the third-biggest ocean in the world, surrounded by Africa, Asia and Australia. "Monsoon" winds blow across it, changing direction between summer and winter.
It has been an ocean of trade since ancient times, with ships carrying spices and cloth.

continents-oceans:10.fact: About 200 million years ago, the continents were all joined together.
continents-oceans:10.about:
About 300 to 200 million years ago, the Earth's continents were one huge continent called "Pangaea." The continents ride on plates and slowly moved into the shapes they have today.
That's why the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like a jigsaw puzzle. The islands of Japan were once part of the Asian continent too.

#islands-world: From the biggest island in the world to brand-new islands. How many islands does Japan, an island country, have?

islands-world:0.fact: The biggest island in the world. About 80% of it is covered in ice.
islands-world:0.about:
Greenland is the biggest island in the world, about 6 times the size of Japan. About 80% of it is covered in thick ice, and if all the ice melted, world sea levels are said to rise by about 7 m.
Its name means "green land," but only parts of the coast are green, in summer.

islands-world:1.fact: The second-biggest island in the world. It has a huge number of languages!
islands-world:1.about:
New Guinea is the second-biggest island in the world, shared by Papua New Guinea and Indonesia.
More than 1,000 languages are said to be spoken on this island, making it one of the places with the most languages in the world.

islands-world:2.fact: The third-biggest island in the world, shared by three countries.
islands-world:2.about:
Borneo is the third-biggest island in the world, shared by three countries: Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei.
In its rainforests, you can see orangutans, proboscis monkeys and rafflesia flowers.

islands-world:3.fact: Many of its living things are found only on this island.
islands-world:3.about:
Madagascar split from India about 88 million years ago and was cut off for a long time, so lots of creatures found nowhere else developed there.
All lemurs live only in Madagascar. Its avenue of baobab trees is famous too.

islands-world:4.fact: An island sitting on the border between two plates.
islands-world:4.about:
Iceland is an island sitting on the border where two of the plates covering the Earth's surface are moving apart. You can walk along cracks in the ground called "gjá."
It has lots of volcanoes and hot springs, and it makes almost all its electricity from geothermal power and water power.

islands-world:5.fact: Volcanic islands born from one of the Earth's "hot spots."
islands-world:5.about:
The Hawaiian Islands are volcanic islands that formed over a "hot spot," where magma rises from deep inside the Earth. Because the plate moves, the islands are lined up in a row.
On the newest one, the Big Island of Hawaiʻi, volcanoes are still active.

islands-world:6.fact: An island born in a 1963 eruption. It's a natural laboratory.
islands-world:6.about:
Surtsey is an island born in an eruption in the sea south of Iceland in 1963. People aren't allowed to go there, so it's a "natural laboratory" for studying how plants and birds arrive.
It's a World Heritage Site too.

islands-world:7.fact: When they were counted again, there were 14,125!
islands-world:7.about:
For a long time, Japan was said to have 6,852 islands, but in 2023 the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan counted again using detailed maps and announced 14,125.
There weren't more islands; the way of counting and the maps just got more detailed.

islands-world:8.fact: Nagasaki has more islands than any other prefecture in Japan.
islands-world:8.about:
With Tsushima, Iki, the Gotō Islands, the Kujūku Islands and more, Nagasaki has the most islands of any prefecture in Japan. The 2023 count said it has 1,479 islands.
Its coastline is the second longest after Hokkaido's. It's a prefecture of sea and islands.

#time-zones-world: "What time is it in London? — It's 11 p.m." When it's morning in Japan, what time is it around the world?

time-zones-world:0.fact: The Earth turns 15 degrees every hour.
time-zones-world:0.about:
The Earth turns once (360 degrees) every 24 hours, so it turns 15 degrees every hour. The time when the Sun is highest in the sky is different from place to place.
So the world is split into "time zones" about 15 degrees of longitude wide, and each uses a different time. That's the time difference.

time-zones-world:1.fact: Greenwich in London is 0 degrees longitude, the starting point for world time.
time-zones-world:1.about:
At an international meeting in 1884, the line passing through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, was chosen as 0 degrees longitude. World time is based on it.
There's a line marking 0 degrees at the observatory, so you can stand with one foot in the Eastern Hemisphere and one in the Western.

time-zones-world:2.fact: Japan's time is set by 135 degrees east, which runs through Akashi in Hyōgo.
time-zones-world:2.about:
Japan Standard Time is the time at 135 degrees east longitude. This line runs through places like Akashi in Hyōgo, and the clock tower of the Akashi Municipal Planetarium marks it.
It's 9 hours ahead of Greenwich, so Japan's time is written "UTC+9."

time-zones-world:3.fact: Cross this line, and the date changes by one day.
time-zones-world:3.about:
If you cross the International Date Line in the middle of the Pacific from west to east, the date goes back one day, and from east to west, it goes forward one day.
The line zigzags so that it doesn't run through the middle of any country.

time-zones-world:4.fact: An island in Kiribati welcomes the New Year first in the world.
time-zones-world:4.about:
Kiribati's Line Islands are at "UTC+14," so they're the first place in the world to start each new day. Their New Year comes 5 hours earlier than Japan's.
The last places to welcome the New Year are at "UTC−11," like American Samoa, a whole 25 hours behind the Line Islands.

time-zones-world:5.fact: A country that's very wide from east to west, but has only one time zone.
time-zones-world:5.about:
China is very wide, about 5,000 km from east to west, and really spans 5 time zones, but the whole country uses one time: Beijing time.
So in the west of China, the sun sometimes doesn't come up until about 10 a.m.

time-zones-world:6.about:
Russia is the biggest country in the world, with 11 time zones from its eastern edge to its western edge. When it's 11 p.m. at the eastern edge, it's still 12 noon at the western edge.
If you travel on the Trans-Siberian Railway, you have to change your watch again and again.

time-zones-world:7.fact: 6 time zones across the mainland, Alaska and Hawaii.
time-zones-world:7.about:
The USA has 6 time zones: from east to west, Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific, plus Alaska and Hawaii.
When it's 9 p.m. in New York, it's only 6 p.m. in Los Angeles. TV programmes are on at different times in different areas.

time-zones-world:8.fact: 9 a.m. in Japan is midnight in the UK (in winter).
time-zones-world:8.about:
The time difference between Japan and the UK is 9 hours (8 hours in the British summer). When school starts in Japan at 9 a.m., it's midnight in the UK.
So if you want to video call a friend in the UK, the evening in Japan is a good time.

time-zones-world:9.fact: Some countries put their clocks forward 1 hour in summer. Japan doesn't now.
time-zones-world:9.about:
Many parts of Europe and America use "daylight saving time," putting their clocks forward 1 hour in summer. It's to make more use of the bright evenings.
Japan used it from 1948 to 1951, but it doesn't now.

#japan-geography: Japan is a mountainous island country that's long from north to south. Why is Nagasaki so warm?

japan-geography:0.fact: Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and more than 10,000 islands.
japan-geography:0.about:
Japan is an island country made of 4 big islands, Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, and more than 10,000 other islands. It stretches about 3,000 km from northeast to southwest, curving like a bow.
That's why it has all kinds of climates, from drift ice in the north to coral reefs in the south.

japan-geography:1.fact: About three quarters of the land is mountains.
japan-geography:1.about:
About three quarters of Japan's land is mountains, and there are only a few plains. That's why lots of people live together on the plains near the sea.
With so many mountains, the rivers are short and fast. There are lots of forests too: about two thirds of the land is forest.

japan-geography:2.fact: Mountains in the middle of Honshu, with peaks around 3,000 m high.
japan-geography:2.about:
The Hida Mountains (Northern Alps), Kiso Mountains (Central Alps) and Akaishi Mountains (Southern Alps) in the middle of Honshu are together called the "Japanese Alps."
They were named by an Englishman, Gowland, in the Meiji period, and another Englishman, Weston, made mountain climbing there popular. Rock ptarmigans live in these mountains.

japan-geography:3.fact: The river with the biggest basin in Japan. It's called "Bandō Tarō."
japan-geography:3.about:
The Tone River is 322 km long, the second longest in Japan, and the area that drains into it (its basin) is the biggest in Japan.
It has long been called "Bandō Tarō" and is an important water source for the Kantō region. In the Edo period, a huge construction project changed its course to flow east.

japan-geography:4.fact: The biggest lake in Japan. An old lake that's more than 4 million years old.
japan-geography:4.about:
Lake Biwa in Shiga is the biggest lake in Japan, covering about a sixth of the prefecture. It formed more than 4 million years ago, making it one of the oldest lakes in the world.
Some fish live only here, and it also supplies water to people in Kyoto and Osaka.

japan-geography:5.about:
The Kantō Plain spreads across Tokyo, Kanagawa, Saitama, Chiba and more. It's the biggest plain in Japan, and about a third of Japan's people live there.
It's covered in red soil called the "Kantō loam," made from piled-up volcanic ash.

japan-geography:6.fact: Warm ocean currents keep Nagasaki warm.
japan-geography:6.about:
The warm "Kuroshio" current flows south of Japan, and part of it passes west of Kyushu as the "Tsushima Current" and flows into the Sea of Japan.
Nagasaki's fairly mild winters and its rich seafood are thanks to this warm current.

japan-geography:7.fact: 208 small islands are scattered across the sea off Sasebo.
japan-geography:7.about:
The Kujūku Islands in Sasebo are a seascape of 208 small islands. "Kujūku" (99) means "very many."
They're an example of a jagged coastline (a ria coast), made when mountains sank into the sea. They're famous for beautiful sunsets too.

japan-geography:8.fact: The east end is Minamitorishima and the west end is Yonaguni.
japan-geography:8.about:
The easternmost point of Japan is Minamitorishima, part of Tokyo, and the westernmost is Yonaguni Island in Okinawa. They're about 3,000 km apart.
On clear days, you can sometimes see the mountains of Taiwan from Yonaguni. It's the island where the sun sets last in Japan.

japan-geography:9.fact: A huge trench that splits the Japanese islands into east and west.
japan-geography:9.about:
The Fossa Magna is a huge trench running from Itoigawa in Niigata to Shizuoka, splitting the Japanese islands into east and west. In Latin, it means "big trench."
It was named by a German, Naumann. The kinds of rock in eastern and western Japan are different on either side of it.

#holidays-world: "When is Halloween? — It's October 31st." Let's look at where the world's festivals come from and how people enjoy them.

holidays-world:0.fact: The first jack-o'-lanterns were made from turnips.
holidays-world:0.about:
Halloween grew from old end-of-autumn festivals in places like Ireland. The first jack-o'-lanterns were made from hollowed-out turnips, and when the custom reached America, they became pumpkins.
Children dress up and go from house to house saying "Trick or treat!" to get sweets.

holidays-world:1.fact: Strawberry shortcake and fried chicken are very Japanese.
holidays-world:1.about:
The classic Japanese Christmas cake is a shortcake with white cream and strawberries. The red and white colours are perfect for Christmas and for Japanese celebrations too.
After an advert in the 1970s, eating fried chicken at Christmas also became a custom. People from abroad are very surprised.

holidays-world:2.fact: In the Netherlands, presents arrive on the night of December 5th.
holidays-world:2.about:
In the Netherlands and Belgium, the night of December 5th (the 6th in some areas) is "Sinterklaas." Children leave their shoes out and get presents and sweets.
Sinterklaas is said to have travelled to America and become the start of Santa Claus.

holidays-world:3.fact: In Italy, an old woman on a broomstick gives out sweets.
holidays-world:3.about:
In Italy, on the night before January 6th, a kind old woman on a broomstick called "La Befana" is said to fill good children's stockings with sweets and naughty children's with candy shaped like lumps of coal.
This day marks the end of the Christmas season.

holidays-world:4.fact: The longest Christmas season in the world, starting in September.
holidays-world:4.about:
In the Philippines, Christmas songs start playing in September (the months ending in "-ber" in English), and it carries on until January. It's said to be the longest Christmas season in the world.
People decorate their homes with "parol," star-shaped lanterns made of bamboo and paper.

holidays-world:5.fact: In spring, people decorate and hunt for painted eggs.
holidays-world:5.about:
At Easter in spring, people decorate eggs painted with colours and patterns, and have "egg hunts" to look for eggs hidden in the garden. Eggs are a symbol of new life.
Chile's Easter Island got its name because Europeans arrived there on Easter Day in 1722.

holidays-world:6.fact: An American day of thanks for the harvest. There's a parade with huge balloons too.
holidays-world:6.about:
Thanksgiving in America is on the fourth Thursday of November. Families get together, eat roast turkey and pumpkin pie, and give thanks for the year's harvest.
New York's huge balloon parade, which has been held since the 1920s, is famous. Canada's Thanksgiving is in October.

holidays-world:7.fact: New Year money in red envelopes. In Nagasaki, it's the Lantern Festival!
holidays-world:7.about:
In China, South Korea, Vietnam and other places, the New Year of the old calendar (in January or February) is a big celebration. Children get money in red envelopes, and people eat feasts with dishes like dumplings.
In Nagasaki, the "Lantern Festival" is held at this time, and the whole city is decorated with thousands of lanterns.

holidays-world:8.fact: India's spring festival. People throw coloured powder to celebrate spring.
holidays-world:8.about:
Holi is a spring festival in India and other places, where people throw coloured powder and coloured water at each other to celebrate the arrival of spring together. Everyone gets covered in colour, whatever their age.
It's known around the world as "the festival of colours."

holidays-world:9.fact: India's "festival of lights." Homes are decorated with lamps and patterns.
holidays-world:9.about:
Diwali is a "festival of lights" celebrated in India and other places. Homes are lit with small oil lamps called "diyas," and patterns called "rangoli" are drawn on the floor with coloured powder.
People wear new clothes and share sweets with family and neighbours.

holidays-world:10.fact: Thailand's New Year. People splash water at each other all over town.
holidays-world:10.about:
Songkran is Thailand's New Year, around April 13th to 15th. Originally, people welcomed the New Year by gently pouring water over Buddha statues and the hands of older people.
Now it's the biggest water festival in the world, with people soaking each other with water pistols and buckets all over town. April is the hottest time of year in Thailand.

holidays-world:11.fact: An Irish holiday. In Chicago, the river turns green!
holidays-world:11.about:
St Patrick's Day, March 17th, is a holiday in Ireland. People wear green and decorate with three-leaf shamrocks.
In Chicago, USA, the river has been dyed green every year since 1962. There's a parade in Tokyo too.

holidays-world:12.fact: It started in America, and people give carnations.
holidays-world:12.about:
Mother's Day started when Anna Jarvis in America gave out white carnations in memory of her mother, who had died. It became a holiday in America in 1914.
In Japan it's the second Sunday of May. The date is different in each country; in the UK it's around March.

holidays-world:13.fact: In 1957, British TV showed a "spaghetti tree"!
holidays-world:13.about:
April 1st is a day for enjoying little fibs and jokes. In 1957, the BBC in the UK broadcast a news story saying "spaghetti is growing on trees in Switzerland," and some people who thought it was true called in to ask about it.
In some countries, you're only allowed to play tricks in the morning.

holidays-world:14.fact: In Japan and South Korea it's May 5th; in Türkiye it's April 23rd.
holidays-world:14.about:
Japan's Children's Day is May 5th. People fly carp streamers and eat kashiwa-mochi. South Korea's Children's Day is May 5th too.
In Türkiye, April 23rd has been Children's Day since the 1920s, and children from all over the world are invited to celebrate. Lots of countries in the world have a Children's Day.

#japanese-holidays: Japan has 16 national holidays a year. What does each one mean?

japanese-holidays:0.fact: A day to celebrate the start of the year.
japanese-holidays:0.about:
New Year's Day, January 1st, is a day to celebrate the start of the new year. People eat osechi and ozōni, read New Year cards and make their first shrine visit of the year.
In Japan, January 1st to 3rd is called "sanganichi," and lots of companies and shops close.

japanese-holidays:1.fact: A day to celebrate and encourage young people who have become adults.
japanese-holidays:1.about:
Coming of Age Day is the second Monday of January. It's a day to celebrate and encourage young people who have become adults and are starting to make their own way in life.
Since 2022 the age of adulthood has been 18, but many towns still hold ceremonies for people who are 20.

japanese-holidays:2.fact: A long string of holidays from late April to early May.
japanese-holidays:2.about:
The time when holidays come one after another, April 29th (Shōwa Day), May 3rd (Constitution Day), 4th (Greenery Day) and 5th (Children's Day), is called "Golden Week."
The name is said to have spread in the 1950s, when a film company called this busy time for cinemas "Golden Week."

japanese-holidays:3.fact: A day to wish for children's happiness and growth.
japanese-holidays:3.about:
By law, Children's Day, May 5th, is a day to respect children as people, wish for their happiness and thank mothers.
People fly carp streamers, eat kashiwa-mochi and chimaki, and take baths with iris leaves.

japanese-holidays:4.fact: A day to give thanks for the sea. Few countries have a holiday for the sea!
japanese-holidays:4.about:
Marine Day is "a day to give thanks for the gifts of the sea and wish for the success of Japan, a country surrounded by sea." It became a holiday in 1996.
Very few countries in the world have a holiday for the sea, so it's a very Japanese holiday for a country surrounded by water.

japanese-holidays:5.about:
Mountain Day, made in 2016, is the newest national holiday. It's "a day to have a chance to get close to the mountains and give thanks for their gifts."
One idea about why it's on August 11th is that "八" (8) looks like a mountain and "11" looks like trees.

japanese-holidays:6.fact: A day to respect older people and celebrate long life.
japanese-holidays:6.about:
Respect for the Aged Day is the third Monday of September. It's a day to respect older people, who have worked for society for a long time, and to celebrate long life.
Japan is one of the countries where people live longest, and more than 90,000 people are 100 or older.

japanese-holidays:7.fact: It comes from the opening day of the 1964 Tokyo Olympics.
japanese-holidays:7.about:
The opening ceremony of the Tokyo Olympics was held on October 10th, 1964. To remember it, "Health and Sports Day" was made in 1966, and in 2020 its name changed to "Sports Day."
Now it's the second Monday of October. Many schools hold their autumn sports days around this time too.

japanese-holidays:8.fact: A day to value culture. The Order of Culture is awarded.
japanese-holidays:8.about:
Culture Day, November 3rd, is "a day to love freedom and peace and to encourage culture." On this day, the Order of Culture is given to people who have done great work in culture and science.
November 3rd is also said to be a day when it's very often sunny.

japanese-holidays:9.fact: A day to thank people who work.
japanese-holidays:9.about:
Labour Thanksgiving Day, November 23rd, is a day to value work, celebrate what we produce, and thank one another. It used to be the day of an old festival celebrating the autumn harvest.
Try saying "thank you" to people in your family and town who work.

japanese-holidays:10.fact: A system that moves holidays to Mondays to make more three-day weekends.
japanese-holidays:10.about:
In 2000, the "Happy Monday system" began, moving holidays like Coming of Age Day and Sports Day to "the ___ Monday of ___." Together with Saturday and Sunday, they make three-day weekends.
That's why these holidays fall on different dates each year.

japanese-holidays:11.fact: Japan has 16. It's a country with lots of public holidays.
japanese-holidays:11.about:
Japan has 16 national holidays a year. America has 11 federal holidays and the UK has about 8, so Japan has a lot.
On the other hand, it's said that few adults in Japan take long summer holidays.

#units-history: "How tall are you? — I'm 140 centimeters." How were the metre and the foot decided?

units-history:0.fact: A unit of length based on the size of the Earth.
units-history:0.about:
In France in the 1790s, "1 metre" was set as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator. It was to make one length for the whole world, when every country had its own.
Now it's defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

units-history:1.fact: A metal "weight" that was used for 130 years retired in 2019.
units-history:1.about:
From 1889, a metal cylinder carefully kept in France, the "International Prototype of the Kilogram," was the standard for 1 kg. But people worried its weight might change very slightly over the decades.
In 2019, the definition changed to one using a fixed number from nature (the Planck constant), and the prototype retired.

units-history:2.fact: Units that came from the length of a foot and the width of a thumb.
units-history:2.about:
The foot came from the length of a foot, and the inch from about the width of a thumb. 1 foot is 12 inches, about 30.5 cm.
In America, people still give their height in feet and inches. "5 feet 2 inches" is about 157 cm.

units-history:3.fact: Legend says it was the length from a king's nose to his thumb.
units-history:3.about:
A yard is about 91 cm. There's a legend that it was set as the length from the tip of King Henry I of England's nose to the tip of his thumb on his outstretched arm.
Yards are still used in golf and American football.

units-history:4.fact: It came from the ancient Roman "1,000 paces."
units-history:4.about:
The mile came from the ancient Roman "1,000 paces" (with one pace being two steps), and today 1 mile is about 1.6 km.
In America and the UK, miles are used on road signs and for car speeds. "60 miles per hour" is about 96 km per hour.

units-history:5.fact: A unit of weight used in America and the UK for things like body weight.
units-history:5.about:
The pound is a unit of weight; 1 pound is about 450 g. In America it's used for body weight and for weighing food. Its symbol, "lb," comes from "libra," an ancient Roman unit of weight.
British money is called the "pound" too. Long ago, money was worth the weight of a pound of silver.

units-history:6.fact: American weather forecasts use Fahrenheit. 100°F is about 38°C!
units-history:6.about:
Celsius (°C), which Japan uses, sets the temperature water freezes at as 0 and the temperature it boils at as 100. It was thought up by Celsius in Sweden.
America uses Fahrenheit (°F), thought up by Fahrenheit in Germany. Water freezes at 32°F, and body temperature is about 98°F.

units-history:7.fact: One sun is about 3 cm. Issun-bōshi is a 3 cm hero!
units-history:7.about:
Shaku and sun are old Japanese units of length. 1 shaku is about 30.3 cm, and 1 sun is a tenth of that, about 3 cm. They're still used by carpenters and kimono makers.
"Issun-bōshi" (One-Inch Boy) is a hero about 3 cm tall. There's also a saying, "One sun ahead is darkness" (no one knows what's coming).

units-history:8.fact: 1 tsubo is 2 tatami mats, about 3.3 m².
units-history:8.about:
The tsubo is a unit for the size of land and houses; 1 tsubo is 2 tatami mats, about 3.3 m². Room sizes are given by the number of tatami mats, like "6 tatami."
By law, Japan uses m², but tsubo and tatami are still often used in home adverts.

units-history:9.fact: One "gō" in a rice cooker is about 180 mL. An old unit that's still alive today.
units-history:9.about:
The gō is a unit for measuring rice and sake; 1 gō is about 180 mL. Rice cooker cups and markings still use "gō."
10 gō make 1 shō (about 1.8 L). The "shō" in "isshō mochi," eaten at a first birthday, is this unit too.

units-history:10.fact: An old unit of distance. 1 ri is about 4 km.
units-history:10.about:
The ri is an old Japanese unit of distance; 1 ri is about 3.9 km, roughly how far a person walks in an hour.
The "ichirizuka" on the old Tōkaidō road were mounds built beside the road every 1 ri as markers. When an old story says someone "walked many ri," it means they walked dozens of kilometres.

#measuring-tools: The man who made a map of Japan on foot, the man who measured the speed of light. Measuring is how we get to know the world.

measuring-tools:0.fact: He walked all over Japan measuring it and made an accurate map of Japan.
measuring-tools:0.about:
Inō Tadataka started studying astronomy at 50, and from 55 he spent about 17 years walking all over Japan surveying it. He's said to have walked about 40,000 km, the same as once around the Earth.
His map of Japan's coasts, finished in 1821 after his death, is very accurate even compared with today's maps.

measuring-tools:1.fact: A tool for comparing weights, used even in ancient Egypt.
measuring-tools:1.about:
A balance is a tool for comparing weights, with pans hanging from both ends of a bar held up in the middle. It was used in ancient Egypt more than about 4,000 years ago.
Today's digital scales measure tiny bends in springs or sensors using electricity.

measuring-tools:2.fact: Galileo's "tool for seeing temperature" is said to be the first.
measuring-tools:2.about:
Around 1593, Galileo in Italy made a tool that showed changes in temperature by how much air expanded. It's said to be the first thermometer.
Later, thermometers using mercury and alcohol were made, and now electronic thermometers can measure your temperature in seconds.

measuring-tools:3.fact: A Japanese clock that's off by only 1 second in 30 billion years.
measuring-tools:3.about:
People long ago measured time with sundials, hourglasses and water clocks. Today, world time is set by "atomic clocks," which count the vibrations of atoms.
The "optical lattice clock" invented by Katori Hidetoshi of Japan is off by only 1 second in 30 billion years, one of the most accurate clocks in the world.

measuring-tools:4.about:
The height of Everest was once calculated by measuring the angles of triangles from faraway points. In 2020, Nepal and China surveyed it from the summit using GPS and other tools and announced it as 8,848.86 m.
Its height can change a little because of earthquakes and movements of the mountain.

measuring-tools:5.fact: The speed of light was first found from the movement of Jupiter's moon.
measuring-tools:5.about:
Light is so fast that people once thought it arrived "instantly." In 1676, Rømer in Denmark showed that light has a speed by noticing timing differences in when Jupiter's moon Io could be seen.
Now we know the speed of light is about 300,000 km per second.

measuring-tools:6.fact: The distance light travels in a year: about 9.5 trillion km!
measuring-tools:6.about:
1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion km. Space is so huge that the numbers in kilometres get too big, so we use light-years.
The nearest star (after the Sun) is about 4.2 light-years away. The starlight you see now set off years ago.

measuring-tools:7.fact: Radio waves from satellites tell you where you are.
measuring-tools:7.about:
GPS works out where you are by measuring the time differences of radio waves from satellites in space. It needs the exact time from atomic clocks.
Japan launched satellites called "Michibiki" so that even in Japan, with all its buildings and mountains, your position can be found to within centimetres.

#how-computers-work: What's going on inside the tablet you use every day? Let's peek into the world of 0s and 1s.

how-computers-work:0.about:
Inside a computer, all information is shown with just two states, whether electricity is flowing or not, written as 0 and 1. This is called "binary."
Letters, photos and music are all long rows of 0s and 1s. "10" in binary is "2" in ordinary numbers.

how-computers-work:1.fact: 8 bits make 1 byte. One English letter is 1 byte.
how-computers-work:1.about:
One 0 or 1 is called a "bit," and 8 bits together make "1 byte." One letter of the English alphabet is 1 byte, and a Japanese character takes 2 or 3 bytes.
1,000 bytes is about 1 kilobyte, and one photo is a few megabytes (a few million bytes).

how-computers-work:2.fact: Pictures on a screen are made of tiny dots of colour.
how-computers-work:2.about:
If you look at a screen through a magnifying glass, you can see rows of tiny red, green and blue lights. Each of these dots is called a "pixel," and by changing the brightness of the three colours, they can show every colour.
The more pixels there are, the sharper and finer the picture.

how-computers-work:3.fact: The computer's "brain," doing billions of calculations every second.
how-computers-work:3.about:
The CPU is the part that works like the computer's "brain," doing billions of calculations and instructions every second.
Inside its tiny chip are billions of switches called "transistors." It gets hot, so it's cooled with things like fans.

how-computers-work:4.fact: The "desk" where the computer keeps what it's working on.
how-computers-work:4.about:
Memory is where a computer keeps the information it's using right now, for a short time. If you think of studying, it's like "the top of your desk." The bigger it is, the more jobs it can do at once.
When you switch off the power, memory is wiped, so important data is saved in "storage" (the bookshelf).

how-computers-work:5.fact: A way of arranging letters that goes back to the age of typewriters.
how-computers-work:5.about:
The top left of a keyboard reads Q, W, E, R, T, Y because it comes from the layout of American typewriters in the 1870s.
It was then passed on to computers, and now it's used all over the world. Japanese keyboards show both Roman letters and kana.

how-computers-work:6.fact: Invented in the 1960s, it was made from a wooden box.
how-computers-work:6.about:
The mouse was invented in the 1960s by Engelbart in America. The first mouse was a wooden box with two wheels.
It looked like a mouse, with its cable like a tail, so it came to be called a "mouse."

how-computers-work:7.fact: It senses the tiny bit of electricity that flows from your finger.
how-computers-work:7.about:
Most smartphones and tablets find where you touched by sensing tiny changes in electricity flowing through your finger. That's why they sometimes don't work when you're wearing gloves.
Moves like spreading or pinching with two fingers work because the screen can sense several places at the same time.

how-computers-work:8.fact: A Japanese supercomputer became number one in the world!
how-computers-work:8.about:
"Fugaku," a supercomputer made by RIKEN and Fujitsu, came first in the world rankings for calculating speed in 2020 and 2021.
It's used for things like researching new medicines, forecasting the weather, and calculating how viruses spread through the air. Its name is another name for Mount Fuji.

#how-internet-works: How do videos and messages reach you? A journey through the internet, all the way to the bottom of the sea.

how-internet-works:0.fact: Most data between countries travels through cables on the seabed.
how-internet-works:0.about:
Most internet data between countries doesn't go via satellites but through fibre-optic cables laid on the bottom of the sea.
There are several cables between Japan and America too, and data travels back and forth at the speed of light. There are even special ships for repairing the cables.

how-internet-works:1.fact: A way of carrying data by radio waves. You can't see them.
how-internet-works:1.about:
Wi-Fi is a way of sending data back and forth between a router and a device using radio waves. They're the same family of waves as radio, and they pass through walls.
Wi-Fi sometimes gets weaker when a microwave oven is on, because they use similar kinds of waves.

how-internet-works:2.fact: Data is cut into small pieces to be sent and put back together when it arrives.
how-internet-works:2.about:
When data is sent over the internet, it's split into small "packets," each with the address it's going to. Packets can take different routes and are put back together in the right order when they arrive.
If one route is busy, another can be used, so it's a tough system.

how-internet-works:3.fact: They collect pages from all over the world in advance and make an index.
how-internet-works:3.about:
Search engines use programs called "crawlers" to collect web pages from all over the world in advance and make an index, like the index at the back of a book.
When you type in words, they instantly pick pages from that index that look useful and show them to you in order.

how-internet-works:4.fact: Buildings with tens of thousands of computers. Keeping them cool is important!
how-internet-works:4.about:
A data centre is a big building with tens of thousands of computers in rows. Videos, photos and emails are stored here.
Computers give off heat, so keeping them cool is very important. Some data centres are in cold northern countries or are cooled with sea water.

how-internet-works:5.about:
The QR code was invented in 1994 by Hara Masahiro and his team at Denso Wave in Japan. He's said to have got the idea from the black and white stones of the game of go.
The square markers in three corners let it be read quickly from any direction. The company let anyone use the patent freely, so it spread all over the world.

how-internet-works:6.fact: Born in Japan, and called "emoji" in English too.
how-internet-works:6.about:
Emoji started in 1999 with 176 tiny pictures made for Japanese mobile phones by Kurita Shigetaka and his team.
Now they're used all over the world, and in English they're called "emoji" too. The first emoji even became part of the collection of the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York.

how-internet-works:7.fact: It learns patterns from lots of examples. But it can make mistakes!
how-internet-works:7.about:
AI (artificial intelligence) learns patterns from lots of examples, like writing and photos, so it can answer questions or recognise pictures.
It's very useful, but sometimes it gives wrong answers as if it's sure. Check important things another way too, like in books or with a teacher.

how-internet-works:8.fact: Don't forget there's a person on the other side of the screen.
how-internet-works:8.about:
On the internet you can't see faces, so words can come across more strongly than you mean. Before you send something, think, "Could I say this to their face?"
Don't share personal information like your name, address, school or photos. If something worries you, talk to a grown-up straight away.

#magnets: They stick, they push apart, they point north. Magnets are hard at work in trains and hospitals too!

magnets:0.fact: Same poles push each other away, and different poles pull together.
magnets:0.about:
Magnets have a north pole (N) and a south pole (S). The same poles push each other away, and different poles pull each other together.
If you cut a magnet in half, each piece becomes a magnet with its own N and S poles. You can't make a magnet with only an N pole.

magnets:1.fact: That's why a compass points north.
magnets:1.about:
The moving iron in the Earth's centre makes the Earth into a giant magnet. That's why the N end of a compass points north.
The Earth's magnetism is also a shield against harmful particles flying from the Sun. When they glow, we see the aurora.

magnets:2.fact: A stone from Magnesia in Greece gave us the word "magnet."
magnets:2.about:
In nature there's a stone that attracts iron, called "magnetite" (lodestone). It was often found in the Magnesia region of ancient Greece, and that's said to be where the word "magnet" came from.
In China, this stone was used to make the tool that led to the compass.

magnets:3.fact: A train that floats and moves using magnets. It holds a record of 603 km per hour!
magnets:3.about:
A maglev train uses powerful magnets to lift the train up and push it forward. The wheels don't touch the rails, so it can go very fast.
In 2015, it set a world record of 603 km per hour on a test line in Yamanashi. The "Chūō Shinkansen" maglev line between Tokyo and Nagoya is being built.

magnets:4.fact: Migrating birds are thought to find their way by sensing the Earth's magnetism.
magnets:4.about:
Migrating birds, sea turtles, salmon and other animals are thought to find their way by sensing the Earth's magnetism. Some research suggests birds have a special system for this in their eyes.
This might also be how pigeons find their way home from far away.

magnets:5.fact: A machine that uses powerful magnets to take pictures inside your body.
magnets:5.about:
An MRI machine uses very powerful magnets and radio waves to take pictures of the inside of the body. It doesn't use X-rays, so it's a gentle kind of scan.
The magnet is so strong that you can't take metal things into the scanning room.

magnets:6.fact: Invented by Honda Kōtarō of Japan, the strongest magnet in the world at the time.
magnets:6.about:
In 1917, Honda Kōtarō of Tōhoku University invented "KS steel," a steel that made magnets several times stronger than before. Its name comes from the initials of Sumitomo Kichizaemon, who supported his research.
Honda was called "the god of iron," and Japanese magnet research went on to lead the world.

magnets:7.fact: One of the strongest magnets today, invented by Sagawa Masato of Japan.
magnets:7.about:
In 1982, Sagawa Masato of Japan invented a very strong magnet made of neodymium, iron and boron. It's still one of the strongest magnets in the world.
They're small but strong, so they're used in lots of everyday machines, like smartphone speakers, earphones and electric car motors.

#senses: Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching. Let's compare our five senses with the amazing senses of animals.

senses:0.fact: They're said to see clearly 4 to 8 times further than people.
senses:0.about:
Eagles and hawks are said to see things clearly 4 to 8 times further away than people can. From high in the sky, they can spot a small rabbit on the ground.
In English, someone with sharp eyes is called "eagle-eyed."

senses:1.fact: They talk to faraway friends with low sounds people can't hear.
senses:1.about:
Elephants make sounds so low that human ears can't hear them, and they're thought to use them to talk to other elephants several kilometres away.
They've been found to feel the vibrations of these low sounds through the soles of their feet too.

senses:2.fact: Its sense of smell is thousands, even tens of thousands of times better than ours!
senses:2.about:
Deep inside a dog's nose are dozens of times more smell-sensing cells than in a person's, and its sense of smell is said to be thousands to tens of thousands of times stronger.
With that power, "working dogs" check luggage at airports and search for people in disasters.

senses:3.fact: The fifth taste, discovered by Ikeda Kikunae of Japan.
senses:3.about:
In 1908, Ikeda Kikunae of Tokyo Imperial University discovered that the delicious taste of kombu broth comes from a substance called "glutamic acid," and he named the taste "umami."
As the fifth taste after sweet, salty, sour and bitter, it's now called "umami" in English too, and it's studied all over the world.

senses:4.fact: "You only taste sweetness on the tip of your tongue" is wrong. You can taste everywhere on your tongue.
senses:4.about:
Old textbooks had a "tongue map" saying "sweet is at the tip and bitter is at the back," but it was wrong.
The "taste buds" that sense taste are spread all over the tongue, and every part can sense every taste.

senses:5.fact: Fingertips are very sensitive. Braille is read with the fingers too.
senses:5.about:
Fingertips are packed with sensors for touch, so they can feel bumps smaller than 1 mm.
People who are blind or can't see well read Braille with their fingertips. Braille is a writing system that Louis Braille of France thought up when he was about 15.

senses:6.fact: It senses its prey's body heat with holes between its eyes and nose.
senses:6.about:
Snakes like pit vipers and rattlesnakes have holes between their eyes and nose called "pit organs," which sense the body heat (infrared) of animals.
Even on a pitch-dark night, they can "see" the shape of their prey as heat.

senses:7.fact: It senses the tiny electricity of fish hiding in the sand.
senses:7.about:
On a shark's snout are lots of tiny holes called "ampullae of Lorenzini," which sense the tiny bits of electricity made by the muscles of living things.
With this sense, it can even find fish hiding in the sand.

senses:8.fact: They can see patterns on flowers that people can't.
senses:8.about:
Honeybees can see ultraviolet light, which people can't. Petals have patterns that only show up in ultraviolet, and they act as "landing markers" showing where the nectar is.
On the other hand, bees are said not to see the colour red well.

#nagasaki-prefecture: Nagasaki is a prefecture of islands and sea. Outside the city, there's lots of nature and history connected to the world!

nagasaki-prefecture:0.fact: A theme park that recreates a Dutch town.
nagasaki-prefecture:0.about:
Huis Ten Bosch is a theme park that recreates Dutch streets, canals and windmills. Its name means "house in the forest" in Dutch, taken from the name of a Dutch royal palace.
It's a place where you can feel Nagasaki's long connection with the Netherlands. Its winter illuminations are famous too.

nagasaki-prefecture:1.fact: Pottery for everyday dishes, with more than 400 years of history.
nagasaki-prefecture:1.about:
Hasami ware is pottery that has been made in Hasami for about 400 years. In the Edo period, potters made lots of tough, cheap rice bowls called "kurawanka bowls," which spread to ordinary people's tables.
Now its simple, stylish designs are popular. Every spring, lots of people come to the pottery fair.

nagasaki-prefecture:2.fact: One of the first places in Japan to be made a national park.
nagasaki-prefecture:2.about:
In 1934, Unzen was chosen along with Kirishima and the Seto Inland Sea as one of Japan's first national parks. It has "Unzen Jigoku" (Unzen Hells), where steam shoots out of the ground.
In the Meiji period, it was a busy summer resort for foreigners. You can enjoy the mountain views of Mount Fugen and the hot springs too.

nagasaki-prefecture:3.fact: A castle town where carp swim in canals of spring water.
nagasaki-prefecture:3.about:
Shimabara has more than 60 places where spring water from the mountains comes up, and colourful carp swim in its canals. It's called "the city of water."
It's the castle town of Shimabara Castle, and streets of samurai houses still remain. Its famous food is hand-stretched "Shimabara sōmen."

nagasaki-prefecture:4.fact: It has "Harunotsuji," the remains of a big village from more than 2,000 years ago.
nagasaki-prefecture:4.about:
Iki is an island between Kyushu and Tsushima. The "Harunotsuji site" is the remains of a big village from more than 2,000 years ago, and it's thought to be the capital of "Ikikoku," which appears in an old Chinese book, the "Records of Wei."
It's rich in seafood, and its sea urchin is famous.

nagasaki-prefecture:5.fact: About 50 km from South Korea. On clear days you can see Korean towns.
nagasaki-prefecture:5.about:
Tsushima is an island between Kyushu and South Korea, about 50 km from Busan. On clear days, you can see Korean towns. It has long been an island of exchange connecting Japan and the Korean Peninsula.
The Tsushima leopard cat lives on the island and is a national Natural Monument. About 90% of the island is mountains and forest.

nagasaki-prefecture:6.fact: More than 140 islands, known for beautiful seas and churches.
nagasaki-prefecture:6.about:
The Gotō Islands are a group of more than 140 islands west of Nagasaki. They have beautiful blue seas and white sand beaches, and plenty of seafood.
There are many old churches built of brick and stone, and some are part of a World Cultural Heritage Site. The famous food is thin "Gotō udon."

nagasaki-prefecture:7.fact: A port town that had a Dutch trading post before Nagasaki's Dejima.
nagasaki-prefecture:7.about:
In 1609, a Dutch trading post (a trading office) was set up in Hirado, and it was the centre of trade between Japan and Europe. In 1641, the trading post moved to Dejima in Nagasaki.
Today, a stone warehouse built in 1639 has been rebuilt and is a museum.

nagasaki-prefecture:8.fact: The world's first full-scale airport built on the sea.
nagasaki-prefecture:8.about:
Nagasaki Airport, opened in 1975 by enlarging an island in Ōmura Bay, was the world's first full-scale offshore airport.
Because it's on the sea, planes can take off and land without flying over towns, so there's less worry about noise. You get to the airport by crossing a bridge.

nagasaki-prefecture:9.fact: A beautiful view of the sun setting between 208 islands.
nagasaki-prefecture:9.about:
The Kujūku Islands in Sasebo are a beautiful sea with 208 islands. The sunset between the islands has been chosen as one of "Japan's 100 Best Sunsets."
You can tour between the islands by sightseeing boat or kayak. At the Kujūku Islands Aquarium, the jellyfish displays are popular.

#nagasaki-festivals: Nagasaki's year is full of festivals! Some were born from contact with China and the Netherlands.

nagasaki-festivals:0.fact: October 7th to 9th. Dragon dances and ship floats parade through the town.
nagasaki-festivals:0.about:
Nagasaki Kunchi is Nagasaki's autumn festival, held on October 7th to 9th, with almost 400 years of history since 1634. Each neighbourhood takes a turn once every 7 years as an "odori-chō" (dancing town) and performs for the shrine.
Performances influenced by China and the Netherlands are famous, like the dragon dance, Kokkodesho and the "hikimono," where huge ship floats are spun around. People shout "Motte kōi!" (Bring it back!) for an encore.

nagasaki-festivals:1.fact: A boat race from China. Rowers row to the rhythm of gongs and drums.
nagasaki-festivals:1.about:
Peiron is said to have started in 1655, when Chinese sailors in Nagasaki Harbour held a boat race to calm the waves.
About 30 people get into a long boat and row to the "don, den, jan" rhythm of gongs and drums. It's a summer tradition in Nagasaki.

nagasaki-festivals:2.fact: At Chinese New Year, about 15,000 lanterns decorate the city.
nagasaki-festivals:2.about:
The Nagasaki Lantern Festival grew from a Chinese celebration of the Lunar New Year (Spring Festival). Around Chinatown, about 15,000 lanterns and big displays decorate the city.
You can see a Chinese emperor's parade, lion dances and Chinese acrobatics. It's the two weeks when winter Nagasaki is at its brightest.

nagasaki-festivals:3.fact: On the night of August 15th, families send off handmade spirit boats.
nagasaki-festivals:3.about:
Shōrō Nagashi is a Nagasaki tradition on the night of August 15th to send off the spirits of people who died that year. Families and neighbours pull handmade spirit boats through the streets.
The noisy firecrackers and the "chankon, chankon" of bells ring through the whole city. It's a farewell that's very Nagasaki.

nagasaki-festivals:4.fact: In spring, Nagasaki kite flyers tangle strings to cut the other side's kite.
nagasaki-festivals:4.about:
In Nagasaki, kites are called "hata," and people enjoy kite flying in spring. "Hata battles," where kite strings coated with glass powder ("bīdoro yori") are tangled to cut the other kite's string, are famous.
Hata patterns are mostly red, white and blue, and some say this comes from the flags of Dutch ships.

nagasaki-festivals:5.fact: The hydrangea is Nagasaki City's flower. Siebold introduced it to the world.
nagasaki-festivals:5.about:
The hydrangea is Nagasaki City's flower. Siebold, a German doctor who came to Dejima in the Edo period, introduced hydrangeas to Europe and named one "Otaksa," after his Japanese wife, "O-Taki-san."
Every year in the rainy season, hydrangea festivals are held around the city.

nagasaki-festivals:6.fact: A summer festival in late July with fireworks over Nagasaki Harbour.
nagasaki-festivals:6.about:
The Nagasaki Port Festival is a summer festival held at Nagasaki Harbour at the end of July. Thousands of fireworks light up the sky over the harbour, and their reflections on the water are beautiful.
There are boat trips around the harbour and stage shows too. It's a treat at the start of the summer holidays.

#japanese-castles: High stone walls, white walls and towering keeps. Let's find out the secrets of Japanese castles.

japanese-castles:0.fact: Keeps, stone walls and moats. Full of ideas for keeping enemies out.
japanese-castles:0.about:
Japanese castles have a "tenshu" (keep) with a good view, "ishigaki" (stone walls) piled high so enemies can't climb them, and a water-filled "hori" (moat) around them.
The entrance gates twist and turn so that enemies can't charge straight in. The way the stones were piled up changed from period to period too.

japanese-castles:1.fact: Only 12 castles in Japan still have keeps from the Edo period or earlier.
japanese-castles:1.about:
Only 12 castles in Japan still have their original keeps built in the Edo period or earlier. Five of them, Himeji, Matsumoto, Inuyama, Hikone and Matsue, are National Treasures.
Most other keeps were rebuilt in the Shōwa period or later.

japanese-castles:2.fact: Called the "White Heron Castle" because it's so white. One of Japan's first World Heritage Sites.
japanese-castles:2.about:
Himeji Castle has beautiful white plaster walls, and because it looks like a white heron landing, it's called the "White Heron Castle."
In 1993, it became one of Japan's first World Cultural Heritage Sites, along with Hōryū-ji. Its keep from more than 400 years ago is still standing.

japanese-castles:3.fact: A National Treasure castle with black walls. It's also called the "Crow Castle."
japanese-castles:3.about:
Matsumoto Castle in Nagano is a National Treasure known for its black lacquered walls, and it's also called the "Crow Castle."
It looks beautiful with the mountains of the Northern Alps behind it, and inside the keep there are very steep stairs.

japanese-castles:4.fact: A small National Treasure keep looking down on the Kiso River.
japanese-castles:4.about:
Inuyama Castle in Aichi is a National Treasure castle standing on a hill overlooking the Kiso River. Its keep is said to be one of the oldest in Japan.
You can walk all the way around the top floor of the keep and enjoy a wonderful view.

japanese-castles:5.fact: A National Treasure castle by Lake Biwa.
japanese-castles:5.about:
Hikone Castle in Shiga is a National Treasure castle near Lake Biwa. Its keep from almost 400 years ago still stands.
Its mascot, "Hikonyan," is based on a legendary cat that saved a lord from lightning long ago.

japanese-castles:6.fact: A castle in a lake town that became a National Treasure in 2015.
japanese-castles:6.about:
Matsue Castle in Shimane stands in the "city of water" on the shores of Lake Shinji, and it became a National Treasure in 2015.
"Horikawa Meguri," a trip around the castle moat in a small boat, is popular. It has a calm look, with dark walls.

japanese-castles:7.fact: Golden shachihoko shine on its roof.
japanese-castles:7.about:
On the roof of Nagoya Castle's keep are shining golden "shachihoko," creatures with a tiger's head and a fish's body. Shachihoko were thought to be charms that protect against fire.
It's the symbol of Nagoya, and an old saying goes "Owari Nagoya is held up by its castle."

japanese-castles:8.fact: The keep today was built in 1931 with donations from the people of the city.
japanese-castles:8.about:
Osaka Castle comes from the castle built by Toyotomi Hideyoshi. The keep today was built in 1931 with donations from the people of Osaka, and inside is a history museum.
The huge stone walls around it include giant stones weighing more than 100 tonnes.

japanese-castles:9.fact: Famous for "mushagaeshi," curved stone walls. It's recovering from an earthquake.
japanese-castles:9.about:
Kumamoto Castle's stone walls curve more and more steeply towards the top, called "mushagaeshi" (warrior repellers), so nobody can climb them.
It was badly damaged in the 2016 Kumamoto earthquake, but repairs to the keep were finished in 2021. Work on the stone walls is still going on, and the people of the city are watching it come back fully.

japanese-castles:10.fact: A castle in Nagasaki, with a five-storey white keep.
japanese-castles:10.about:
Shimabara Castle in Shimabara, Nagasaki, was built at the start of the Edo period. The keep today was rebuilt in 1964, and its five white storeys are beautiful.
Inside the keep is a museum, and nearby are streets of samurai houses and canals where carp swim.

#trains-japan: On time, fast and clean. The history and famous trains of Japan's railways, which amaze the world.

trains-japan:0.fact: It linked Shimbashi and Yokohama in about 53 minutes.
trains-japan:0.about:
In 1872, Japan's first railway opened, running about 29 km between Shimbashi (Tokyo) and Yokohama. A journey that took half a day on foot now took about 53 minutes.
The locomotives were imported from Britain, and British engineers helped. October 14th is "Railway Day."

trains-japan:1.fact: "Degoichi." A steam locomotive of which more than 1,000 were built.
trains-japan:1.about:
The D51 steam locomotive was built from 1936, and with more than 1,000 made, it's the most-built steam locomotive in Japan. It was loved by the nickname "Degoichi."
It burns coal to boil water, and the steam powers it. Some steam trains still run as sightseeing trains today.

trains-japan:2.fact: The world's first high-speed railway, which started running in the year of the Tokyo Olympics.
trains-japan:2.about:
On October 1st, 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics, the Tōkaidō Shinkansen opened. The 0 Series Shinkansen ran at 210 km per hour and amazed the world as the first high-speed railway.
Its round nose was designed using aeroplane technology.

trains-japan:3.fact: A yellow Shinkansen that checks the tracks. People say "seeing it brings happiness."
trains-japan:3.about:
Doctor Yellow is a yellow Shinkansen that checks the condition of the tracks and wires as it runs. The days it ran weren't announced, so people said "if you see it, you'll be happy," and it was very popular.
On the Tōkaidō Shinkansen, it began to retire in 2025. Now checking machines are fitted to ordinary passenger trains instead.

trains-japan:4.fact: 320 km per hour. The fastest Shinkansen in service in Japan.
trains-japan:4.about:
The E5 Series "Hayabusa" runs at 320 km per hour on the Tōhoku Shinkansen. It's the fastest Shinkansen in passenger service in Japan.
Its long nose is shaped to reduce the "boom" when it goes into a tunnel. Look for its green and pink stripe.

trains-japan:5.fact: A Shinkansen that can run on its own battery when an earthquake cuts the power.
trains-japan:5.about:
The N700S, which made its debut in 2020, runs on the Tōkaidō Shinkansen. Even if the power goes off in an earthquake, it can run on its own batteries to a safe place nearby.
The "S" stands for "Supreme." Every seat has a power socket.

trains-japan:6.fact: Nagasaki's own Shinkansen, linking Takeo-Onsen and Nagasaki!
trains-japan:6.about:
The Nishi-Kyushu Shinkansen "Kamome" opened in September 2022, linking Takeo-Onsen Station in Saga and Nagasaki Station in as little as about 23 minutes.
It's white with red lettering. Nagasaki Station was rebuilt too, and more people now come to Nagasaki by Shinkansen.

trains-japan:7.fact: "Ching-ching trains" that have run through the city for more than 100 years.
trains-japan:7.about:
Nagasaki's streetcars opened in 1915 and have carried the people of the city for more than 100 years. They're called "ching-ching trains" after the sound of the bell when they set off.
Old trams are looked after and still used, and the fare is the same however far you go. They run along the flat parts of hilly Nagasaki.

trains-japan:8.fact: A loop line that goes all the way around Tokyo. One lap takes about an hour.
trains-japan:8.about:
Tokyo's Yamanote Line is a loop that links places like Tokyo, Shinjuku, Shibuya and Ikebukuro. One lap is about 35 km and takes about an hour.
At rush hour, trains come every 2 to 3 minutes. Each station has its own departure melody too.

trains-japan:9.fact: Reach your destination while you sleep. Now only the "Sunrise" is left.
trains-japan:9.about:
