Sleeper express trains leave at night and reach faraway towns while you sleep in a bed. Long ago, "Blue Trains" ran all over the country.
Now the only sleeper express that runs every day is the "Sunrise Izumo / Seto," linking Tokyo with San'in and Shikoku.

trains-japan:10.fact: A luxury sightseeing train that tours Kyushu for several days.
trains-japan:10.about:
"Seven Stars in Kyushu," which started running in 2013, is a luxury sleeper train that tours Kyushu over several days. It's named after Kyushu's 7 prefectures and 7 sightseeing attractions.
Traditional craft skills are used inside the train, and it's even called "a museum on wheels."

trains-japan:11.fact: The Tōkaidō Shinkansen's average delay is less than a minute!
trains-japan:11.about:
The average delay per train on the Tōkaidō Shinkansen over a year is said to be less than a minute. If it's even a few minutes late, there's an apology announcement at the station.
The punctuality of Japan's railways is thanks to the daily hard work of drivers, maintenance staff and station staff.

#crafts-japan: All over Japan, there are handcrafts that have been passed down for hundreds of years. Are there any in your home?

crafts-japan:0.fact: The first porcelain made in Japan. Even European kings collected it.
crafts-japan:0.about:
Arita ware is the first porcelain made in Japan, after the stone needed to make it was found in Arita, Saga, at the start of the Edo period. Bright blue and red pictures are painted on its white surface.
It was carried to Europe on Dutch ships from the port of Nagasaki, and kings and nobles collected it.

crafts-japan:1.fact: Wooden dolls born in the hot spring towns of Tōhoku.
crafts-japan:1.about:
Kokeshi are wooden dolls born near the end of the Edo period in hot spring towns in the Tōhoku region, as souvenirs for people who came to bathe.
The wood is shaped on a lathe, and the face and patterns are painted with a brush. Each area has its own shapes and patterns.

crafts-japan:2.fact: When your wish comes true, you paint in the other eye.
crafts-japan:2.about:
Daruma dolls are lucky charms for "fall down seven times, get up eight," because they pop back up when knocked over. When you make a wish, you paint in one eye, and when it comes true, you paint in the other.
Takasaki in Gunma is famous for making daruma; many of Japan's daruma are made there.

crafts-japan:3.fact: Sparkling patterns are cut into the surface of glass.
crafts-japan:3.about:
Edo kiriko is a glass craft that began in Tokyo at the end of the Edo period. Fine patterns are cut into the surface of coloured glass.
When light shines through, it sparkles beautifully. There are traditional patterns like "asa no ha" (hemp leaf) and "nanako" (fish roe).

crafts-japan:4.fact: Tough iron teapots. They're popular abroad too.
crafts-japan:4.about:
Nambu ironware from Iwate is an iron craft with almost 400 years of history. Its teapots and kettles with bumpy patterns on the surface are famous.
They're tough and last a long time, used by grandmothers and then by their grandchildren. Colourful teapots are popular in Europe too.

crafts-japan:5.fact: On UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list. Paper said to last 1,000 years.
crafts-japan:5.about:
Washi is Japanese paper made from the fibres of plants like kōzo (paper mulberry) and mitsumata. It's thin but strong, and it's said to last more than 1,000 years.
In 2014, "Washi, craftsmanship of traditional Japanese hand-made paper" was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list. Washi skills live on in shōji paper and banknote paper too.

crafts-japan:6.fact: A Kyoto skill for dyeing picture-like patterns onto kimono.
crafts-japan:6.about:
Kyō-yūzen is a skill for dyeing picture-like patterns onto kimono, said to have been spread by a painter called Miyazaki Yūzensai in the Edo period.
Lines are drawn with paste so the colours don't run, and colours are added one at a time with brushes. Long ago, you could see "yūzen nagashi," cloth being washed in Kyoto's rivers.

crafts-japan:7.fact: Expressive dolls made of fired clay and painted.
crafts-japan:7.about:
Hakata dolls are a traditional craft from Fukuoka, made by painting fired clay. Their faces are so expressive that they look alive.
There are all kinds: beautiful women, children, kabuki actors, seasonal events and more.

crafts-japan:8.fact: Folding fans are said to have been born in Japan.
crafts-japan:8.about:
Folding fans (sensu) are said to have been born in Japan around the Heian period. They started as "hiōgi," thin wooden slats tied together with thread.
They spread to China and Europe and came to be used all over the world. They're also props in rakugo and traditional Japanese dance.

crafts-japan:9.fact: A town of kitchen knives and scissors that inherited sword-making skills.
crafts-japan:9.about:
Seki in Gifu has thrived on making Japanese swords since the Kamakura period. It has carried on those skills, and today it's known around the world as a town of blades like kitchen knives, scissors and nail clippers.
It's said to be one of the "world's three great cutlery towns," along with Solingen in Germany and Sheffield in the UK.

crafts-japan:10.fact: Pottery from Nagasaki. Now it's popular for its stylish designs too.
crafts-japan:10.about:
Hasami ware from Nagasaki has been used to make lots of everyday dishes for about 400 years. Long ago, it was sometimes sold as Arita ware.
Now, with new designs like stackable mugs and simple plates, it's hugely popular with young people too.

#wagashi-seasons: Wagashi are sweets that let you taste the seasons. Let's travel through the year, from spring cherry blossoms to winter kagami-mochi.

wagashi-seasons:0.fact: In Kantō it's wrapped in a pancake; in Kansai it's made of grainy dōmyōji rice.
wagashi-seasons:0.about:
Sakura-mochi is a spring sweet wrapped in a salted cherry leaf. In Kantō, the classic is "Chōmei-ji," a thin pancake wrapped around red bean paste, and in Kansai it's "Dōmyō-ji," made of grainy sticky rice.
Whether you eat the leaf too is up to you!

wagashi-seasons:1.fact: A sweet for Children's Day. Its oak leaf carries a family wish.
wagashi-seasons:1.about:
Kashiwa-mochi is a rice cake wrapped in an oak leaf, eaten on Children's Day. Old oak leaves don't fall until new buds come out, so the leaf carries the wish "may the family carry on."
Inside there can be smooth bean paste, chunky bean paste or miso bean paste.

wagashi-seasons:2.about:
Mizu-yōkan is a summer sweet made softer than ordinary yōkan by adding more water. Eaten chilled, it's smooth and feels cool in your mouth.
In Fukui, there's a custom of eating it under the kotatsu in winter.

wagashi-seasons:3.fact: A wobbly summer sweet sprinkled with kinako.
wagashi-seasons:3.about:
Warabi-mochi is a wobbly sweet originally made from starch from bracken (warabi) roots. It's eaten with kinako (roasted soybean flour) and kuromitsu (black sugar syrup).
It's popular chilled on hot summer days. Now it's often made with other kinds of starch.

wagashi-seasons:4.fact: For moon-viewing, 15 dumplings are piled up into a pyramid.
wagashi-seasons:4.about:
For autumn moon-viewing on the night of the harvest moon, people decorate with pampas grass and offer 15 white dumplings piled up like a pyramid.
In some areas, people offer dumplings wrapped in red bean paste or long, thin dumplings.

wagashi-seasons:5.fact: An autumn sweet that lets you taste the sweetness of chestnuts as they are.
wagashi-seasons:5.about:
Kuri kinton is an autumn wagashi made by mashing steamed chestnuts with sugar and squeezing the mixture in a cloth into a chestnut shape. Nakatsugawa in Gifu is famous for it.
The "kuri kinton" in New Year osechi is a different dish: sweet potato paste with candied chestnuts.

wagashi-seasons:6.fact: Displayed at New Year, then eaten at "kagami biraki" around January 11th.
wagashi-seasons:6.about:
Kagami-mochi is two round rice cakes, a big one and a small one, displayed at New Year to welcome the New Year god. A daidai (a kind of orange) is placed on top with the wish "may the family prosper for generations."
At "kagami biraki" around January 11th, it's broken up with a wooden mallet and eaten in things like sweet red bean soup.

wagashi-seasons:7.fact: It's said to have been started by a Tokyo shop in the Meiji period.
wagashi-seasons:7.about:
Taiyaki is a baked sweet shaped like a sea bream, said to have been started around 1909, in the Meiji period, by a shop in Azabu-Jūban, Tokyo.
Sea bream is a lucky fish, but it was too expensive to buy, so it was a fun idea to have the shape at least. Do you eat it head first or tail first?

wagashi-seasons:8.fact: Named because its shape looks like a "dora," a gong.
wagashi-seasons:8.about:
Dorayaki is a sweet made of red bean paste sandwiched between two pieces of castella-like pancake. It got its name because its round shape looks like a "dora," a gong.
Now it's known abroad as "dorayaki" too.

wagashi-seasons:9.fact: Spiky sugar sweets that came to Nagasaki from Portugal.
wagashi-seasons:9.about:
Konpeitō are sugar sweets that came to Nagasaki from Portugal about 450 years ago, and their name comes from the Portuguese "confeito" (sugar sweet).
A big pan is turned while sugar syrup is added little by little over many days, slowly growing the spiky shapes.

#pref-hokkaido-tohoku: Japan's northern regions. Snow, apples and festivals! Summers are cool, and winters bring the fun of snow country.

pref-hokkaido-tohoku:0.fact: The biggest prefecture, about a fifth of Japan's area.
pref-hokkaido-tohoku:0.about:
Hokkaido produces more milk, potatoes, wheat and lots of other foods than anywhere else in Japan.
People from all over the world come to the "Sapporo Snow Festival" in winter.

pref-hokkaido-tohoku:1.fact: It grows more than half of Japan's apples.
pref-hokkaido-tohoku:1.about:
At the summer "Nebuta Festival," huge glowing figures on floats move through the town.
It's at the very north of Honshu, connected to Hokkaido by the Seikan Tunnel.

pref-hokkaido-tohoku:2.about:
"Wanko soba," where bowl after bowl of soba is tipped into your bowl, is famous.
It's the home town of Miyazawa Kenji, and Nambu ironware is made here too.

pref-hokkaido-tohoku:3.fact: Sendai's Tanabata Festival is said to be the most splendid in Japan.
pref-hokkaido-tohoku:3.about:
Matsushima, one of the Three Views of Japan, has about 260 islands floating in its bay.
Sendai is a green city called "the city of trees."

pref-hokkaido-tohoku:4.fact: The home of the Akita dog, famous because of Hachikō.
pref-hokkaido-tohoku:4.about:
At the summer "Kantō Festival," people balance long poles hung with lots of paper lanterns on their hands and foreheads.
Hot pot with "kiritanpo," rice grilled on sticks like chikuwa, is a famous dish.

pref-hokkaido-tohoku:5.fact: About 70% of Japan's cherries come from Yamagata.
pref-hokkaido-tohoku:5.about:
"Imoni-kai," parties where taro is stewed in huge pots, are an autumn treat.
In winter on Mount Zaō, you can see "snow monsters," trees covered in snow and ice.

pref-hokkaido-tohoku:6.about:
"Akabeko," a folk toy from the Aizu area, is a red cow doll with a nodding head.
Lots of delicious farm produce grows here, like peaches, pears and rice.

#pref-kanto: The region around Tokyo, Japan's capital. About a third of Japan's people live here.

pref-kanto:0.fact: Japan's capital, home to about 14 million people.
pref-kanto:0.about:
There's lots to see, like Tokyo Skytree, Asakusa and Shibuya.
In fact, Tokyo also includes islands far to the south, like the Ogasawara Islands.

pref-kanto:1.fact: Yokohama Chinatown is the biggest Chinatown in Japan.
pref-kanto:1.about:
Kamakura has a Great Buddha about 11 m tall.
Yokohama is a city where the port opened at the end of the Edo period and Western culture came in.

pref-kanto:2.fact: A prefecture with no sea, but the highest share of its area covered by rivers in Japan.
pref-kanto:2.about:
Kawagoe, "Little Edo," still has streets of old storehouses and its "Bell of Time."
It also makes more hina dolls than anywhere else in Japan.

pref-kanto:3.fact: About 80% of Japan's peanuts come from Chiba.
pref-kanto:3.about:
Narita Airport is one of Japan's main gateways by air.
Surfing is popular on the seas of the Bōsō Peninsula.

pref-kanto:4.fact: Number one in Japan for melons.
pref-kanto:4.about:
Kairakuen in Mito is one of Japan's Three Great Gardens and is famous for plum blossoms.
In Tsukuba Science City, research into space and science goes on.

pref-kanto:5.fact: Number one in Japan for strawberries.
pref-kanto:5.about:
The three wise monkeys of Nikkō Tōshō-gū, "see no evil, speak no evil, hear no evil," are famous.
Utsunomiya is known as "the gyōza city."

pref-kanto:6.fact: It grows more than 90% of Japan's konnyaku potatoes.
pref-kanto:6.about:
Kusatsu Onsen is one of Japan's most famous hot spring towns, known for "yumomi," stirring the hot water with big boards.
The Tomioka Silk Mill is a World Heritage Site. Lots of daruma are made here too.

#pref-chubu: The region with the Japanese Alps and Mount Fuji. From rice country to the kingdom of fruit to towns of craftsmanship.

pref-chubu:0.fact: Rice country, competing for the top spot in Japan for rice.
pref-chubu:0.about:
The Shinano River, the longest in Japan, flows into the Sea of Japan here.
It gets lots of snow in winter and has lots of ski resorts.

pref-chubu:1.fact: At Tateyama's "Yuki no Ōtani," you can walk between walls of snow almost 20 m high.
pref-chubu:1.about:
White shrimp, called "the jewels of Toyama Bay," are a famous food.
It's a "town of medicine," where medicine sellers have travelled around the country for a long time.

pref-chubu:2.fact: Almost all of Japan's gold leaf is made in Kanazawa.
pref-chubu:2.about:
Kenroku-en is one of Japan's Three Great Gardens.
Traditional crafts like Wajima lacquerware and Kutani ware are thriving.

pref-chubu:3.fact: Many of Japan's dinosaur fossils have been found in Fukui.
pref-chubu:3.about:
The Dinosaur Museum in Katsuyama is one of the world's top dinosaur museums.
It makes more glasses frames than anywhere else in Japan.

pref-chubu:4.fact: Number one in Japan for grapes and peaches.
pref-chubu:4.about:
You can see beautiful views of Mount Fuji from the Fuji Five Lakes on its north side.
"Hōtō," thick noodles stewed with vegetables and miso, is a famous dish.

pref-chubu:5.fact: The Winter Olympics were held here in 1998.
pref-chubu:5.about:
It's "the roof of Japan," with mountains around 3,000 m high.
It's known as a prefecture where people live long lives. Its apples and lettuce are famous too.

pref-chubu:6.fact: The gasshō-style farmhouses of Shirakawa-gō are a World Heritage Site.
pref-chubu:6.about:
In "ukai" on the Nagara River, people use birds called cormorants to catch sweetfish.
Seki is known around the world as a town of blades.

pref-chubu:7.fact: Almost all of Japan's plastic model kits are made in Shizuoka.
pref-chubu:7.about:
Tea is grown in big tea fields at the foot of Mount Fuji.
Making instruments like pianos is a big industry here too.

pref-chubu:8.fact: Number one in Japan for manufacturing. It has lots of car factories.
pref-chubu:8.about:
The golden shachihoko of Nagoya Castle are its symbol.
"Nagoya-meshi," Nagoya food like miso katsu, hitsumabushi (grilled eel on rice) and chicken wings, is popular.

#pref-kinki: A region rich in history, where the capital was for more than 1,000 years. It has old temples and a city famous for eating till you drop.

pref-kinki:0.fact: A merchant city once called "the nation's kitchen."
pref-kinki:0.about:
As the city of "kuidaore" (eating till you drop), it's famous for takoyaki and okonomiyaki.
The Osaka-Kansai Expo was held here in 2025.

pref-kinki:1.fact: A city that was Japan's capital for about 1,000 years.
pref-kinki:1.about:
17 temples, shrines and a castle, like Kiyomizu-dera and Kinkaku-ji, are World Heritage Sites.
The Gion Festival is a summer festival with more than 1,000 years of history.

pref-kinki:2.fact: The line of 135 degrees east, which sets Japan's time, runs through it.
pref-kinki:2.about:
Himeji Castle is a white castle and a World Heritage Site.
The port city of Kobe has a foreign feel, with its old Western houses and Chinatown.

pref-kinki:3.fact: About 1,300 deer live in Nara Park.
pref-kinki:3.about:
Buildings from Japan's oldest times still stand here, like the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji and Hōryū-ji.
It's an old capital, where Heijō-kyō was built in 710.

pref-kinki:4.fact: The first place in the world to succeed in farming pearls.
pref-kinki:4.about:
In 1893, Mikimoto Kōkichi succeeded in farming pearls.
F1 races are held at Suzuka Circuit.

pref-kinki:5.fact: About a sixth of the prefecture is Lake Biwa.
pref-kinki:5.about:
Lake Biwa is "the water jar of Kinki," supplying water to people in Kyoto and Osaka too.
Shigaraki ware tanuki statues are famous.

pref-kinki:6.fact: Number one in Japan for ume plums and mikan oranges.
pref-kinki:6.about:
At Adventure World in Shirahama, 17 panda babies have been born and raised so far.
The Kumano Kodō is an ancient pilgrimage trail and a World Heritage Site.

#pref-chugoku-shikoku: Sand dunes, whirlpools and "Udon Prefecture"! Let's tour the two regions on either side of the Seto Inland Sea.

pref-chugoku-shikoku:0.fact: The prefecture with the fewest people in Japan.
pref-chugoku-shikoku:0.about:
You can even ride a camel on the Tottori Sand Dunes.
It's also one of the top places in Japan for landing crabs.

pref-chugoku-shikoku:1.fact: Iwami Ginzan, which once produced much of the world's silver, is a World Heritage Site.
pref-chugoku-shikoku:1.about:
Matsue Castle is a National Treasure.
It's also known for the shijimi clams of Lake Shinji and its beautiful sunsets.

pref-chugoku-shikoku:2.fact: The "Land of Sunshine," said to be the home of Momotarō.
pref-chugoku-shikoku:2.about:
Kōraku-en is one of Japan's Three Great Gardens.
It has a town famous for making jeans too.

pref-chugoku-shikoku:3.fact: Number one in Japan for oysters.
pref-chugoku-shikoku:3.about:
The great torii gate standing in the sea at Miyajima is part of a World Heritage Site.
Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, with noodles inside, is a famous dish.

pref-chugoku-shikoku:4.fact: Shimonoseki's pufferfish is called "fuku," which sounds like "good luck."
pref-chugoku-shikoku:4.about:
Akiyoshidai is the biggest karst plateau in Japan, with Akiyoshi-dō Cave underneath.
Kintai Bridge is a wooden bridge with 5 arches in a row.

pref-chugoku-shikoku:5.fact: The Naruto whirlpools can be up to about 20 m across!
pref-chugoku-shikoku:5.about:
More than a million people come to the "Awa Odori" dance festival in summer.
Almost all of Japan's sudachi citrus fruit comes from Tokushima.

pref-chugoku-shikoku:6.about:
Udon is so popular that it calls itself "Udon Prefecture."
The Great Seto Bridge connects it to Okayama.

pref-chugoku-shikoku:7.fact: Dōgo Onsen is one of the oldest hot springs in Japan.
pref-chugoku-shikoku:7.about:
It's a "land of mikan," with a huge number of kinds of citrus fruit.
It's the home town of Masaoka Shiki and is known as a town of haiku too.

pref-chugoku-shikoku:8.fact: The Shimanto River is called "Japan's last clear stream."
pref-chugoku-shikoku:8.about:
It's the home town of Sakamoto Ryōma.
"Tataki," bonito seared over burning straw, is a famous dish.

#pref-kyushu-okinawa: Our Kyushu! Volcanoes, hot springs and southern islands. Let's see what each prefecture is proud of.

pref-kyushu-okinawa:0.fact: The prefecture with the most people in Kyushu.
pref-kyushu-okinawa:0.about:
Hakata's food stalls and mentaiko (spicy cod roe) are famous.
Students preparing for exams visit Dazaifu Tenmangū, the shrine of the god of learning.

pref-kyushu-okinawa:1.fact: Number one in Japan for nori seaweed, from the Ariake Sea.
pref-kyushu-okinawa:1.about:
It's the home of pottery like Arita ware and Imari ware.
The Yoshinogari site is the remains of a big village from the Yayoi period.

pref-kyushu-okinawa:2.fact: The prefecture with the most islands in Japan.
pref-kyushu-okinawa:2.about:
In the Edo period, it became Japan's window to Europe through Dejima.
It has flavours born from contact with other countries, like castella, champon and sara udon.

pref-kyushu-okinawa:3.fact: Number one in Japan for watermelons and tomatoes.
pref-kyushu-okinawa:3.about:
Mount Aso has one of the biggest calderas in the world.
Kumamoto Castle is still being restored after the earthquake.

pref-kyushu-okinawa:4.fact: "Onsen Prefecture," with the most hot springs and the most hot spring water in Japan.
pref-kyushu-okinawa:4.about:
The hot springs of Beppu and Yufuin are famous.
Almost all of Japan's kabosu citrus fruit comes from Ōita.

pref-kyushu-okinawa:5.fact: "Japan's sunny spot," with lots of hours of sunshine.
pref-kyushu-okinawa:5.about:
Ripe mangoes are a famous food.
It's also famous for the beautiful Takachiho Gorge and as a place where professional baseball teams hold training camps.

pref-kyushu-okinawa:6.fact: Number one in Japan for sweet potatoes.
pref-kyushu-okinawa:6.about:
Sakurajima is a volcano that still sends up smoke.
Yakushima was one of Japan's first World Natural Heritage Sites.

pref-kyushu-okinawa:7.fact: Japan's most southwestern prefecture, with more than 160 islands.
pref-kyushu-okinawa:7.about:
It has its own culture, with coral reef seas, sanshin music and eisā dancing.
It's also known for having lots of people who live long lives.

#african-mammals: Gorillas, chimpanzees, black rhinos… Africa has so many more animals to meet!

african-mammals:0.fact: Big males have silver backs and are called "silverbacks."
african-mammals:0.about:
Mountain gorillas live in the volcanic forests of Rwanda, Uganda and the Congo. Thanks to work to protect them, their numbers are slowly growing.
They're very strong but gentle, and they live in family groups.

african-mammals:1.fact: An ape that uses tools, fishing for termites with twigs.
african-mammals:1.about:
Chimpanzees are one of our closest animal relatives, sharing about 98% of their genes with humans.
Each group has its own "culture," like cracking nuts with stones.

african-mammals:2.fact: A friendly ape that lives only south of the Congo River.
african-mammals:2.about:
Bonobos look a lot like chimpanzees, but they fight less, and females hold the group together.
They're studied as peaceful apes that avoid fights by being friendly.

african-mammals:3.fact: Its big horns join together on top of its head.
african-mammals:3.about:
African buffalo live in big herds of hundreds, and they'll even stand up to lions.
When one of the herd is attacked, they sometimes all go to help.

african-mammals:4.fact: It can jump 3 m high and 10 m long.
african-mammals:4.about:
Impalas are very nimble antelopes. When they sense danger, the whole herd leaps high into the air and runs away.
Only males have long, spiralling horns.

african-mammals:5.fact: It uses its pointed upper lip to pick leaves off trees.
african-mammals:5.about:
Black rhinos fell a lot in number because of poaching for their horns, but conservation work is helping them slowly recover.
Their colour is almost the same as white rhinos'. The difference is the shape of the mouth.

african-mammals:6.fact: A scaly mammal that rolls up into a ball to protect itself.
african-mammals:6.about:
A pangolin's scales are made of the same material as our fingernails. It has no teeth and licks up ants with its long tongue.
It's one of the most poached mammals in the world, and protecting it is urgent.

african-mammals:7.fact: A penguin that lives on the warm coasts of Africa.
african-mammals:7.about:
African penguins call with a "donkey-like" bray. At Boulders Beach in South Africa, you can see them living right next to people.
The fish they eat are decreasing, and their numbers have fallen a lot.

african-mammals:8.fact: A small primate with big eyes and ears that's active at night.
african-mammals:8.about:
Galagos make huge leaps from tree to tree at night. Their calls sound like a baby crying, so they're called "bush babies."
They move their big ears to pick out even the tiny sounds of insects.

african-mammals:9.fact: The biggest zebra, with thin stripes.
african-mammals:9.about:
Grévy's zebras have thin stripes and big round ears.
Every zebra's stripes are different, so they can be used to tell zebras apart, like human fingerprints.

#asian-mammals: Elephants, rhinos, monkeys with amazing noses. Asia's forests and grasslands have lots of rare animals.

asian-mammals:0.fact: It has smaller ears than an African elephant and a rounded back.
asian-mammals:0.about:
Asian elephants have worked alongside people for a long time. Females have almost no tusks.
They eat more than 150 kg of plants a day.

asian-mammals:1.fact: The smallest bear. It licks up honey with its long tongue.
asian-mammals:1.about:
The sun bear has an orange, sun-like patch on its chest.
Its tongue is 20 to 25 cm long, for licking honey and insects out of holes in trees.

asian-mammals:2.fact: It spends almost its whole life up in the trees.
asian-mammals:2.about:
Orangutan means "person of the forest" in Malay. Every night, it makes a new bed in the trees to sleep in.
Young ones live with their mothers for 7 to 8 years, learning how to live in the forest.

asian-mammals:3.fact: The males have huge, drooping noses.
asian-mammals:3.about:
The big nose of a male proboscis monkey is thought to make its calls louder and to impress females.
It's a good swimmer and crosses rivers with its webbed feet.

asian-mammals:4.fact: A slow-moving primate of the night. It has venom in its elbows.
asian-mammals:4.about:
The slow loris moves slowly through the night forest with its big eyes. It's a rare mammal with venom that comes from its elbows.
Its numbers are falling because they're caught to be sold as pets.

asian-mammals:5.fact: A one-horned rhino with skin that looks like armour.
asian-mammals:5.about:
Indian rhinos once fell to about 200, but conservation work has brought them back to more than 4,000. It's a success story for protecting animals.
They're good swimmers and live in grasslands near rivers.

asian-mammals:6.fact: The only truly wild horse in the world.
asian-mammals:6.about:
Przewalski's horse once disappeared from the wild, but it was bred in zoos and returned to the grasslands of Mongolia.
It has a short mane that stands up.

asian-mammals:7.fact: Bhutan's national animal. It looks like a mix of a goat and a cow.
asian-mammals:7.about:
The takin is a member of the cattle family that lives in steep mountains, and it's Bhutan's national animal.
The inside of its nose is wide, so it warms cold air before breathing it in.

asian-mammals:8.about:
The binturong lives in the trees and wraps its tail around branches to hold itself up.
The smell comes from its wee, which has the same chemical that gives popcorn its smell.

asian-mammals:9.fact: Cloud-like patterns and very long fangs.
asian-mammals:9.about:
The clouded leopard is a member of the cat family with long fangs for its size. It's a great climber and can even hang upside down from branches.
It's rarely seen and is still full of mysteries.

#americas-animals: From northern forests to southern grasslands, the Americas have lots of animals found nowhere else.

americas-animals:0.fact: The national bird of the USA. A big eagle with a white head.
americas-animals:0.about:
Bald eagles once fell a lot in number, but they recovered after harmful pesticides were banned.
The nests they build in trees can weigh more than 1 tonne.

americas-animals:1.fact: The heaviest land animal in North America.
americas-animals:1.about:
There were once tens of millions of American bison on the grasslands, but at one time they fell to fewer than 1,000. Now they're protected in places like national parks.
Even with their big bodies, they can run at about 55 km per hour.

americas-animals:2.fact: It feels for food in the water with its clever front paws.
americas-animals:2.about:
Its Japanese name means "washing bear," because the way it feels around in water with its front paws looks like "washing."
It's not originally from Japan, and escaped pets that have multiplied are causing problems.

americas-animals:3.fact: It sprays a smelly liquid more than 3 m away.
americas-animals:3.about:
Before spraying, a skunk warns you to "stay back" by stamping its feet and raising its tail.
Its black-and-white pattern is a sign that says "touch me and you'll smell!"

americas-animals:4.fact: It protects itself with bands of hard shell.
americas-animals:4.about:
The nine-banded armadillo is an unusual animal that always gives birth to identical quadruplets.
It can hold its breath for about 6 minutes and walk across the bottom of a river.

americas-animals:5.fact: With its 60 cm tongue, it eats 30,000 ants a day.
americas-animals:5.about:
The giant anteater has no teeth. It flicks its long tongue in and out 150 times a minute to lick up ants.
Babies ride on their mother's back.

americas-animals:6.fact: A huge beak that's a third of its body length.
americas-animals:6.about:
The toco toucan's beak is big but very light, with a sponge-like inside.
It's also been found to use its beak to give off heat and control its body temperature.

americas-animals:7.about:
Manatees are close relatives of elephants, and they eat about a tenth of their body weight in seagrass every day.
In winter they gather in rivers with warm springs. There's work to protect them from boat accidents.

americas-animals:8.fact: The biggest deer in the world. Its antlers can be 1.8 m wide.
americas-animals:8.about:
The moose is the biggest deer in the world, up to 2 m tall at the shoulder. It's a good swimmer and eats plants underwater too.
The male's big, flat antlers fall off every winter and grow back.

americas-animals:9.fact: It builds an underground "town" and lives in a big family.
americas-animals:9.about:
Prairie dogs are members of the squirrel family. They build underground towns of tunnels where thousands live together.
Their calls are said to tell the others what kind of danger is coming, like "a hawk!" or "a person!"

#australia-animals: Animals that raise babies in pouches, mammals that lay eggs! Australia is a treasure house of amazing animals.

australia-animals:0.about:
Wombat poo is cube-shaped, like dice. Wombats leave it on rocks to mark their territory.
Their pouch opens backwards, so no dirt gets in when they dig.

australia-animals:1.fact: A mammal that lays eggs. It senses electricity with its bill.
australia-animals:1.about:
The platypus is an egg-laying mammal with a bill like a duck and a tail like a beaver.
When the first specimen reached Britain, people thought it was a fake. Males have venomous spurs on their back legs.

australia-animals:2.fact: An egg-laying mammal, just like the platypus.
australia-animals:2.about:
The echidna's back is covered in spines, and when it senses danger, it digs into the ground so only its spines show.
It keeps its egg warm in a pouch on its belly, and the baby that hatches is called a "puggle."

australia-animals:3.fact: A meat-eating marsupial with an amazing screech.
australia-animals:3.about:
The Tasmanian devil is about the size of a small dog, but it has a very powerful bite.
Its numbers have fallen because of a disease that spreads between them, and people are working to protect groups without the disease.

australia-animals:4.fact: The "happiest animal in the world," which always seems to be smiling.
australia-animals:4.about:
The quokka is a small relative of the kangaroo, and the shape of its mouth makes it look like it's smiling.
It isn't very scared of people, but touching or feeding quokkas is not allowed.

australia-animals:5.fact: The second-biggest bird in the world. It runs at about 50 km per hour.
australia-animals:5.about:
The emu can't fly, but it runs fast on its long legs. Its eggs are a beautiful dark green.
Keeping the eggs warm and raising the chicks is the father's job.

australia-animals:6.fact: A big bird with a helmet-like crest on its head.
australia-animals:6.about:
The southern cassowary is a big bird with a blue neck and a "helmet" on its head. It swallows fruit whole and carries seeds all over the forest, so it's a "gardener of the forest."
Its claws are sharp, so it's dangerous to get close.

australia-animals:7.fact: It calls "ha-ha-ha!" like a person laughing.
australia-animals:7.about:
Laughing kookaburras call loudly together as a family in the morning and evening to announce their territory.
It's one of the biggest kingfishers in the world, and it even catches and eats snakes.

australia-animals:8.fact: A cockatoo with a yellow crown of feathers on its head.
australia-animals:8.about:
Sulphur-crested cockatoos are very clever. Research in Sydney found they learn how to open the lids of wheelie bins from each other.
They're long-lived birds that can sometimes live more than 80 years.

australia-animals:9.fact: It glides from tree to tree using the skin between its arms and legs.
australia-animals:9.about:
The sugar glider looks like a flying squirrel, but it's a marsupial with a pouch on its belly.
It loves sweet tree sap, which is where the "sugar" in its English name comes from.

australia-animals:10.fact: It spreads the frill around its neck to startle its enemies.
australia-animals:10.about:
When the frilled lizard is surprised, it spreads the frill around its neck like an umbrella and opens its mouth wide to scare off its attacker.
If that doesn't work, it stands up on its back legs and runs away.

#whales-dolphins: Whales and dolphins are mammals that live in the sea. Some have teeth, and some have baleen.

whales-dolphins:0.fact: The biggest toothed whale. It dives more than 2,000 m.
whales-dolphins:0.about:
The sperm whale has the biggest brain of any animal. Some even have marks on their bodies from fighting giant squid in the deep sea.
It talks to others and finds prey with "click-click" sounds.

whales-dolphins:1.fact: The king of the sea. Each family talks in its own "dialect."
whales-dolphins:1.about:
The orca is the biggest member of the dolphin family and has a black-and-white pattern.
Each group has its own ways of hunting and calling, passed down from mothers to their young.

whales-dolphins:2.fact: One of the smallest baleen whales.
whales-dolphins:2.about:
The minke whale is a baleen whale about 8 m long. It filters water through the "baleen plates" in its mouth to eat small shrimp and fish.
It's very curious and sometimes comes close to boats.

whales-dolphins:3.fact: A dolphin that loves to jump, seen in Japan's seas too.
whales-dolphins:3.about:
Its Japanese name, "kama iruka," means "sickle dolphin," because its back fin is shaped like a sickle.
It swims in groups of hundreds and sometimes plays by riding the waves made by boats.

whales-dolphins:4.fact: A small, smiley-faced porpoise with no back fin.
whales-dolphins:4.about:
The finless porpoise is a small porpoise about 1.8 m long, with no back fin. It lives in Japan's shallow seas and can be seen in Ōmura Bay and the Ariake Sea in Nagasaki too.
With its round head and smiley face, it's popular at aquariums.

whales-dolphins:5.fact: A pink dolphin that lives in rivers.
whales-dolphins:5.about:
The Amazon river dolphin is a river dolphin that turns pink as it grows up. It can bend its neck, so it swims skilfully between the trees of flooded forests.
In the Amazon, there are even legends of "dolphins that turn into people."

whales-dolphins:6.fact: One of the smallest dolphins, found only in New Zealand.
whales-dolphins:6.about:
Hector's dolphin is a small dolphin about 1.5 m long, with a round back fin like a mouse's ear.
Protected areas have been made to keep it safe from getting caught in fishing nets.

whales-dolphins:7.fact: A whale that travels almost 20,000 km every year.
whales-dolphins:7.about:
The gray whale scoops up mud from the seabed and filters out small shrimp and other creatures to eat.
Every year, it makes a long journey from northern seas to warm lagoons in Mexico to raise its calves.

whales-dolphins:8.fact: A dolphin with lots of white scars on its body.
whales-dolphins:8.about:
Risso's dolphins get whiter as they get older. The white lines are marks from playing with each other and from squid suckers.
It has a round head and a face with no beak.

whales-dolphins:9.fact: The most endangered dolphin family member in the world.
whales-dolphins:9.about:
The vaquita is a small porpoise about 1.5 m long, with black markings around its eyes.
Its numbers have fallen because of accidents in fishing nets, and there are said to be only about 10 left. Work to protect it continues.

whales-dolphins:10.fact: A big whale with white, bumpy patches on its head.
whales-dolphins:10.about:
North Pacific right whales can be told apart by the pattern of white bumps (callosities) on their heads.
They swim slowly, so long ago many were hunted, and there are still very few today.

#sharks-rays: Sharks have been in the sea since before the dinosaurs. Only a very few kinds of shark ever attack people.

sharks-rays:0.fact: It can smell prey several kilometres away.
sharks-rays:0.about:
The great white shark is a big shark that grows to 6 m long. It can keep its body warmer than the water, so it can swim fast even in cold seas.
Films make people afraid of it, but attacks on people are very rare.

sharks-rays:1.fact: With its T-shaped head, it sees a wide area and senses electricity.
sharks-rays:1.about:
The hammerhead shark has eyes at both ends of its head, so it can see almost 360 degrees. Its whole head senses the electricity of rays hiding in the sand.
In the daytime, they sometimes form big schools of hundreds.

sharks-rays:2.fact: When young, its body has stripes like a tiger.
sharks-rays:2.about:
The tiger shark eats almost anything; tyres and empty cans have even been found in their stomachs.
When it grows up, the stripes fade.

sharks-rays:3.fact: A mysterious big-mouthed shark discovered in 1976.
sharks-rays:3.about:
The megamouth is a big shark first found in Hawaii in 1976. It opens its huge mouth to eat plankton.
Many of the sightings so far have been in the seas near Japan. There's still a lot we don't know about it.

sharks-rays:4.fact: A deep-sea "living fossil" whose jaws shoot forward.
sharks-rays:4.about:
The goblin shark is a pink shark that lives in the deep sea, and its jaws shoot far forward the moment it catches prey.
Its Japanese name honours the Japanese zoologist Mitsukuri Kakichi. In English it's called the "goblin shark."

sharks-rays:5.fact: The second-biggest fish in the world. It filters plankton to eat.
sharks-rays:5.about:
The basking shark is a huge shark more than 10 m long, but it's gentle: it swims with its big mouth open and filters out tiny plankton to eat.
It's said to filter about a swimming pool's worth of water every hour.

sharks-rays:6.fact: A relaxed shark that rests quietly on the sea floor.
sharks-rays:6.about:
The nurse shark can pump water over its gills to breathe even without swimming, so it can rest still on the sea floor.
It catches prey in gaps between rocks by sucking hard with its mouth.

sharks-rays:7.fact: A deep-sea shark that has hardly changed in 300 million years.
sharks-rays:7.about:
The frilled shark is an eel-shaped shark with frilly edges on its gills.
Its pregnancy is said to last more than 3 years, one of the longest of any animal.

sharks-rays:8.fact: It catches fish by hitting them with its long, saw-like snout.
sharks-rays:8.about:
The sawfish looks like a shark, but it's actually a ray. Tooth-like spikes line both sides of its long snout.
Its snout senses the electricity of prey in the sand. It easily gets caught in nets, and people worry it will die out.

#noodles-world: "I like ramen." Noodles are loved all over the world. Every country has its own shapes and ways of eating them!

noodles-world:0.fact: Chinese noodles reborn in Japan as a national favourite.
noodles-world:0.about:
Ramen comes from Chinese noodle dishes and spread in the Meiji period from Chinatowns like Yokohama's.
In 1958, Andō Momofuku invented the world's first instant ramen, "Chicken Ramen."

noodles-world:1.fact: Thick and chewy. Kagawa is "Udon Prefecture"!
noodles-world:1.about:
Udon is a thick noodle made from wheat flour. Each area has its own kind, like Sanuki udon from Kagawa, Inaniwa udon from Akita and Gotō udon from Nagasaki.
Gotō udon is a thin udon stretched with camellia oil.

noodles-world:2.about:
Soba is made from the flour of the seeds of a plant called buckwheat (soba). On New Year's Eve, people eat "toshikoshi soba," wishing to live a long life, like a long noodle.
There was also a custom of giving soba to the neighbours when you moved house.

noodles-world:3.fact: Born in Nagasaki! Noodles packed with vegetables and seafood.
noodles-world:3.about:
Champon is said to have been made around 1899 by the owner of "Shikairō," a Chinese restaurant in Nagasaki, who wanted to give students from China a cheap, nourishing meal.
Its thick noodles are cooked in the soup. It spread all over Japan as a taste of Nagasaki.

noodles-world:4.about:
Phở is a Vietnamese dish of flat rice noodles in a clear beef or chicken broth.
It's eaten with lots of herbs, lime and bean sprouts on top. In Vietnam, it's a classic breakfast.

noodles-world:5.fact: A Thai street food of stir-fried rice noodles.
noodles-world:5.about:
Pad thai is a Thai dish of rice noodles stir-fried with shrimp, egg and bean sprouts, with a sweet-and-sour flavour.
It's eaten with peanuts and lime. It's a favourite at Thai street stalls.

noodles-world:6.fact: There are more than 300 shapes of pasta!
noodles-world:6.about:
Spaghetti is one kind of Italian pasta, and its name means "little strings." Pasta comes in more than 300 shapes, like butterfly-shaped farfalle and tube-shaped penne.
"Napolitan" spaghetti, which was born in Japan, isn't found in Italy.

noodles-world:7.fact: Dough is stretched again and again to make thin noodles in an instant!
noodles-world:7.about:
In places like Lanzhou in China, cooks pull dough with both hands and fold it again and again, making hundreds of thin noodles in an instant. They're called "lamian," which is said to be where the Japanese word "ramen" comes from.
The cooks' skill is like a show.

noodles-world:8.fact: A Korean dish of glass noodles made from sweet potato starch.
noodles-world:8.about:
Japchae is a Korean dish of glass noodles made from sweet potato starch, stir-fried with vegetables and meat and seasoned with sesame oil and soy sauce.
It's often served as a feast on special days.

noodles-world:9.fact: Noodles in a spicy coconut milk soup.
noodles-world:9.about:
Laksa is a noodle dish from Malaysia and Singapore, with a spicy soup of coconut milk and spices.
In some areas, laksa has a sour soup instead. It was born from a mix of Chinese and Malay cooking.

#bread-world: "Pan" is a Portuguese word! The world's breads come in all kinds of shapes and are made in all kinds of ways.

bread-world:0.fact: A long, thin French bread. The skill of making it is on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
bread-world:0.about:
The baguette is a French bread made only from flour, water, salt and yeast. Millions are eaten in France every day.
In 2022, the skills and culture of baguette making were added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

bread-world:1.fact: Shaped like a crescent moon. Its roots are an Austrian bread.
bread-world:1.about:
Croissant means "crescent" in French. Butter is folded into the dough in many layers to make it flaky.
It's said to have come from the "kipferl," a crescent-shaped Austrian bread that travelled to France.

bread-world:2.fact: A bread baked by sticking it to the wall of an oven.
bread-world:2.about:
Naan is a bread from places like India, baked by sticking it to the inside wall of a pot-shaped clay oven called a "tandoor."
In Indian homes, people often eat thin "chapati."

bread-world:3.fact: A flat bread with a hollow inside like a pocket.
bread-world:3.about:
Pita is a flat bread from the Middle East and the Mediterranean. When it's baked at a high temperature, it puffs up and makes a pocket inside.
People fill the pocket with vegetables, meat or "falafel," fried chickpea balls.

bread-world:4.fact: A thin Mexican flatbread made from corn flour.
bread-world:4.about:
Tortillas are thin flatbreads made from corn or wheat flour, used for tacos and burritos.
In Mexico, corn has been the staple food for thousands of years.

bread-world:5.fact: A German bread shaped like folded arms.
bread-world:5.about:
The pretzel is a German bread. Its surface is dipped in an alkaline liquid before baking, so it turns shiny brown.
This shape is used on bakery signs too.

bread-world:6.fact: A chewy ring-shaped bread that's boiled before it's baked.
bread-world:6.about:
Bagel dough is boiled first and then baked, which makes it chewy.
A bread of Jewish people in Poland came to New York with people who moved there, and it became famous.

bread-world:7.fact: Born in Japan. But there's no melon in it!
bread-world:7.about:
Melon pan is a Japanese bread baked with a layer of cookie dough on top. It got its name because the criss-cross pattern on top looks like a melon.
Now it's popular in places like Taiwan and Hong Kong too.

bread-world:8.fact: A blend of Japanese and Western, made by a Tokyo bakery in the Meiji period.
bread-world:8.about:
In 1874, Kimuraya in Ginza, Tokyo, made anpan by wrapping red bean paste in bread dough. It became hugely popular as a bread that suited Japanese tastes.
It's known for the salted cherry blossom in the middle.

bread-world:9.fact: A flat Italian bread made with lots of olive oil.
bread-world:9.about:
Focaccia is an Italian bread baked with lots of olive oil brushed on the dough. The dimples on top are made by pressing with your fingers.
Sometimes it's baked with rosemary, salt or tomatoes on top.

#street-food: "What would you like? — I'd like takoyaki." Let's tour the world's flavours from street stalls.

street-food:0.about:
Takoyaki is said to have been born around 1935 at a street stall in Osaka. It's cooked on an iron plate with round holes, turned around and around as it cooks.
It's eaten with sauce, mayonnaise, katsuobushi and green laver.

street-food:1.fact: Chicken on skewers, grilled over charcoal.
street-food:1.about:
Yakitori is chicken cut into bite-sized pieces, put on skewers and grilled over charcoal. It's flavoured with either "tare" (sauce) or "shio" (salt).
There are lots of kinds for different parts, like thigh, breast and tsukune (meatballs).

street-food:2.fact: Born in France, it became a sweet treat in Harajuku.
street-food:2.about:
Crêpes are thin French pancakes. In France, buckwheat "galettes" are wrapped around egg or ham for a meal.
In Japan in the 1970s, the style of wrapping cream and fruit in crêpes and eating them while walking spread in Harajuku.

street-food:3.fact: A Mexican classic: meat and vegetables wrapped in tortillas.
street-food:3.about:
Tacos are corn tortillas topped with grilled meat, vegetables and salsa, eaten with your hands.
In Mexico, street stalls are open from morning to night. In 2010, traditional Mexican cooking was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

street-food:4.fact: Southeast Asian skewers eaten with sweet peanut sauce.
street-food:4.about:
Satay is grilled skewers from Indonesia and Malaysia. Chicken or beef is soaked in spices and grilled over charcoal.
It's eaten dipped in a sweet, rich peanut sauce.

street-food:5.fact: Star-shaped fried dough. You dip them in chocolate.
street-food:5.about:
Churros are a Spanish treat made by piping dough through a star-shaped nozzle and frying it.
In Spain, people dip them in thick hot chocolate for breakfast.

street-food:6.fact: A drink born in Taiwan in the 1980s.
street-food:6.about:
Bubble tea was born in tea shops in Taiwan in the 1980s. The tapioca pearls are made from the starch of a root called cassava.
The chewy pearls you suck up through a fat straw are popular, and it spread all over the world.

street-food:7.fact: Melty brown sugar syrup inside! A Korean winter snack.
street-food:7.about:
Hotteok is a Korean snack: dough filled with brown sugar and nuts, pressed flat and cooked on a hot plate.
The syrup inside is very hot when it's freshly cooked, so eat it carefully.

street-food:8.fact: Grilled corn spread with mayonnaise and cheese.
street-food:8.about:
Elote is grilled corn on the cob from Mexican street stalls, eaten with mayonnaise, cheese, chilli powder and lime.
Corn is a crop that first came from Mexico.

street-food:9.fact: A huge block of meat that cooks as it spins.
street-food:9.about:
Döner kebab, which was born in Türkiye, is thin slices of meat stacked into a big block, cooked as it turns on a vertical spit, and shaved off the outside to eat.
It's eaten in bread with vegetables. It's very popular in Germany too.

#soups-world: Hot soups and cold soups. The world's soups warm your body and your heart.

soups-world:0.fact: On the table every day. Miso is made by fermenting soybeans.
soups-world:0.about:
Miso soup is a Japanese soup made by mixing miso into dashi broth, with things like tofu, wakame seaweed and green onions.
Miso is made by fermenting soybeans, kōji and salt for months. Different areas have white miso, red miso, barley miso and more.

soups-world:1.fact: A spicy and sour Thai shrimp soup.
soups-world:1.about:
Tom yum goong is a spicy, sour Thai soup made with lemongrass, lime and chillies. "Goong" means shrimp.
In 2024, tom yum goong was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

soups-world:2.fact: An Italian soup packed with vegetables.
soups-world:2.about:
Minestrone is an Italian soup of tomatoes, lots of vegetables, beans and small pasta, all cooked together.
There's no set recipe; it's made with whatever seasonal vegetables are in the house.

soups-world:3.fact: A cold tomato soup made without any cooking.
soups-world:3.about:
Gazpacho is a cold Spanish soup made by blending tomatoes, cucumber, peppers, bread and more.
It's drunk on hot summer days and called "a salad you drink."

soups-world:4.fact: A creamy soup of clams and potatoes.
soups-world:4.about:
Clam chowder is a soup of clams and potatoes, famous in places like Boston on America's east coast.
Boston style is white and creamy, and New York style is red and tomatoey. Sometimes it's served in a bread bowl.

soups-world:5.fact: In Japan, you can even buy it from vending machines!
soups-world:5.about:
Corn potage is a thick, smooth soup made of mashed corn and milk.
In Japan, hot cans of corn soup are sold in vending machines in winter, which surprises people from other countries.

soups-world:6.fact: Onions are slowly fried, then it's topped with cheese and baked.
soups-world:6.about:
French onion soup is made by frying onions slowly for a long time until they're brown and sweet, then topping it with bread and cheese and baking it in the oven.
People working at the markets in Paris used to eat it as a late-night meal.

soups-world:7.fact: A seaweed soup eaten on birthdays in South Korea.
soups-world:7.about:
Miyeok-guk is a Korean seaweed soup that mothers eat to get their strength back after having a baby.
So there's a custom of eating it on birthdays, as a way of saying "thank you for giving birth to me."

soups-world:8.fact: Hot soup in hot summer! A Korean dish to give you energy.
soups-world:8.about:
Samgyetang is a Korean soup of a whole young chicken stuffed with sticky rice, ginseng and jujubes and simmered.
In South Korea, people eat hot samgyetang on the hottest days of the year to beat summer tiredness.

#tropical-fruits: Spiky, fluffy and star-shaped! Let's look at the amazing fruits of hot countries.

tropical-fruits:0.fact: The fruit of a kind of cactus.
tropical-fruits:0.about:
Dragon fruit is the fruit of a plant in the cactus family, with pink skin covered in scale-like flaps. Inside it's white or red, with lots of tiny black seeds.
Its flowers open at night and close by morning. It's grown in Okinawa too.

tropical-fruits:1.fact: "The king of fruits." It smells so strong that some countries ban it on trains!
tropical-fruits:1.about:
The durian is a big, spiky fruit with sweet, creamy flesh and a very, very strong smell.
In Singapore, you're not allowed to take durians on the underground.

tropical-fruits:2.fact: Clear white fruit inside a red, scaly skin.
tropical-fruits:2.about:
The lychee is a fruit from southern China. When you peel off its red, rough skin, you find soft, white, jelly-like fruit.
There's a story that an ancient Chinese emperor's consort loved lychees so much that she had them brought from far away by horse.

tropical-fruits:3.fact: A hairy fruit. Its name means "hair" in Malay.
tropical-fruits:3.about:
The rambutan is a fruit with red skin covered in lots of soft hairs, and its name comes from the Malay word "rambut" (hair).
Inside is white fruit like a lychee, sweet and juicy.

tropical-fruits:4.fact: "The queen of fruits." White fruit inside a purple skin.
tropical-fruits:4.about:
The mangosteen is a fruit with white segments like a mikan inside a hard, deep purple skin. Its delicate sweetness has earned it the name "the queen of fruits."
The number of "petals" in the pattern on its bottom is the same as the number of segments inside.

tropical-fruits:5.fact: A sweet fruit, and also a vegetable when it's green.
tropical-fruits:5.about:
Papaya is a sweet orange fruit, but green (unripe) papaya is used as a vegetable in salads and stir-fries.
In Okinawa, "papaya irichī," stir-fried green papaya, is a home-cooked favourite.

tropical-fruits:6.fact: A sweet-and-sour fruit you eat seeds and all.
tropical-fruits:6.about:
Passion fruit comes from South America. Inside its hard skin are lots of seeds wrapped in jelly, and you scoop them out with a spoon and eat them, seeds and all.
Its flower looks like a clock, so in Japanese the plant is called "tokeisō" (clock plant).

tropical-fruits:7.about:
Star fruit has 5 pointed ridges, so when you slice it, it makes beautiful star shapes.
It's used to decorate salads and desserts too. It has a fresh, sweet-and-sour taste.

tropical-fruits:8.fact: The biggest fruit that grows on a tree. It can weigh up to 50 kg!
tropical-fruits:8.about:
Jackfruit is a huge fruit that grows straight from the trunk, and it can weigh 30 to 50 kg. It's the biggest tree fruit in the world.
The sweet flesh is eaten as fruit, and unripe jackfruit is cooked as a meat substitute.

tropical-fruits:9.fact: A seed that floats across the sea to faraway islands.
tropical-fruits:9.about:
The coconut is the fruit of the coconut palm. People drink the juice inside (coconut water), and the white flesh is made into coconut milk and oil.
Coconuts float, so they can drift thousands of kilometres across the sea and sprout on faraway islands.

#spices: Pepper was once as valuable as gold! The story of spices that make food delicious.

spices:0.fact: "Black gold," once as valuable as gold.
spices:0.about:
Pepper is the fruit of a climbing plant from southern India. In Europe long ago, it was so valuable that it was sometimes used instead of money.
The "Age of Discovery," when European ships set off for Asia, began partly so people could get spices like pepper.

spices:1.fact: A spice made of dried tree bark.
spices:1.about:
Cinnamon is the bark of a tree in the laurel family, peeled off and dried, so it curls up into rolls.
It's used in apple pie, chai and Kyoto's yatsuhashi sweets (as "nikki").

spices:2.fact: A root used all over the world that warms you up.
spices:2.about:
Ginger is a spice that uses the underground stem (the part that looks like a root). It has a zingy heat and a fresh smell.
It's used in all kinds of food, like "gari" with sushi, shōga-yaki (ginger pork) and ginger ale.

spices:3.fact: What makes curry yellow. In Japanese it's called "ukon."
spices:3.about:
Turmeric is a yellow spice made from the dried root of a plant in the ginger family, and it's what gives curry its colour.
Its colour is so strong that long ago it was also used to dye cloth yellow.

spices:4.fact: It comes from the Americas. Its heat is measured in "Scoville" units.
spices:4.about:
Chilli peppers originally came from the Americas. After Columbus and others took them back to Europe about 500 years ago, they spread all over the world.
Measured in "Scoville" units of heat, the hottest chilli in the world is millions of times hotter than an ordinary green pepper.

spices:5.fact: A Japanese spice grown in clean spring water.
spices:5.about:
Real wasabi is the stem of a plant native to Japan, grown in "wasabi fields" with cold, clean spring water flowing through them. Shizuoka and Nagano are famous for it.
When it's grated, it makes a heat that shoots up your nose. The wasabi with sushi also takes away the fishy smell.

spices:6.fact: A Japanese spice that makes your tongue tingle and go numb.
spices:6.about:
Sanshō is the fruit of a Japanese tree in the citrus family, sprinkled on grilled eel. When you eat it, your tongue tingles and goes numb.
"Sanshō may be small, but it's hot" is a saying about people who are small but very talented.

spices:7.fact: The most expensive spice in the world, made from flowers.
spices:7.about:
Saffron is made by picking the stigmas of a kind of crocus flower one by one by hand and drying them. It takes more than about 150 flowers to make 1 g.
The yellow colour of Spanish paella comes from saffron.

spices:8.fact: The fruit of an orchid. A 12-year-old boy discovered how to grow it!
spices:8.about:
Vanilla is made by fermenting the pods of an orchid from Mexico. Outside Mexico, there were no bees to carry its pollen, so it didn't make pods.
In 1841, on an island in the Indian Ocean, a 12-year-old boy called Edmond Albius discovered how to pollinate the flowers by hand, and vanilla could then be grown all over the world.

spices:9.fact: A mix of dozens of kinds of spices.
spices:9.about:
Curry powder is a mix of dozens of kinds of spices, like turmeric, cumin and coriander. It was made in Britain based on Indian cooking and came to Japan in the Meiji period.
Japan's thick curry rice is now one of Japan's favourite national dishes.

#simple-machines: Levers, pulleys and wheels. Ideas for doing big jobs with small forces have been used for thousands of years.

simple-machines:0.fact: Fulcrum, effort and load. A long bar can lift heavy things!
simple-machines:0.about:
A lever is a bar resting on one point, used to move heavy things with a small force. Seesaws, scissors and claw hammers are levers too.
Archimedes of ancient Greece is said to have said, "Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth."

simple-machines:1.fact: A rope and a wheel make lifting heavy things easy.
simple-machines:1.about:
A pulley is a tool made of a rope over a wheel with a groove. With a moving pulley, you can lift things with half the force.
Pulleys are used in well buckets, flagpoles and cranes on building sites.

simple-machines:2.fact: Doorknobs and steering wheels both use this idea.
simple-machines:2.about:
When a big wheel and a thin axle turn together, turning the big wheel with a little force makes a big force at the axle.
Doorknobs, bicycle pedals, car steering wheels and taps all use this idea.

simple-machines:3.fact: A slope makes it easier to push heavy things up.
simple-machines:3.about:
Things that are hard to lift straight up can be raised with a small force using a gentle slope (an inclined plane). But you have to move them a longer distance.
Ramps, winding mountain roads and maybe even the building of the ancient pyramids use this idea.

simple-machines:4.fact: The blades of axes and knives are wedge-shaped.
simple-machines:4.about:
A wedge is a pointed, triangle-shaped tool. When you hammer it in, it makes a big sideways force, so it can split or cut things.
Axes, kitchen knives, nails and doorstops are all kinds of wedges.

simple-machines:5.fact: A slope that goes round and round. Archimedes made a screw that lifts water.
simple-machines:5.about:
A screw is a slope wrapped around a rod. When you turn it, it can hold things very tightly or move things with a small force.
The "Archimedes' screw," named after Archimedes, is a tool that turns a screw to carry water from low places up to high places.

simple-machines:6.fact: Gears of different sizes can change speed and force.
simple-machines:6.about:
Gears are wheels with jagged teeth that fit together and turn. By combining big gears and small gears, you can change how fast they turn and how strong the force is.
There are gears in bicycles, clocks and toys.

simple-machines:7.fact: Robots from Edo-period Japan! A doll that carries tea.
simple-machines:7.about:
Karakuri dolls were made in Edo-period Japan and moved using springs and gears. When you put a teacup on the "tea-serving doll," it walks to the guest, and when the empty cup is put back, it turns around and goes back.
They're said to be the roots of robot-making in Japan.

#electricity: Press a switch and the light comes on. Let's explore the mysteries of invisible electricity.

electricity:0.fact: Take off a jumper and… zap! A tiny bit of what electricity really is.
electricity:0.about:
When things rub together, tiny particles that carry electricity (electrons) move from one to the other, making static electricity.
In ancient Greece, people knew that rubbing amber made dust stick to it. The word "electricity" comes from the Greek word for "amber."

electricity:1.fact: Giant static electricity in the clouds. Hundreds of millions of volts in one strike!
electricity:1.about:
Lightning is giant static electricity made when bits of ice crash into each other inside clouds. One strike can be hundreds of millions of volts.
In 1752, Franklin in America used a kite to show that lightning is electricity (it's extremely dangerous, so never try it).

electricity:2.fact: The first battery, made by Volta in Italy.
electricity:2.about:
In 1800, Volta in Italy stacked copper and zinc plates to make a "battery" that kept giving electricity. The unit of voltage, the "volt," comes from his name.
Now we use batteries that can be recharged again and again, like the lithium-ion batteries in smartphones. Yoshino Akira of Japan won a Nobel Prize for helping develop them.

electricity:3.fact: When the path for electricity makes a loop, electricity flows.
electricity:3.about:
The path that electricity takes from a battery, through wires, lighting up a bulb and back to the battery, is called a "circuit."
A switch is a "gate" that joins or breaks this path. Try making one in a science experiment!

electricity:4.fact: Metals let electricity through. Rubber and plastic don't.
electricity:4.about:
Metals like iron, copper and aluminium let electricity through easily; they're "conductors." Rubber, glass and plastic don't let electricity through; they're "insulators."
Inside a cable is copper wire, and around it is plastic, so it's safe to touch.

electricity:5.fact: They make electricity by turning turbines.
electricity:5.about:
At many power stations, flowing water, steam or wind turns a bladed wheel called a "turbine," and magnets and coils make electricity.
Solar power turns light straight into electricity, without any turbine.

electricity:6.fact: The "War of the Currents" between Edison and Tesla!
electricity:6.about:
Electricity from a battery flows in one direction; that's "direct current" (DC). Electricity from a wall socket changes direction dozens of times a second; that's "alternating current" (AC).
In the 1880s, Edison, who backed DC, competed with Tesla and others, who backed AC, and AC, which is easier to send long distances, spread.

electricity:7.fact: An electric light was lit for the first time in Tokyo.
electricity:7.about:
On March 25th, 1878, the first electric light in Japan (an arc lamp) was lit at the Imperial College of Engineering in Tokyo. This day is now "Electricity Day."
Then, in 1887, a business sending electricity to homes started in Tokyo.

electricity:8.fact: Switch off electricity you're not using.
electricity:8.about:
Much of our electricity is still made by burning coal and gas, which gives off carbon dioxide.
Little ideas protect the Earth: switching off the lights when you leave a room, changing the air conditioner's temperature a little, and switching to LEDs.

#light-color: Why do rainbows appear? Why is the sky blue? Let's solve the mysteries of light.

light-color:0.fact: In Japan rainbows have 7 colours. But the number of colours is different in different countries.
light-color:0.about:
A rainbow appears when sunlight goes into drops of water in the air and each colour bends at a different angle and separates. You see it with the sun behind you.
In Japan rainbows have 7 colours, but some people in America say 6 and some in Germany say 5. How colours are counted depends on culture.

light-color:1.fact: White light is really a mix of lots of colours.
light-color:1.about:
Around 1666, Newton in England used a glass prism to split sunlight into rainbow colours, showing that white light is a mix of light of many colours.
The back of a CD looks rainbow-coloured because light splits up there too.

light-color:2.fact: Because blue light bumps into the air and scatters easily.
light-color:2.about:
When sunlight hits the tiny particles in air, blue light scatters the most. That blue light spreads across the whole sky, so the sky looks blue.
Space has no air, so to astronauts the sky looks pitch black even in the daytime.

light-color:3.fact: In the evening, light travels a long way, and only red light gets through.
light-color:3.about:
In the evening the sun is low, so its light travels a long way through the air. The blue light scatters away on the way, and only red and orange light reaches our eyes.
There's a saying: "A red sunset means a sunny day tomorrow."

light-color:4.fact: They bounce light back and show you a back-to-front reflection.
light-color:4.about:
A mirror bounces light back almost exactly as it is, so it shows the shapes of things. The you in the mirror is back to front.
"AMBULANCE" is written back to front on the front of ambulances so it reads the right way in the rear-view mirror of the car in front.

light-color:5.fact: They bend light to make things look bigger.
light-color:5.about:
A lens is a tool that bends light. A "convex lens," which bulges in the middle, makes things look bigger. Lenses are used in magnifying glasses, glasses, cameras, microscopes and telescopes.
If you use a magnifying glass in the sunshine, the light focuses and gets very hot, so be careful.

light-color:6.fact: The dark area where light is blocked.
light-color:6.about:
Light travels in straight lines, so when something blocks it, a shadow forms behind it. In the morning and evening, when the sun is low, shadows get long.
People long ago made "sundials" that tell the time from the direction and length of shadows.

light-color:7.fact: Mixing light makes white, but mixing paint makes it darker.
light-color:7.about:
The three primary colours of light are red, green and blue. Put all three together and you get white. TV and smartphone screens make every colour from these three.
The three primary colours of paint are magenta, cyan and yellow, and the more you mix them, the darker they get.

light-color:8.fact: A tool with two mirrors for seeing over a wall.
light-color:8.about:
A periscope has two mirrors set at an angle inside a tube. It bounces light twice so you can see things from a high or hidden place.
Submarines use them to look above the sea from underwater. You can even make one from milk cartons.

#sound-science: Sound is things "shaking." How does it reach our ears?

sound-science:0.fact: If you touch a drum skin, you can feel it shaking.
sound-science:0.about:
Sound is made when something vibrates and shakes the air around it. That shaking travels like a wave and reaches our ears.
When you speak, you can feel the vibration if you put your hand on your throat.

sound-science:1.fact: About 340 m a second in air. More than 4 times faster in water!
sound-science:1.about:
Sound travels about 340 m a second in air. It's even faster in water, about 1,500 m a second, and in iron, about 5,000 m a second.
You can work out how far away lightning is from the time between the flash and the thunder.

sound-science:2.fact: Shout "Yoo-hoo!" at a mountain, and the sound bounces back.
sound-science:2.about:
Sound bounces back when it hits walls or mountains. That's why your voice comes back when you shout in the mountains (an echo).
Bats and dolphins use these echoes to learn what's around them.

sound-science:3.fact: Your voice travels through the shaking string.
sound-science:3.about:
If you join paper cups with string, pull it tight and talk, the vibrations of your voice travel along the string and shake the other cup, so your friend can hear you.
If the string goes slack or you pinch it, you can't hear anymore, because the vibrations can't get through.

sound-science:4.fact: The shorter, thinner and tighter the string, the higher the sound.
sound-science:4.about:
The faster something vibrates, the higher the sound, and the slower it vibrates, the lower the sound. A guitar's thin strings make high notes and its thick strings make low notes.
If you tap glasses with water in them, the note changes with the amount of water.

sound-science:5.fact: The smallest bone in your body is in your ear.
sound-science:5.about:
Inside your ear, vibrations in the air shake your "eardrum," three tiny bones make the vibrations bigger, and they pass them to the spiral-shaped "cochlea." There they turn into electrical signals and go to your brain.
The smallest bone, the "stirrup," is about the size of a grain of rice.

sound-science:6.fact: An ambulance siren sounds lower after it goes past.
sound-science:6.about:
When something making a sound comes towards you, the sound waves get squashed together and sound higher; when it moves away, the waves stretch out and sound lower. This is called the "Doppler effect."
Astronomers use the Doppler effect of light to check whether stars are moving away from us.

sound-science:7.fact: Space has no air, so sound can't travel there.
sound-science:7.about:
Sound travels as vibrations in things like air and water, so it can't travel in space, where there's no air. Even if there were a huge explosion in space, you wouldn't hear anything.
Astronauts talk by radio. If they touch their space helmets together, their voices can sometimes get through.

#water-cycle: The water you drink might be water a dinosaur drank long ago! Water's journey around the Earth.

water-cycle:0.fact: Water in seas and rivers, warmed by the sun, turns into invisible water vapour.
water-cycle:0.about:
When the sun's heat warms the water in seas, rivers and the ground, the water turns into invisible "water vapour" and rises into the sky. Washing drying on the line is evaporation too.
Most of the Earth's evaporation is from the sea.

water-cycle:1.fact: Water vapour cools high in the sky and turns into tiny drops of water.
water-cycle:1.about:
High in the sky the air is cold, so the rising water vapour cools down and turns into tiny drops of water or bits of ice. When lots of them gather, they make a cloud.
Water drops forming on the outside of a cold glass work the same way.

water-cycle:2.fact: When cloud drops get big, they get heavy and fall.
water-cycle:2.about:
When drops in a cloud bump into each other and grow, they get heavy and fall to the ground as rain or snow.
Japan is a rainy country, getting about twice as much rain as the world average.

water-cycle:3.fact: Rain that falls on the mountains becomes rivers and goes back to the sea.
water-cycle:3.about:
Rain that falls on the ground gathers into small streams, which become rivers flowing to the sea.
Japan's rivers are short and steep, so rain that falls on the mountains rushes quickly to the sea. That's why dams are used to store water.

water-cycle:4.fact: Water that soaks into the ground takes years to become spring water.
water-cycle:4.about:
Some rain soaks into the ground and becomes "groundwater," flowing slowly between soil and rocks. It takes years, sometimes decades, to come out of the ground as spring water.
The spring water in Shimabara, Nagasaki, is rain that fell on the Unzen mountains and travelled underground.

water-cycle:5.fact: Only about 2.5% of the Earth's water is fresh water, and most of that is ice.
water-cycle:5.about:
About 97.5% of the Earth's water is sea water, and only about 2.5% is fresh water. Most of that fresh water is ice in Antarctica and Greenland.
Water that people can use easily, like rivers and lakes, is only a tiny amount. Water is a precious resource.

water-cycle:6.fact: The Earth's water goes round and round and never runs out.
water-cycle:6.about:
The Earth's water has been going round for hundreds of millions of years, changing form from evaporation to clouds, rain, rivers and seas. Hardly any is newly made or lost.
So some of the water you drank today might once have been drunk by a dinosaur.

water-cycle:7.fact: People in Japan use about 200 L of water each per day.
water-cycle:7.about:
In Japan, each person uses about 200 L of water a day. Most of it goes on baths, toilets, cooking and washing clothes.
If you leave the tap running while you brush your teeth, about 12 L flows away in a minute. Just using a cup saves water.

#states-of-matter: Ice, water and steam. The same water can change its form! Let's explore the three states of matter.

states-of-matter:0.about:
Things can be in three states: a "solid," whose shape doesn't change; a "liquid," whose shape changes freely; and a "gas," which is sometimes invisible.
When the temperature changes, the same thing can change its state.

states-of-matter:1.fact: Water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C.
states-of-matter:1.about:
Water turns to ice below 0°C and boils into water vapour at 100°C. These temperatures became the basis of the Celsius scale.
On top of a mountain, the air pressure is lower, so water boils below 100°C.

states-of-matter:2.fact: Most things are heavier as solids, but water is the opposite!
states-of-matter:2.about:
Most things shrink and get heavier (denser) when they become solid, but water gets about 10% bigger when it freezes, so it gets lighter. That's why ice floats on water.
Thanks to this, lakes freeze from the top in winter, and fish can survive in the water below.

states-of-matter:3.fact: Sometimes things turn straight into a gas without melting.
states-of-matter:3.about:
On very cold, dry days, snow and ice can turn straight into a gas without becoming water. This is called "sublimation."
Dry ice, and ice cubes slowly shrinking in the freezer, work this way too.

states-of-matter:4.fact: Hard when you hit it, runny when you touch it slowly.
states-of-matter:4.about:
If you mix potato starch with a little water, you get an amazing goo that's hard like a solid when you hit it, but flows like a liquid when you touch it gently.
It's called "dilatancy," a property where something behaves differently depending on how force is applied.

states-of-matter:5.fact: 1 L of air weighs about 1.2 g.
states-of-matter:5.about:
Even invisible air has weight: 1 L weighs about 1.2 g. The air in a whole classroom weighs about 200 kg!
Air is always pushing on us, but our bodies push back with the same force from the inside, so we don't notice.

states-of-matter:6.fact: Warm air gets lighter and rises.
states-of-matter:6.about:
When air is warmed, it expands, gets lighter and rises. Hot-air balloons float by heating the air inside with a burner.
In 1783, the Montgolfier brothers in France flew the first hot-air balloon carrying people. Every autumn, a world-famous balloon festival is held in Saga.

states-of-matter:7.fact: The "fourth state," after solid, liquid and gas.
states-of-matter:7.about:
When a gas is made very hot or has a strong electric current passed through it, it turns into a state called "plasma" and gives off light.
Lightning, the aurora, the Sun and neon signs are all plasma. Most of the visible things in the universe are made of plasma.

#volcanoes-world: Places where hot magma from inside the Earth comes out. Volcanoes make islands and hot springs too.

volcanoes-world:0.fact: Underground magma bursts out of cracks in the ground.
volcanoes-world:0.about:
"Magma," melted rock inside the Earth, is lighter than the rock around it, so it rises. The places where it comes out are volcanoes.
Japan has 111 active volcanoes, about 10% of the world's active volcanoes.

volcanoes-world:1.fact: A belt of volcanoes that goes all the way around the Pacific.
volcanoes-world:1.about:
Around the Pacific Ocean, volcanoes line up in a ring along the edges of the plates, called the "Pacific Ring of Fire." Many of the world's volcanoes are here.
Japan, Indonesia, Chile and the west coast of the USA are on this ring too.

volcanoes-world:2.fact: Japan's highest mountain (3,776 m) is a volcano too.
volcanoes-world:2.about:
Mount Fuji is still an active volcano, and its last eruption was the "Hōei eruption" in 1707. Volcanic ash even fell on the city of Edo.
Its beautiful cone shape was made by layers built up over many eruptions. It became a World Cultural Heritage Site in 2013.

volcanoes-world:3.fact: A Hawaiian volcano where red-hot lava flows.
volcanoes-world:3.about:
Kīlauea on the Big Island of Hawaiʻi is one of the most active volcanoes in the world. Its runny lava flows like a river, pouring into the sea and making new land.
In Hawaiʻi, the legend of "Pele," the goddess of volcanoes, is treasured.

volcanoes-world:4.fact: The biggest volcano in the world by volume. Measured from the sea floor, it's about 9,000 m!
volcanoes-world:4.about:
Mauna Loa on the Big Island of Hawaiʻi is about 4,170 m above sea level, but measured from the sea floor, it's about 9,000 m. It's the biggest volcano in the world by volume.
Because of its gentle shape, it's called a shield volcano, "like a shield lying on the ground."

volcanoes-world:5.fact: On Mars, the biggest volcano in the solar system.
volcanoes-world:5.about:
Olympus Mons on Mars is about 22 km tall, about 6 times the height of Mount Fuji, making it the biggest volcano in the solar system. Its base is about as big as Honshu.
Mars has no moving plates, so it kept erupting in the same place and grew huge.

volcanoes-world:6.fact: A moon of Jupiter. The most volcanically active place in the solar system.
volcanoes-world:6.about:
Jupiter's moon Io has more than 400 active volcanoes, the most volcanic activity in the solar system.
Jupiter's strong gravity squeezes the inside of the moon and heats it up. Its yellowish colour comes from sulphur.

volcanoes-world:7.fact: "The lighthouse of the Mediterranean," which has been erupting for thousands of years.
volcanoes-world:7.about:
Stromboli in Italy has small eruptions every few minutes to every few dozen minutes. At night its red glow can be seen from far away, and sailors long ago used it as a landmark.
Small eruptions like these are called "Strombolian eruptions."

volcanoes-world:8.fact: A volcano born from a Mexican cornfield in 1943.
volcanoes-world:8.about:
In 1943, the ground in a Mexican farmer's field cracked open and smoke started coming out. In one year, it became a mountain more than 300 m tall.
It's one of the world's rare examples where people could watch a volcano being born from the very start.

volcanoes-world:9.fact: Hot springs, geothermal power and rich soil.
volcanoes-world:9.about:
