Volcanoes aren't only dangerous; they also give us lots of gifts, like hot springs, geothermal power and volcanic ash soil where crops grow well.
Many of Kyushu's hot springs, like those in Ōita, Kagoshima and Unzen in Nagasaki, are thanks to volcanoes.

#clouds: Look up at the sky. Sometimes you can tell how the weather will change from the shapes of clouds.

clouds:0.fact: Howard in England gave clouds Latin names.
clouds:0.about:
In 1802, an English chemist called Luke Howard sorted clouds by shape and gave them names like "cumulus," "stratus" and "cirrus." His ideas are still used today.
Clouds are divided into 10 types by height and shape.

clouds:1.fact: Clouds like candyfloss on a sunny day.
clouds:1.about:
Cumulus clouds are white, puffy clouds seen on sunny days, also called "cotton clouds." They form when the ground warms up and air rises.
When these clouds keep growing taller, they become cumulonimbus clouds.

clouds:2.fact: More than 10 km tall. Clouds of thunder and heavy rain.
clouds:2.about:
Cumulonimbus clouds tower up like mountains and are often seen in summer. Their tops can be more than 10 km high.
When one comes near, there can be thunder, heavy rain and hail. If you see one, go inside a building early.

clouds:3.fact: The highest clouds, made of ice.
clouds:3.about:
Cirrus clouds form very high up, 5 to 13 km, and look like they've been brushed on with a thin brush. They're made of tiny bits of ice.
When cirrus clouds increase, it can be a sign that the weather is about to turn bad.

clouds:4.fact: Autumn sky clouds that look like fish scales.
clouds:4.about:
Cirrocumulus clouds are made of lots of little cloud puffs in rows, also called "sardine clouds" in Japanese. They're an autumn season word in haiku.
They form high in the sky, so they look very small.

clouds:5.fact: Round clouds like a flock of sheep.
clouds:5.about:
Altocumulus clouds are round clumps of cloud lower than cirrocumulus. They look like a flock of sheep.
You can tell them apart because each clump looks bigger than in cirrocumulus.

clouds:6.about:
Fog forms when air near the ground cools and water vapour turns into tiny drops of water. It's just like a cloud that has come down to the ground.
If you can't see 1 km ahead, it's called "fog"; if you can see further, it's called "mist."

clouds:7.fact: Clouds made when water vapour from plane engines cools.
clouds:7.about:
Contrails are clouds made when water vapour from the engines of planes flying high in the sky freezes straight away in the cold air.
On days when contrails last a long time, the air is damp, and it can be a sign that the weather will turn bad.

clouds:8.fact: A hat-like cloud on top of Mount Fuji.
clouds:8.about:
Cap clouds and lenticular clouds are UFO-shaped clouds made by damp wind blowing over mountains. They're often seen on Mount Fuji.
There's a saying, "When Mount Fuji wears a hat, it will rain," and they're said to be a sign that the weather will turn bad.

#constellations: Join the stars in the night sky with lines, and stories appear. People all over the world have made constellations.

constellations:0.fact: Worldwide, the whole sky is divided into 88 constellations.
constellations:0.about:
People all over the world have made constellations since ancient times, but in 1922 the International Astronomical Union decided to divide the whole sky into 88 constellations.
Many of them are people and animals from ancient Greek myths.

constellations:1.fact: The star of the winter night sky. Look for its three stars in a row.
constellations:1.about:
Orion is a constellation of a hunter from Greek myth, seen in the southern sky in winter. Look for the three stars lined up in the middle.
Betelgeuse, the red star at the top left, is an old star about 1,000 times the size of the Sun. In Japan, it was called "tsuzumi-boshi" because of its drum-like shape.

constellations:2.fact: Follow the shape of the dipper, and you'll find the North Star.
constellations:2.about:
The Big Dipper is part of Ursa Major (the Great Bear), with 7 stars in the shape of a ladle. If you extend the two stars at the end of the ladle by 5 times their distance, you'll find the North Star.
The North Star hardly moves, so travellers have used it to find north since ancient times.

constellations:3.fact: A W-shaped constellation. Another way to find the North Star.
constellations:3.about:
Cassiopeia is a constellation of 5 bright stars in the shape of a W (or M), seen all year in the northern sky.
It's named after Queen Cassiopeia from Greek myth, and it's on the opposite side of the North Star from the Big Dipper.

constellations:4.fact: In the southern summer sky. Antares, the red star at its heart.
constellations:4.about:
Scorpius is an S-shaped constellation seen in the southern sky in summer. Antares, the red star where the scorpion's heart would be, means "rival of Mars."
In the myth, the scorpion defeated Orion, so people say the two are never in the sky at the same time.

constellations:5.fact: A cluster of stars in Taurus. Sei Shōnagon praised "Subaru" too.
constellations:5.about:
Subaru is a group of stars (a star cluster) in Taurus, and you can see 6 or 7 stars with your eyes. In English it's called the "Pleiades."
"The Pillow Book" from the Heian period says "Of the stars, Subaru is best," and it has been loved by Japanese people for a long time.

constellations:6.fact: A Southern Hemisphere constellation. It's on flags like Australia's.
constellations:6.about:
The Southern Cross (Crux) is the smallest of the 88 constellations, but it stands out in the Southern Hemisphere. Sailors long ago used it to find south.
In Japan, you can see it for a short time in spring from southern islands of Okinawa.

constellations:7.fact: Birthday constellations are the ones along the Sun's path.
constellations:7.about:
The 12 constellations along the path the Sun takes through the stars over a year (the ecliptic) are called the "12 zodiac constellations." Birthday constellations come from these.
But around your birthday, your constellation is in the daytime sky with the Sun, so you can't see it.

constellations:8.fact: Our galaxy, seen from the side.
constellations:8.about:
The Milky Way is how the stars of our own galaxy, the "Milky Way Galaxy," where our solar system is, look from the inside. Hundreds of billions of stars are gathered there.
In English it's called the "Milky Way," from a Greek myth about a goddess's milk spilling across the sky.

constellations:9.fact: Town lights are making the stars harder to see.
constellations:9.about:
When town lights make the night sky brighter and stars harder to see, it's called "light pollution." In big cities, you can hardly see the Milky Way.
There's work to protect starry skies too, and places like Bisei in Ibara, Okayama, have been certified as "Dark Sky Places."

#comets-asteroids: Comets with long tails and small rocky asteroids. A Japanese probe even brought sand back from an asteroid!

comets-asteroids:0.fact: A comet that comes back about every 76 years. Next time is 2061.
comets-asteroids:0.about:
Halley's Comet comes back near the Earth about every 76 years. In 1705, Halley in England predicted "the same comet will come back," and it really did.
The last time was 1986. The next time you can see it is 2061.

comets-asteroids:1.fact: Their tails always point away from the Sun.
comets-asteroids:1.about:
A comet is a "dirty snowball" made of ice and dust. When it gets close to the Sun, the ice melts and it gives off gas and dust, making a long tail.
The wind from the Sun pushes it, so the tail always points away from the Sun.

comets-asteroids:2.fact: Millions of asteroids between Mars and Jupiter.
comets-asteroids:2.about:
Between Mars and Jupiter is the "asteroid belt," where millions of small bodies made of rock and metal, called "asteroids," are gathered.
But they're very far apart, so space probes can pass through without hitting any.

comets-asteroids:3.fact: It was the first in the world to bring back sand from an asteroid, Itokawa.
comets-asteroids:3.about:
The Japanese probe "Hayabusa" landed on the asteroid Itokawa and came back to Earth in 2010. It was the first probe in the world to bring back sand from an asteroid.
It overcame lots of problems, like engine trouble, and took 7 years to get back.

comets-asteroids:4.fact: It brought back stones from the asteroid Ryugu, and building blocks of life were found.
comets-asteroids:4.about:
Hayabusa2 landed on the asteroid Ryugu, collected stones from under the surface too, and delivered them to Earth in 2020.
In those stones, amino acids, which are building blocks of life, and signs of water were found. It's still travelling on to another asteroid.

comets-asteroids:5.fact: Space dust that glows when it shoots into the atmosphere.
comets-asteroids:5.about:
A shooting star is a tiny bit of space dust that shoots into the Earth's atmosphere at tens of kilometres a second and glows from rubbing against the air.
Around the "Perseid meteor shower" in August and the "Geminid meteor shower" in December, you can sometimes see dozens an hour.

comets-asteroids:6.fact: Stones from space that fell to the ground.
comets-asteroids:6.about:
A stone from space that reaches the ground without burning up is called a "meteorite."
The "Nōgata meteorite" in Nōgata, Fukuoka, is recorded as falling in 861, and it's said to be the oldest meteorite in the world that people saw fall.

comets-asteroids:7.fact: About 66 million years ago, a big asteroid hit Mexico.
comets-asteroids:7.about:
About 66 million years ago, an asteroid about 10 km across hit what's now the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. The Earth's climate changed a lot, and it's thought that many dinosaurs died out.
But birds are still alive today as the descendants of dinosaurs.

comets-asteroids:8.fact: A spacecraft was crashed into an asteroid to change its path.
comets-asteroids:8.about:
In 2022, NASA in the USA deliberately crashed the spacecraft "DART" into the asteroid Dimorphos and succeeded in changing its path.
It was an experiment to find a way to protect the Earth from asteroids heading our way in the future.

#space-japan: "I want to be an astronaut." Let's follow the story of Japan's astronauts and rockets.

space-japan:0.fact: A TV reporter who was the first Japanese person to go to space.
space-japan:0.about:
In 1990, TV reporter Akiyama Toyohiro went to the Soviet space station "Mir," becoming the first Japanese person to travel to space.
He's also known for asking, during a broadcast from space, "Is this live?"

space-japan:1.fact: The first Japanese astronaut to fly on the Space Shuttle.
space-japan:1.about:
In 1992, Mōri Mamoru flew on the American Space Shuttle "Endeavour" and did lots of experiments in space.
He's famous for saying, "I couldn't see any borders from space."

space-japan:2.fact: The first Japanese woman in space. She was a doctor.
space-japan:2.about:
In 1994, Mukai Chiaki, a heart doctor, became the first Asian woman to go to space.
She did an experiment raising medaka fish eggs in space, and the medaka born in space made the news.

space-japan:3.fact: The centre of Japan's space research and development.
space-japan:3.about:
JAXA (the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) was formed in 2003 when three organisations joined together. It works on rockets, satellites, space probes and astronaut training.
You can visit the Tsukuba Space Center in Ibaraki.

space-japan:4.fact: Japan's laboratory on the International Space Station.
space-japan:4.about:
"Kibō" is Japan's laboratory module on the International Space Station (ISS), attached in 2008 and 2009. It's the biggest laboratory on the ISS.
It can do experiments that are only possible in space, and it can even release small satellites into space.

space-japan:5.fact: A Japanese supply ship that delivered cargo to the space station.
space-japan:5.about:
"Kounotori" (HTV) was a Japanese spacecraft that carried food, water and experiment equipment to the International Space Station. All 9 missions, from 2009 to 2020, were successful.
Its way of docking, by being caught with a robot arm, became a model for the world.

space-japan:6.fact: He was the first Japanese commander of the ISS.
space-japan:6.about:
Wakata Kōichi is an astronaut who has been to space 5 times, and in 2014 he became the first Japanese commander of the International Space Station.
He has spent more than 500 days in space in total.

space-japan:7.fact: A pinpoint Moon landing, right where it aimed!
space-japan:7.about:
In January 2024, Japan's small lunar lander "SLIM" landed on the Moon, making Japan the fifth country to land successfully on the Moon.
It was a very accurate "pinpoint landing," within 100 m of where it aimed.

space-japan:8.about:
The H3 rocket is Japan's new main rocket, and it was launched successfully in February 2024. It's designed to be cheaper than the H-IIA before it and to launch more often.
It's launched from the Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima. Tanegashima is said to be "the most beautiful rocket launch site in the world."

#moons: Not just our Moon: other planets have lots of moons too.

moons:0.fact: About 380,000 km away. It's moving away by 3.8 cm every year.
moons:0.about:
The Moon is about 380,000 km away, about 30 Earths. Even light takes about 1.3 seconds to get there.
The Moon is slowly moving away from the Earth, by about 3.8 cm a year.

moons:1.fact: In about 29.5 days, it goes from new moon to full moon and back to new moon.
moons:1.about:
The Moon doesn't shine by itself; it shines by reflecting sunlight. As the positions of the Moon, Sun and Earth change, the part that looks bright changes.
From one new moon to the next is about 29.5 days. The "month" of the old calendar was based on these phases of the Moon.

moons:2.fact: The Moon always shows the same face to the Earth.
moons:2.about:
In the time it takes the Moon to go around the Earth once, it also spins exactly once itself. So from the Earth, we only ever see the same side.
The far side of the Moon was first photographed by a Soviet probe in 1959.

moons:3.fact: In Japan, it's a rabbit pounding mochi. People see different things in different countries.
moons:3.about:
The dark patterns on the Moon are flat areas, called "seas," where lava spread out long ago.
In Japan, people see "a rabbit pounding mochi," but in southern Europe some see "a crab," in Arabia "a roaring lion," and among some Native Americans "a woman's face."

moons:4.fact: Humans walked on the Moon for the first time.
moons:4.about:
In July 1969, Commander Armstrong of America's Apollo 11 became the first human to stand on the Moon. His words, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind," are famous.
There's no wind on the Moon, so his footprints are thought to still be there.

moons:5.fact: The four big moons that Galileo found.
moons:5.about:
In 1610, Galileo in Italy used a telescope to find Jupiter's four big moons. One of them, Europa, is thought to have a big ocean under its ice.
Ganymede is the biggest moon in the solar system, bigger than Mercury.

moons:6.fact: A moon of Saturn with lakes and rivers of liquid methane.
moons:6.about:
Titan, a moon of Saturn, is a big moon covered by a thick atmosphere. Instead of water like on Earth, very cold liquid methane falls as rain and forms lakes and rivers.
In the 2030s, a drone-like probe called "Dragonfly" is planned to fly around and explore it.

moons:7.fact: A moon of Saturn that shoots water out of its icy surface.
moons:7.about:
Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, is a pure white icy moon that sprays water out into space from around its south pole.
It's thought to have an ocean under its ice, and it's getting attention as a place where there might be life.

moons:8.fact: More than 200 moons have been found around Saturn.
moons:8.about:
The planet with the most moons found so far is Saturn, with more than 200 confirmed. Jupiter has more than 90 too.
Mercury and Venus don't have any moons. The Earth has one.

#thought-experiments-2: No equipment needed. Try these "what if" experiments that happen only in your head!

thought-experiments-2:0.fact: If you've only ever seen shadows, would you think the shadows are real?
thought-experiments-2:0.about:
There were people who grew up in a cave, seeing only shadows on the wall. When one of them went outside, saw the real world and came back to tell the others, nobody believed him.
This is a story by Plato of ancient Greece. It asks, "Are the things we think are real really real?"

thought-experiments-2:1.fact: If you got a ring that made you invisible, what would you do?
thought-experiments-2:1.about:
This is a story about a shepherd who found a ring that made him invisible when he wore it. If people knew nobody could see them, would they keep doing good things?
With this story, Plato thought about whether "people do good because they're being watched, or because it's right."

thought-experiments-2:2.fact: Two exactly equal piles of hay. Which one does the donkey choose?
thought-experiments-2:2.about:
A hungry donkey stands with two piles of hay on its left and right, exactly the same distance away and exactly the same size. It can't decide on either… so what happens?
It's a story for thinking about "how do you decide when there's no reason to choose?" Are you a rock-paper-scissors person?

thought-experiments-2:3.fact: Your body's cells are replaced every day. Will you in 10 years be the same you?
thought-experiments-2:3.about:
Skin and blood cells are being replaced by new ones every day. After many years, lots of your body has been replaced.
So why do you still feel "I'm me"? It's the body version of the "Ship of Theseus."

thought-experiments-2:4.fact: If you knew everything about colour, would you learn something new when you saw red for the first time?
thought-experiments-2:4.about:
Mary, a scientist who grew up in a black-and-white room, learned everything about colour from books. One day she leaves the room and sees a red apple for the first time.
Did Mary learn something new? It's about the difference between "knowing" and "experiencing."

thought-experiments-2:5.fact: A machine that lets you have happy dreams forever. Would you go in?
thought-experiments-2:5.about:
If there were a machine where you could have happy dreams for your whole life, would you want to go in? In the dream, anything can come true, but you can't see your real friends and family.
It's a question by American philosopher Nozick: "What is real happiness?"

thought-experiments-2:6.fact: If you didn't know which slice of cake would be yours, how would you cut it?
thought-experiments-2:6.about:
If the person cutting the cake didn't know which slice they'd get, they'd probably cut all the slices the same size.
American philosopher Rawls thought that "if we make the rules without knowing what position we'll end up in, we can make a fair society."

thought-experiments-2:7.fact: Does a machine that can give answers understand what they mean?
thought-experiments-2:7.about:
A person who doesn't know Chinese sits in a room, follows a thick manual to put characters together, and answers questions in Chinese correctly. People outside think, "This person understands Chinese."
This question by American philosopher Searle is used when people think about "whether AI really understands meaning."

#paradoxes: "Paradoxes" seem to make sense but lead to strange answers. Stretch your brain and think!

paradoxes:0.fact: "This sentence is a lie." True or false?
paradoxes:0.about:
If the sentence "This sentence is a lie" is true, then it's a lie; but if it's a lie, then it's true.
It's a puzzle about language that people have been thinking about since Greece more than 2,500 years ago.

paradoxes:1.fact: A barber who "shaves only people who don't shave themselves." What about his own beard?
paradoxes:1.about:
A barber in a village decided he would "shave everyone who doesn't shave themselves, and only them." So who shaves the barber?
If he shaves himself, he breaks the rule; if he doesn't, then he has to shave himself. It's a story thought up by the mathematician Russell.

paradoxes:2.fact: If you went back in time and changed history, what would happen to future you?
paradoxes:2.about:
If you went back in a time machine and changed something that happened before you were born, you might not be born, and then you couldn't go back in time.
It's a puzzle that comes up a lot in time-travel stories. Each story imagines its own "answer."

paradoxes:3.fact: "There'll be a surprise test next week." Can there be a test?
paradoxes:3.about:
A teacher said, "Some day next week, there'll be a surprise test you won't be able to guess the day before." If there's no test by Friday, you'd know it's Friday, so it can't be Friday. Then it can't be Thursday either… so there can't be a test at all!
But when the test came on Wednesday, everyone was surprised. Where's the mistake?

paradoxes:4.fact: A full hotel that can still fit in a new guest!
paradoxes:4.about:
A hotel with infinitely many rooms is full. When a new guest arrives, you ask everyone to "move to the room with the next number up," and Room 1 becomes free.
It's a story the German mathematician Hilbert thought up to explain the strangeness of "infinity."

paradoxes:5.fact: With 23 people, the chance that two share a birthday is more than half!
paradoxes:5.about:
Even though there are 365 days in a year, if there are 23 people in a class, the chance that two of them share a birthday is about 50%, and with 40 people it's about 90%.
That's because there are so many "pairs" of people. Try it in your class!

paradoxes:6.fact: Three doors. Are you more likely to win if you switch?
paradoxes:6.about:
There's a prize behind one of three doors. You choose one, and then the host, who knows the answer, opens one of the losing doors. Should you switch?
The answer is "if you switch, your chance of winning is two thirds." It goes against your gut feeling, so it's a famous problem that even many mathematicians got wrong.

paradoxes:7.fact: At every instant, an arrow is still. So how does it move?
paradoxes:7.about:
If you look at a flying arrow at one single instant, it's not moving. However many still instants you add up, it shouldn't move…?
This is a paradox by Zeno of ancient Greece. When "calculus" was born in maths, people got a tool for thinking about this puzzle.

#logic-puzzles: Line up the clues and think step by step. The answer is in the explanation!

logic-puzzles:0.fact: People who always tell the truth and people who always lie. Can you tell them apart?
logic-puzzles:0.about:
On an island live "knights," who always tell the truth, and "knaves," who always lie. A says, "We are both knaves."
Answer: If A were a knight, A would have told a lie, so A is a knave. That means "we are both knaves" is a lie, so B is a knight.

logic-puzzles:1.fact: Take a wolf, a goat and a cabbage across by boat.
logic-puzzles:1.about:
The boat can only carry you and one other thing. If you leave the wolf alone with the goat, the goat gets eaten, and if you leave the goat with the cabbage, the cabbage gets eaten.
Answer: Take the goat across → go back → take the wolf across and bring the goat back → take the cabbage across → go back and take the goat across. It's a puzzle more than 1,200 years old.

logic-puzzles:2.fact: "Cats are animals. Tama is a cat. So Tama is an animal."
logic-puzzles:2.about:
Reasoning that gets true things from true things like this is called a "syllogism." Aristotle put it together.
But "Cats are animals. Dogs are animals. So dogs are cats" is wrong. Can you see where it goes wrong?

logic-puzzles:3.about:
From "Some people in the class wear glasses," you can't say "Everyone in the class wears glasses." Using "all," "some" and "none" correctly is the first step in logic.
It's the same in English: all, some, no.

logic-puzzles:4.fact: When ice cream sales go up, sunburn goes up. Is it the ice cream's fault?
logic-puzzles:4.about:
In summer, lots of ice cream is sold and lots of people get sunburnt. But ice cream doesn't cause sunburn. Both are caused by "hot, sunny days."
Even if two things happen together, one isn't always the cause of the other. It's a useful way of thinking when you watch the news too.

logic-puzzles:5.fact: The basics of thinking that computers use too.
logic-puzzles:5.about:
"If it's sunny AND a holiday, we'll go to the park" means you only go when both are true. "If it's sunny OR a holiday, we'll go" means one is enough.
Inside computers, these "AND" and "OR" steps are combined billions of times to do calculations.

logic-puzzles:6.fact: Look into the room only once and work out which switch is for the bulb.
logic-puzzles:6.about:
There are 3 switches outside a room and one light bulb inside. You can only go into the room once.
Answer: Turn switch A on for a while and then off, turn B on, and go in. If the bulb is lit, it's B; if it's off but warm, it's A; if it's cold, it's C. The clever part is using the clue of "heat."

logic-puzzles:7.fact: One guard always tells the truth, and one always lies. You can ask only one question.
logic-puzzles:7.about:
There's a treasure door and a losing door. One guard is a truth-teller and one is a liar, but you don't know which.
Answer: Ask either guard, "Which door would the other guard say is the treasure door?" and choose the opposite door.

#eastern-thinkers: Are people born good? What does it mean to value harmony? Let's meet the words of Asia's great thinkers.

eastern-thinkers:0.fact: People are born with "sprouts of goodness" in their hearts.
eastern-thinkers:0.about:
Mencius was a Chinese thinker who carried on the teachings of Confucius. He said that if anyone saw a child about to fall into a well, they would want to help without thinking. So he believed people's hearts are born with sprouts of goodness (the idea that "human nature is good").
He taught that it's important to help those sprouts grow.

eastern-thinkers:1.about:
Xunzi believed that people, left as they're born, easily become selfish, so it's important to improve yourself through learning and rules (the idea that "human nature is bad").
The saying "Blue comes from the indigo plant but is bluer than it" (a student can go beyond the teacher) is also from Xunzi.

eastern-thinkers:2.fact: Care for everyone, just as you care for your own family.
eastern-thinkers:2.about:
Mozi was a Chinese thinker about 2,400 years ago who taught "universal love": caring for all people equally, not just the people close to you.
He aimed for a society where fighting stopped, waste was cut, and everyone could live well.

eastern-thinkers:3.fact: Clear rules that everyone can follow are important.
eastern-thinkers:3.about:
Han Feizi was a Chinese thinker who believed that to run a country, what matters isn't people's moods but clear laws that apply the same to everyone.
The story of "mujun" (contradiction), about a spear that can pierce any shield and a shield that can stop any spear, comes from the book "Han Feizi" too.

eastern-thinkers:4.fact: A South Indian poet who put life's wisdom into 1,330 short verses.
eastern-thinkers:4.about:
Tiruvalluvar was a poet and thinker from southern India about 2,000 years ago. He wrote the "Tirukkural," 1,330 short verses about living rightly, friendship, work and more.
It's written in Tamil and is still read by lots of people today.

eastern-thinkers:5.fact: "Harmony is to be valued." Talking things through is important.
eastern-thinkers:5.about:
Prince Shōtoku was a Japanese statesman of the Asuka period, said to have made the "Seventeen-Article Constitution," a guide for how officials should behave.
Its first article, "Harmony is to be valued," means "let's value getting along and talking things through," and it still lives on in the way Japanese people think.

eastern-thinkers:6.fact: He wrote "Yōjōkun," a book about health in the Edo period.
eastern-thinkers:6.about:
Kaibara Ekiken was a scholar from the Fukuoka domain. At 83, he wrote "Yōjōkun," a book about living a long, healthy life.
It's full of wisdom that still fits today's ideas about health, like "hara hachibunme" (eat until you're 80% full), walking a lot and not worrying too much.

eastern-thinkers:7.about:
Ishida Baigan was an Edo-period thinker in Kyoto who taught merchants to "do business honestly, without waste, so that both your customer and you do well" (Sekimon Shingaku).
His idea, "the other side stands, and I stand too," still lives on in Japanese companies today.

eastern-thinkers:8.fact: Asia's first Nobel Prize in Literature. He made a school in the forest.
eastern-thinkers:8.about:
In 1913, the Indian poet Tagore became the first person from Asia to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. He valued learning freely in nature and made a school where lessons were held under the trees.
He visited Japan several times and loved Japanese culture. He also wrote the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

#western-thinkers: What is the world made of? What is happiness? Let's follow the questions of Europe's thinkers.

western-thinkers:0.fact: "Everything comes from water." The first philosopher.
western-thinkers:0.about:
Thales lived in Greece about 2,600 years ago. He's called "the first philosopher" because he looked for how the world works in nature, not in myths.
He believed "everything comes from water." He's also said to have predicted a solar eclipse.

western-thinkers:1.fact: He found an amazing link between numbers and music.
western-thinkers:1.about:
Pythagoras was a Greek mathematician and thinker, famous for the "Pythagorean theorem." He noticed that the beauty of music can be shown with numbers; for example, halving the length of a string makes a note one octave higher.
He believed "the world is made of numbers."

western-thinkers:2.fact: "You can't step into the same river twice."
western-thinkers:2.about:
Heraclitus said that the water in a river is always flowing, so the second time you step in, it's already a different river.
The idea is that everything in the world is always changing. Maybe you're a little different from the you of yesterday too?

western-thinkers:3.fact: A philosopher who lived very simply, inside a big jar.
western-thinkers:3.about:
Diogenes was a Greek philosopher who is said to have owned almost nothing and lived in a big jar.
A famous story says that when a great king asked him, "Is there anything you want?", he answered, "Please don't block my sunlight." He believed we really need very little.

western-thinkers:4.fact: Happiness is friends and simple pleasures.
western-thinkers:4.about:
Epicurus believed happiness isn't luxury but talking with friends, enjoying simple food like bread and water, and having a calm mind.
He started a school where friends studied together in a garden.

western-thinkers:5.fact: A Roman emperor's notebook for his own mind.
western-thinkers:5.about:
Marcus Aurelius was a Roman emperor who, between his busy duties, wrote words in a notebook to calm his mind. That became the "Meditations."
His idea, "focus on what you can change, and don't worry about what you can't" (Stoicism), still helps lots of people today.

western-thinkers:6.fact: "What do I know?" The father of the essay.
western-thinkers:6.about:
Montaigne was a French thinker who wrote the "Essays," freely writing about his own thoughts and experiences. It's where the word "essay" comes from.
He always asked himself, "What do I know?", and valued not jumping to conclusions.

western-thinkers:7.fact: When we're born, our minds are a "blank sheet of paper."
western-thinkers:7.about:
Locke from England believed that when people are born, they're like a blank sheet of paper with nothing written on it, and they build their ideas by learning from experience.
He also taught that all people are born with natural rights, which had a big influence on how society thinks today.

#philosophy-of-happiness: What is happiness? Here are "hints for happiness" found by scientists and people around the world.

philosophy-of-happiness:0.fact: Finding things to say "thank you" for helps you feel happy.
philosophy-of-happiness:0.about:
Research shows that writing down 3 things you're thankful for every day helps you feel happier.
It's practice in noticing everyday things. What are your 3 for today?

philosophy-of-happiness:1.fact: "Flow," when you're so absorbed in something that you lose track of time.
philosophy-of-happiness:1.about:
Psychologist Csikszentmihalyi called the state of being so absorbed in something you love that you forget the time "flow."
He said it happens most easily when you take on a challenge that's not too hard and not too easy. When do you lose track of time?

philosophy-of-happiness:2.fact: The biggest key to happiness, found by a long study.
philosophy-of-happiness:2.about:
Harvard University in America has studied the same people for more than 80 years, and found that "good relationships are the biggest key to health and happiness."
Connections with the people close to you matter more than money or fame.

philosophy-of-happiness:3.fact: Being kind to others makes you happy too.
philosophy-of-happiness:3.about:
Research shows that people feel happier spending money or time on others than on themselves.
Even small kindnesses make the giver, the receiver and even people watching feel good.

philosophy-of-happiness:4.about:
Hygge is a Danish word for cosy, comfortable times, like enjoying warm drinks with family and friends by candlelight.
Denmark is always near the top of the "World Happiness Report."

philosophy-of-happiness:5.about:
Lagom is a Swedish word meaning "not too much, not too little: just right." Just the right amount of food and just the right amount of work is best.
It's a lot like the Japanese idea of "hara hachibunme" (eat until you're 80% full).

philosophy-of-happiness:6.about:
Sisu is a Finnish word for the strong spirit to keep going without giving up, even when things are hard. It's like "fall down seven times, get up eight."
Finland has been number one in the World Happiness Report for many years.

philosophy-of-happiness:7.fact: South Africa's "I am because we are."
philosophy-of-happiness:7.about:
Ubuntu is a word from southern Africa meaning "I am who I am because of who we all are." It's the idea that people become people through their connections with others.
It's a way of life where everyone becomes happy together, not "it's fine as long as I'm OK."

philosophy-of-happiness:8.fact: "Ikigai," a reason to get up in the morning.
philosophy-of-happiness:8.about:
Ikigai is said to be where things like "what you love," "what you're good at" and "what helps others" overlap, and it's become known abroad as "ikigai."
It doesn't have to be a big dream: small everyday pleasures can be your ikigai too.

#ethics-for-kids: What does it mean to do the right thing? Let's think together about questions that have more than one answer.

ethics-for-kids:0.fact: 3 sweets and 4 friends. How do you share them?
ethics-for-kids:0.about:
Sharing means having less for yourself. So why do people share?
"Give everyone the same number," "give more to someone who's hungry," "break them into smaller pieces"… Talk about different ways of sharing.

ethics-for-kids:1.fact: Aesop's "The Boy Who Cried Wolf." What happens if you keep telling lies?
ethics-for-kids:1.about:
A shepherd boy played tricks on the villagers by shouting "A wolf is coming!" When a wolf really came, nobody believed him.
It's a story by Aesop from about 2,500 years ago. It teaches us how important it is to be trusted.

ethics-for-kids:2.fact: What should you do if you made a promise you can't keep?
ethics-for-kids:2.about:
When you keep promises, people trust you. But sometimes you can't keep one.
Then it's important to say sorry early and explain why. "Don't make promises you can't keep" is another answer.

ethics-for-kids:3.fact: What do you do when you see someone in trouble?
ethics-for-kids:3.about:
When everyone who sees someone in trouble thinks "someone else will help," sometimes nobody helps at all.
Think about what you can do. Even just calling a grown-up is a big help.

ethics-for-kids:4.fact: The same box for everyone? Or the box each person needs?
ethics-for-kids:4.about:
Three people of different heights are trying to watch a game over a fence. Giving everyone one box of the same height is "equality." Giving each person the box they need so they can all see is "fairness."
Which is better depends on the situation. Let's think about it together.

ethics-for-kids:5.about:
Many animals are thought to feel pain, fear and happiness.
Let's think about what we can do, like caring for pets until the very end and not disturbing wild animals' lives.

ethics-for-kids:6.fact: What can we do now for people in the future?
ethics-for-kids:6.about:
The way we live now affects the Earth of future children too.
Thinking about people who haven't even been born yet may be an amazing power only humans have. Rubbish, electricity, water… choose one thing you can do today.

ethics-for-kids:7.fact: What if a friend is being treated badly?
ethics-for-kids:7.about:
When someone is being teased, things can change if someone nearby says "Let's stop," or talks to them kindly afterwards.
When it's hard to do alone, telling a teacher or another grown-up takes courage too.

#critical-thinking: Is that story really true? Here are "thinking tools" for a world full of information.

critical-thinking:0.fact: It helps you see the real cause of a problem.
critical-thinking:0.about:
Asking "Why?" five times when a problem happens is a method born at the Japanese car company Toyota, and it's used all over the world.
"I was late → Why? → I overslept → Why? → I stayed up late…" and you reach the real cause.

critical-thinking:1.fact: "Mount Fuji is 3,776 m" and "Mount Fuji is beautiful" are different.
critical-thinking:1.about:
A fact is something you can look up and check; an opinion is a view that's different from person to person. "Mount Fuji is 3,776 m tall" is a fact, and "Mount Fuji is the most beautiful sight in Japan" is an opinion.
When you watch the news or adverts, think about which is which.

critical-thinking:2.fact: Who wrote it, when, and why?
critical-thinking:2.about:
Anyone can write things on the internet. Check who wrote it, how old the information is, and whether other books or teachers say the same thing.
The more "amazing" a story sounds, the more important it is to stop and check.

critical-thinking:3.fact: In an argument, don't decide after hearing only one side.
critical-thinking:3.about:
When friends argue, if you only hear one side's story, the other side can look bad.
Listening to both sides and thinking about what really happened shows you a different picture. Courts work this way too.

critical-thinking:4.fact: The same thing can look different depending on where you stand.
critical-thinking:4.about:
The number "6" looks like "9" from the other side. Neither is wrong.
When you try seeing things from the other person's side, you can sometimes understand why your opinions are different.

critical-thinking:5.fact: Grow ideas by drawing branches out from the middle.
critical-thinking:5.about:
Writing a topic in the middle of a page and joining the things you think of like branches is called a "mind map."
When you can see your thoughts, you find new ideas and connections.

critical-thinking:6.fact: Disagree with the idea, not the person.
critical-thinking:6.about:
In discussions and debates, talk about what the opinion says, not about the person who said it.
Listen to the end, give your reasons, keep to time. Even if you disagree, you're still friends when it's over.

critical-thinking:7.fact: Changing your mind when you learn something new is cool.
critical-thinking:7.about:
Changing your mind after learning new facts isn't losing; it's proof that you learned something. Scientists have changed their ideas when new discoveries were made too.
Being able to say "I used to think that, but now I think this" is a great strength.

#philosophy-of-science: Look, think, test. Science is the wisdom of "how to check."

philosophy-of-science:0.about:
The first step of science is looking carefully and noticing "Huh?" Keeping a morning glory observation diary is real science too.
Darwin observed the differences in the beaks of birds on the Galápagos and reached the idea of evolution.

philosophy-of-science:1.fact: Coming up with an idea: "Maybe it's like this."
philosophy-of-science:1.about:
Making a guess about something you noticed, like "maybe this is what's happening," is called a "hypothesis."
It's fine if a hypothesis turns out to be wrong. It's a starting point for testing and checking.

philosophy-of-science:2.fact: Change just one thing and compare.
philosophy-of-science:2.about:
In an experiment, you change only the one thing you want to compare and keep everything else the same. This is called a "fair test."
For example, to test whether plants need light, you keep the water and soil the same and change only the light.

philosophy-of-science:3.fact: Which falls first, something heavy or something light?
philosophy-of-science:3.about:
People once believed "heavier things fall faster." Using experiments and reasoning, Galileo showed that without air resistance, things fall at the same speed whatever their weight.
In 1971, an astronaut on the Moon dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time, and they really did land together.

philosophy-of-science:4.fact: If two ideas explain something equally well, choose the simpler one.
philosophy-of-science:4.about:
When there are several ideas that explain something, the simple explanation with fewer assumptions is often the right one.
"No homework → Did the dog eat it? Did aliens take it? Did I leave it at home?" Which is most likely?

philosophy-of-science:5.fact: Other scientists check the work to make sure it's right.
philosophy-of-science:5.about:
Before scientists publish a new discovery, other scientists read it and check whether the methods and results are right. This is called "peer review."
It's important that other people get the same results when they do the same experiment.

philosophy-of-science:6.about:
Pluto was the ninth planet for a long time, but lots of similar bodies were found, and in 2006 it became a "dwarf planet."
Ideas changing because of new discoveries is a sign that science is working properly.

philosophy-of-science:7.fact: A medicine was born from a mouldy experiment!
philosophy-of-science:7.about:
In 1928, Fleming in Britain noticed that bacteria wouldn't grow around mould on an experiment dish he'd forgotten to clear away. This led to the medicine "penicillin," which has saved many lives.
Microwave ovens and Post-it notes were also born from unexpected discoveries.

#time-philosophy: Fun times fly by, and waiting feels long. What is time, really?

time-philosophy:0.fact: "What is time? If no one asks me, I know."
time-philosophy:0.about:
Augustine, a thinker from about 1,600 years ago, wrote, "What is time? If no one asks me, I know. But if I try to explain it, I don't know."
We use it every day, but it's very hard to explain. Time is one of the big mysteries of philosophy.

time-philosophy:1.fact: Is it because we don't think about time when we're having fun?
time-philosophy:1.about:
When you're absorbed in something, you don't look at the clock much, so time feels short. When you're waiting, you think about the time all the time, so it feels long.
But when you look back later, the fun days can sometimes feel longer. Strange, isn't it?

time-philosophy:2.fact: People say a year feels shorter the older you get.
time-philosophy:2.about:
For a 10-year-old, one year is a tenth of their life, but for a 50-year-old it's a fiftieth. One idea (Janet's law) says that's why a year feels shorter for grown-ups.
It's also said that time feels longer when you have lots of new experiences.

time-philosophy:3.fact: If you travel very fast, time goes more slowly!
time-philosophy:3.about:
According to Einstein's theory of relativity, if one twin travels through space close to the speed of light and comes back, they'll be younger than the twin who stayed on Earth.
In fact, clocks on satellites drift slightly from clocks on the ground, so GPS corrects for this.

time-philosophy:4.fact: A person's heart beats about 3 billion times in a lifetime.
time-philosophy:4.about:
A person's heart beats about 60 to 100 times a minute, about 3 billion times in a lifetime.
A mouse's heart beats very fast, and an elephant's beats slowly. Maybe "how time flows" is different depending on body size.

time-philosophy:5.fact: Does a fly see the world in slow motion?
time-philosophy:5.about:
A fly can take in what's in front of it many more times a second than a person can. So our hand movements look slow to it, and it's hard to catch.
It's thought that different animals feel the same second differently.

time-philosophy:6.fact: Japan switched to today's calendar in 1873.
time-philosophy:6.about:
The calendar used around the world today (the Gregorian calendar) was made in Europe in 1582. Japan switched from its old moon-based calendar in 1873, in the Meiji period.
So in the 5th year of Meiji, the day after December 2nd suddenly became January 1st, 1873.

time-philosophy:7.fact: Write a letter to your future self.
time-philosophy:7.about:
A box where you put your thoughts and favourite things now, to open many years later, is called a "time capsule." Some Japanese schools bury one at graduation.
At the Osaka Expo (1970), a time capsule was buried to be opened 5,000 years later.

#mind-and-feelings: Remembering, dreaming, feeling happy, feeling sad. Where is the mind?

mind-and-feelings:0.fact: While you sleep, your brain sorts out what you learned.
mind-and-feelings:0.about:
It's thought that while you sleep, your brain sorts out what you learned that day so you can remember it for a long time.
So the night before a test, a good sleep works better than staying up late. Practising remembering again and again helps too.

mind-and-feelings:1.fact: People dream several times every night.
mind-and-feelings:1.about:
Sleep has light sleep and deep sleep, and we dream most during light sleep (REM sleep). We dream several times a night, but forget most of it.
Why we dream is still a mystery being researched.

mind-and-feelings:2.fact: Happy, sad, angry, scared. They're all important feelings.
mind-and-feelings:2.about:
Feeling sad or angry is an important signal that protects your body and mind. Fear protects you from danger.
Giving your feelings a name, like "I feel frustrated right now," helps your mind calm down a little.

mind-and-feelings:3.fact: What you do again and again makes who you are.
mind-and-feelings:3.about:
Aristotle of ancient Greece believed that "by doing good things again and again, we become good people."
One study suggests it takes about 2 months for a new habit to stick. Start with something small and keep going every day.

mind-and-feelings:4.about:
American psychologist Dweck showed in her research that people who believe "abilities grow with effort" keep taking on hard challenges.
Mistakes are proof that your brain is growing. Try adding "yet"!

mind-and-feelings:5.fact: Breathe in counting to 4, breathe out counting to 4.
mind-and-feelings:5.about:
When you feel nervous or cross, slow, deep breathing helps calm your mind. One way is to breathe in for 4 seconds, hold for 4 seconds and breathe out for 4 seconds.
Practising focusing on the here and now is called "mindfulness."

mind-and-feelings:6.fact: The power to imagine how someone else feels.
mind-and-feelings:6.about:
The power to imagine "how would I feel if this happened to me?" is called "empathy" or "kindness."
You can practise and grow this power by listening to people until they finish and watching their faces carefully.

mind-and-feelings:7.fact: When someone laughs, you can't help laughing too.
mind-and-feelings:7.about:
People are said to laugh many times more when they're with someone than when they're alone. When you hear laughter, your brain gets ready to laugh along.
Laughing relaxes your mind and body. How many times have you laughed today?

#world-wisdom-words: One word can show you the heart of a country. Here are some wonderful words from around the world.

world-wisdom-words:0.about:
Aloha is used as a greeting in Hawaiian, but it has deeper meanings too, like "kindness," "love" and "life."
The "aloha spirit" is the Hawaiian heart that cares for the people and nature around you.

world-wisdom-words:1.about:
Pura vida means "pure life" in Spanish. In Costa Rica it's also used to mean hello, thank you and "it's all fine."
It shows the heart of Costa Rican people, who enjoy every day simply.

world-wisdom-words:2.about:
Carpe diem is a phrase from Horace, a Roman poet from about 2,000 years ago, meaning "make the most of today."
Instead of "I'll do it tomorrow," enjoy what you can do now.

world-wisdom-words:3.about:
Hakuna matata is a phrase in Swahili, spoken in East Africa, meaning "no problem" or "no worries."
In Kenya and Tanzania, people use it in everyday conversation.

world-wisdom-words:4.fact: Mending broken pottery with gold, making it more beautiful than before.
world-wisdom-words:4.about:
Kintsugi is a Japanese craft of gluing a broken bowl back together with lacquer and decorating the joins with gold. Instead of hiding the cracks, it turns them into a new kind of beauty.
It's popular abroad too, as the idea that "mistakes and scars are an important part of your story."

world-wisdom-words:5.about:
Gemütlichkeit is a German word for the warm, cosy feeling of relaxing together with friends.
It's like Danish hygge, a feeling that people in cold countries have always treasured.

world-wisdom-words:6.fact: Italian for "the joy of doing nothing."
world-wisdom-words:6.about:
Dolce far niente is an Italian phrase meaning "the sweetness of doing nothing." It values time spent not rushing, just looking at the view.
Resting is an important part of life too.

world-wisdom-words:7.about:
Fika is a Swedish custom of taking a break from work or study for coffee or tea and something sweet, and chatting with the people around you.
It's so important that companies and schools have fika time.

world-wisdom-words:8.fact: Japanese for "giving it everything without giving up."
world-wisdom-words:8.about:
"Ganbaru" is a Japanese word for doing your very best without giving up, even when things are hard. "Ganbatte!" is used every day to cheer people on.
There's no exact English word, so people say things like "Do your best!", "Good luck!" or "You can do it!"

#onomatopoeia: In Japan, dogs say "wan wan," and in English they say "Woof!" The same sound is heard differently!

onomatopoeia:0.about:
In English, a dog's bark is written "woof" or "bow-wow." Little dogs can go "yap yap" too.
In a different country, the same bark sounds different. Language shapes the way our ears hear.

onomatopoeia:1.about:
In English, a cat says "meow." The rumbling sound it makes in its throat is a "purr."
In French it's "miaou," and in Korean it's "yaong." They're all a bit alike, aren't they?

onomatopoeia:2.about:
In English, roosters say "cock-a-doodle-doo." That's very long!
In German it's "kikeriki," and in Spanish it's "quiquiriquí."

onomatopoeia:3.about:
In English, pigs say "oink oink."
It's a word for a snorting sound, quite different from the Japanese "bū bū."

onomatopoeia:4.about:
In English, frogs say "ribbit." That's very different from the Japanese "kero kero" and "geko geko."
In Korean, frogs say "gaegul gaegul."

onomatopoeia:5.about:
In English, ducks say "quack quack."
A fake doctor is called a "quack" in English, and it's said to be because they chatter on like a duck.

onomatopoeia:6.about:
In English, sheep say "baa."
The nursery rhyme "Baa, Baa, Black Sheep" is a British song that has been sung for more than 300 years.

onomatopoeia:7.about:
A cow's moo is almost the same in Japanese and English: "mō" and "moo."
Like this, some sounds are similar even in different countries.

onomatopoeia:8.fact: Japanese has lots of sound words for feelings!
onomatopoeia:8.about:
Japanese has lots of words that show feelings and how things are, like "doki doki," "waku waku" and "niko niko" (onomatopoeia). There are said to be 4,000 to 5,000 of them.
In English, you'd say "My heart is pounding" (doki doki) or "I'm excited!" (waku waku).

onomatopoeia:9.about:
In Japanese, the sound changes with how the rain falls: "shito shito," "para para" and "zā zā."
In English, the sound of light rain is "pitter-patter," and for heavy rain people say "It's pouring" or "It's raining cats and dogs."

#uk-us-english: Even in English, the UK and America sometimes use different words!

uk-us-english:0.about:
In America it's an "elevator," and in the UK it's a "lift." "Lift" means "to raise up."
The Japanese word "erebētā" comes from American English.

uk-us-english:1.about:
A home in a block of flats is an "apartment" in America and a "flat" in the UK.
Careful: the Japanese "manshon" (mansion) means "a huge house" in English.

uk-us-english:2.about:
An American "cookie" is called a "biscuit" in the UK.
But an American "biscuit" is a soft bread like a scone. Sometimes the same word means different things!

uk-us-english:3.about:
Fried potato sticks are "French fries" in America and "chips" in the UK. They're the chips in "fish and chips."
So what about potato chips? In America they're "chips," and in the UK they're "crisps." Confusing!

uk-us-english:4.about:
In the UK, soccer is called "football." In America, "football" means American football.
"Soccer" was actually a short form of a word, first made up in England.

uk-us-english:5.about:
A big vehicle for carrying goods is a "truck" in America and a "lorry" in the UK.
The tongue twister "Red lorry, yellow lorry" uses British English.

uk-us-english:6.about:
In America people spell "color" and "favorite," and in the UK "colour" and "favourite."
It started in the 1800s, when Webster in America changed the spellings in his dictionary to make them simpler and closer to how they sound.

uk-us-english:7.about:
Car fuel is "gas" (gasoline) in America and "petrol" in the UK.
A place to fill up is a "gas station" in America and a "petrol station" in the UK.

uk-us-english:8.about:
American "pants" are trousers, but in the UK, "pants" means underpants.
In the UK, trousers are "trousers." Mix them up and it might be a bit embarrassing!

uk-us-english:9.fact: The British "first floor" is the Japanese 2nd floor!
uk-us-english:9.about:
In America, the floor at ground level is the "first floor," but in the UK it's the "ground floor," and the one above it is the "first floor."
If you're going to the "first floor" in a British department store, go up one!

#tongue-twisters: Try English and Japanese tongue twisters! Can you say them fast three times?

tongue-twisters:0.about:
"She sells seashells by the seashore" is a famous tongue twister for practising the difference between "sh" and "s" sounds.
Some say it was inspired by Mary Anning, a woman in England who collected and sold fossil shells almost 200 years ago.

tongue-twisters:1.fact: "Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers."
tongue-twisters:1.about:
"Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers" is a tongue twister found in a British book from more than 200 years ago.
It's good practice for saying the "p" sound clearly.

tongue-twisters:2.fact: Take turns with the "r" and "l" sounds!
tongue-twisters:2.about:
"Red lorry, yellow lorry" is a tongue twister that switches between "r" and "l," sounds that Japanese speakers often find hard.
For "r," curl your tongue back without touching anything; for "l," touch the tip of your tongue to the back of your top teeth.

tongue-twisters:3.fact: It's short but really hard to say!
tongue-twisters:3.about:
If you say "Unique New York" over and over fast, your mouth slowly gets tangled up.
Actors and announcers use it for voice practice too.

tongue-twisters:4.fact: "How much wood would a woodchuck chuck?"
tongue-twisters:4.about:
"How much wood would a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood?" is an American tongue twister more than 100 years old.
A woodchuck is an animal in the squirrel family.

tongue-twisters:5.about:
"Toy boat" is only two words, but when you repeat it fast, it turns into "boy tote"!
The shorter the tongue twister, the more surprisingly hard it can be!

tongue-twisters:6.about:
"Namamugi namagome namatamago" is one of the most famous tongue twisters in Japan, with "ma," "go" and "mu" sounds one after another.
In English it means "raw wheat, raw rice, raw egg." Teach it to your English-speaking friends!

tongue-twisters:7.fact: "Ki," "ku" and "ka" come up again and again!
tongue-twisters:7.about:
"Tonari no kyaku wa yoku kaki kuu kyaku da" is a Japanese tongue twister full of "k" sounds.
In English it's "The guest next door is a guest who eats a lot of persimmons." When you think about the meaning, it's a bit funny.

tongue-twisters:8.fact: It's actually the name of a government office that doesn't exist!
tongue-twisters:8.about:
"Tōkyō tokkyo kyoka kyoku" (Tokyo Patent Approval Office) is a tongue twister full of hard-to-say sounds. But actually, there's no office with this name.
Announcers often use it for practice too.

#words-from-languages: Lots of English words came from all over the world! Some came from Japanese too.

words-from-languages:0.fact: From a word for "fish sauce" in a southern Chinese language.
words-from-languages:0.about:
Ketchup is said to come from a word in the Hokkien language of southern China meaning a fish sauce. When it reached Britain, it changed into a tomato sauce.
As words travel the world, their meanings change too.

words-from-languages:1.about:
"Kindergarten" means "children's garden" in German. It was the name of the kindergarten Fröbel set up in Germany in 1840, and English kept the word as it was.
The idea is to help children grow like plants in a garden.

words-from-languages:2.about:
The piano's full name is "pianoforte," which means "it can play both soft and loud" in Italian.
Lots of music words are Italian, like "tempo" and "soprano."

words-from-languages:3.about:
"Safari" means "journey" in Swahili, spoken in East Africa. It first came from Arabic.
Now it means a trip to see wild animals.

words-from-languages:4.fact: From an Indian word meaning "to massage."
words-from-languages:4.about:
"Shampoo" comes from a Hindi word in India meaning "to massage." It reached Britain in the 18th century.
"Pyjamas" is another word that came into English from India.

words-from-languages:5.fact: From Japanese into the world's languages.
words-from-languages:5.about:
"Tsunami" is a Japanese word that came to be used all over the world. In English it's used as a science word too.
There are lots of other English words from Japanese, like "karaoke," "emoji," "sushi," "anime" and "kawaii."

words-from-languages:6.fact: From Nahuatl, an old language of Mexico.
words-from-languages:6.about:
"Chocolate" is said to come from "xocolatl" (bitter water) in Nahuatl, the language of the Aztec people of Mexico.
"Tomato," "avocado" and "chilli" come from Nahuatl too.

words-from-languages:7.fact: From "alpha" and "beta," the first two Greek letters.
words-from-languages:7.about:
"Alphabet" is made by joining the first two letters of the Greek alphabet, "α" (alpha) and "β" (beta).
In Japanese, "iroha," the first three kana of an old poem, also means "the order of letters."

words-from-languages:8.fact: From the name of an Arabic maths book.
words-from-languages:8.about:
"Algebra" comes from "al-jabr," a word in the title of a book by al-Khwārizmī, an Arab mathematician from about 1,200 years ago.
The computer word "algorithm" comes from this mathematician's name.

words-from-languages:9.about:
"Robot" is a word the Czech writer Čapek used in a play in 1920, made from a Czech word meaning "forced labour."
Now it's used all over the world.

#codes: Ways to send messages without words, and ways to send secret messages. Welcome to the world of codes!

codes:0.fact: Letters are shown with dots (·) and dashes (–).
codes:0.about:
Morse code was thought up in the 1830s by Morse and others in America. It sends letters as combinations of short sounds (·) and long sounds (–).
"SOS," a call for help, is "··· ––– ···." It can be sent with light, sound or tapping.

codes:1.fact: Letters are shown by the positions of two flags.
codes:1.about:
Semaphore is a way of sending one letter at a time by the angles of flags held in both hands. It's been used where voices can't reach, like between ships.
Japanese flag semaphore is based on the shapes of katakana.

codes:2.fact: A code that shifts letters by a set number.
codes:2.about:
This code is said to have been used by Julius Caesar of ancient Rome. Each letter is shifted 3 places along the alphabet: A becomes D, B becomes E.
If you shift "KHOOR" back 3 places… the answer is "HELLO."

codes:3.fact: A code that shows letters with lines and dots in grids.
codes:3.about:
The pigpen cipher puts letters of the alphabet into grids shaped like "#" and "×," and shows each letter by the shape of its box.
If you just look at the shapes, they look like strange symbols. Try writing secret letters with your friends!

codes:4.fact: Writing in lemon juice appears when you warm it!
codes:4.about:
If you write on paper with lemon or mikan juice and let it dry, it disappears. If you warm it with a hair dryer or similar, with a grown-up, brown writing appears.
That's because things in the juice burn slightly with the heat.

codes:5.fact: Stripes that show a product's number.
codes:5.about:
A barcode shows numbers with lines of different thicknesses. When it's scanned at the till, the product's name and price come up.
In 1974, the first product sold with a barcode at an American supermarket was a packet of chewing gum.

codes:6.fact: A stone that became the key to reading ancient Egyptian writing.
codes:6.about:
The Rosetta Stone had the same text written in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek.
In 1822, Champollion of France compared them with the Greek and managed to read the hieroglyphs. The stone is now in the British Museum in London.

codes:7.fact: A is Alfa, B is Bravo. A way of spelling that stops mishearing.
codes:7.about:
On the phone and radio, it's easy to mishear similar sounds like "B" and "D," so each letter is sent with a set word, like A = Alfa, B = Bravo, C = Charlie.
Pilots and sailors use it all over the world.

#symbols-signs: Signs whose meaning gets across even if you don't know the language. Lots of them were born in Japan!

symbols-signs:0.fact: Born in Japan, it became a world standard.
symbols-signs:0.about:
The emergency exit sign, with a white figure running on a green background, was designed in Japan and chosen as an international standard (ISO) in 1987. Now it's used all over the world.
Its colours and shape were designed to be easy to see even in smoke.

symbols-signs:1.fact: They really started to be used at the 1964 Tokyo Games.
symbols-signs:1.about:
At the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, "pictograms," pictures showing sports, toilets and more, were made properly for the first time so that visitors who didn't know Japanese could understand.
At the 2021 Tokyo Games, moving pictograms got lots of attention.

symbols-signs:2.fact: A sign with three arrows going round and round.
symbols-signs:2.about:
The three-arrow recycling symbol was designed by Gary Anderson, an American university student, for a contest in 1970.
Japan also has recycling marks for each material, like plastic bottles, plastics and paper.

symbols-signs:3.fact: Japan's hot spring sign, with three lines of steam.
symbols-signs:3.about:
♨ is the symbol for hot springs on Japanese maps. In 2016, when map symbols for foreign visitors were being made, changing it to "people sitting in a bath" was considered, but it was decided to keep ♨ too.
Now it's known abroad as the sign for a "Japanese hot spring."

symbols-signs:4.fact: A worldwide sign showing that anyone can use a place.
symbols-signs:4.about:
The wheelchair symbol was designed by a Danish student in 1968 and became an international symbol. It shows places that are "easy for anyone to use," not only wheelchair users.
Japan also has the "Help Mark," which lets people show they have a disability or condition that's hard to see.

symbols-signs:5.fact: Blocks for people who can't see well, invented in Japan.
symbols-signs:5.about:
The yellow bumpy blocks on pavements and station platforms were thought up in 1965 by Miyake Seiichi of Okayama, and in 1967 they were laid on a road in Okayama for the first time in the world.
Lines mean "go," and dots mean "stop / take care." Now they're used all over the world.

symbols-signs:6.fact: A symbol that came to be used in email addresses.
symbols-signs:6.about:
@ was originally a symbol merchants used to mean "at the price of." In 1971, Tomlinson in America chose it to separate the name and the place when he sent the first email.
In English it's "at," but some people in Italy call it "snail," and some in the Netherlands call it "monkey's tail."

symbols-signs:7.fact: A symbol made from the Latin "et" (and) written as one letter.
symbols-signs:7.about:
& was born from writing the two letters of the Latin "et," meaning "and," joined together as one.
In old English alphabet songs, & was sung after Z.

symbols-signs:8.fact: In Japan it's 110 and 119. It's different in each country!
symbols-signs:8.about:
In Japan, the police is 110, and fire and ambulance is 119. America and Canada use 911, the UK uses 999, and many European countries use 112.
Before travelling abroad, it's good to check that country's numbers.

#ancient-civilizations: Thousands of years ago, people built towns beside rivers and invented writing and calendars.

ancient-civilizations:0.fact: One of the oldest kinds of pottery in the world was made in Japan.
ancient-civilizations:0.about:
The Jōmon period began about 16,000 years ago, and people lived by hunting and gathering nuts. "Jōmon pottery," decorated with rope patterns, is one of the oldest kinds of pottery in the world.
The Sannai-Maruyama site in Aomori has the remains of a big village, and it's a World Heritage Site.

ancient-civilizations:1.fact: "The land between two rivers," where the wheel and writing were born.
ancient-civilizations:1.about:
About 5,000 years ago, the Mesopotamian civilisation flourished between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in today's Iraq. "Cuneiform," one of the first kinds of writing, and the wheel were used there.
Counting in 60s, which gives us 60 minutes in an hour, comes from here too.

ancient-civilizations:2.fact: It flourished thanks to the Nile and built the pyramids.
ancient-civilizations:2.about:
In ancient Egypt, people grew crops in the soil carried by the Nile's yearly floods. The Great Pyramid of Giza was built about 4,500 years ago with more than 2.3 million stones.
"Papyrus," the ancestor of paper, was also born in Egypt.

ancient-civilizations:3.fact: A town 4,500 years ago had drains!
ancient-civilizations:3.about:
Planned towns like Mohenjo-daro were built beside the Indus River, which flows through today's Pakistan. Brick houses stood in rows, and the towns had drains and public baths.
It's a mysterious civilisation, with writing that nobody can read yet.

ancient-civilizations:4.fact: Writing on turtle shells is the root of kanji.
ancient-civilizations:4.about:
In the Shang dynasty, which flourished by the Yellow River, people carved characters on turtle shells and animal bones to tell fortunes. This is "oracle bone script," the root of today's kanji.
Japanese kanji are characters that came from China too.

ancient-civilizations:5.fact: The Olympics, theatre and philosophy were born here.
ancient-civilizations:5.about:
In ancient Greece, games (the Olympics) were held at Olympia, and in Athens there was democracy, where people decided things by discussing them together.
Theatre, philosophy and maths also developed a lot. "Democracy" comes from the Greek for "power of the people."

ancient-civilizations:6.fact: "All roads lead to Rome." Experts at roads and water supply.
ancient-civilizations:6.about:
Ancient Rome laid stone roads across Europe and built "aqueducts" to carry water from faraway mountains. They used concrete too, and some of their buildings are still standing more than 2,000 years later.
Today's English alphabet is the Roman alphabet (Latin letters).

ancient-civilizations:7.fact: They used "0" and made accurate calendars.
ancient-civilizations:7.about:
The Maya civilisation of Central America built pyramid temples in the jungle and watched the movements of the stars to make accurate calendars.
It was one of the first civilisations in the world to use the number "0." Maya people still live there today.

ancient-civilizations:8.fact: Instead of writing, they kept records with "knots in strings."
ancient-civilizations:8.about:
The Inca Empire, which flourished in the Andes Mountains of South America, built the town of Machu Picchu high on a mountain.
They had no writing, but they kept numbers and records with knots in strings of different colours, called "quipu." They also built thousands of kilometres of roads through the mountains.

#writing-history: From pictures to letters, from handwriting to printing. The invention of writing carried human wisdom into the future.

writing-history:0.fact: One of the oldest kinds of writing, pressed into clay tablets with a reed pen.
writing-history:0.about:
About 5,000 years ago in Mesopotamia, people made writing by pressing wedge-shaped marks into soft clay tablets with pointed reed stems.
At first it was used to keep count of things like wheat and sheep.

writing-history:1.fact: Picture-like Egyptian writing, with birds, eyes, hands and more.
writing-history:1.about:
Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs used pictures like birds, eyes and snakes, and they were carved on the walls of temples and tombs.
For a long time nobody could read them, but thanks to the Rosetta Stone, people can read them now.

writing-history:2.about:
Oracle bone script is writing carved on turtle shells and cattle bones in China about 3,300 years ago. "日" (sun) was a circle with a dot in it, and "山" (mountain) was the shape of three peaks.
Kanji have been used for more than 3,000 years while changing shape, which is rare for a writing system.

writing-history:3.fact: The letters of Mediterranean traders became the root of the world's alphabets.
writing-history:3.about:
About 3,000 years ago, the Phoenicians, who traded around the Mediterranean, used 22 letters that showed sounds.
These became the ancestors of many of the world's writing systems, like the Greek alphabet and the Latin alphabet (today's English alphabet).

writing-history:4.fact: Writing born in Japan from kanji in the Heian period.
writing-history:4.about:
Hiragana came from writing kanji in a flowing, simplified way, and katakana came from taking parts of kanji. "あ" comes from "安," and "ア" comes from "阿."
"The Tale of Genji," written in hiragana, is said to be one of the oldest novels in the world.

writing-history:5.fact: It made it possible to make lots of books.
writing-history:5.about:
Around 1450, Gutenberg in Germany made a printing machine that put together metal letters. Books that had been copied by hand could now be made quickly and in large numbers.
Thanks to this invention, knowledge spread to many people.

writing-history:6.fact: Writing you read with your fingers, thought up by a 15-year-old boy.
writing-history:6.about:
In 1824, Louis Braille, a blind boy in France, thought up Braille, which shows letters with combinations of 6 dots.
Japanese Braille was made by Ishikawa Kuraji in 1890, and now there's Braille on station ticket machines and even on drink cans.

writing-history:7.fact: Pencils that Tokugawa Ieyasu is said to have used.
writing-history:7.about:
A pencil's lead is made of graphite. Pencils spread after good-quality graphite was found in England in the 1560s.
In Japan, a pencil said to have been used by Tokugawa Ieyasu is kept at Kunōzan Tōshō-gū in Shizuoka.

#communication-history: Smoke signals, runners, letters, telephones, smartphones. How have the ways of connecting with faraway people changed?

communication-history:0.fact: People sent smoke up to signal to people far away.
communication-history:0.about:
People long ago lit fires on mountaintops and sent signals to faraway people with smoke or firelight. Passed on like a relay, a message could travel hundreds of kilometres quickly.
All over Japan, you can still find the remains of "noroshi-dai," signal fire stations.

communication-history:1.fact: The running postmen of the Edo period.
communication-history:1.about:
In the Edo period, "hikyaku" runners carried letters and money. By running in relays, they could cover the roughly 500 km from Edo to Osaka in about 3 days.
The image of a hikyaku has even been used in a delivery company's logo.

communication-history:2.fact: In 1840, the world's first stamp was born in Britain.
communication-history:2.about:
In 1840, the world's first stamp, the "Penny Black," was issued in Britain, and anyone could send a letter cheaply.
In Japan, Maejima Hisoka set up the postal system in 1871. He's called "the father of Japan's postal service," and he's on the 1-yen stamp.

communication-history:3.fact: It became possible to send words instantly along wires.
communication-history:3.about:
In 1844, the telegraph using Morse code came into use in America, and messages could be sent to faraway towns in an instant.
In Japan, the telegraph started between Tokyo and Yokohama in 1869. Telegraph cables were even laid on the bottom of the sea.

communication-history:4.fact: Bell turned voices into electricity and sent them.
communication-history:4.about:
In 1876, Bell in America got a patent for the telephone. The first words on a telephone are said to have been "Mr Watson, come here."
In Japan, telephone service started in Tokyo and Yokohama in 1890. At first, operators connected the lines by hand.

communication-history:5.fact: It sends voices and music far away by radio waves.
communication-history:5.about:
In 1901, Marconi of Italy succeeded in sending a radio signal across the Atlantic. Later, radio broadcasting of voices and music began.
Radio broadcasting in Japan began in 1925. Radio exercises were born from radio too.

communication-history:6.fact: In 1973, a phone you could carry around was born.
communication-history:6.about:
In 1973, the first call on a mobile phone was made in America. It weighed about 1 kg and was the size of a brick.
In Japan, car phones started in 1979, and mobile phones spread quickly in the 1990s.

communication-history:7.fact: Phone, camera, map and internet, all in one.
communication-history:7.about:
From around 2007, touchscreen smartphones spread around the world. Not just calls, but photos, maps, games and the internet fit in the palm of your hand.
Even before that, Japanese mobile phones were advanced, with email, cameras and emoji, and they're now called "garakei."

#transport-history: Walking, rowing, driving, flying. How did people learn to travel far?

transport-history:0.fact: Invented in Mesopotamia about 5,500 years ago.
transport-history:0.about:
The wheel was invented in Mesopotamia about 5,500 years ago. At first it was a potter's wheel, and later it was used on carts.
The combination of a round wheel and an axle lives on in today's cars, bicycles and trains.

transport-history:1.fact: The taxis of the Edo period! People carried them on their shoulders.
transport-history:1.about:
In the Edo period, people used "kago," carriers in which a passenger was carried by two or more people. High-ranking people rode in grand ones.
In post towns along roads like the Tōkaidō, kago carriers waited for customers.

transport-history:2.fact: A bike with no pedals, pushed along with your feet.
transport-history:2.about:
The "Draisine," made by Drais in Germany in 1817, had no pedals; you moved by pushing the ground with your feet. It's like today's children's balance bikes.
Later, pedals and chains were added, and it became the bicycle we know.

transport-history:3.fact: The world's first public railway ran in Britain.
transport-history:3.about:
In 1825, Stephenson's steam locomotive ran on the world's first public railway in Britain. It burned coal to boil water, and the steam made it move.
In Japan, the railway between Shimbashi and Yokohama started running in 1872.

transport-history:4.fact: A vehicle invented in Japan that spread all over Asia.
transport-history:4.about:
The jinrikisha is a two-wheeled vehicle pulled by a person, invented in Japan around 1869. In the Meiji period, tens of thousands of them ran in Tokyo alone.
The English word "rickshaw" comes from the Japanese "jinrikisha." Now you can ride one at tourist spots.

transport-history:5.fact: A car that ran on petrol was born in Germany.
transport-history:5.about:
In 1886, Karl Benz in Germany made a three-wheeled car with a petrol engine. His wife Bertha made a long drive of about 100 km, showing people how amazing cars were.
Now more and more cars run on electricity.

transport-history:6.fact: The Wright brothers flew for the first time.
transport-history:6.about:
In 1903, the Wright brothers in America flew an aeroplane with an engine for the first time. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and went 36 m.
About 66 years later, people were standing on the Moon.

transport-history:7.about:
In 1964, Japan became the first country in the world to run a high-speed railway at more than 200 km per hour: the "Shinkansen."
After seeing its success, high-speed railways like France's TGV were built all over the world.

transport-history:8.fact: A huge plane that can carry more than 400 people.
transport-history:8.about:
The Boeing 747 "jumbo jet," which appeared in 1970, was a huge plane that could carry more than 400 people, and it made trips abroad possible for many more people.
Japan was one of the countries that used the most jumbo jets in the world.

#toys-history: Spinning tops, kites, marbles and blocks. Children long ago and children today all love to play!

toys-history:0.fact: They're said to have been born in China about 2,400 years ago.
toys-history:0.about:
Kites are said to have been born in China about 2,400 years ago, and they came to Japan around the Heian period.
All over Japan there are different kites, like New Year kites and Nagasaki's hata.

toys-history:1.fact: They were already in Japan in the Nara period.
toys-history:1.about:
Spinning tops are old toys found all over the world, and they're said to have come to Japan from China around the Nara period. They've been loved as a New Year game too.
The secret of why they keep spinning is the "gyroscopic effect," the same force that stops a bicycle falling over.

toys-history:2.fact: A Japanese game with cloth balls filled with beans.
toys-history:2.about:
Otedama is a game where you throw and catch small cloth balls filled with things like red beans, while singing.
It started as a game with pebbles, and there are similar games all over the world. It's a kind of juggling.

toys-history:3.fact: Their Japanese name comes from the Portuguese "vidro" (glass).
toys-history:3.about:
The "bī" in "bīdama," glass marbles, is said to come from "bīdoro," from the Portuguese word for glass. Glassmaking skills spread through Japan from Nagasaki.
The ball inside a bottle of rāmune soda is a kind of marble too.

toys-history:4.fact: It began as a learning tool made by cutting up a map.
toys-history:4.about:
