In the 1760s, an English mapmaker called Spilsbury stuck a map onto a wooden board and cut it up along the countries' borders to make a tool for learning geography. This was the start of the jigsaw puzzle.
Now there are puzzles with thousands of pieces.

toys-history:5.fact: Named after an American president's nickname.
toys-history:5.about:
In 1902, a story spread that American President Roosevelt refused to shoot a weak bear while hunting, and from his nickname, "Teddy," toy bears came to be called "teddy bears."
Around the same time, toy bears were also made in Germany, and they came to be loved all over the world.

toys-history:6.fact: A spring that walks down stairs. It was born from an accident.
toys-history:6.about:
Around 1943, an American engineer dropped a spring and saw it keep bouncing along, and he had the idea for a toy. It went on sale in 1945 and was a huge hit.
It's an example of an unexpected discovery becoming a toy.

toys-history:7.fact: In 1958, blocks in today's shape were born.
toys-history:7.about:
The blocks made by a Danish company in 1958, which fit together firmly with studs on top and tubes underneath, are played with all over the world.
They're made so that blocks from decades ago still fit perfectly with today's blocks.

toys-history:8.fact: Born in Japan in 1996, it became a craze around the world.
toys-history:8.about:
The egg-shaped digital pet (Tamagotchi), released in Japan in 1996, was a toy you raised by feeding and looking after it, and it became hugely popular around the world.
Lots of other toys played all over the world were born in Japan too, like video games and card games.

#edo-life: Edo (today's Tokyo), about 300 years ago. Let's peek at daily life in a city of a million people.

edo-life:0.fact: In the 1700s, Edo was one of the biggest cities in the world.
edo-life:0.about:
In the 1700s, about a million people lived in Edo, making it one of the world's great cities, bigger than London or Paris.
It had lots of rivers and canals, and goods were carried by boat. Nihonbashi was the starting point of all the country's roads.

edo-life:1.fact: Broken things were mended and used again and again.
edo-life:1.about:
In Edo there were craftspeople who mended pots, umbrellas and geta sandals, and even old clothes, scraps of paper and ashes from the stove were collected and sold.
This life without waste fits today's SDGs too. It was a city of "mottainai" (don't waste it).

edo-life:2.fact: Town children learned reading, writing and the soroban.
edo-life:2.about:
In the Edo period, there were lots of small schools called "terakoya" all over the country, where children from towns and villages learned reading, writing and the soroban.
That's why the people of Edo are said to have had one of the highest reading and writing rates in the world.

edo-life:3.fact: Sushi, soba and tempura were street-stall food.
edo-life:3.about:
Edo had lots of street stalls, and nigiri sushi, soba and tempura were fast food that busy townspeople ate quickly, standing up.
Today's style of nigiri sushi is said to have been born in the Edo period.

edo-life:4.about:
Many homes in Edo had no bath, so people went to "sentō," public bathhouses. Sentō were also places for chatting with the neighbours.
Even today, sentō walls sometimes have big paintings of Mount Fuji.

edo-life:5.fact: The newspapers of Edo, sold by reading them aloud in the street.
edo-life:5.about:
Kawaraban were sheets of paper printed with big events and unusual news, something like the newspapers of the Edo period.
Sellers read the news aloud in the streets as they sold them, so they were also called "yomiuri" (read and sell).

edo-life:6.fact: "Fires and fights are the flowers of Edo." The firefighters who protected the city.
edo-life:6.about:
Edo had lots of wooden houses and lots of fires, so each neighbourhood set up "machi-bikeshi" (town firefighters). The "Iroha 48 Companies" protected the city.
They waved their company's standard, the "matoi," on rooftops to gather their team. They were the beginning of today's fire brigades.

edo-life:7.fact: From Edo to Kyoto, about two weeks on foot.
edo-life:7.about:
The Tōkaidō road from Edo to Kyoto (about 500 km) had 53 post towns, and travellers took about two weeks to walk it.
Utagawa Hiroshige's pictures, "The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō," show what the journey was like.

edo-life:8.fact: Instead of clocks, people knew the time from the sound of bells.
edo-life:8.about:
Edo had "toki no kane" (time bells), which rang at set times to tell people the time.
The old way of telling time split day and night into 6 parts each, so the length of an "hour" changed with the seasons. "Oyatsu" (snack) comes from eating at "yatsu-doki," around 2 to 3 in the afternoon.

#jobs-hospital: "I want to be a nurse." At a hospital, lots of people work as a team to protect lives.

jobs-hospital:0.fact: They find out what's wrong and treat illnesses and injuries.
jobs-hospital:0.about:
To become a doctor, you study at university for 6 years, pass a national exam, and then train in a hospital for several more years.
There are lots of specialties, like internal medicine, surgery and paediatrics. Some doctors, called paediatricians, look after children.

jobs-hospital:1.fact: They take turns 24 hours a day to stay with patients in hospital.
jobs-hospital:1.about:
Nurses work with doctors to give injections and drips, check temperatures and look after patients. They take turns to look after the hospital at night too.
Florence Nightingale from Britain helped make nursing known as an important job.

jobs-hospital:2.fact: Medicine experts. They teach you the right way to take your medicine.
jobs-hospital:2.about:
Pharmacists read the doctor's prescription, get the medicine ready and explain how much to take, when to take it and which medicines not to take together.
They work in pharmacies, hospitals and companies that make medicines.

jobs-hospital:3.fact: Doctors who protect the health of your teeth.
jobs-hospital:3.about:
Dentists treat tooth decay, clean teeth and straighten teeth.
Japan has the "8020 campaign," which encourages people to keep 20 teeth until they're 80.

jobs-hospital:4.about:
Vets treat illnesses and injuries in pets like dogs and cats, farm animals like cows and pigs, and zoo animals.
Animals can't say "it hurts here," so being good at watching them carefully is important.

jobs-hospital:5.fact: They help people walk again after an injury.
jobs-hospital:5.about:
Physiotherapists exercise together with people whose bodies have become hard to move because of an injury or illness, helping them walk and move again.
Some help athletes recover from injuries too.

jobs-hospital:6.fact: They rush to help in an ambulance and keep people safe until they reach hospital.
jobs-hospital:6.about:
Paramedics ride in ambulances to help people who are ill or injured, and they give them first aid on the way to hospital.
In Japan, the number to call for an ambulance is 119.

jobs-hospital:7.fact: They plan the meals for hospital patients and school lunches.
jobs-hospital:7.about:
Registered dietitians plan meals that suit people who are ill, and school lunch menus, thinking about a good balance of nutrients.
It's a job that helps people get healthy through "eating."

jobs-hospital:8.about:
A "doctor heli" is a helicopter carrying a doctor and a nurse that rushes quickly to faraway places like mountains and islands.
In places with lots of islands, like Nagasaki, they do a very important job.

#jobs-airport: "I want to be a pilot." It takes the work of hundreds of people to fly one plane.

jobs-airport:0.fact: Two people fly the plane: the captain and the co-pilot.
jobs-airport:0.about:
A passenger plane is flown by two pilots: the captain and the co-pilot. Some airlines have a rule that they eat different meals, so they can't both get ill from the same food.
They check the weather and fuel, and they're responsible for the lives of hundreds of people.

jobs-airport:1.fact: They look after safety and service up in the sky.
jobs-airport:1.about:
Flight attendants don't just serve drinks; they do important jobs to keep passengers safe, like showing the emergency exits and helping anyone who suddenly gets ill.
They talk with passengers from lots of countries, so they use English too.

jobs-airport:2.fact: A job directing traffic in the sky.
jobs-airport:2.about:
Air traffic controllers watch the positions of lots of planes from the control tower and on radar, and give pilots instructions by radio so they don't crash into each other.
So that everyone around the world can talk the same way, air traffic control is mostly done in English.

jobs-airport:3.fact: They check planes so they can fly safely.
jobs-airport:3.about:
Aircraft mechanics check the engines, tyres and wings every time a plane lands, and in big checks they take parts apart one by one to inspect them.
They often work through the night, keeping air travel safe.

jobs-airport:4.fact: They check people in and help them at the counter.
jobs-airport:4.about:
Ground staff check passengers in, take their luggage and help them with connecting flights at the airport counters.
Getting passengers to the gate on time so the plane can leave as planned is an important job too.

jobs-airport:5.fact: They guide planes to the right spot with two paddles.
jobs-airport:5.about:
Aircraft marshallers stand in front of a plane that has landed and signal to the pilot with paddles in both hands, guiding it to stop in exactly the right place.
At the end, you can sometimes see them waving the plane off as it leaves.

jobs-airport:6.fact: They check for things that aren't allowed into the country.
jobs-airport:6.about:
Customs officers check luggage brought in from abroad to make sure there's nothing the rules don't allow.
"Detector dogs" with excellent noses work there too. To protect Japan's animals and plants, sometimes you can't bring in fruit or meat from abroad.

jobs-airport:7.fact: They watch the wind and fog to help planes fly safely.
jobs-airport:7.about:
At airports, weather experts carefully measure the wind's direction and strength, fog, snow and more, and pass it on to pilots and air traffic controllers.
Strong crosswinds and thunder are very important information for planes taking off and landing.

jobs-airport:8.fact: Airports have their own huge fire engines.
jobs-airport:8.about:
Airports have their own fire brigades, with chemical fire engines much bigger than ordinary ones, ready in case of an accident.
They train so they can reach anywhere at the airport within 3 minutes.

#jobs-creative: "I want to be a manga artist." Pictures, sounds, stories and designs: jobs that turn ideas into something real.

jobs-creative:0.fact: They draw pictures for books, posters and games.
jobs-creative:0.about:
Illustrators draw pictures for things like book illustrations, posters, product packaging and game characters.
Now lots of illustrators draw digital pictures on tablets.

jobs-creative:1.fact: Japanese manga are read all over the world.
jobs-creative:1.about:
Manga artists think up stories, plan the panels and draw the pictures to make manga. They often work in a team with assistants and editors.
Japanese manga are translated all over the world and called "manga" in English too.

jobs-creative:2.fact: One second of anime needs lots of drawings.
jobs-creative:2.about:
Anime looks like it's moving because slightly different pictures are shown very quickly. One second of film uses about 8 to 24 drawings.
Animators draw each one of those pictures and bring the characters to life.

jobs-creative:3.fact: They think up the rules and worlds of games.
jobs-creative:3.about:
Game creators work in teams to make a game's rules, stages, characters, music and more. Programmers, designers, composers and others work together.
Japan is a country that has made lots of world-famous games.

jobs-creative:4.fact: They play characters using only their voices.
jobs-creative:4.about:
Voice actors show characters' feelings using only their voices, in anime, games and dubbed foreign films.
In Japan, being a voice actor is a very popular job, and the word "seiyuu" is known abroad too.

jobs-creative:5.fact: They capture a moment and tell a story.
jobs-creative:5.about:
Photographers show all kinds of things through photos, like nature, animals, people, sports and food.
Good photos need the right direction of light and the right time of day, and the patience to wait for hours.

jobs-creative:6.fact: They think up clothes designs and make them real.
jobs-creative:6.about:
Fashion designers think about the shape, colour and material of clothes, draw designs, and make the clothes together with pattern makers and craftspeople.
Japanese designers do well at fashion shows in Paris and New York too.

jobs-creative:7.fact: Craftspeople who make cakes and sweets.
jobs-creative:7.about:
"Pâtissier" is French for a pastry chef. They carefully make cakes, chocolates and baked sweets, weighing ingredients to the gram.
Making sweets is even said to be like "a science experiment."

jobs-creative:8.fact: They make melodies and create music.
jobs-creative:8.about:
Composers write music for songs, films, games, adverts and more. Long ago they wrote it on music paper, but now many make it on computers.
Even school chimes and train departure melodies were written by someone.

#jobs-nature: "I want to be a zookeeper." Here are jobs that work with nature: the sea, mountains, fields and animals.

jobs-nature:0.fact: They grow rice and vegetables to make food for everyone.
jobs-nature:0.about:
Farmers grow rice, vegetables and fruit. They read the weather and seasons and work all year round, from preparing the soil to the harvest.
Now "smart farming" is spreading, like spraying with drones and controlling water with sensors.

jobs-nature:1.fact: They go out to sea to catch fish. Nagasaki is a big fishing prefecture.
jobs-nature:1.about:
Fishers go out to sea by boat and catch fish with nets or lines. They set off early in the morning, or sometimes in the middle of the night.
Nagasaki has a huge variety of fish and is one of the top prefectures in Japan for the amount of fish caught.

jobs-nature:2.fact: They plant, grow and cut trees, and look after forests.
jobs-nature:2.about:
Foresters plant trees, grow them for decades, thin them out to keep the forest healthy, and turn them into timber.
About two thirds of Japan is forest, so it's a forest country.

jobs-nature:3.fact: Food, cleaning and health checks for animals.
jobs-nature:3.about:
Keepers at zoos and aquariums prepare the animals' food, clean up and check on their health every day.
Finding fun ways to give food, so the animals don't get bored, is an important part of the job too.

jobs-nature:4.fact: They protect nature and visitors in national parks.
jobs-nature:4.about:
Rangers protect nature and animals in places like national parks, look after the hiking trails, and teach visitors how to enjoy nature and follow the rules.
Japan has "nature conservation officers" (rangers) from the Ministry of the Environment too.

jobs-nature:5.fact: They study living things in the sea.
jobs-nature:5.about:
Marine biologists go out on ships and dive into the sea to study creatures like fish, whales and coral.
It's thought that the deep sea still has lots of creatures that don't even have names yet.

jobs-nature:6.fact: They keep honeybees and collect honey.
jobs-nature:6.about:
Beekeepers look after hives of honeybees and collect the honey. Honeybees also do an important job carrying pollen between crop flowers.
Some people even keep bees on the roofs of buildings in cities.

jobs-nature:7.fact: They look at the sky and data to forecast tomorrow's weather.
jobs-nature:7.about:
Weather forecasters predict the weather using satellites, radar, and data like temperature and air pressure. You have to pass a national exam to become one.
Forecasts aren't just for TV; they're useful for farming, transport and planning events too.

jobs-nature:8.fact: They check old, weak trees and help them get healthy.
jobs-nature:8.about:
Tree doctors are experts who examine and treat trees weakened by disease or insects, and big old trees. It's a qualification that started in Japan in 1991.
They also protect sacred shrine trees that have lived for hundreds of years and trees that are Natural Monuments.

#explorers: To places nobody had ever been. Let's follow the journeys of the world's explorers.

explorers:0.fact: He travelled from Italy to China.
explorers:0.about:
About 750 years ago, Marco Polo travelled from Venice in Italy along the Silk Road to China and lived there for many years.
In "The Travels of Marco Polo," the book of his stories, Japan was described as "Zipangu, the land of gold."

explorers:1.fact: He travelled more than 120,000 km over about 30 years.
explorers:1.about:
Ibn Battuta was a traveller born in Morocco who is said to have travelled more than 120,000 km over about 30 years, through Africa, the Middle East, India, China and more.
His travel records are important for learning what the world was like back then.

explorers:2.fact: He sailed all the way to Africa with a huge fleet.
explorers:2.about:
In the Ming dynasty of China, Zheng He led fleets of dozens of huge ships on 7 voyages to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and the east coast of Africa.
There are even records that he brought a giraffe back to China from Africa.

explorers:3.fact: Magellan's fleet was the first to sail around the world.
explorers:3.about:
In 1519, a fleet led by Magellan left Spain, went through the strait at the southern tip of South America and crossed the Pacific. Magellan died on the way, but in 1522 one ship returned to Spain, completing the first voyage around the world.
It was a journey that actually showed the Earth is round.

explorers:4.fact: He explored the northern seas, and his name stayed on the map.
explorers:4.about:
Mamiya Rinzō, an Edo-period explorer, explored the northern island of Karafuto (Sakhalin) and confirmed that it's an island, not joined to the mainland.
The strait between Sakhalin and the mainland is still called the "Mamiya Strait" on world maps.

explorers:5.fact: The first people to stand at the South Pole.
explorers:5.about:
In December 1911, Roald Amundsen's team from Norway used dog sleds to become the first people to reach the South Pole.
The key to their success was learning from Arctic peoples' wisdom to prepare, with warm clothes and dog sleds.

explorers:6.fact: The first two people to stand on top of Everest.
explorers:6.about:
In 1953, Edmund Hillary from New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa from Nepal, became the first to stand on top of Everest, the highest mountain in the world.
They cared more about "we climbed it together" than "who was first."

explorers:7.fact: The first woman to climb Everest.
explorers:7.about:
In 1975, Tabei Junko became the first woman in the world to stand on top of Everest. Later, she also became the first woman to climb the highest mountain on all 7 continents.
She worked hard to protect mountain nature too.

explorers:8.fact: He reached the North Pole alone by dog sled.
explorers:8.about:
Uemura Naomi was a Japanese adventurer who, in 1978, became the first person in the world to reach the North Pole alone by dog sled.
He was also the first person to climb the highest peaks of 5 continents. You can learn about his adventures at the Uemura Naomi Adventure Museum in Hyōgo.

#women-science: "My hero is Marie Curie." Let's meet women scientists whose discoveries changed the world.

women-science:0.fact: The first person to win two Nobel Prizes.
women-science:0.about:
Marie Curie, born in Poland, carried out her research in France and discovered two new elements that give off radiation: polonium and radium.
She's the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911.

women-science:1.fact: The person who wrote the world's first "program."
women-science:1.about:
In the 1840s, Ada Lovelace from England wrote out the steps of a calculation for a computing machine that hadn't even been finished. This is said to be the world's first computer program.
She imagined the future, saying "machines might be able to make music, not just numbers."

women-science:2.about:
In a time when women weren't allowed to take the doctors' exam, Ogino Ginko kept asking again and again, and in 1885 she became Japan's first officially licensed woman doctor.
Her wish to "help women patients like me" opened the way.

women-science:3.fact: In "Silent Spring," she warned about the dangers of pesticides.
women-science:3.about:
Rachel Carson, an American biologist, wrote the book "Silent Spring" in 1962, telling people how pesticides harm birds and nature.
Her book helped start movements to protect the environment all over the world.

women-science:4.fact: The first woman to go to space.
women-science:4.about:
In 1963, Valentina Tereshkova of the Soviet Union became the first woman to fly in space, going around the Earth 48 times in about 3 days.
Her first words from space, "I am Seagull," are famous.

women-science:5.fact: A mathematician who worked out spacecraft paths by hand.
women-science:5.about:
Katherine Johnson, an American mathematician, worked out the flight paths of spacecraft at NASA. The astronaut Glenn is said to have said, "If she checks the computer's numbers, I'll fly."
She also worked on the calculations for Apollo 11's trip to the Moon.

women-science:6.fact: She captured the spiral shape of DNA in a photo.
women-science:6.about:
Rosalind Franklin from England used X-rays to take pictures of DNA, giving a big clue that showed DNA has a double spiral (double helix) shape.
It was important research that brought us closer to the secrets of the blueprint of living things.

women-science:7.fact: She studied wild chimpanzees for more than 60 years.
women-science:7.about:
From 1960, Jane Goodall from England watched wild chimpanzees in the forests of Tanzania in Africa, and discovered that chimpanzees use tools.
She also spread "Roots & Shoots," a programme where children around the world protect nature.

women-science:8.fact: She found a medicine for malaria in an old book of herbs.
women-science:8.about:
Tu Youyou, a Chinese scientist, searched through thousands of old medicine books and found "artemisinin," a medicine that works against malaria, in a plant related to mugwort.
This medicine has saved millions of lives around the world, and she won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2015.

#olympic-sports: "I want to play ___ at the Olympics." The world of the Olympics, with more and more new sports.

olympic-sports:0.fact: 42.195 km. This distance comes from the 1908 London Games.
olympic-sports:0.about:
The marathon distance of 42.195 km is said to have been set at the 1908 London Games, when the start was put in front of a castle and the finish in front of the royal box.
Its name comes from "Marathon," a place in ancient Greece.

olympic-sports:1.fact: Floor, high bar, rings… Japan is strong at gymnastics.
olympic-sports:1.about:
Gymnastics has been an event since the very first Games in Athens in 1896. Men compete in 6 events and women in 4, for beauty and difficulty.
Japan has won lots of gold medals in gymnastics. Some moves are even named after Japanese gymnasts.

olympic-sports:2.fact: It became an Olympic sport for the first time at Tokyo 2020.
olympic-sports:2.about:
Skateboarding became an Olympic sport for the first time at the Tokyo Games in 2021. Japanese teenagers won gold medals, which got lots of attention.
It's said to have started with surfers on the west coast of America playing in the streets on days without waves.

olympic-sports:3.fact: A sport where you climb a wall by holding on to holds.
olympic-sports:3.about:
Sport climbing is a sport where you climb a wall by gripping "holds" attached to it with your hands and feet, and it joined the Olympics at the Tokyo Games.
There's "speed" (who's fastest), "boulder" (how many problems you can climb) and "lead" (how high you can get).

olympic-sports:4.fact: Competing at riding waves. It comes from Hawaiian tradition.
olympic-sports:4.about:
Surfing is a sport that comes from the traditions of Pacific peoples like the Hawaiians. At the Tokyo Games, it was held in the sea in Chiba.
Natural waves are different every time, so choosing waves well is important too.

olympic-sports:5.about:
Breaking (breakdancing) is a dance born in New York in the 1970s, and it became an Olympic sport at the 2024 Paris Games. A Japanese dancer won the gold medal.
Dancers compete in expression with spinning moves and freezes, in time to the music.

olympic-sports:6.fact: Electricity is used to judge whether a hit landed.
olympic-sports:6.about:
Fencing is a sport that grew from European sword skills, and it's been an Olympic event since the first Games.
When the tip of the sword touches, an electric signal lights a lamp to judge it. Japanese fencers have won medals too.

olympic-sports:7.fact: Chess on ice. Brushes make a path for the stone.
olympic-sports:7.about:
Curling is a Winter Olympics sport where you slide a stone of about 20 kg across the ice to get it close to the centre of the target. Brushing the ice changes how the stone moves.
Planning tactics is so important that it's called "chess on ice."

olympic-sports:8.fact: They fly more than 100 m through the air.
olympic-sports:8.about:
Ski jumping is a winter sport where athletes launch off a jump and compete in the distance and beauty of their flight. Jumps go over 100 m, and in some events more than 200 m.
At the Nagano Olympics (1998), the Japanese team won the gold medal.

#paralympic-sports: With clever ideas and equipment, everyone can compete for real. Let's find out how amazing para sports are.

paralympic-sports:0.fact: It started with a wheelchair sports event at a British hospital.
paralympic-sports:0.about:
It started in 1948, when Dr Guttmann held a sports event for wheelchair users at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in Britain. The first Paralympic Games were held in Rome in 1960.
The name "Paralympics" started being used at the 1964 Tokyo Games.

paralympic-sports:1.fact: The hoop is 3.05 m high, the same as in ordinary basketball!
paralympic-sports:1.about:
In wheelchair basketball, the hoop height and court size are the same as in ordinary basketball. Pushing your wheelchair 3 times while holding the ball is a foul.
Each player has points depending on their disability, and there's a limit on the team's total points.

paralympic-sports:2.fact: How close can you get to the white target ball?
paralympic-sports:2.about:
Boccia is a sport where players throw or roll red or blue balls towards a white target ball, and whoever gets closest wins.
Players who find it hard to throw can kick the ball or use a ramp. It's a sport you can enjoy at school too.

paralympic-sports:3.fact: Players defend by listening to a ball with bells inside.
paralympic-sports:3.about:
Goalball is a sport for teams of 3 wearing blindfolds, who roll a ball with bells inside back and forth to get it into the other team's goal.
The crowd has to keep quiet too. Using only sound, players stop the ball by lying sideways across the court.

paralympic-sports:4.fact: Players shout "Voy!" to show where they are.
paralympic-sports:4.about:
Blind football is 5-a-side football played by players who can't see, with a ball that makes a sound. The goalkeeper and the "guide" behind the goal can see, and they give instructions by voice.
There's a rule that players must call out "Voy!" when they go to win the ball.

paralympic-sports:5.fact: An exciting sport where wheelchairs crash into each other.
paralympic-sports:5.about:
Wheelchair rugby is a sport where players with disabilities in their arms and legs carry the ball in extra-tough wheelchairs to score. Wheelchair-to-wheelchair tackles are allowed.
Men and women can play on the same team. Japan is one of the strongest teams in the world.

paralympic-sports:6.fact: For swimmers who can't see, a "tapper" tells them the wall is near.
paralympic-sports:6.about:
In para swimming, so that swimmers who can't see don't hit the wall at turns and the finish, a "tapper" at the poolside touches them with a soft-tipped pole to let them know.
Teamwork between swimmer and tapper is important.

paralympic-sports:7.fact: Players play with their bottoms touching the floor.
paralympic-sports:7.about:
Sitting volleyball is volleyball played with your bottom touching the floor, with a lower net and a smaller court.
Players can't jump, but they keep the ball going with quick moves and teamwork.

#martial-arts: Begin with a bow, end with a bow. The world's martial arts are paths for training the mind and body.

martial-arts:0.fact: In martial arts, people bow at the start and the end.
martial-arts:0.about:
In Japanese martial arts, you begin by bowing to your opponent and the dōjō, and you end with a bow too. Win or lose, it shows that you respect your opponent.
"Begin with a bow, end with a bow" is an important spirit of martial arts.

martial-arts:1.fact: Born in Okinawa, it spread all over the world.
martial-arts:1.about:
Karate is a martial art born in Okinawa, and "karate" means "empty hand," fighting without weapons. It has "kata," set sequences of moves, and "kumite," where you face a partner.
About 100 million people are said to practise it around the world now, and it became an Olympic sport at the Tokyo Games.

martial-arts:2.fact: If you go outside the ring or touch the ground with anything but the soles of your feet, you lose.
martial-arts:2.about:
Sumo is a traditional wrestling sport, sometimes called Japan's national sport. Salt is thrown into the ring to purify it.
Sumo wrestlers can weigh more than 150 kg, and wrestlers from other countries do well too.

martial-arts:3.fact: A martial art that uses the attacker's force to redirect them.
martial-arts:3.about:
Aikido is a Japanese martial art where you don't clash with your opponent's strength, but use the direction of their force to redirect them or throw them.
Many dōjō don't hold matches to decide winners and losers, so people can practise whatever their age or size.

martial-arts:4.fact: The Japanese way of the bow, aiming at a target 28 m away.
martial-arts:4.about:
Kyūdō is a martial art where you aim at a target 28 m away with a Japanese bow about 2 m long. Not only hitting the target, but also good posture and a calm mind are valued.
Holding the bow below its middle is a special feature of the Japanese bow.

martial-arts:5.fact: A Korean martial art. Lots of kicks!
martial-arts:5.about:
Taekwondo is a martial art born in South Korea, famous for its high spinning kicks. It's been an Olympic sport since the 2000 Sydney Games.
There are dōjō all over the world, and commands are given in Korean.

martial-arts:6.fact: A Chinese martial art with forms that copy animal movements.
martial-arts:6.about:
Chinese martial arts (wushu, kung fu) include forms based on the movements of animals like tigers, cranes and snakes.
In China, lots of people do slow-moving "tai chi" in parks in the morning to stay healthy.

martial-arts:7.fact: A Brazilian martial art where people fight as if dancing to music.
martial-arts:7.about:
Capoeira is a martial art born in Brazil, with dance-like movements. People form a circle, playing instruments and singing, while two players show their moves without hitting each other.
It's on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

martial-arts:8.fact: Born in Japan, it spread to more than 200 countries and regions.
martial-arts:8.about:
Judo is a Japanese martial art created by Kanō Jigorō, and now it's practised in more than 200 countries and regions. France is said to have even more judo players than Japan.
At world competitions, Japanese words like "hajime" (begin) and "ippon" (full point) are used just as they are.

#japanese-games: From New Year games to playground games, here are the traditional games Japanese children have played.

japanese-games:0.fact: Listen to the reading card and grab the matching card fast!
japanese-games:0.about:
Karuta is a game where you quickly grab the picture or word card that matches the card the reader reads out. The name "karuta" comes from the Portuguese word for "card."
In "competitive karuta," played with the Hyakunin Isshu poems, players react in less than a second.

japanese-games:1.fact: Roll the dice and race to the finish.
japanese-games:1.about:
In sugoroku, you roll the dice, move that many spaces, and whoever reaches the goal first wins. In the Edo period, "dōchū sugoroku," based on a journey along the Tōkaidō, was popular.
It's a tradition to play it with the family at New Year.

japanese-games:2.fact: A funny game where you place parts of a face while blindfolded.
japanese-games:2.about:
Fukuwarai is a New Year game where you wear a blindfold and place the eyebrows, eyes, nose and mouth on the outline of a face. Everyone laughs at the funny face you make.
It's linked to the saying "Good luck comes to the house that laughs."

japanese-games:3.fact: A New Year game of hitting a shuttlecock with wooden paddles.
japanese-games:3.about:
In hanetsuki, players hit a shuttlecock, a soapberry seed with feathers, back and forth with wooden paddles called hagoita. Whoever drops it gets an × or ○ drawn on their face with ink.
The shuttlecock looks like a dragonfly, and like dragonflies, which eat mosquitoes, it was believed to "keep illness away."

japanese-games:4.fact: Flip over the menko on the ground with your own menko!
japanese-games:4.about:
Menko is a game where you slam a cardboard card onto the ground to flip over your opponent's card or knock it out of the area.
Menko had pictures of popular sumo wrestlers and baseball players on them, and they were children's treasures long ago.

japanese-games:5.fact: Flick the pieces with your finger, and win the ones you hit.
japanese-games:5.about:
Ohajiki is a game where you flick flat glass or stone pieces with your finger to hit other pieces and win them.
There's also a rule that before you flick, you have to draw your finger between the two pieces you want to hit, like drawing a line.

japanese-games:6.fact: Make a broom or Tokyo Tower with a single string.
japanese-games:6.about:
Ayatori is a game where you loop a string around your fingers to make all kinds of shapes. You can play alone or take turns with a partner.
String games are found all over the world, and in English it's called "cat's cradle."

japanese-games:7.fact: If the oni tags you, you're the next oni!
japanese-games:7.about:
In onigokko, the "oni" (it) chases everyone else and tries to tag them. There are lots of kinds, like "taka-oni," where you're safe if you're up high, and "kōri-oni," where you freeze when you're tagged.
There are similar games all over the world; in English it's called "tag."

japanese-games:8.fact: Don't move when the oni turns around!
japanese-games:8.about:
When the oni says "Daruma-san ga koronda" and turns around, anyone who's moving is caught.
There are similar games all over the world. In English it's called "Red light, green light," and in the UK "Grandmother's footsteps."

japanese-games:9.fact: A word game where each word starts with the last sound of the one before.
japanese-games:9.about:
In shiritori, you say a word that starts with the last sound of the word the person before you said. If your word ends in "n," you lose!
You can play shiritori in English too, linking the last letters, like "apple → egg → grape."

#playground-world: Rock-paper-scissors, hopscotch, tug of war. Children around the world play similar games too!

playground-world:0.fact: A game born in Japan that spread all over the world.
playground-world:0.about:
Janken, with rock, scissors and paper, is said to have taken its present form in Japan between the Edo and Meiji periods and then spread around the world.
In English, people say "Rock, paper, scissors!" There are even world championships.

playground-world:1.fact: A game where you hop through squares on the ground on one foot.
playground-world:1.about:
Games where you draw squares on the ground and hop through them on one or two feet are found all over the world. In English it's called "hopscotch."
It's such an old game that some say similar squares have been found on ancient Roman roads.

playground-world:2.fact: It used to be an Olympic sport!
playground-world:2.about:
Tug of war was an official Olympic sport from 1900 to 1920. There are still world championships today.
It's a popular event at Japanese sports days too. The Naha Ōtsunahiki in Okinawa is in the Guinness World Records for using the world's biggest rope.

playground-world:3.fact: "Mō ii kai?" (Ready?) "Mā da da yo!" (Not yet!)
playground-world:3.about:
In hide-and-seek, everyone hides while the seeker closes their eyes and counts, and then the seeker looks for them. It's played all over the world.
In English, the seeker shouts, "Ready or not, here I come!"

playground-world:4.fact: A game where you copy only when "Simon says."
playground-world:4.about:
You copy an action only when it starts with "Simon says," like "Simon says, touch your nose." If you move when it doesn't, you're out!
It's a fun way to learn English action words.

playground-world:5.fact: Sit in a circle, and when you hear "Goose!", it's a chase.
playground-world:5.about:
Everyone sits in a circle, and "it" walks around touching each person's head, saying "duck, duck…" The person who hears "goose!" stands up and chases "it."
It's an American game similar to the Japanese game "handkerchief drop."

playground-world:6.fact: An American game of bouncing a ball between four squares.
playground-world:6.about:
In four square, one person stands in each of four squares drawn on the ground, and they hit the ball into other squares after one bounce. If you make a mistake, you swap with the next person.
It's a classic at break time in American schools.

playground-world:7.fact: A game where the "piggy" in the middle tries to grab the ball.
playground-world:7.about:
Two people throw a ball to each other, and one person standing in the middle (the piggy) tries to grab it. If they get it, they swap with the person who threw it.
It's a British game, similar to the Japanese game "torikago."

playground-world:8.fact: Jumping over elastic held by people's legs, a game played around the world.
playground-world:8.about:
Two people stretch elastic around their legs, and others jump over it or step on it in time to a song. This game is found all over the world, in Japan, China, Europe and more.
The challenge is that the elastic gets higher and higher.

#stadiums: Stadiums ringing with the voices of tens of thousands. Let's tour the world's great stadiums, from ancient times to now.

stadiums:0.fact: The venue of the first modern Olympics, made entirely of marble.
stadiums:0.about:
The Panathenaic Stadium in Athens, Greece, is a rare stadium made of marble, and it was the venue for the first modern Olympics in 1896.
The ceremony to send the Olympic flame off from Greece is still held there.

stadiums:1.fact: A huge round arena from Rome, about 2,000 years ago.
stadiums:1.about:
The Colosseum in Rome is a round building built about 2,000 years ago, and it held about 50,000 people. It even had a system for stretching huge cloths overhead for shade.
It's said to be a model for the shape of today's stadiums, and it's a World Heritage Site.

stadiums:2.fact: The sacred ground of high school baseball, with more than 100 years of history.
stadiums:2.about:
Kōshien Stadium in Hyōgo, built in 1924, is the oldest professional baseball stadium in Japan. The national high school baseball tournaments are held there in summer and spring.
The tradition of players from losing teams taking home some soil from the field, and the ivy covering its walls, are famous.

stadiums:3.fact: Wood from all 47 prefectures is used in it.
stadiums:3.about:
Japan National Stadium in Tokyo was finished in 2019 and was the main venue of the Tokyo 2020 Games. It was designed by architect Kuma Kengo and others, and the eaves of its roof use wood from all 47 prefectures.
It's built to let the wind through so it stays cool even in summer.

stadiums:4.fact: A football stadium built in the middle of the city.
stadiums:4.about:
Nagasaki Stadium City in Nagasaki opened in 2024. Around the football stadium are an arena, a hotel, shops and more.
The stands are very close to the pitch, so it's an exciting stadium where you can even hear the players' voices.

stadiums:5.fact: The home of English football. Look for its huge arch.
stadiums:5.about:
Wembley Stadium in London, England, is the home of English football and holds about 90,000 people. A white arch about 130 m high holds up its roof.
Big matches like the final of England's FA Cup are held there.

stadiums:6.fact: A Brazilian stadium where about 200,000 fans gathered in 1950.
stadiums:6.about:
The Maracanã Stadium in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, is known for the World Cup final match in 1950, when about 200,000 people came.
Now it has seats for about 78,000, but it's still the spiritual home of Brazilian football.

stadiums:7.fact: A university stadium that holds more than 100,000 people!
stadiums:7.about:
The University of Michigan's stadium in America is called "The Big House." It holds more than 100,000 people, making it one of the biggest stadiums in America.
Huge crowds come to every university American football game.

#traditional-clothes: Clothes born to suit the climate and way of life of each place. Let's look at the traditional clothes of the world.

traditional-clothes:0.fact: Japanese clothes made by sewing straight pieces of cloth together.
traditional-clothes:0.about:
A kimono is made by sewing straight pieces of a long roll of cloth called a "tanmono" together, with hardly any cloth cut off and thrown away. If you undo the stitches, it turns back into one piece of cloth, so there's no waste.
The yukata worn at summer festivals is a kind of kimono too.

traditional-clothes:1.fact: A full skirt and a short jacket.
traditional-clothes:1.about:
Hanbok is traditional Korean clothing. Women wear a short jacket called a "jeogori" and a long, full skirt called a "chima."
It's worn at New Year, weddings, first birthday celebrations and more. Its bright colours stand out.

traditional-clothes:2.fact: Known for its high collar and slits at the sides.
traditional-clothes:2.about:
The qipao (cheongsam) is based on clothes from China's Qing dynasty, and it took its present form in Shanghai in the 1920s.
It's known for its high collar, close-fitting shape and bright embroidery.

traditional-clothes:3.fact: A single cloth 5 to 9 m long, wrapped around the body.
traditional-clothes:3.about:
The sari is worn by women in India and nearby countries. It's a single cloth 5 to 9 m long, wrapped around the body without any sewing.
There are dozens of ways to wrap it, depending on the region. It's airy, so it's good for hot countries.

traditional-clothes:4.about:
The kilt is a traditional knee-length Scottish skirt worn by men. Its checked pattern, called "tartan," has different designs for each family (clan).
Some people wear it at festivals and weddings and play the bagpipes.

traditional-clothes:5.fact: Traditional clothes from southern Germany and Austria.
traditional-clothes:5.about:
In southern Germany and Austria, women wear the "dirndl," a dress with an apron, and men wear "lederhosen," leather shorts.
They started as work clothes in mountain villages, but now they're popular for festivals.

traditional-clothes:6.fact: A colourful Ghanaian cloth made by joining narrow strips.
traditional-clothes:6.about:
Kente is a cloth made in Ghana, Africa, by sewing together long, narrow woven strips. Each colour and pattern has a meaning.
Gold is said to stand for wealth, green for growth and blue for peace.

traditional-clothes:7.fact: One piece of cloth with a hole in the middle. A warm coat from the Andes.
traditional-clothes:7.about:
A poncho is a piece of cloth with a hole in the middle for your head. It was born in the Andes of South America and is made from alpaca or llama wool.
It's warm and easy to move in, perfect for the cold highlands.

traditional-clothes:8.fact: A Vietnamese outfit of a long tunic and trousers.
traditional-clothes:8.about:
The áo dài is traditional Vietnamese clothing: a long, close-fitting tunic worn with loose trousers.
In Vietnam, it's used as a uniform for high school students and staff at hotels and airports.

traditional-clothes:9.fact: Beautiful patterns on cloth woven from tree-bark fibre.
traditional-clothes:9.about:
The traditional clothing of the Ainu people, who live in places like Hokkaido, uses "attush," cloth woven from the bark fibres of trees like the elm.
Ainu patterns, with swirls and thorn-like shapes, are said to protect against evil, and they're still passed down today.

#world-new-year: "Happy New Year!" The way people welcome the New Year is very different from country to country!

world-new-year:0.fact: Osechi, ozōni, New Year cards and otoshidama.
world-new-year:0.about:
At New Year in Japan, people put up kadomatsu and shimekazari decorations and eat osechi and ozōni. On New Year's Day, New Year cards arrive, and children get otoshidama (New Year money).
Each osechi dish carries a wish, like black beans for "living a hard-working, healthy life."

world-new-year:1.fact: They eat 12 grapes, one with each chime of the bell.
world-new-year:1.about:
In Spain, at midnight on New Year's Eve, people eat one grape with each of the 12 chimes of the bell, wishing for good luck in all 12 months.
Eating them all in time is surprisingly hard! Some people choose small grapes.

world-new-year:2.fact: The first person to come to your house in the New Year brings good luck.
world-new-year:2.about:
At "Hogmanay," Scotland's New Year's Eve festival, the first visitor to step into a house in the New Year (the "first-footer") is said to bring good luck to that home for the year.
Everyone holds hands and sings a song to welcome the New Year.

world-new-year:3.fact: Eat "tteokguk" rice cake soup and you're a year older.
world-new-year:3.about:
At "Seollal," the Korean Lunar New Year, families get together and eat "tteokguk," a soup with white rice cakes. People have long said that "eating tteokguk makes you a year older."
Children bow deeply to grown-ups and get New Year money.

world-new-year:4.fact: The New Year is on the spring equinox. It has more than 3,000 years of history.
world-new-year:4.about:
Nowruz is a New Year on the spring equinox, celebrated in Iran, Central Asia and other places. It means "new day" and has more than 3,000 years of history.
There's a custom of displaying 7 things whose Persian names start with "S," like sprouted wheat and apples. It's on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

world-new-year:5.fact: People throw old plates at their friends' doors!
world-new-year:5.about:
In Denmark, there's a New Year's Eve custom of smashing old plates in front of friends' and family members' front doors. The more broken plates in front of your door in the morning, the more friends you have.
There's also a custom of "jumping" into the New Year from a chair.

world-new-year:6.fact: Wearing white, people jump over 7 waves in the sea.
world-new-year:6.about:
In Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, millions of people dressed in white gather on the beach on New Year's Eve. It's said that if you jump over 7 waves, your wishes will come true.
Brazil is in the Southern Hemisphere, so New Year is in the middle of summer.

world-new-year:7.fact: They lay out 12 kinds of round fruit that look like coins.
world-new-year:7.about:
In the Philippines, on New Year's Eve, people put 12 kinds of round fruit, shaped like coins, on the table and wish for a year of plenty.
Some people wear polka-dot clothes too, which also stand for round coins.

world-new-year:8.fact: The New Year comes in September, when the rainy season ends.
world-new-year:8.about:
Ethiopia's New Year, "Enkutatash," is around September 11th. The long rainy season is over, and yellow flowers are in full bloom.
Children pick flowers and go from house to house singing. The Ethiopian calendar has 13 months in a year.

world-new-year:9.fact: In New York, a big glowing ball comes down.
world-new-year:9.about:
In Times Square, New York, a big glowing ball has slowly come down every New Year's Eve since 1907, reaching the bottom at exactly midnight.
Nearly a million people gather and count down, "10, 9, 8…"

#markets-world: "How much is it?" Busy markets are packed with the life of their country.

markets-world:0.fact: Tokyo's fish market. Its morning tuna auctions are famous.
markets-world:0.about:
Toyosu Market in Tokyo, which moved from Tsukiji Market in 2018, is one of the biggest fish markets in the world. Every morning, huge tuna are lined up and their prices are decided in an "auction."
The auctions use special hand signals, showing prices with finger shapes.

markets-world:1.fact: A covered market in Türkiye with more than 4,000 shops.
markets-world:1.about:
The Grand Bazaar in Istanbul, Türkiye, has been open since around 1461 and is one of the oldest and biggest covered markets in the world. More than 4,000 shops line its maze-like streets.
It sells things like carpets, lamps, spices and tea.

markets-world:2.fact: In Thailand, people sell vegetables and fruit from small boats.
markets-world:2.about:
At floating markets in Thailand, like Damnoen Saduak, fruit, vegetables and noodle dishes are sold from small boats on the canals.
Long ago, canals were used instead of roads, and people went shopping by boat.

markets-world:3.fact: A square in Morocco, busy at night with food stalls and street performers.
markets-world:3.about:
Jemaa el-Fnaa square in Marrakesh, Morocco, is busy in the daytime with fruit juice stalls and sellers, and at night with hundreds of food stalls, music and storytellers.
Its culture of storytelling and performance is on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

markets-world:4.fact: Wooden stalls fill the squares of Germany in winter.
markets-world:4.about:
In Germany and other countries, Christmas markets with wooden stalls fill town squares for about 4 weeks before Christmas.
They sell decorations, toys, grilled sausages, gingerbread and more. Now they're held in Japan too.

markets-world:5.fact: A weekend market in Thailand with 15,000 shops!
markets-world:5.about:
The Chatuchak Weekend Market in Bangkok, Thailand, is one of the biggest markets in the world, with more than 15,000 shops.
It has everything: clothes, plants, pet supplies, food and more. It's so big you could get lost without a map.

markets-world:6.fact: A colourful food market in Spain.
markets-world:6.about:
La Boqueria in Barcelona, Spain, is a food market with more than 800 years of history. Colourful fruit, cured ham and seafood are on display.
Counters where you can eat what you've just bought are popular too.

markets-world:7.about:
All over Taiwan, there are "night markets" that open from evening until the middle of the night. Rows of small stalls sell things like pan-fried soup dumplings and bubble tea for eating as you walk.
Going out at night with family and friends is a fun part of the culture.

markets-world:8.fact: A Japanese street market that has run for more than 300 years.
markets-world:8.about:
Kōchi's Sunday Market is a street market that has carried on for more than 300 years since the Edo period. On Sunday mornings, about 300 stalls line about 1 km of road.
Farmers sell vegetables and fruit they grew themselves, country-style sushi and more, and chatting with the customers is part of the fun.

#mythical-creatures: Kappa, dragons, unicorns. Amazing creatures that people around the world have told stories about.

mythical-creatures:0.fact: If the water in the dish on its head runs out, it loses its strength!
mythical-creatures:0.about:
The kappa is a creature said to live in Japan's rivers and ponds, with a dish on top of its head and a shell on its back. It loves cucumbers, which is where the name "kappa maki" (cucumber sushi rolls) comes from.
One story says that if you bow to a kappa, it can't help bowing back, and the water spills out of its dish.

mythical-creatures:1.fact: A mysterious long-nosed being that lives in the mountains.
mythical-creatures:1.about:
Tengu are said to live in Japan's mountains, and they're shown with red faces, long noses and feather fans. They can fly and are said to watch over people training in the mountains.
In Japanese, showing off is called "becoming a tengu," because of their long noses.

mythical-creatures:2.fact: A spirit like a child that brings happiness to the house it lives in.
mythical-creatures:2.about:
The zashiki-warashi is a child-like spirit from stories of the Tōhoku region, and a house with a zashiki-warashi is said to prosper.
It likes playing tricks, but it isn't scary; it's been treasured as a spirit that protects the home.

mythical-creatures:3.fact: A lucky creature that brings rain.
mythical-creatures:3.about:
Chinese and Japanese dragons have long, snake-like bodies. They fly through the sky and are thought to be lucky creatures that bring rain. The dragon dance at Nagasaki Kunchi is this kind of dragon.
European dragons usually have wings and breathe fire, so they look different.

mythical-creatures:4.fact: An immortal bird that's reborn from fire.
mythical-creatures:4.about:
The phoenix is a legendary bird that, after living for hundreds of years, burns in a fire and is born again from the ashes.
So it's used in many countries as a symbol of "getting back up again and again."

mythical-creatures:5.fact: Scotland's national animal is the unicorn!
mythical-creatures:5.about:
The unicorn is a legendary creature like a white horse with one horn on its head. It's the national animal of Scotland.
Long ago, narwhal tusks were sometimes sold as "unicorn horns."

mythical-creatures:6.fact: A mysterious creature that might live in a Scottish lake.
mythical-creatures:6.about:
There's a story that "Nessie," a big creature with a long neck, lives in Loch Ness in Scotland. A photo made the news in the 1930s, but it was later found to be fake.
It's still a fun mystery, and lots of people come looking for Nessie.

mythical-creatures:7.fact: A legend of creatures that are human on top and fish below.
mythical-creatures:7.about:
There are stories of mermaids all over the world. Danish author Andersen's fairy tale "The Little Mermaid" is famous, and there's a mermaid statue from 1913 in the harbour in Copenhagen.
Some say sailors who saw dugongs or manatees mistook them for mermaids.

mythical-creatures:8.fact: The snowman of the Himalayas. Were its footprints found?
mythical-creatures:8.about:
The yeti is a big "abominable snowman" said to live in the Himalayas. Photos of huge footprints in the snow made the news, but research found that some were bear footprints.
It appears in old stories from Bhutan and Nepal too.

mythical-creatures:9.fact: A creature that eats your bad dreams.
mythical-creatures:9.about:
The baku of Chinese and Japanese legend is said to eat people's bad dreams. People long ago slept with a picture of a baku under their pillows.
The Japanese name for the Malayan tapir, "baku," comes from this legendary creature.

#lucky-symbols: Four-leaf clovers, maneki-neko and lucky number seven. Here are the world's "signs of good luck."

lucky-symbols:0.fact: The right paw calls money, and the left paw calls customers.
lucky-symbols:0.about:
A maneki-neko is a cat figure with a raised paw that beckons good luck. A cat with its right paw raised is said to call money, and one with its left paw raised calls customers.
Abroad, it's popular as a "lucky cat" that waves its paw back and forth.

lucky-symbols:1.fact: You find one in about every 10,000!
lucky-symbols:1.about:
White clover leaves usually have 3 leaflets, but sometimes you find one with 4. The chance is said to be about 1 in 10,000.
In Ireland and other parts of Europe, they've long been treasured as a sign of good luck.

lucky-symbols:2.fact: Hang one above the door, and good luck will come.
lucky-symbols:2.about:
In Europe and America, people say that hanging a horseshoe above the door brings good luck. Some believe that with the U shape facing up, it "holds in the luck."
Iron has long been thought to keep away evil.

lucky-symbols:3.fact: In English-speaking countries it's 7; in China it's 8.
lucky-symbols:3.about:
In English-speaking countries, 7 is a lucky number, as in "lucky seven." In China, "8" sounds like a word for "getting rich," so it's a very good number.
The 2008 Beijing Olympics began at 8 p.m. on August 8th.

lucky-symbols:4.fact: In China and Japan, red is a colour for celebrations.
lucky-symbols:4.about:
In China, red is the colour of good luck and joy, so New Year money envelopes and decorations are red. In Japan too, red is used for celebrations, in sekihan (red bean rice) and red-and-white decorations.
The meaning of colours is different in each country.

lucky-symbols:5.fact: In Europe, it's "the insect that brings good luck."
lucky-symbols:5.about:
In many European countries, the ladybird is thought to be a lucky insect. For farmers, it's a welcome bug, because it eats the aphids that eat their crops.
The Japanese name "tentōmushi" comes from how it climbs up and up and flies towards the sun ("otentō-sama").

lucky-symbols:6.fact: Lucky dreams to have at New Year.
lucky-symbols:6.about:
In Japan, the first dream of the New Year is called "hatsuyume," and dreams of Mount Fuji, a hawk or an aubergine have long been thought lucky.
Mount Fuji is Japan's highest mountain, the hawk is a strong, clever bird, and "nasu" (aubergine) sounds like "nasu" (to achieve).

lucky-symbols:7.fact: If a tea stalk stands up in your tea, something good will happen.
lucky-symbols:7.about:
When you pour tea and a stalk floats upright in the cup, it's called "chabashira ga tatsu" (a tea stalk stands), and it's thought to be lucky.
It rarely happens, so it makes people happy, thinking "maybe something good will happen today."

lucky-symbols:8.fact: A charm that catches bad dreams in its net.
lucky-symbols:8.about:
The dreamcatcher is a charm from the Ojibwe, an Indigenous people of North America. It has a net like a spider's web inside a hoop.
It's said that bad dreams get caught in the net, and only good dreams slide down the feathers to the sleeper.

lucky-symbols:9.about:
The nazar boncuğu is a blue glass eye charm seen in Türkiye and other places, said to protect people from bad things.
It's hung in homes and cars and on babies' clothes. It's a popular souvenir from Türkiye too.

#birthdays-world: "When is your birthday? — My birthday is May 5th." Let's look at birthday celebrations around the world.

birthdays-world:0.fact: Blow out one candle for each year and make a wish.
birthdays-world:0.about:
The custom of putting one candle for each year on a cake and blowing them out while making a wish is said to have spread from children's birthday celebrations in Germany.
There's also a saying that if you blow them all out in one go, your wish will come true.

birthdays-world:1.fact: One of the most sung songs in the world.
birthdays-world:1.about:
The melody of the birthday song comes from a children's song written by two American sisters in the 1890s.
Now it's sung in languages all over the world. In English, people sing "Happy birthday to you."

birthdays-world:2.fact: Hit it while blindfolded, and sweets come out!
birthdays-world:2.about:
In Mexico and other countries, a colourful paper figure full of sweets called a "piñata" is hung up, and blindfolded children hit it with a stick to break it.
When it breaks, sweets rain down and everyone picks them up.

birthdays-world:3.fact: Long noodles for a long life.
birthdays-world:3.about:
In China, people eat long "longevity noodles" on their birthdays, wishing for a long life. It's important to eat them without cutting them.
Peach-shaped buns called "shoutao" are also eaten to celebrate.

birthdays-world:4.fact: A soup that thanks your mother for giving birth to you.
birthdays-world:4.about:
In South Korea, people have seaweed soup, "miyeok-guk," on the morning of their birthday. It's the soup mothers have after giving birth, so it's a way to remember the day you were born and thank your mother.
When a friend asks, "Did you have your seaweed soup?", it means "Happy birthday!"

birthdays-world:5.fact: Butter on your nose so bad luck slides off.
birthdays-world:5.about:
In parts of Atlantic Canada, there's a custom of putting butter on the birthday person's nose. It means "may bad luck slide off."
It's quite a surprise when it happens suddenly!

birthdays-world:6.fact: It's bad luck to say "happy birthday" before the day.
birthdays-world:6.about:
In Germany, saying "happy birthday" or giving presents before the actual birthday is sometimes thought to be bad luck.
So some people have a party the night before and all celebrate together at midnight.

birthdays-world:7.fact: Long ago, everyone got a year older together at New Year.
birthdays-world:7.about:
In Vietnam long ago, instead of celebrating each person's birthday, people thought everyone got a year older together at the Lunar New Year (Tết).
In Japan too, people used to count age in "kazoedoshi," getting a year older at New Year.

birthdays-world:8.fact: A birthday breakfast of yam and egg.
birthdays-world:8.about:
In Ghana, there's a custom of eating "oto," mashed yam with boiled eggs, on the morning of your birthday.
After that, people celebrate at a party with family and friends.

birthdays-world:9.fact: Celebrating with strawberry cake and candles.
birthdays-world:9.about:
In Japan today, many families celebrate birthdays with strawberry shortcake and favourite foods. Long ago, people used "kazoedoshi," getting older at New Year.
Milestone birthdays, like turning 1, kanreki (60) and beiju (88), have special celebrations.

#paintings-italy-spain: From beautiful Renaissance pictures to faces made of vegetables. Let's tour the great paintings of southern Europe.

paintings-italy-spain:0.fact: Even ideas for flying machines! Notebooks written in mirror writing.
paintings-italy-spain:0.about:
Leonardo da Vinci didn't only paint; he filled notebooks with detailed notes on how birds fly, how water flows, the human body, how machines work and more. About 7,000 pages still survive.
There are even ideas for flying machines like helicopters. He wrote in back-to-front "mirror writing."

paintings-italy-spain:1.fact: Raphael's painting of ancient philosophers gathered together.
paintings-italy-spain:1.about:
This huge painting by Raphael, painted on the wall of a room in the Vatican around 1510, shows ancient Greek philosophers and thinkers like Plato and Aristotle gathered together and talking.
Using perspective, the building looks like it goes back and back into the distance.

paintings-italy-spain:2.fact: Velázquez's mysterious painting. The painter himself is in the picture too!
paintings-italy-spain:2.about:
"Las Meninas" (The Ladies-in-Waiting), painted by Velázquez of Spain in 1656, shows a little princess, the people who look after her, and the painter himself standing at a big canvas.
In the mirror at the back, the king and queen are reflected, small, making you wonder, "Who's looking at whom?" It's in the Prado Museum in Madrid.

paintings-italy-spain:3.fact: Human faces made of vegetables and fruit!
paintings-italy-spain:3.about:
Arcimboldo of Italy is famous for strange paintings of human faces made by putting together vegetables, fruit, flowers, fish and more.
Up close it's a pile of fruit; from far away it's a face. In his "Four Seasons" series, the faces are made of each season's vegetables.

paintings-italy-spain:4.fact: The city on the water, painted in photo-like detail.
paintings-italy-spain:4.about:
Canaletto of Italy painted the canals, buildings and gondolas of 1700s Venice in such fine detail they look like photos.
British travellers bought them as souvenirs, so many of his works are in Britain. They show us very well what the city looked like 300 years ago.

paintings-italy-spain:5.fact: Spain's "painter of light." Dazzling summer beaches.
paintings-italy-spain:5.about:
Sorolla of Spain painted the dazzling Mediterranean sunlight and is called "the painter of light." The light on white clothes and the sparkle of the sea are beautiful in his paintings.
"Walk on the Beach" (1909) shows two women whose white clothes ripple in the sea breeze.

paintings-italy-spain:6.fact: Stars, birds and eyes. Free colours and shapes, like a child's drawing.
paintings-italy-spain:6.about:
Miró of Spain painted dreamlike pictures with bright red, blue and yellow, and strange shapes like stars, birds and eyes.
His works are on a wall of Barcelona airport and all around the city. He wanted to "paint freely, like a child."

paintings-italy-spain:7.fact: Gentle portraits with long necks and faces.
paintings-italy-spain:7.about:
Modigliani, born in Italy, worked in Paris and painted portraits in his own style, with long necks and faces and almond-shaped eyes.
He's said to have been influenced by African sculpture. There are works by him in Japanese museums too.

#paintings-uk-usa: Country scenes, seas of light and a late-night diner. Masterpieces by painters from Britain and America.

paintings-uk-usa:0.fact: Constable's painting of a summer in the English countryside.
paintings-uk-usa:0.about:
"The Hay Wain," painted by Constable of England in 1821, shows a horse and cart crossing a river under a sky of big clouds.
He watched clouds and changing light carefully, and he influenced French painters too. It's in the National Gallery in London.

paintings-uk-usa:1.fact: The British painter who painted light and air.
paintings-uk-usa:1.about:
Turner of England painted the movement of light and air, like sunsets, mist and stormy seas. "The Fighting Temeraire" (1839) shows an old sailing warship being towed through the sunset.
Turner's portrait and this painting are on the British £20 note.

paintings-uk-usa:2.fact: A quiet painting of a mother sitting in a chair, seen from the side.
paintings-uk-usa:2.about:
This painting by American-born Whistler from 1871 shows the painter's mother sitting side-on, in calm greys and blacks.
It later became one of America's symbols of "mother" and was even put on a stamp.

paintings-uk-usa:3.fact: Two people standing in front of a farmhouse. One of America's most famous paintings.
paintings-uk-usa:3.about:
In this painting by Grant Wood from 1930, a man holding a pitchfork and a woman stand straight in front of a house with a pointed window.
The models were the painter's sister and his dentist. It's so famous that lots of parodies have been made.

paintings-uk-usa:4.fact: A painting that feels like looking into a late-night diner on a street corner.
paintings-uk-usa:4.about:
In this painting by Edward Hopper from 1942, a few customers and a worker sit quietly in a bright diner on a night-time street corner.
The contrast between the light of the big glass window and the dark town around it is striking. It's in a museum in Chicago.

paintings-uk-usa:5.fact: An American painter who painted flowers really big.
paintings-uk-usa:5.about:
Georgia O'Keeffe of America is famous for painting big close-ups of flowers, as if looking inside them with a magnifying glass.
She thought, "If I paint flowers big, even busy people will look at them." She also painted the desert landscapes and animal bones of New Mexico.

paintings-uk-usa:6.fact: Painting by dripping paint onto a canvas on the floor.
paintings-uk-usa:6.about:
Jackson Pollock of America laid big canvases on the floor and walked around them, dripping and flicking paint.
It's called "action painting," and the movement of painting itself became the artwork.

paintings-uk-usa:7.fact: Blue California swimming pools and splashes.
paintings-uk-usa:7.about:
British-born David Hockney painted the bright light of California and the surfaces of swimming pools in vivid colours. "A Bigger Splash" (1967) shows only the splash at the moment someone has jumped into a pool.
Now he's also known for making pictures on an iPad.

#art-asia: Long scroll paintings, calligraphy, a tiger and a magpie, wax-resist dyeing. Treasures of Asian art.

art-asia:0.fact: A 5 m Chinese scroll painting with more than 800 people.
art-asia:0.about:
"Along the River During the Qingming Festival," by Zhang Zeduan, a painter of China's Song dynasty, is a scroll about 5 m long that shows the capital city and its river in great detail.
Boats, bridges, shops, camels and more than 800 people are painted in a lively way, so we can learn a lot about life in old China.

art-asia:1.fact: A Chinese master of calligraphy called "the Sage of Calligraphy."
art-asia:1.about:
Wang Xizhi was a Chinese calligrapher from about 1,700 years ago, and his beautiful writing earned him the name "the Sage of Calligraphy."
None of his original works survive, but copies reached Japan and had a big influence on Japanese calligraphy too.

art-asia:2.fact: Korean folk paintings with a funny tiger and a magpie.
art-asia:2.about:
Minhwa are paintings that hung in ordinary people's homes in Korea's Joseon period. "Tiger and Magpie" paintings, with a funny-looking tiger and a magpie, a bird that brings good news, are famous.
With their bright colours, they carry wishes for happiness and long life.

art-asia:3.fact: Tiny Indian paintings with a fine, beautiful world inside.
art-asia:3.about:
In Mughal India, lots of small "miniature paintings" were made to go inside books. They're so detailed they look as if they were painted with a one-hair brush, showing royal hunts, animals and flowers.
Paintings of animals like elephants, tigers and birds were popular too.

art-asia:4.fact: Indonesian cloth dyed after drawing patterns with wax.
art-asia:4.about:
Batik is Indonesian wax-resist dyeing: patterns are drawn on cloth with melted wax, then the cloth is dipped in dye. The waxed parts don't take the colour, so the patterns show up.
It was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2009, and in Indonesia there's a custom of wearing batik shirts on Fridays.

art-asia:5.fact: Shiny pictures made by layering and polishing lacquer again and again.
art-asia:5.about:
Vietnamese lacquer painting (sơn mài) is made by layering lacquer dozens of times, setting in eggshell, gold leaf, seashells and more, and polishing it all up.
With its glowing deep reds, blacks and golds, it's one of Vietnam's best-known art forms.

art-asia:6.fact: Fish and flower patterns from one sheet of red paper.
art-asia:6.about:
Chinese paper cutting (jianzhi) is a traditional art of cutting red paper with scissors or a small knife to make patterns of animals, flowers and characters. There's a custom of putting them on windows at New Year.
It was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2009.

art-asia:7.fact: Paintings passed down by women in Indian villages.
art-asia:7.about:
Mithila (Madhubani) paintings have been painted by women on the walls and floors of their homes in the Mithila region of northeastern India. Fish, peacocks, the sun and trees are drawn with fine lines and bright colours.
Now they're painted on paper and cloth and are popular around the world.
